# ATCS6 Desired Design Model

This document describes how ATCS6 should work after the refactor.
It lists the rules the new code must follow and the behavior that changes between components.
Its job is to guide the engineer doing the refactor, not to be a full spec that replaces the code.
Fields, helper internals, and save/load details that this document does not mention stay the way the current code has them.
When the current code and a changed rule here disagree, this document wins.

## About this document

AI agents (and human reviewers) use this document to write code for a train control simulator. It describes the v1 system as it should be built. It does not record how the design got to this point. Keep these points in mind as you read:

- **`TrainController` stands in for a real train's computer.** A real train computer is one unit made of many modules: ATC, ATO, EB, the cab interface, the mode manager, and operational state. `TrainController` is wide on purpose because it models all of them. Each sub-module is its own separate concern, even when one sentence mentions several at once.
- **A latch models hardware that cannot drop work while the train is moving.** A latch is a command the controller saves and holds in its own state until some test (usually `is_stopped()`) lets it run. A plain flag is not a latch. Before you add a latch, first decide which test must pass before it can run.
- **The runtime uses one thread.** Every API, UI, and admin request runs between ticks, on the same thread as the per-tick stage loop. Every "always recompute live" rule in this document depends on this. If you break the single-thread model, you break several core design choices. The one exception is the Real Hardware safety-only `OutputWatchdog` daemon, which touches no runtime model state (see **Out of Scope**, Multi-threaded runtime, and **Power**, Loss-of-control watchdog).
- **v1 means v1.** Anything that is not in v1 must not appear in this document, not even as "removed," "legacy," or "deprecated" text. If a row is missing from a schema table, that absence is the statement that the thing does not exist. Use git for design history.
- **Performance is already checked for the v1 scope.** The compute-live patterns (`lookahead`, the `received_path_plan` projection, derived properties) are there on purpose. They are not performance bugs to optimize away.
- **Tests are out of scope for this document.** This document sets the contracts that generated code must meet. Test plans live elsewhere.
- **This document changes often.** When a design changes, every cross-reference is updated in the same edit. You will never see a half-updated doc. If you find one, that is a bug, not history.

## Core Runtime Loop

**Observe, Plan, and Action structure**

### Per-train tick transaction

1. Advance `simulation_time`.
2. **Observe every train, all together.** Before any train plans, read every block's detector once and retain that one layout-wide detector snapshot for the rest of Observe. Then calculate movement over the elapsed time for each train whose movement is calculated this pass. A train whose movement is not calculated — a stopped, powered-off, or ghost-frozen train, per **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs** — skips that calculation, but no train opts out of the detector work: debounce and attribute the retained snapshot across the whole layout, commit occupancy for every known and unidentified train, reconcile every train against its attributed readings, notice any train that reached its stop or ran off its route, and free the track of any that arrived. The controller decides how its train responds to the attributed observation; controller state never suppresses detector sampling, attribution, occupancy reconciliation, or detector-driven recovery. This whole step runs once as a batch over every train — its full contents are the **Observe, Plan, and Action Table** Observe row and **Power**, Block occupancy detection. It commits every train's observed position before the planning in step 4, so each train plans against where every other train really is (not a stale guess for the trains that plan later in the tick).
3. `RouteExecutor` owns the order trains run in for the planning and command steps that follow, and `SimulationController` owns running each train's Plan and Action in that order.
   - **Building the order.** `SimulationController.update(...)` advances time and calls `RouteExecutor.update(delta_seconds)` to refresh route-managed scheduling state, then passes the candidate train IDs to `RouteExecutor.order_runnable_trains(...)` and uses the ordered list that call returns. This is the canonical runnable-train ordering rule; every other site that mentions the ordering cross-references it instead of restating it.
   - **Ordering criteria.** Route-managed trains are ordered by both of these, in order:
     - ordering tier first — a `RouteRun` already running its route (`RouteRun.is_starting == False`) comes ahead of one still finishing its first task (`RouteRun.is_starting == True`). Putting running runs ahead of starting runs keeps trains that are already moving flowing through shared track, and lets a fresh departure fill the gaps in that movement instead of making a running train wait behind one that has not started moving.
     - effective priority within that tier, highest first (`RouteRun.effective_priority(route_registry)`, the override-aware read per **RouteRun overrides**; priority is an integer where `9` is highest, `0` is lowest, and the default is `5`)
   - **No-`RouteRun` default.** A train with no current `RouteRun` is ordered like a running-tier (not-starting) run at effective priority `5`; a one-off route's run is route-managed like any other and uses its own tier and effective priority.
   - **Powered-off trains stay in the order.** A train that is powered off at the start of its transaction still appears in the runnable order, ordered by its current `RouteRun` like any other train, so its Action-stage command drain can accept `TrainController.commands.power_on_cmd()`. It skips Plan, because route planning cannot run until the command drain has had that chance. Its exact order position carries no behavioral weight, since ordering only governs Plan and a powered-off train skips it.
   - **Ties.** Ties keep the existing stable iteration order.
   - **Running each transaction.** During each train transaction, `SimulationController.update(...)` calls `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(train_id, delta_seconds)` as the whole Plan-stage route-executor tick for that train, before it calls `SimulationController._act_train(train, delta_seconds)` for the Action stage.
4. For each train in that order, run Plan then Action to completion before starting the next train:
  - **Plan (top-down planning for that train)**: `RouteExecutor` runs the canonical Planning Kernel steps `c9e1`–`66aa`. The step chain, its order, and its gating rules are defined once in the **Planning Kernel** section, and the **Observe, Plan, and Action Table** lists the same chain by step ID. Plan reads the position that step 2 already committed for this train.
    - **`received_path_plan` updates automatically.** After any successful `create_path(...)` / `extend_path(...)` call, `PathDispatcher` has updated its own `Path` registry. The controller's `received_path_plan` property then returns that updated record on its next read, so there is no separate controller write step.
    - **Same-tick retry stays inside Plan.** Plan may retry or loop within the same tick only while it stays inside Plan-owned procedures, such as covered-task index advance, target resolution, candidate selection, and `create_path(...)` / `extend_path(...)` acquisition-and-rollback.
    - **Replacing a live path.** Sometimes live-path target re-resolution or a route/controller invariant check decides the current live path must be replaced. In that case Plan must not call `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` directly, and must not keep a hidden desired-target override attached to the still-live path. Instead it latches `pending_path_cancel_request` for the Action stage, stops planning for that train this tick, and waits for the normal cancel flow: cancel, then callback, then route-deviation cleanup. Operator retargeting and explicit route swap use "abort current run + create new run" instead (see **Route Edit And Reconciliation**), driven by `pending_route_abort` plus its inclusive cancel. After the authority cancellation commits and the train stops, the next eligible Plan replans from current physical progress and requests a brand-new path. Eligibility for this fresh create/replan branch uses the canonical Plan-stage eligibility predicate defined in the **Planning Kernel** section.
  - **Action (command, dispatcher cleanup, transitions, control, drive, and teardown for that train)**: `TrainController.tick(...)` first drains queued operator commands. Immediately afterward, Action consumes `pending_path_cancel_request` when its stopped gate holds; this is the early-Action dispatcher slot, so a cancel written by Observe, Plan, or the command drain commits before the controller evaluates authority for output. Action then consumes `departure_request` by calling `TrainController.depart()` and `station_entry_request` by calling `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()`, performing the transitions Plan requested. It then calls `OperationalStateMachine.evaluate_reactive_conditions()`, validates calibration, applies safety restrictions, and selects calibration or ordinary ATC/ATO/manual output. `TrainPhysics` sets the resulting block track voltage for the next tick's movement. Action next consumes `pending_route_abort`, `pending_power_off`, and `pending_route_deactivate` in that order, and finally consumes `station_exit_request` by calling `TrainController.finish_dwell()` when dwelling (or its named no-op clear otherwise). Action does not calculate movement, plan a target, or write `RouteRun` task-walk fields. `RouteExecutor` owns dwell and route-run timing writes in the procedures listed below.
5. After all trains finish their per-train transactions, drain the de-energize queue per **Power**, De-energize against the same source, then update signals from blocks once for the tick.
6. `SimulationController.update(...)` accrues `Block.occupied_seconds` once for the tick, for every block whose `occupied_by` is set (see **Maintenance counters**).

- So Observe runs once for every train first, then Plan and Action are interleaved per train — one train's Plan and Action fully commit before the next train's Plan begins.
- Stage ownership in v1 is strict:
  - **Observe scope.** Observe owns finding where every train is and writing it down. It first takes one detector snapshot for the whole layout. For each train whose movement is calculated this pass (per **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs**), it then calculates movement over the elapsed time and applies the controller-owned span/speed update through `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)`. It next attributes the retained detector snapshot and writes occupancy through the coordinator and managers for every train regardless of controller state; a train whose movement is not calculated still receives detector-derived progress through `TrainController.build_detected_progress_report()`. Observe detects a train that ran off its route and a train that reached its stop. `RouteExecutor`'s head-advance and completion callbacks run here too, because they record route progress for movement or detector reconciliation that has already happened — which is why `RouteExecutor` writes `RouteRun` in Observe as well as Plan (and, for the teardown status and cancellation-callback writes, Action).
  - **Plan scope.** Plan owns downward resolution, the planning-side `RouteRun` writes, the transition-request writes (`departure_request`, `station_entry_request`, `station_exit_request`), and same-stage retries. The owned steps are the **Planning Kernel** steps `c9e1`–`66aa`, plus route reconciliation. Plan decides departure and dwell entry/exit and writes the matching request; Action performs the transition.
  - **`RouteExecutor` is the sole `RouteRun` writer.** `RouteExecutor` is the only owner of all `RouteRun` writes, including the writes it makes outside Plan. Three sites define that full write set, and no other site restates it: the Observe, Plan, and Action Table's Observe row (the head-advance and stop-arrival finishes) and Action row (the teardown status write plus the `path_cancelled` / `path_cancel_was_deviation` cancellation-callback writes) list every write it makes outside Plan, the **`current_route_status` write contract** gives the per-writer rules, and **RouteRun overrides** covers the between-tick operator writes through `RouteExecutor.set_run_override(...)` and `RouteExecutor.clear_run_override(...)`. Of the Observe-stage writes, the head-advance callback and the stop-arrival step are the two that route through `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(walk_position)` (see that helper's own canonical definition), per the Observe commit-order bullet below.
  - **The closed runtime progress-writer set.** This set is defined by **`RouteRun.advance_walk_position(walk_position)`** plus its two explicit direct-write exceptions: the start-mode pre-finish of the skipped prefix at step `9c4f` (see **Run start-mode seeding**), and the broken-task skip's direct `finished_at` / `finished_at_operating` writes at steps `c481` / `592a` (see **Unreachable and broken task handling**).
  - **Fresh-read requirement after a progress move.** Within Plan, covered-task advance moves progress before later work and therefore requires a fresh `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` read. Dwell completion and run completion move progress and return for the tick (dwell completion writes `station_exit_request` before returning), while broken-task skipping re-runs its lookup internally. Deviation cleanup and dwell entry do not move progress. The helper's last result is never reused across a progress change.
  - **Action scope.** Action owns the command drain, early dispatcher-cancel callback, transition-request consumption (depart, dwell entry, dwell exit), control and voltage selection, and later teardown-latch consumption. Calculating movement and writing span/speed remain Observe work. The command drain is the first substep of `TrainController.tick(...)`; `SimulationController` supplies only the narrow callback that runs immediately afterward. Calibration uses `SpeedCalibration.get_propulsion_override(train_id)` and remains under every ordinary safety restriction. Action does not resolve route targets, write task-walk progress, or decide dwell/deviation timing — it performs the depart/dwell transition a request latch names, but never owns its timing.
  - **Observe commit order.** Observe commits dispatcher and physical state for the train in this canonical order:
    - **(a)** (`3e9b`) Drain and clear the controller-owned progress mailbox (`physics_sync.queued_progress_reports`) for this same transaction. This includes movement-derived deviation detection (which writes `pending_path_cancel_request` with the report's own `ErrorRecord`, `origin = "out_of_sequence"`, per the **Physical progress / deviation procedure**), physical entry and tail-vacate writes, and callback-by-callback route-progress checks against the current task (each `RouteExecutor.handle_train_advanced(...)` callback writes `task_runs[i].finished_at` for the consumed task).
    - **(b)** (`9d8b`) Evaluate normal stop arrival: `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(train_id)` releases the authority and hands the arrival to `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(...)`, which writes `task_runs[walk_position].finished_at` for the just-served stop. Skip this step whenever `pending_path_cancel_request` is set, because a pending cancel outranks completion. The check reads the latch after every earlier Observe writer, including movement-derived deviation and authority-truncation failure.
  - **Action dispatcher and teardown order.** After Plan, Action runs these commits in canonical order:
    - **(c)** (`7b40`) Immediately after the command drain, consume an explicit `pending_path_cancel_request`, gated by `TrainController.is_stopped() == True`; the latch survives while the train is rolling. Next consume `departure_request` by calling `TrainController.depart()` and `station_entry_request` by calling `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()`, each recording its result and clearing its own request. Then run reactive evaluation, calibration validation, control selection, and the voltage write against the resulting live authority.
    - **(d)** (`5d2c`) After the voltage write, consume an explicit `pending_route_abort`, gated by `pending_path_cancel_request is None` — the inclusive cancel committed earlier in this Action pass or was never written because no live path existed.
    - **(e)** (`9a81`) Consume an explicit `pending_power_off`, gated by `pending_path_cancel_request is None` per the Latch Table.
    - **(f)** (`4f6e`) Consume `pending_route_deactivate`, gated by `pending_path_cancel_request is None` per the Latch Table.
    - **(g)** (`bf3d`) After the teardown consumers, consume `station_exit_request`: when the controller is `RUNNING_AT_STATION`, call `TrainController.finish_dwell()`; otherwise emit the named no-op clear; then clear the request. Placing this last lets a run removal in steps (d)–(f) that wrote the request leave station state in the same Action pass.
  - **Calibration drive is gated in propulsion; a lighting run is ended in teardown.** An open calibration drives only through `SpeedCalibration.get_propulsion_override(train_id)`, which the controller reads while selecting propulsion and which returns `None` — withholding any drive — under EB, pending power-off, output safe state, and the other safety caps. Separately, step `26f5` (`SimulationController._reevaluate_lighting_run`) runs later in the Action teardown, after the voltage write and after the route/power/deactivation consumers (d)–(f), and cancels an open lighting-voltage run whose conditions no longer hold; it is a `SimulationController`-level step because the run registry and the run-ending route-assignment check live at that level. Cancelling a tick after the write moves nothing, because the drive was already gated in propulsion and a still-valid lighting candidate is a sub-drive-threshold holding voltage.
  - **Terminal route completion is not on either list.** When Plan detects the terminal walk with no live path remaining, it calls `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)` directly inside `tick_train_plan(...)`, instead of handing off through the Action cleanup; the broken-skip case first latches the ordinary cancel, per **Unreachable and broken task handling**.
  - **Latches written mid-pass wait for the next pass.** Latches written *during* this Action cleanup by step (c) or later (for example, the `path_cancelled` diagnostic latch the cancellation callback writes, or a fresh `pending_path_cancel_request`) are not consumed in the same pass; they wait for the next tick's Plan (route-deviation cleanup) or the next tick's Action (dispatcher cleanup). The one exception is `station_exit_request`: a teardown consumer (d)–(f) writes it through `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(...)`, and the later step (g) consumes it in this same Action pass under the within-stage step-ordering rule. A latch written by Observe step (a)'s deviation detection counts as an earlier-stage write under the Latch-table step-ordering rule: Action step (c) consumes it this same tick when its `is_stopped()` gate already holds, and otherwise it survives like any rolling-train cancel latch.
  - **Observe and Action must not plan.** Neither Observe nor Action may arm a fresh planning target, create fresh authority, decide dwell entry or dwell-completion timing, or do route-deviation cleanup; those wait for the next eligible Plan for that train. Action does perform the depart/dwell transitions Plan requested through the transition latches: its transition-consumer steps call `TrainController.depart()`, `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()`, and `TrainController.finish_dwell()`. A teardown consumer that removes a run writes `station_exit_request` through `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(...)`, and the same Action station-exit consumer performs the transition.

**Running and stopped**

A session is either **running** or **stopped**. `AppState.simulation_running` holds which one. `POST /api/simulation/control` writes it for ordinary start/stop, and the two fatal halt entries `SimulationController.enter_failed_runtime()` and `SimulationController.enter_hardware_failure()` write it `False` through the same stop-state transition before latching their failure gates. No other writer exists.

Stopped does not mean the railway stops. In Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware the layout carries whatever it carried a moment ago: a locomotive stands on a block, a hand pushes a cut of wagons, a train left from the last session sits in a siding. The detectors go on reporting all of it. One rule therefore divides the loop:

> **While stopped and not fatally halted, the runtime causes nothing and keeps observing everything.**

Every step of the tick is either **authoring** or **observing**:

- **Authoring** decides what happens next and drives the layout to make it happen: advancing `operating_time` and `simulation_time`, refreshing route scheduling state, building the runnable order, the contention snapshot, the wedge report, and the meet assignment, route planning and switch alignment (Plan), the movement calculation that advances each train's span (the authoring part of Observe), the Action operator-command drain, the ATC/ATO/manual command generation and the block track voltage it sets, and every latch consumption. Authoring runs only while the session is running.
- **Observing** reads the detectors and makes the model agree with them: the global detector read, debounce, attribution, unidentified-train minting, authority truncation, the forward-only span correction, the occupancy commit, unidentified-train reconciliation, the de-energize drain, the signal refresh, and the `Block.occupied_seconds` accrual (the observing part of Observe, plus the tick-tail drains). An observing step cannot invent motion — every write it makes is forced by a reading — so it runs whether the session is running or stopped. While stopped, Observe skips its movement calculation (nothing moved) and runs only these observing steps.

**An observing step may remove power and must not apply it.** The de-energize drain is the one observing step that writes to the output boundary, and it belongs there only because it drives toward `0` and never away from it. No observing step may raise a block voltage, throw a point motor, or energize anything else. That constraint is what lets the drain and the signal refresh follow a detector-driven commit in a stopped session without breaking the rule above.

**Stopping is a physical act.** `stop` writes `simulation_running = False` and calls `SimulationController.enter_output_safe_state()`, which advances the runtime safe-state generation and delegates to `OutputSafety.enter_safe_state()`, so every block voltage goes to `0` and every point motor de-energizes (see **Power**, Safe state / fail-safe). A train under power coasts to a stand. Every block is then in the **idle** zone, where the digital detector decides (see **Hardware setup**, Occupancy source follows drive state), so a stopped session reads its detectors through the one zone that carries no drive to disturb them.

**The stopped pass.** While a Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware session is stopped, each pass of the runtime loop runs the observing steps and nothing else, in this order. `failed_runtime` always gates this pass; `hardware_failure` gates it because this paragraph applies only to the two hardware-backed environments. An active Simulation environment is not gated by `hardware_failure` (see **Fatal physical-entry conflict procedure**, step `ee19`).

1. The observing steps of Observe — the global detector read, debounce, attribution, unidentified-train minting/reconciliation, authority truncation, forward-only span correction, and ghost detection (Observe's movement calculation is skipped, because a stopped train moves nothing). A ghost rising edge synchronously releases that train's confirmed block occupancy through `BlockManager.release_train_occupancy(train_id)`, which queues those just-cleared holdings for the de-energize drain through its own occupancy-release writer; reevaluates affected caution chains; and excludes the train from the energized set. Its retained span reaches the same de-energize drain on the next running pass through the ordinary `TrainPhysics` emission-set difference, not through an Observe write — on a stopped pass that `TrainPhysics` half of the drain is moot, because every block already sits at the safe-state `0`. This step also writes the ordinary power-off/cancel latches (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection and Ghosted trains).
2. For each train Observe attributed a confirmed change to, `TrainController.build_detected_progress_report()` (an observing step) drains `physics_sync.pending_detected_entered_blocks` / `pending_detected_vacated_blocks` into one `ControllerProgressReport` with `current_head_sequence_index = None` and `deviation = False` — a detection-only report carrying no movement-derived head mapping — clears both sets, and appends the report to the controller-owned per-train progress mailbox (`physics_sync.queued_progress_reports`), returning `None`. Observe step `3e9b` then drains that mailbox exactly as it does on a running pass, so the report is the occupancy commit alone. `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` runs the route head-advance callback only for a report whose `current_head_sequence_index is not None`, so a stopped-pass report suppresses it for the same reason it carries `deviation = False` — the suppression is a property of the report, not a session-mode branch. No latch is consumed, and no other Observe or Action step runs.
3. Unidentified-train reconciliation.
4. The de-energize drain and the signal refresh. Stopping already drove every block to `0`, so on an ordinary stopped pass the drain commands nothing new; it stays in the sequence because a detector-driven commit changes block state the same way whether the session is running or stopped. While a commissioning session owns outputs, detector processing and model commits still run, but this drain issues no device write: it clears the queued IDs as already covered by commissioning's exclusive output ownership and mandatory exit safe-state sequence (see **Power**, Commissioning owns the writes; the detectors stay shared). The queue therefore still survives no tick.
5. The `Block.occupied_seconds` accrual (see **Maintenance counters**).

A stopped Simulation session runs no such pass. `SimulatedOccupancyDriver` builds its current map from live train spans, so with no span moving the read can only repeat what is already committed. This is one gate applied to both, not a second rule: in Simulation the observing steps take their input from the authoring steps, so gating the authoring half leaves the observing half nothing to find.

**Latches wait for the resume.** No latch is consumed by a stopped pass; the rule and its scope live in the **Latch Table**. The de-energize drain (step 4 above) is not a counterexample: it only ever drives toward `0`, and the world-level queue behind it is not a latch (see **Power**, De-energize against the same source). Stopping settles nothing a latch is waiting on and undoes nothing: the physical effect of `pending_power_off` has already happened, because the safe state cut the rails, and a train under a latched cancel coasts to a stand during the stop, so that latch's `is_stopped()` gate is already satisfied when the session resumes.

**No deviation verdict is reached while stopped.** A deviation is a statement about live authority, and a stopped session exercises none. A train pushed off its `resource_sequence` while the session is stopped has its blocks committed like any other detected change, and the first *running* tick's Observe `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)` callback after the resume finds the head outside the sequence and sets `deviation = true` on that report; Observe step `3e9b` latches the cancellation through the ordinary **Physical progress / deviation procedure** (step `389a`), and step `7b40` commits it once the train is stopped.

**Operator-command processing slot**

- Operator commands targeted at a train (`TrainController.commands.power_on_cmd()`, `TrainController.commands.set_cab(...)`, `TrainController.commands.set_mode(...)`, `TrainController.commands.set_manual_mode_type(...)`, `TrainController.commands.set_handle(...)`, `TrainController.commands.set_manual_power_percent(...)`, `TrainController.eb.activate()`, `TrainController.eb.release()`, `TrainController.commands.power_off_cmd()`) are queued onto the targeted train's `TrainController` as they arrive from the API/UI layer. `TrainController.tick(...)` drains them as its first substep for that train, before any controller decision. For a powered-on train, this substep runs after Plan has finished planning. For a powered-off train, Plan is skipped, but this Action tick entry still runs so `TrainController.commands.power_on_cmd()` can be accepted. Operator intent therefore changes the same tick's controller command and block-voltage output; the movement produced by that voltage is calculated in the next tick's Observe batch. Route planning after power-on also waits for a later Plan tick.
- Within that drain slot, queued commands run in the canonical order below, so that higher-urgency commands see the lower-urgency control selections applied earlier in the same tick:
  1. `power_on_cmd()`
  2. `set_mode(...)`
  3. `set_cab(...)`
  4. `set_manual_mode_type(...)`
  5. `set_handle(...)` / `set_manual_power_percent(...)`
  6. `eb.activate()`
  7. `eb.release()`
  8. `power_off_cmd()`

  The drain order enforces three prerequisite pairs:

  - **Mode before cab and manual-mode-type.** `set_mode(...)` (slot 2) always runs before `set_cab(...)` (slot 3) and `set_manual_mode_type(...)` (slot 4). Both of those commands need `control_mode == "manual"` to be accepted (operator cab selection is manual-only in v1, and `set_manual_mode_type(...)` needs manual mode). This way a same-tick "switch to manual, then pick a cab" batch is accepted in one drain.
  - **Cab before handle.** `set_cab(...)` (slot 3) runs before `set_handle(...)` (slot 5). `set_handle(...)` needs a selected cab.
  - **Power percent before EB release.** `set_manual_power_percent(...)` (slot 5) runs before `eb.release()` (slot 7). This lets a driver holding a retained percentage under EB satisfy the **driver-control interlock** and release in one batch, because the release sees the zero the same drain just wrote.
- Each command's preconditions (stopped-only, power-on, EB-not-latched, cab-selected) are re-checked the moment it is drained, against the controller state that earlier commands in the same drain have set. A command that fails its preconditions is rejected (`success=False`) and does not block later commands in the same queue.
- **Latches written during the tick-entry drain.** Controller commands may write `pending_path_cancel_request` from operator-issued EB and `pending_power_off` from `power_off_cmd()`. The early-Action callback consumes an eligible command-drain cancel immediately. ATC-derived EB may write the cancel latch later in the same `TrainController.tick()` call, after that slot has passed; that request survives to the next Action pass. The path stays live in the meantime, so the braking train retains its authority and locks.
- **`pending_route_abort` is not drain-written.** It is not a controller command: API/UI/admin request services call its canonical writer helper between ticks.
- **External operations follow the same internal workflow.** External API/UI/admin operations must follow this same internal workflow: they enqueue controller commands or set the controller-owned Action handoff payloads, then let the per-train stage loop commit the dispatcher, route, and resource changes. They must not call `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)`, clear controller authority, remove route runs, or release resources inline from the request handler.
- **EB has two trigger paths.** `TrainController.eb.activate()` is the canonical operator-issued EB command. ATC overspeed escalation can also raise EB from inside `TrainController.tick()` — including the zero-limit branch in step `826a`, where the canonical lookahead has dropped to `atc_limit = 0` with `atc_limit_reason_code = "deviation"` or `"no_authority"`. Both paths perform the **canonical EB activation effects** defined in the **EB workflow state machine**, so Action commits any resulting cancellation through the same dispatcher cancel-and-release path used by every other cancellation kind.
- Submitting an API/UI command and executing it give separate results. The request service returns success once it enqueues the command or writes an Action handoff; the handler maps that accepted/pending result. The real command result comes when `TrainController.tick(...)` drains the command and emits its result event.
- `TrainController.eb.release()` is latch-based. Its full gate is defined in the **`TrainController.eb.release()`** contract. On acceptance it clears only `eb.active`; it never writes the operational state, calls `RouteExecutor`, or writes `RouteRun`. The ordinary controller-state evaluator runs immediately after the command drain: it preserves `RUNNING_AT_STATION`, and it moves any other powered, stopped, authority-free controller to **`READY`**. Ordinary Plan recovery/replanning follows on the next eligible tick.

**Runtime notifications**

- `NotificationCenter` owns the one runtime event stream in v1. It is exposed through `SimulationController.notification_center`. Every component that has something to report — a command result, a failure, a latch write, a state change worth reviewing later — reports it by calling `NotificationCenter.emit(...)`. No component keeps an event queue, a toast buffer, or a log of its own. There is exactly one stream, and every operator-facing "what happened" surface is a filter over it.
- **Event schema.** Every event carries exactly these fields:
  - `notification_id` — `int`, assigned by `NotificationCenter` in emit order. It is the order the stream reads back in.
  - `event_time` — `float`, system-time Unix seconds, sampled by the emitting function at the moment it emits (per **Time sampling**).
  - `source` — `str`, the class that emitted the event (`"PathDispatcher"`, `"RouteExecutor"`, `"TrainController"`, `"BlockManager"`, `"SwitchManager"`, `"SimulationController"`).
  - `operation` — `str`, the name of the function that emitted the event (`"cancel_path"`, `"set_path_cancel_request"`, `"handle_path_completion"`, `"set_handle"`). Every emitting function writes its own name here and never another function's. `source` plus `operation` is the "where did this come from" key a reader filters on.
  - `kind` — `"debug" | "info" | "warning" | "error"`, how serious the event is. This is the only level field on an event, and the only field runtime code may branch on. `debug` is per-tick detail a developer reads; `info` is a normal thing that happened; `warning` is a recoverable problem or safety action; `error` is reserved for entry into fatal failed-runtime or hardware-failure state.
  - `entities` — an ordered list of `{entity_type, entity_id}` refs naming everything the event is about: the train, the route run, the walk-position, the path, the blocks and switches involved. One event may name several entities, and every per-entity view is a membership filter over that one list. It is the only entity routing key: a per-train view filters for an `entity_type == "train"` ref rather than reading a separate scalar.
  - `message` — `str`, one human-readable line saying what the operation did. Always present, on every event at every level.
  - The v1 `entity_type` values are `"train"`, `"route_run"`, `"walk_position"`, `"path"`, `"block"`, and `"switch"`. `entity_id` is that entity's own id, except for `"walk_position"`, whose id is the `RouteRun` id and the integer walk index joined by `"#"` (`"<run_id>#<index>"`). An event about a task names both a `"route_run"` ref and a `"walk_position"` ref, so a run-level filter and a task-level filter both find it.
  - `error` — `Optional[ErrorRecord]`, diagnostic context (see **Errors and diagnostic classification**). It may accompany `info`, `warning`, or `error`; normal successful events usually leave it `None`. `message` says what happened or was attempted; `error.text` supplies the diagnostic detail.
  - `payload` — the structured per-operation data, whatever that operation needs a reader to have. A command result carries `{command_id, success, reason}`; a latch write carries the latch name and its payload; a cancellation carries its two classification booleans.
- **The emit call.** `NotificationCenter.emit(source, operation, kind, message, entities=None, error=None, payload=None, event_time=None, latch_event=False, condition_key=None)` is the one way an event enters the stream. `event_time` is optional: `NotificationCenter` samples `time.time()` itself when the caller omits it, and because `emit(...)` runs inline inside the calling function, that sample is taken at the writer's own execution point per **Time sampling** — so an omitted `event_time` is equivalent to one the caller sampled. A caller passes `event_time` explicitly only when it must match a status timestamp it writes in the same step: for example `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` samples `time.time()` once and uses that one value for both `Path.last_status_updated_time` and the `cancel_path` event. The caller also supplies the non-stored `latch_event` and `condition_key` control arguments; `NotificationCenter` assigns only `notification_id` as it appends. Neither control argument is part of the persisted **Event schema**. `condition_key` is required for a suppressible error condition and identifies that one live occurrence until its owner calls `NotificationCenter.resolve_condition(condition_key)`. Every event field except `error` and `payload` is required, so an event can never reach the stream without a level, a message, or an entity list. A component with many emit sites may wrap this in a thin per-component adapter that fills in its own `source` and its usual `entities` — `TrainController` does, through `controller.notifications` — but the adapter holds no queue and no state, and the stream it writes to is this one.
- **Retention.** `NotificationCenter` keeps the most recent `NOTIFICATION_RETENTION_ROWS` events and drops the oldest beyond that. The v1 default is `10000`, and it lives in `constants.py` as a **Runtime settings** tunable, so an operator running a long session may raise it. `notification_id` keeps counting past a drop, so a gap in the ids means events aged out rather than that the stream lost order. At startup `NotificationCenter` seeds the counter from the highest `notification_id` in the persisted **Event log**, so ids stay strictly increasing across a session restart and `since_notification_id` never straddles two sessions' worth of the same number. `NotificationCenter` is also the only component that decides read/ack state and how the frontend gets events.
- Command execution results are ordinary events: `source` is the class holding the command surface, `operation` is the drained command's kind (`"set_handle"`, `"power_on"`, `"set_cab"`), `kind` is `"info"` on acceptance and `"warning"` on rejection, and `payload`'s closed core is `{command_id, success, reason}`. A command result that targets a specific entity additionally carries that entity's id field alongside the core three (for example `switch_id` for a switch-state command, or `<entity>_id` for an entity PATCH command); no other extension is permitted. Path cancellation, latch writes, fatal runtime failures, route-run errors, and blocked planning are all the same core shape. The component that caused the event still owns the underlying state change; `NotificationCenter` owns only the event record and the delivery surface.
- Request handlers must not read controller internals to find out about later command failures. They return accepted/pending for an enqueue or a latch write, and then frontend/API consumers see the later results on this stream.
- Per-entity reads are filters over this one stream, not separate queues. `GET /api/trains/<train_id>/notifications` returns the events whose `entities` include that train, most recent first, and takes optional `kind` and `since_notification_id` filters. It is a read: it acknowledges nothing and empties nothing.
- The persisted, operator-facing view of this stream is the **Event log** (see that section): the same stream kept on disk, read in a viewer, and scrubbed in replay. It is not a second sink.

**Error events**

This is the canonical home for where error state lives in v1.

- No ordinary entity stores an error. Every error, failure, and blocked-planning reason is emitted once into the `NotificationCenter` stream described above, and every "what went wrong here" read — the train-panel no-authority banner, the Quick Route toast, the run panel, the event-log viewer — is a filter over that one stream. No `RouteRun`, `RouteTaskRun`, `Path`, `Block`, or `Switch` field holds an `ErrorRecord` as entity state. Exactly two bounded runtime carriers may retain one across ticks: an Action latch payload holds its writer's record only until its consumer commits and hands it to the event, and `SimulationController.failed_runtime_payload` holds one complete `FatalPhysicalEntryConflict` only while `failed_runtime == True`, until `SimulationController.clear_failed_runtime()` clears both. Neither carrier reads the record for branching. Hardware I/O failure retains only `hardware_failure_activation_generation`; its diagnostics remain events.
- `kind` and `error` are independent. `kind` is the writer-declared operator severity; `error` is present whenever the writer has a diagnostic record, including an ordinary `kind = "info"` cancellation. A `run_complete` release alone carries `error = None` because nothing failed. `kind = "error"` is reserved for the two fatal session entries: `SimulationController.enter_failed_runtime()` and `SimulationController.enter_hardware_failure()`. Recoverable safety actions, including EB cancellation, use `"warning"`; normal operator/system cancellations use `"info"`. Nothing derives severity from `ErrorRecord.origin` or a classification boolean. A `"debug"` event carries no diagnostic.
- **Emit on change, not per tick.** Plan retries a blocked task on every eligible tick, so an error event is emitted when the condition first appears and not again while the same entity stays blocked with the same `operation`, the same `ErrorRecord.origin`, and the same `payload`. A changed reason — including a changed payload, such as a meet ceiling moving to a different block — is a new event.
  - **Suppression mechanism.** `NotificationCenter` owns an in-memory map of active error conditions keyed by the caller-supplied `condition_key`. `NotificationCenter.emit(...)` applies suppression only to events carrying an `ErrorRecord`, with `latch_event == False`, and with a non-`None` condition key. It drops the call only when that key is already active with the same `entities`, `operation`, `ErrorRecord.origin`, and `payload`; a changed fingerprint is appended and replaces the active value. Events with `error is None` — command results, error-free latch writes and consumptions, and operational events — are always appended.
  - **Resolution and recurrence.** The component that owns the live predicate must call `NotificationCenter.resolve_condition(condition_key)` on the first transition to false. Resolution removes the active key and is idempotent; it does not delete or rewrite the historical event. If the same condition later becomes true, its key is no longer active and the otherwise-identical event is emitted again. Active keys are runtime-only and start empty after restart, so the first still-present condition observed in a new process emits once for that process.
  - **Latch events are exempt.** Every latch writer helper and every latch's consume-side emitter (`TrainController.consume_service_stop()`, the only `consume_*()` accessor in v1; `RouteRun.path_cancelled`'s clear call in Plan step `5fc7`; and — for the seven `phase_latches` fields — each field's own named Action consumer call per the **Latch consumption events** table) passes `latch_event=True`, so a latch-write or latch-consume event is never suppressed even when it carries an `ErrorRecord`. The point of the pair is to show intent and commit separately.
  - **No open-ended inference, no per-caller event memory.** Suppression does not infer latch membership from operation names. The condition owner detects its own predicate becoming false and calls the resolver, but it keeps no duplicate-event history; `NotificationCenter` alone owns the active fingerprints.
  - This is the rule **Wedge detection** and **Meet coordination** already state for their own diagnostics, applied to every error.
- **Reading the current reason.** `NotificationCenter.latest_error_for(entity_type, entity_id, operation=None, origin=None)` returns the most recent retained `warning`/`error` event whose condition key is still active and whose entities and optional filters match, or `None`. It never returns a resolved condition. Historical viewers read the event stream directly when they need past rather than current reasons.
- `NotificationCenter.latest_error_for(...)` combines the retained event row with the runtime active-condition map. After restart the map begins empty and is repopulated as live predicates are evaluated, so a still-present condition emits a fresh event and becomes current again. Historical event-log filters remain available independently of current-condition reads.
- **Deferred actions are events too.** A latch records an action the runtime intends to take and cannot commit yet (see the **Latch Table**). Setting one emits an event and consuming one emits another, so the operator can see both that the runtime decided to cancel a path and that it later did. Both calls pass `latch_event=True`, so the suppression in **Emit on change, not per tick** never drops either of them, whether or not the latch write carried an `ErrorRecord`: without those two events the intent is invisible whenever a second writer overwrites the latch payload before Action reaches it. The **Writer-helper rule** owns which function emits which.
- Nothing branches on an error event. The rule in **Errors and diagnostic classification** still holds: `kind` is the one branchable field, and no runtime code reads `message`, `ErrorRecord.text`, or `ErrorRecord.origin` to decide behavior. Filtering a view by `operation` or `origin` is a display choice, not a runtime branch.

**Plan departure-request writes (manual + ATO)**

- In both manual and ATO modes, every eligible Plan pass that sees live authority for the current target writes `phase_latches.departure_request` through `set_departure_request()`, whether or not the driver has already started rolling manually; Action consumes it by calling `TrainController.depart()`. This makes route-managed manual operation go through the canonical depart-acceptance path too. Manual pre-depart movement by the driver is allowed (and protected by ATC), but the route-side gate "depart accepted, route progress can complete a stop" (`controller.state == RUNNING_MOVING`) is not skipped just because the train moved early. If the Action `TrainController.depart()` consumer rejects (for example: EB latched, no cab in manual mode, `pending_power_off` set; see the **`TrainController.depart()` canonical contract** for the full precondition list), that consumer clears the request and Plan may write a fresh one on the next eligible tick.

**Stage handoff rule**

- A stage may retry immediately only when every operation stays inside that same stage.
- If logic in one stage needs a later tick or pass to change live runtime state, it must write a per-train retained latch instead of calling across stages directly.
- **Within-Observe handoffs are not latches.** The controller-owned per-train progress mailbox (`physics_sync.queued_progress_reports`), the `physics_sync.pending_detected_entered_blocks: Set[str]` / `pending_detected_vacated_blocks: Set[str]` slices, and `physics_sync.pending_block_exit_edges` are all written and consumed inside one Observe pass. Attribution writes the slices (`pending_detected_vacated_blocks` carries only the clears the holding train's calculated tail has reached the exit seam of; every other confirmed clear is held and re-offered on a later read, see **Power**, A clear read from under the train is a detection fault), and the occupancy-commit step folds them into a `ControllerProgressReport` that the mailbox drain (step `3e9b`) then consumes and clears — for a train whose movement is not calculated this pass (per **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs**), `TrainController.build_detected_progress_report()` builds that report instead. `pending_block_exit_edges` carries an unidentified train's tail-vacate direction and is consumed on that same tick (see **Power**, Unidentified trains). All are within-tick transients, not retained across ticks.
- **Observe's only cross-stage latch fields are the two Action latches in the Latch Table.** Observe writes `phase_latches.power_off` on a ghost rising edge. It writes `phase_latches.path_cancel_request` for movement-derived deviation, authority-truncation failure, and the inclusive cancel produced by that same ghost power-off request. Every cause goes through the latch's canonical writer helper, and Action consumes both fields under the Latch Table gates.
- **The span correction and the ghost cleanup are Observe-internal direct calls, not handoffs.** Observe calls `TrainPhysics.reconcile_to_detected_occupancy(train, controller)` and, on a ghost rising edge, `BlockManager.release_train_occupancy(train_id)` (which clears those owned blocks and reevaluates caution) and excludes the train from the energized set — all synchronously, within Observe. Observe does not itself queue a block for de-energize: `release_train_occupancy(...)` exercises `BlockManager`'s own occupancy-release writer for the just-cleared holdings, and the train's retained span reaches `TrainPhysics`'s de-energize store afterward through the ordinary per-tick `TrainPhysics` emission-set difference, because the train's emission set now reads empty (see **Power**, De-energize against the same source).
- **A read is not a handoff.** `SpeedCalibration` also reads the calibration train's `physics_sync.pending_detected_entered_blocks` inside Observe, after attribution writes it (see **Speed calibration**); this is a read against Observe-internal state, not a handoff, and it writes nothing into the slice.
- **What this list does not cover.** The Observe, Plan, and Action Table row `0d70` owns the full Observe write set, including detector debounce state, the stored `presence_unknown` flag Observe overwrites each pass (and reads as its own edge memory), unidentified-train lifecycle, and `Path.resource_sequence` truncation plus the dropped tail's reservations/locks. `presence_unknown` is not a latch: Observe recomputes and overwrites its verdict every pass.
- **The boundary is between procedures, not between objects.** Observe runs once over all trains, then each train's transaction runs Plan and Action in that order. A stage must not start a procedure owned by another stage. A procedure may synchronously call another component when that call is one of the closed commit/callback chains below; the component that owns a field still writes that field. This is not a cross-stage handoff because the whole call chain finishes inside the initiating procedure before the next procedure starts. Observe's committed position is complete before Plan begins. Route resolution runs before dispatcher acquisition near the end of Plan. Dispatcher cancellation is the first cleanup commit in Action, immediately after the command drain and before reactive evaluation, calibration validation, command/control output selection, and voltage application; route/power/deactivation teardown remains after voltage application. The closed list is:
  - `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(train_id)` releasing the authority and handing the arrival to `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(...)`, which records the finished stop.
  - `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` calling its injected `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(...)` callback.
  - `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` calling `RouteExecutor.handle_train_advanced(...)` and `ResourceCoordinator.on_physical_entry(...)` / `ResourceCoordinator.release_tail_vacated(...)` (which fan out to `BlockManager.occupy_blocks(...)` / `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated(...)` and `SwitchManager.on_physical_entry(...)` / `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(...)`).
  - The Action `pending_power_off` consumer calling `TrainController.complete_power_off()` (the controller-owned OFF-cleanup entry point).
  - The Action transition-consumer steps calling `TrainController.depart()`, `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()`, and `TrainController.finish_dwell()` — the transitions Plan (or, for `station_exit_request`, a teardown consumer) requested through `departure_request` / `station_entry_request` / `station_exit_request`.
  - Plan run step `6a0d` calling `TrainController.begin_service_stop()` / `TrainController.consume_service_stop()`. `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(...)`, EB activation, OFF cleanup, and `TrainController._apply_power_off_request()` (at power-off acceptance) must call `consume_service_stop()` to clear an interrupted run's `ops.service_stop_active` latch, per the **Latch Table**. These calls own the operational service-stop transitions.
- The calls above are part of their initiating procedures even when the callee owns the written field. Plan's authority-acquisition, dwell-entry, and dwell-complete procedures write the matching transition request (`departure_request` / `station_entry_request` / `station_exit_request`); the Action transition-consumer steps call the named `TrainController` transitions. Plan's run-timer procedure calls `TrainController.begin_service_stop()` / `consume_service_stop()` directly. Observe's movement procedure may call `OperationalStateMachine.evaluate_reactive_conditions()` inside `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)`. Cross-train and cross-tick requests still use the retained latches.
- The per-train Action retained latch / flag table is controller-owned in v1. Its canonical home is the nested aggregate `TrainController.route_hooks.phase_latches: PhaseLatches`, documented in the **Latch Table** (see the Naming-convention paragraph) in this section.
- The v1 retained latch table contains:
  - `departure_request` / `station_entry_request` / `station_exit_request` (controller-owned transition requests written by Plan — or, for `station_exit_request`, by an Action teardown consumer — and consumed by Action)
  - `pending_path_cancel_request`
  - `pending_route_abort`
  - `pending_power_off` (controller-owned latch consumed by Action)
  - `pending_route_deactivate` (controller-owned latch written by the route-deactivation service per assigned train; consumed by Action)
- `ControllerProgressReport` values are deliberately left out of this retained latch table. Observe appends them to the controller-owned per-train progress mailbox (`physics_sync.queued_progress_reports`): the final `on_physics_updated(...)` callback for a train whose movement is calculated, or `TrainController.build_detected_progress_report()` for a train whose movement is not calculated (per **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs**), and that same Observe pass drains and clears the mailbox right away either way. The mailbox is a within-tick transient: written and drained inside Observe, and never surviving across ticks. So it is not a retained latch.
  - `pending_path_cancel_request` is an optional payload, not a bare boolean. It is the **canonical owner** of "cancel my path" — the only latch that ever drives `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)`.
    - **Writers.** Every writer that needs a cancel (EB activation, movement-derived deviation, live-path replan revocation, operator/admin path cancellation, route-abort, power-off, route-deactivate, ghosting, Observe authority-truncation failure, normal run-completion authority release, and the broken-skip terminal-walk cancel at steps `c481` / `592a`) routes through `controller.route_hooks.phase_latches.set_path_cancel_request(...)` directly, or through one of the higher-level helpers (`set_route_abort`, `set_power_off` via `_apply_power_off_request`, `set_route_deactivate`) that fans out to it per the **Writer-helper rule**. A speed-calibration leg is an ordinary one-off route: normal stop completion releases its path, and abandonment uses `set_route_deactivate(...)`. Once a writer writes a latch, it walks away.
    - **One commit per pass.** Action commits exactly one cancellation per pass for that train. It resolves the actual live path from `PathDispatcher.active_path_id_by_train(train_id)` and commits at most one explicit latched cancellation for that train that tick. Because v1 allows at most one active path per train, the payload needs no required `path_id` routing key.
    - **Payload fields.** The payload's canonical fields are all four of these:
      - `kind` — the event level the writer declares for this cancellation: `"info"` for a normal cancellation and `"warning"` for a recoverable problem or safety action. Latch writers never use `"error"`.
      - `error: Optional[ErrorRecord]` — required (non-`None`) on every request except a `run_complete` release, where it must be `None`. It carries diagnostic context, including on an ordinary `"info"` cancellation. Its `origin` carries a free-form notification label such as `"eb"`, `"operator_cancelled"`, `"power_off"`, `"out_of_sequence"`, `"revoked"`, `"idle_hold_release"`, or `"contention_release"`; `controller.route_hooks.phase_latches.set_path_cancel_request(...)` validates this pairing at write time.
      - `deviation: bool` — set only by movement-derived deviation.
      - `run_complete: bool` — set only by Plan step `6a0d` (Run timer, service stop, and normal-progress authority release).
    - **The two booleans classify the cancellation.** The two booleans, never anything read out of `error`, drive the only cancellation-callback classifications: `deviation` produces the deviation diagnostic latch, while `run_complete` marks a normal route-progress release that must not set `RouteRun.path_cancelled`. The payload does not decide whether the `RouteRun` must be removed.
    - **Most-recent payload wins.** If several same-tick writers set the request, the most recent complete payload wins; higher-priority teardown writers set `run_complete = False`, so a teardown cannot be misclassified as run completion.
- `pending_route_abort` is the Action bare-boolean latch for intentionally tearing down the current `RouteRun`. API/UI/admin abort, operator retarget, and explicit route-swap requests call `set_route_abort(...)`; it sets the abort latch and fans out to the inclusive path cancel when authority exists. Structural shared-route edits use `pending_route_deactivate` plus held same-route reassignment, not abort. Every other writer of `pending_path_cancel_request` — the full list is the Latch Table row `c832`'s Written-by column together with the **Public callers** enumeration below, including same-`RouteRun` live-path target re-resolution, structural extend failure, EB, movement-derived deviation, run-completion release, ordinary authority revocation, and the operator/admin path-cancel request — writes it without any route teardown latch. The three workflows must not be conflated.
- Plan requests the depart transition through a latch: on every eligible pass with live authority for the current target, `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` writes `phase_latches.departure_request` through `set_departure_request()`, and Action consumes it by calling `TrainController.depart()`, records the result, and clears the request. If depart rejects (for example: EB latched, no cab in manual mode, power off; see the **`TrainController.depart()` canonical contract**), Plan may write a fresh request on a later tick. Dwell entry and dwell exit are latch-based the same way. `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` writes `phase_latches.station_entry_request` when the dwell-entry preconditions are met, after `RouteExecutor` itself samples and writes the dwell row's `started_at` (see step `3a37` in the **Planning Kernel**). It writes `phase_latches.station_exit_request` (after writing `task_runs[walk_position].finished_at`) when `RouteTask.should_depart(...)` is satisfied. Action consumes them by calling `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()` and `TrainController.finish_dwell()` respectively. The controller never reads `RouteRun` to decide any of these transitions.

**Action latched-cancel consumption: stopped-train gating and no-active-path skip**

- The `pending_path_cancel_request` consumer is the **canonical owner** of the "is there a live path to cancel?" decision. The other latches (`pending_route_abort`, `pending_power_off`, `pending_route_deactivate`) "assign and forget": their writers already wrote `pending_path_cancel_request` through the inclusive-latch helpers, and Action commits that cancel before it reaches their consumer steps. They do not check active-path emptiness themselves.
- When Action reaches the `pending_path_cancel_request` consumption step, it first checks `TrainController.is_stopped()`. If the train is still rolling, it keeps the latch and reconsiders it on the next eligible Action pass. Action must NOT call `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` against a moving train, because that would release future block reservations and switch locks ahead of the still-rolling train. No cancellation commits while a train is rolling — deviation included. The stop is always emergent; the cancel itself never forces it. A train can reach rest before its latched cancel commits in any of these ways:

  - a deviated train brakes under the zero ATC limit with `atc_limit_reason_code = "deviation"`
  - an EB'd train brakes at the emergency rate
  - a train whose route was cleanly cancelled, aborted, revoked, or deactivated while its authority is still valid (head still maps into `resource_sequence`, so it is not a deviation) keeps running under that authority and stops on its own at the current `authority_end_block_id` (`atc_limit_reason_code = "authority_stop"`)
  - a train finishing a timed `run` brakes under the route-owned service-stop override (step `b41e`) while its `run_complete` cancel is latched, and that cancel commits once the brake brings it to rest
  - a ghosted train coasts to a stand under `_apply_power_off_request(...)`'s neutralized propulsion while its inclusive cancel is latched, and that cancel commits once it reaches rest

  So only EB, deviation, and the service-stop override force a stop before the authority end; an orderly operator/admin cancel lets the train run out its current granted authority and halt at that boundary, and only then does the latched cancel commit. (While the cancel is latched, Plan cannot extend the authority — the eligibility precondition excludes `PATH_CANCEL_PENDING` — so the train runs only to its current authority end, not the full route.) Once `is_stopped()` is true, the pending latch is consumed on the next eligible Action pass. Several writers in the rolling window just overwrite the same single payload slot (most-recent payload wins per the latch table); no extra blocking is needed.
- Sometimes Action reaches the cancel consumer with the train stopped but no active path. It emits one event per the **Event schema** — `operation` the consuming step's own function name, `kind = "info"`, `error = None`, `entities` naming the train — recording that the latched cancel found no live path, and consumes the latch. Route-run teardown happens only from `pending_route_abort`, `pending_power_off`, `pending_route_deactivate`, or Plan terminal completion. Operator removal of an app-controlled train is out of scope and is not a hidden teardown trigger. Retiring an unidentified train is owned by **Power**, Unidentified trains, and reaches no route-run teardown because such a train never holds a `RouteRun`.
- When the `pending_path_cancel_request` latch survives across ticks because the train was rolling when it was written, no cross-stage coordination is needed: the train protects itself. For a deviation, the live path stays `ACTIVE` and keeps its locks while the canonical lookahead reads `atc_limit = 0` at distance 0 with `atc_limit_reason_code = "deviation"` (the head is unmappable — see the **canonical lookahead payload**). So ATC brakes the train, and the overspeed branch escalates a still-rolling train to EB. Once `is_stopped() == True`, the next eligible Action explicit-cancel step (`7b40`) consumes the latch. `PathDispatcher` does not reach across stages to clear the latch early.
- The `pending_route_abort` consumer is an assign-and-forget step (per the first bullet above): it does only its own teardown. It calls `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)` to fully remove the route assignment — that helper writes `current_route_status = DEACTIVATED` and, when the controller is `RUNNING_AT_STATION`, writes `station_exit_request` so the later Action station-exit consumer calls `TrainController.finish_dwell()` — then clears `pending_route_abort`.
- The `pending_power_off` consumer is assign-and-forget. Its inclusive cancel commits on the same Action pass **when the Action operator writer set it**, because `_apply_power_off_request()` neutralizes every propulsion input and prevents later command generation from moving the train after stopped acceptance. When the Observe ghosted-train rising edge set it, the train may still be rolling, so the consumer waits across ticks for the inclusive cancel's `is_stopped()` gate (see the `power_off` row in the **Latch Table**). The consumer then removes the route run and calls `TrainController.complete_power_off()`.
- **Terminal route completion.** Plan handles it with a direct call, not an Action latch consumption step. When `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` detects the terminal walk (the final task is finished and `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` returns `None`) with no live path (`PathDispatcher.active_path_id_by_train(train_id) is None`), it calls `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)` directly inside that same Plan call.
  - **Why the path is already gone.** In the ordinary case the matching live path is already absent by then: a terminal stop cleared it through the step-`09b0` authority release/status transition before step `bc55` recorded route progress, while a terminal run cleared it through run step `6a0d`'s normal-progress release before finishing its task row.
  - **Broken-skip exception.** A path can also still be live at this point when every remaining task was broken-skipped (see **Unreachable and broken task handling**). Step `592a` latches the ordinary cancel for that case instead of finishing the run, and `finish_route_run(...)` runs on the later pass this same terminal-walk check finds no live path. `finish_route_run(...)` itself is therefore called only once no dispatcher cancel is needed.
  - **What `finish_route_run(...)` does.** It calls `Route.unassign_train(train_id)`, sets `RouteRun.current_route_status = FINISHED`, and moves the run to `_historical_runs`. `RouteExecutor.assigned_route_id_for(train_id)` then returns `None`.
  - **`ONE_OFF` cascade.** When the route is `RouteMode.ONE_OFF` and the unassign left it with no assigned trains, it also calls `route.deactivate()`, whose per-train latch walk writes nothing because no assigned trains remain.
- The `pending_route_deactivate` consumer is assign-and-forget too; it does only its own teardown, in this order:
  1. Call `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)`. The helper writes `current_route_status = DEACTIVATED`, unassigns the train from the run's `route_id`, and — when the controller is `RUNNING_AT_STATION` — writes `station_exit_request` (the Action station-exit consumer performs the transition).
  2. Resolve any held re-assignment per the **Shared-route edit teardown**, but only when this consumer owned the teardown:
     - When `_pending_reassign[train_id]` is set AND this step's own `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)` just cleared a still-`RUNNING` run (`RouteExecutor.execution_state_for(train_id)` was not `None` when this step began) — apply the re-assignment (`Route.assign_train(train_id)` on the recorded route) and clear the stash.
     - When an earlier Action consumer (`pending_route_abort` or `pending_power_off`) or a natural finish had already ended the run — so `execution_state_for(train_id)` was already `None` at this step — the operator/admin teardown wins: discard `_pending_reassign[train_id]` without re-assigning, so a powered-off or aborted train is never silently re-assigned to the edited route.
  3. Clear `pending_route_deactivate`.
  - `RouteExecutor.assigned_route_id_for(train_id)` returns the re-assigned route after a structural-edit re-assignment, and `None` otherwise.

**Observe, Plan, and Action Table**

Observe runs once as a batch over every train before any train plans; then, for each train in order, Plan then Action run to completion. The boundary controls which procedure may begin and when it may begin; it does not forbid the synchronous commit/callback calls listed under **Stage handoff rule**. Retained work that cannot commit in its initiating pass uses only the latches defined in the Latch Table below. Same-transaction movement progress uses the controller-owned per-train progress mailbox (`physics_sync.queued_progress_reports`), which is drained and cleared within Observe.

**Why this shape.** Observe runs once for every train before any train plans, then Plan and Action are interleaved per train — one train's Plan and Action commit before the next train's Plan begins. Working out every train's position first means each train plans against where every other train really is, not a stale guess for the trains that plan later in the tick; interleaving Plan and Action after that keeps one train's reservations visible to the next train that plans. The ownership split is strict: Observe owns finding and committing position (the movement calculation, the occupancy write, and the off-route and reached-its-stop checks); Plan owns route planning and the planning-side `RouteRun` writes; Action owns the controller, the block track voltage, and the cleanup latch consumption. Of the `RouteRun` writes `RouteExecutor` makes outside Plan, the head-advance callback and the stop-arrival step — both Observe — route through `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(...)` (`task_runs[i].finished_at`, `delay_class`, and the appended next walk-position); and the Action writes are the teardown status write (`current_route_status`) plus the cancellation callback `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(...)` setting `RouteRun.path_cancelled` / `RouteRun.path_cancel_was_deviation`. `RouteRun.direction` is not among them: it is a Plan write, set from the projection Plan consumes (see **Route-run state**, the `direction` row). So each field has exactly one owning component, and because a single Observe batch runs before each train's Plan and Action, which themselves run in order, there is never a concurrent writer. That is what makes "always recompute live" reads safe across the rest of the document.
