Neither case re-runs the release, the route callback, or the notification, and neither resamples `Path.last_status_updated_time`. Callers therefore never have to check `Path.status` before cancelling.
- When the path is currently `ACTIVE`, `cancel_path(...)` performs the normal cancellation flow described below and returns `committed = True` with `new_status = CANCELLED`.
- Three conditions are caller-contract violations rather than outcomes, and raise rather than returning a result, because `cancel_path(...)` carries no `failure_kind` to report one on: a `path_id` that is not present in `paths_by_id`; a call carrying both `deviation = True` and `run_complete = True`; and a call whose `error` / classification pairing violates the **`pending_path_cancel_request` payload** contract (`error is None` on any call that is not a `run_complete` release, or `error is not None` on a `run_complete` release). In v1 the only writer of this payload is `set_path_cancel_request(...)`, which validates this same pairing at write time and so already guarantees the third condition never fires; `cancel_path(...)` still raises on a violated pairing rather than silently accepting a malformed call.
- `reason` is optional plain-text diagnostic context. Callers may display or log it, but they must never branch on exact reason text; control flow branches only on `committed` and `new_status`.

**Authority truncation**

- **`truncate_path_before_block(path_id, block_id, reason)`.** A block a path reserved may be physically taken by another train before this train reaches it — an unidentified train appears on it, or a train running under its own authority gets there first (see **Power**, Attribution) — and when that happens, `PathDispatcher.truncate_path_before_block(path_id, block_id, reason)` pulls the path back to end at the last block in front of the train and behind the taken one. Authority that runs through a block another train is standing on is not authority, which is why the path must pull back rather than keep it.
  - **Where the cut lands.** Observe truncation applies the same item-11 truncation-terminal rules that govern `create_path(...)` and `extend_path(...)` (see **Path And PathDispatcher**, the truncation-terminal rules paragraph below): the cut lands at the furthest legal terminal at or behind the last `block` entry before the taken block, preferring a holding point and honoring the reversal-trap and junction-fouling exclusions. When no legal terminal remains at or behind that cut, `truncate_path_before_block(...)` returns `False`. The path stays `ACTIVE` when it returns `True`.
  - **Release of the dropped tail.** Everything from the new end onward is dropped: those blocks' reservations and the claim families sourced by those tail main switches are released together through `ResourceCoordinator.release_authority_tail(<tail block ids>, <tail main switch ids>, path_id)` — never the whole-path `release_path_resources(...)`, which would drop locks the surviving head still needs. The source-keyed release removes `(path_id, None)` on each dropped main switch and `(path_id, main_switch_id)` on its flank neighbours, preserving claims sourced by main switches in the surviving head.
- The authority end is derived from `resource_sequence` and the controller reads its plan live from the dispatcher, so the shortened authority reaches the canonical lookahead on its next read with no separate republish step. ATC then brakes the train to a stop at the new end exactly as it does for any other authority end. The train keeps every resource it has already entered, and the route layer extends the path again through the ordinary acquisition step once the block clears; truncation itself never retries.
- A path must end on a block (see **Path invariants**), so the cut lands at the item-11 legal terminal identified in the previous bullet — the furthest legal terminal at or behind the last `block` entry before the taken block — and any switches and blocks between that terminal and the taken block go with the dropped tail.
  - **Return value.** `truncate_path_before_block(...)` returns whether the path survived with a valid remainder.
  - **When it returns `False`.** It returns `False` when no legal terminal remains at or behind that cut, for **either of these reasons**:
    - the taken block is the first thing ahead of the train, so there is no shorter authority to hold
    - every remaining candidate terminal is barred by an item-11 exclusion
  - **After a `False` return.** `truncate_path_before_block(...)` itself releases every reservation the path held ahead of the train through `ResourceCoordinator.release_authority_tail(...)` before returning. Observe then calls `controller.route_hooks.phase_latches.set_path_cancel_request(error=<ErrorRecord with origin = "revoked">, kind="info")` on the reserving train's controller instead, so the whole path comes down through the ordinary Action cancellation while the train may still be rolling.
  - **The train brakes under ordinary obstruction, not EB.** The `resource_sequence` and the head mapping are unchanged by this call, so the train stops under the ordinary `"obstruction"` ATC restriction against the now-occupied block ahead, not the zero-limit / EB protocol (see **A revocation under unchanged authority stops the train through ordinary obstruction braking, not the zero-limit protocol**); the latched cancel commits once that braking brings the train to rest.
  - **Diagnostic event on a surviving truncation.** When the call returns `True` — the path survived with a shorter valid remainder — `truncate_path_before_block(...)` emits one `NotificationCenter` event recording the shortening, for logs and the UI. Nothing branches on it. The event carries `source = "PathDispatcher"`, `operation = "truncate_path_before_block"`, `kind = "warning"`, a `message` naming the path and its new authority-end block, `entities` naming the train and the path, an `error` whose `ErrorRecord.origin` is `"authority_truncated"` and whose `text` is the caller's `reason`, and a `payload` of `{blocked_block_id, authority_end_block_id, released_block_ids, released_switch_ids}` — the taken block that forced the pull-back, the block the shortened authority now ends on, and the block and main-switch ids of the dropped tail. A `False` return emits no truncate event; the cancellation it hands off produces the `cancel_path` event instead.
- Observe is the only caller: after attribution, every block a train has just physically entered that is still reserved for a different train is truncated out of the reserving train's authority. Doing it there means the reservation is released before Observe commits the entry, so a legitimate arrival is never reported as the `reserved_for_other_train` fatal physical-entry conflict (see **BlockManager**, `occupy_blocks(...)`).

**Resource acquisition**

- The caller's `manual_override` flag (default `False`) flows through the acquisition chain (see the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags** canonical home for the full chain and override contract). Pathfinder and candidate-search calls invoked from inside `create_path(...)` / `extend_path(...)` also pass the same flag into the `RailwayPathfinder.query_graph_walks(...)` request, so manual resources are included or excluded consistently with the acquisition step.
- **Switch-first acquisition order.** Acquire switches first, then blocks, so switch conflicts are discovered before any blocks are reserved. One `ResourceCoordinator.reserve_segment(...)` call acquires a whole block-terminated prefix in this order, all-or-nothing: on any switch or block failure it releases everything it took before returning and names the first resource that failed.
  - **Best-effort prefix scan.** In `best_effort`, dispatcher decides the storable prefix by re-attempting whole prefixes, not by one forward walk that stops at the first failure. It starts at the prefix length the first failing resource implies — that resource's index is the truncation point — and scans toward shorter prefixes, attempting each whole block-terminated prefix atomically through its own `reserve_segment(...)` call. The scan stops at the furthest-forward prefix that both acquires and passes the item-11 terminal rules (holding-point preference, reversal-trap and junction-fouling exclusions).
  - **Each attempt cleans up after itself.** A failed attempt's `reserve_segment(...)` has already released its own holds, so the next-shorter attempt starts from a clean slate. When an attempt acquires a longer non-holding-point prefix but dispatcher keeps scanning for a nearer holding point, dispatcher releases that discarded attempt's exact holds through `ResourceCoordinator.rollback_probe(...)` — the blocks it still owns plus the exact switch claim keys that attempt inserted — so a switch the path legitimately still holds is never dropped.
  - **Final acquisition.** The chosen prefix is acquired atomically using the same switch-first, blocks-second order. When that final prefix contains no storable block authority, `create_path(...)` fails; for `extend_path(...)`, appending nothing is still a success when the existing path remains a valid blocked prefix.
- **Per-switch main claim and flank acquisition.** For each switch in path order, `SwitchManager.acquire_locks_for_segment(...)` calls `switch.acquire_lock(claim)` with a `claim` carrying `path_id`, `train_id`, `locked_state`, `route` (copied unchanged from the `SwitchLockRequest`, always non-`None` for a main claim), and `source_switch_id=None` (the `None` source marks the claim as a main-usage claim), then expands that main request into that switch's non-exempt `flank_protection` neighbour claims and immediately acquires them before moving to the next switch in path order.
  - **Transaction insertion journal.** For rollback, acquisition records every exact `SwitchClaimKey` newly inserted by the probe and records no idempotently pre-existing key. Failed-probe rollback deletes only that list. Whole-family release is reserved for authority truncation after the corresponding main route point has been removed from the live path.
  - **Route-point exemption.** A `flank_protection` entry is skipped when its `neighbour_switch_id` is itself a main-usage switch in the same acquisition request set (a route point this path traverses). That neighbour is already set and locked by its own main claim, so issuing an opposing flank claim on it would make the path self-conflict and `Switch.acquire_lock` would reject the route's own main claim. This is the canonical home for the rule. Two switches in series on one route — for example a depot-throat pair where the path runs out of one switch straight onto the lead through the next — each appear in the other's `flank_protection` list, so this exemption is what lets a route through such a throat acquire its switches at all.
  - **Same-path conflict exemption** (the switch-triangle case). A `flank_protection` entry is also skipped when two of this path's route points would lock the same `neighbour_switch_id` to opposite `safe_state` values: that neighbour sits at the apex with one route point on each of its two diverging legs (for example a depot-lead crossover apex whose legs reach the mainline switch on one side and the N-track switch on the other). No single position of that neighbour aims its branch away from both route points, so it cannot flank-protect the path, and locking it to either state would reject one route point's own main claim. The two route points need not be acquired in the same call: in `best_effort` the prefix scan truncates a path into separately-acquired segments, so the earlier route point may already be committed, with its flank claim recorded on the apex — as a future flank lock keyed `(path_id, earlier_route_point)` before the train reaches that route point, or as a `train_protection_claim` owned by this train once the train has entered it. The exemption therefore skips the apex whenever the opposite-state demand is already held there by this same path or train, not only when both route points appear in the current call. This exemption leaves the apex protected only as the path's earlier route point already set it (and unlocked when both route points are in one call), rather than failing the segment — the path's own block reservations and route-point switch locks still keep a second train from intruding through it. Like the route-point exemption it is applied at acquisition time, where path membership — including route points committed by this path's earlier segments — is known.
  - **`safe_state` computation.** For each remaining (non-exempt) `flank_protection` entry `(neighbour_switch_id, blocking_state)`, `SwitchManager.acquire_locks_for_segment(...)` calls `neighbour_switch.acquire_lock(claim)` with `source_switch_id=switch.switch_id` (the originating main switch ID marks the claim as a flank-protection claim) and `locked_state=safe_state`, where `safe_state` is the neighbour's state whose active branch does **not** point toward the main switch's track — that is, the state that keeps the neighbour's diverging path aimed away, preventing a head-on approach. `safe_state` is computable from switch geometry: it is the neighbour state whose selected branch exit edge is not the edge facing the main switch. In v1, because switches are binary, `safe_state` is simply the opposite of the neighbour's `blocking_state` recorded at placement time.
  - **Flank claim provenance.** Every acquired flank claim stores `source_switch_id = switch.switch_id` so later switch head-entry can convert only the flank claims sourced from that main switch into train-owned protection.
- Acquire blocks atomically through `BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)`.
- Resource acquisition writes `Block.reserved_direction` through `BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)` for every reserved block. Tile-level traversal direction is carried by `resource_sequence[*].entry_edge` / `exit_edge` and nested `path_tiles[*].entry_edge` / `exit_edge`; there is no `Tile.path_direction` field.
- Distinguish retained geometry, static allowed travel, and temporary reservation direction: v1 does not define a track-level `traffic_direction_policy` field. Static allowed travel direction lives on `Block.allowed_travel_directions`; `Block.reserved_direction` is only the dispatcher-owned temporary reservation direction for one path; and the path plan geometry carries the finer-grained per-tile traversal frame inside that block.
- On failure, roll back in reverse acquisition order — block reservations first, then exact inserted switch claims — per `ResourceCoordinator.rollback_probe(...)`. There is no separate tile-level `path_direction` assignment to clear.
- That rollback releases the acquired claims/reservations only; it does not restore an earlier physical `Switch.position`. The live switch alignment remains at the last successfully written value until some later switch command or path acquisition changes it again.
- Completion and cancellation release blocks through `BlockManager.release_path_block_reservations(...)`, not direct `block.release()` calls.
- In v1, block reservations remain single-train/single-path resources even though `Switch.locks` can have multiple compatible owners. `Block.reserved_direction` therefore has at most one active value per reserved block and must be cleared when that block reservation is released.
- `create_path(..., acquisition_mode: PathDispatcher.AcquisitionMode)` and `extend_path(..., acquisition_mode: PathDispatcher.AcquisitionMode)` must share the same `PathDispatcher.AcquisitionMode` enum, with two v1 behaviors:
  - `AcquisitionMode.all_or_nothing`: dispatcher acquires only the full requested authority or returns failure after full rollback
  - `AcquisitionMode.best_effort`: dispatcher may truncate to the furthest forward acquirable resource prefix, but the acquisition of that chosen prefix is still atomic
- In `best_effort` mode, `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` must either create a block-terminated live path record or fail; a create never succeeds without appending. `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` carries no such rule, and appending nothing is not by itself a failure. Extend fails on an outcome in exactly one situation: no legal forward walk from the live authority end to the caller's current requested target exists, which returns `success = False` with `failure_kind = no_viable_path` and leaves the existing path unchanged. (A caller-contract violation is reported as its own `failure_kind`, per the **`create_path()` / `extend_path()` return contract**.) Every other outcome is `success = True`, because the existing live path is still a legal prefix toward that target and the caller's job is to keep it. A success that appended nothing reports `reached_target = True` when `Path.reaches_target(requested_destination_block_id)` is already true, and `reached_target = False` when the path is still short of it; the caller branches on those two fields and never on why the tick produced no growth. The controller projection reflects any same-path growth on the next read.
- A head-on-switch acquisition remains a failure because v1 does not allow storing a head-on-switch live authority end.
- In all acquisition modes, the stored live authority end must be block-terminated. A same-tick acquisition result that reaches a switch but no following block is not a valid stored live authority in v1; dispatcher must roll that trailing switch/flank acquisition back before storing the path.

**Controller-mediated progress**

- `TrainPhysics.tick(...)` must compute the next `TrainSpan`, next `current_speed_kmh`, and the ordered tile-level delta for that movement, then call `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)` at least once on each pass it runs — that is, each pass this train's movement is calculated (per **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs**). `TrainPhysics` does not call dispatcher progress, completion, or release APIs directly and does not own the stored span.
- `TrainPhysics.tick(...)` integrates from the already-reconciled `controller.physics_sync.current_span` that Observe's `TrainPhysics.reconcile_to_detected_occupancy(...)` committed before Plan. `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)` then atomically writes each physics-integrated `span_update.new_span` and speed. It derives switch observations from that update's tile delta. Only the final callback for the train's tick folds the named `physics_sync.pending_detected_entered_blocks` / `pending_detected_vacated_blocks` into block observations, appends those observations in the specified order, and clears both sets immediately; earlier boundary callbacks leave them untouched. For a train whose movement is not calculated this pass (per **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs**), `TrainController.build_detected_progress_report()` is the sole equivalent producer. Stop completion remains a separate later Observe check.
- The controller progress report payload follows the canonical **ControllerProgressReport schema** defined in the **Dispatcher progress/completion flow** section. `current_head_sequence_index` is the `sequence_index` of the train head's current position in `received_path_plan.resource_sequence`, resolved by the **Head-mapping rule** in that schema, or `None` when no active resource-sequence mapping is available. When live authority exists and the controller cannot map the head to that active `resource_sequence` under the **Head-mapping rule** (no entry anywhere in the sequence matches), the report must set `deviation = true`, a `deviation_error` whose `origin` is `"out_of_sequence"`, and `current_head_sequence_index = None`; dispatcher treats that report as deviation input rather than as ordinary active-path progress. For a single report, dispatcher processing order is entered resources first, then deviation latching if `report.deviation == true`, then tail-vacated resources.
- Observe is the only normal consumer of these reports. It drains the controller-owned progress mailbox (`physics_sync.queued_progress_reports`) in order, calls `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` for each one, and clears the mailbox. Within that same drain, each route head-advance callback compares its single reported block advance with the current next waypoint; if that callback consumes a waypoint, the following report in the mailbox is what may discover and test the next waypoint. After local progress reports have been consumed, if an active path still exists for that train and `pending_path_cancel_request` is `None` (a pending cancel — deviation or explicit — outranks completion), `SimulationController` calls `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(train_id)` and, on success, that step releases the authority and hands the arrival to `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(...)`, which records the finished stop (timestamps per **Time sampling**). `pending_route_abort`, `pending_power_off`, and `pending_route_deactivate` are consumed only after that normal arrival chance.
- The controller report carries `deviation_error` as a diagnostic for the dispatcher / route callback chain, but v1 route progression does not branch on it. Once the active path has been cancelled in Action, the next eligible Plan always returns to the ordinary covered-task index advance plus `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` flow from the train's current physical position; already-covered pass-through handling and stop handling follow the normal task-kind rules.
- **Multiple resource boundaries in one tick.** When physical movement crosses multiple resource boundaries within one simulation tick, `TrainPhysics` must fire multiple sequential `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)` calls — one per resource boundary crossed, in physical traversal order — rather than batching them into a single multi-resource report.
  - `TrainPhysics` computes each incremental `span_update` up to the next boundary, calls `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)` for that boundary, which appends that step's report to the controller-owned per-train progress mailbox (`physics_sync.queued_progress_reports`), then computes the next boundary update and repeats.
  - The boundary `event_time` on each returned `ControllerProgressReport` is the timestamp `TrainPhysics` sampled once for that movement pass via `time.time()` and passed into `on_physics_updated(event_time, span_update)`; the controller stores it unchanged and never resamples per report. The `ControllerProgressReport` is a within-tick transient, so this sits outside the stored-field **Time sampling** rule under the **Units contract**.
  - The per-boundary reports carry the switch observations (calculated traversal, this tick). The detector-confirmed block observations are folded into that tick's final no-boundary report instead, ordered by `sequence_index` when the entries map into the active `resource_sequence` — each such `sequence_index` resolved by the **Head-mapping rule** — and by physical entry order otherwise (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection). Consumers must therefore tolerate the one-tick detector lag between block and switch observations; the monotonic `Path.current_resource_index` rule below absorbs the skew.
  - After the last boundary in that tick, or on a tick with no boundary crossing, `TrainPhysics` must still emit one final callback for that tick. When no resource boundary was crossed, that final update carries `added_tiles=[]` and `removed_tiles=[]`; when nothing changed physically, it may be an explicit no-change callback.

  This guarantees that Observe always has a final progress report to drain and that downstream side effects (lock consumption, tail-vacate release, route head-advance callbacks, switch state notifications) commit in the same physical order as the local progress reports. So the Observe progress-mailbox drain (step `3e9b`) has one deterministic pass every tick, independent of whether movement crossed a boundary.

  Within any single `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)` call, `entered_resources` and `tail_vacated_resources` therefore typically carry one entry each at most. When a single call legitimately needs to carry more (for example simultaneous head entry and tail vacate at the same boundary), events within each list must still be ordered by physical traversal / vacate order, and dispatcher still processes the entered list before the vacated list.
- Entry ownership is resource-typed and dispatcher-mediated; `PathDispatcher` does not branch on `resource_type` — it routes every entry through `ResourceCoordinator.on_physical_entry(resource_type, resource_id, train_id, path_id, route)`:
  - on block entry, the coordinator routes to `BlockManager.occupy_blocks([block_id], train_id)`; this is the only normal runtime path that writes `Block.occupied_by`
  - on clean switch entry, the coordinator routes to `SwitchManager.on_physical_entry(switch_id, train_id, path_id, route)`, which records `Switch.physical_occupants[route] = train_id`, consumes the entering train's compatible main switch lock, and converts applicable flank locks into train-owned protection. Two trains using non-conflicting routes coexist (per `switch.routes_conflict(...)`); the hard-failure case is an incoming `route` that conflicts with a route held by a different train, or the intrusion case where the entering train holds no compatible lock for its route (see the **Switch entity** intrusion check). A conflict must not overwrite the prior owner
- Dispatcher progress must update `Path.current_resource_index` using the reported path-step `sequence_index`, not by searching for the first matching raw `resource_id`. The producer-side companion is the **Head-mapping rule** in the **ControllerProgressReport schema**: because one `resource_id` may sit at more than one index, `TrainController` resolves each reported `sequence_index` against its own progress anchor, so a lapping path's second visit to a block reports the later index and advances progress instead of being swallowed by the monotonic rule in this bullet. `Path.current_resource_index` is head-based progress only; it advances when the train head enters a new resource and does not wait for the later tail-based release of earlier resources. Because switch observations (calculated, same tick) and block observations (detector-confirmed, one tick later) interleave with that skew, `current_resource_index` is monotonic: an entry whose `sequence_index` is at or behind the current value leaves it unchanged (`current_resource_index = max(current, reported sequence_index)`).
- A live path must remain `ACTIVE` after creation, through intermediate resources, and after entering the final block/resource. Entering the terminal resource must not change lifecycle state by itself.
- **Only Observe may finish a `stop` task against a live authority.** After local progress reports have been consumed, if an active path still exists for that train and `pending_path_cancel_request` is `None` (a pending cancel outranks arrival), step `9d8b` has `SimulationController` call `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(train_id)`. Step `8df5` is the predicate. If it is true, step `09b0` releases future resources, writes `Path.status = COMPLETED`, and delivers the callback; step `bc55` is the route callback's finished-stop commit (timestamps per **Time sampling**). Dispatcher invents no additional acceptance test.
  - **Depart-acceptance signal.** The single canonical depart-acceptance signal is `controller.state == RUNNING_MOVING`, set by any canonical transition into that state listed in the Controller state machine table — either a successful `TrainController.depart()` call or `OperationalStateMachine.evaluate_reactive_conditions()` observing motion from a cab-selected `READY` controller.
  - **Manual driving before `depart()`.** Manual driving input may command motion under live authority before Plan's `depart()` call lands; ATC still protects the train.
  - **The reactive transition is equally legitimate.** The reactive transition into `RUNNING_MOVING` is treated as equally legitimate to depart-acceptance: `ato.running` setting (when `control_mode == "ato"` and `received_path_plan is not None`) and other readers all key on `state == RUNNING_MOVING` regardless of which transition fired.
  - **Head-entry route progress is not state-gated.** Head-entry route progress, including `task_kind == "waypoint"` consumption through `RouteExecutor.handle_train_advanced(...)`, is not state-gated.
  - **Admin teardown waits for this arrival chance.** Explicit latched admin teardown such as `pending_path_cancel_request` and `pending_power_off` is consumed only after this normal arrival chance.
- A distance-0 ATC limit at its floor is not by itself stop completion. No-cab, no-authority, deviation, EB, obstruction/conflict, wrong-direction cab, and truncated best-effort authority all drive the distance-0 limit to zero without being stop completion; only `atc_limit_reason_code == "authority_stop"` (with the controller stopped and the other `8df5` (Stop-arrival check) conditions) is.
- For a `task_kind == "stop"` task whose live authority already reaches its requested target block, a post-physics controller stop at the safety-margin-adjusted usable authority stop satisfying the **Stop-arrival check** (step `8df5`) completes the path normally. The head may be short of the physical requested block when the safety margin/ATC boundary requires that; ATC remains the higher-priority rule and there is no "go back and try again" prompt for a within-block or before-block safety-margin stop.
- EB activation records `pending_path_cancel_request` per the **canonical EB activation effects** (when a live path exists), and that request is committed by the same train's Action consume pass through `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` once the train is stopped. That pending cancel is what keeps a latched EB out of arrival — no condition in the **Stop-arrival check** mentions EB: step `9d8b` skips the check entirely while `pending_path_cancel_request` is set, and the distance-0 reason-code tie-break makes `"eb"` outrank `"authority_stop"`. After EB release any route continuation uses a fresh path request.
- Controller-reported deviation produces a `cancel_path` event carrying the report's own `ErrorRecord` (`origin = "out_of_sequence"`) unchanged on the event's `error` field, with `deviation = true` and a `message` naming the deviation, per the **Cancellation** subsection. Cancellation wins over any same-tick completion attempt. Recovery follows the canonical recovery table. A `task_kind == "waypoint"` target the train has entered, passed, or later covers counts as served and does not produce a separate overshot-waypoint deviation.
- A best-effort truncated path must not complete just because the train has stopped at the current authority boundary while the current authorized target is still short of the requested target. In that case the same path remains `ACTIVE`, the controller stays in `RUNNING_MOVING` (stopped under zero ATC clearance against the still-live authority), and `RouteExecutor` keeps trying `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` on that same `path_id` until `RouteExecutor` releases the truncated authority under the **idle-hold maintenance and release** rule in Planning Kernel step `66aa` — either after the authority makes no progress for `IDLE_HOLD_RELEASE_TICKS` consecutive Plan ticks, or as soon as a strictly-higher-priority run is blocked on a block this run holds but has not yet physically entered — and re-plans after a cooldown so the held reservations/locks return to higher-priority runs.
- Completed paths must release only not-yet-entered block reservations through `BlockManager.release_path_block_reservations(..., completed=True)`, because reservations for already-entered blocks were consumed on head entry. That reservation release may force-clear terminal `CAUTION` only for matching still-reserved owned blocks, but it must not force-clear any physical `OCCUPIED` block early. On this `ACTIVE -> COMPLETED` transition, dispatcher follows the step `09b0` release order in the **Stop-arrival procedure**. The retained record may remain in `paths_by_id` for history, but physical release of a switch or block still under the train resolves from the resource itself. When a later tail-vacate resource event arrives through `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)`, it clears `Block.occupied_by` (for a block) or removes the `Switch.physical_occupants` entry (for a switch, so `Switch.occupied_by` reads `None`) and any train-owned switch protection through the resource-specific release path. `RouteExecutor` records the arrival in step `bc55` from the `handle_path_completion(...)` callback that step `09b0` delivers after this transition, and does not re-check safety-margin projection itself.
- On extension, the only stored `Path` update is `Path.resource_sequence`. On creation, `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` initializes every stored field in the **Path field schema** — `path_id`, `status`, `train_id`, `resource_sequence`, `current_resource_index`, and `last_status_updated_time`; path geometry still has only one stored source, `resource_sequence`. `Path.get_authority_end_block_id()` and `Path.reaches_target(block_id)` are derived reads of that list and update automatically. The controller's `received_path_plan` property reads them live on the next access; there is no separate controller write step. An extension that appends nothing stores nothing, and the caller learns the outcome from `appended_resource_count` and `reached_target` in the result rather than from any refreshed field on the record.
- Drive resource release from tail-vacate observations (detector-confirmed for blocks per **Power**, Block occupancy detection; controller-reported traversal for switches). `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` routes every vacate through `ResourceCoordinator.release_tail_vacated(resource_type, resource_id, train_id, direction, route)` (the single `resource_type` branch lives inside the coordinator; `PathDispatcher` does not branch on it):
  - vacated blocks go through `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated(block_id, train_id, direction)`
  - vacated switches go through `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(switch_id, train_id, route)`. The physical state is cleared first — the matching `Switch.physical_occupants[route]` entry owned by this train is removed — and only then, when no `physical_occupants` entries remain for that train on this switch, the manager clears train-owned protection sourced from that switch via `Switch.release_train_protection_from(source_switch_id=switch_id, train_id=train_id)` on each protected neighbour. The physical-vacate handler never decides which lock to drop; the manager does, keyed by `(path_id, source_switch_id)`, so a switch that holds both a main lock and a flank lock for the same route releases the correct one (per the **Switch entity** tail-vacate contract)
- All normal block release goes through `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated()` so `OCCUPIED -> CAUTION -> FREE` stays a single-manager state machine.

**Path extension**

- The controller has no lookahead cache to invalidate (lookahead is computed live each read; see the lookahead section). Path updates therefore have no per-controller invalidation step.
- A change to `Block.allowed_travel_directions` (static config edit) does **not** invalidate any already-active path's reservations; the block-direction eligibility test in `BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)` ran once at acquisition against the candidate `ReservedBlockTraversal.block_direction`, and no re-check runs for the life of the path; the stored `Block.reservation` carries only `path_id`, `train_id`, and `exit_edge`, so there is nothing on the block for a policy edit to invalidate. The new direction policy takes effect only at the next `BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)` call. Operator/admin code must not edit `allowed_travel_directions` to indirectly cancel a live path; cancellation goes through `pending_path_cancel_request`.
- Truncated best-effort authority where the train physically stops at the temporary boundary while no resolved target is armed (the one-tick gap between task-completion and the next Plan target arm) is permissible: the controller stays in `RUNNING_MOVING` against the still-live truncated authority with zero ATC clearance, and the next Plan may extend authority once the next target resolves.
- Extension is forward-only. **`RouteExecutor` must call `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` with the `stored_resolved_target` returned by `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)` for the live planning chain.** Extend identity is the target block alone. Any other target block is a route-side invariant violation expressed through cancel-and-replan. While the same block stays armed, Plan passes the stored pair unchanged and does not resolve direction again. Arming a new target block is a fresh resolve; when the path already reaches it, **Already-reached success** applies.
- `extend_path(...)` appends only the new suffix's resources (with their nested `path_tiles` slices) to `resource_sequence`; `Path.get_path_tiles()` reflects the growth on its next call. The existing prefix's entries — including the connecting tile the new suffix starts from, already seeded by the prior `create_path(...)` / `extend_path(...)` call — are not re-appended.
- Reject any extension that would make the path hold one resource twice at once, per the **repeated-resource rule** under **Path invariants**: dispatcher fails it with `no_viable_path`, not the retry result. A resource the train has already passed and released — block or switch — is not held, so an extension may take authority into it again.
- **Already-reached success.** When `Path.reaches_target(requested_destination_block_id)` is already true there is nothing to append: return `success = True` with `appended_resource_count = 0` and `reached_target = True`, and leave `resource_sequence` unchanged. This covers both shapes — the target is the live authority end, and the target sits behind the authority end on the stored walk — because both mean the same thing to the caller: the authority already runs to that block, so no forward growth is owed. It is reached whenever Plan arms a target block the live path already holds, which the **Waypoint lookahead** produces routinely: that step arms the next target while the current one is still unserved, so a later arm of the same block finds the authority already there.
- `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` must take the same argument contract as `create_path(...)`, except that it identifies the existing live path by `path_id`: `path_id`, `requested_destination_block_id`, `requested_destination_direction`, `acquisition_mode`, `manual_override`, optional `acquisition_cap_block_id`, and optional `required_candidate_resource_keys` (mirroring `create_path(...)`'s full signature). `manual_override` flows through the acquisition chain exactly as for create, `acquisition_cap_block_id` caps the appended suffix per the **Acquisition-cap rule**, and `required_candidate_resource_keys` applies the same exact-candidate filtering as `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)`: when the named candidate is no longer viable, return the ordinary blocked/no-growth result without falling through to another candidate. The live path identified by `path_id` is the fixed already-acquired prefix; `extend_path(...)` grows that existing path forward from its current authority end toward the caller-supplied requested target for this extend attempt. Dispatcher does not run a separate shared-walk prefix-compatibility test. When the requested extension cannot continue forward from the existing live path without breaking the ordinary path rules, the outcome splits by the **viable-but-unavailable rule**: an extension that no legal forward walk can serve — including one whose only walk would revisit a resource the path still holds — fails with `no_viable_path`, while an extension whose forward walk exists but whose next forward resource is held by another train's live claim returns the `0` / `False` retry result. Neither outcome changes the existing path's `resource_sequence`.
- The shared request contract between `extend_path(...)` and `create_path(...)` is the same, but `extend_path(...)` adds extra constraints: it requires a live `path_id`, and the newly appended suffix must continue forward from that live path's current authority-end edge in the same travel direction the existing prefix was built in. The caller-supplied `requested_destination_direction` applies only to the new terminal block `requested_destination_block_id`; it is not a license to reverse at the current authority end. A `requested_destination_direction` that would require the train to reverse 180 degrees at the current authority end (for example, the requested new terminal block lies behind the current authority-end edge on the existing prefix's travel frame, or reaching it would require exiting the authority-end block backward out of its current `exit_edge`) is invalid for `extend_path(...)` and must be rejected with `success = False`, `failure_kind = no_viable_path`, and a diagnostic `reason` such as `"extend would reverse at authority end"`: extension is forward-only, so no forward suffix reaches that target. The existing live path must remain unchanged in that rejection. Callers that actually need the train to turn back at the current terminal must cancel the existing path and issue a fresh `create_path(...)` from the train's current span instead.
- `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` requires a live `ACTIVE` path. A `path_id` that does not exist, or that references a path which is not currently `ACTIVE`, is a caller-contract violation and fails with `failure_kind = missing_or_inactive_path` per the **`create_path()` / `extend_path()` return contract**. `RouteExecutor` passes the id it just read from `PathDispatcher.active_path_id_by_train(train_id)`, so it cannot reach this case in normal operation.
- In `all_or_nothing` mode, `extend_path(...)` must either acquire the full requested suffix to `requested_destination_block_id` or leave the existing path unchanged, so an all-or-nothing extend never returns the truncated `appended_resource_count > 0` / `reached_target = False` shape a `best_effort` extend can. The **Already-reached success** result (`appended_resource_count = 0`, `reached_target = True`, `resource_sequence` unchanged) applies in `all_or_nothing` exactly as it does in every other mode, since it fires whenever the live authority already reaches the requested target and there is nothing left to append. An all-or-nothing extend that does append anything reports `reached_target = True` and `appended_resource_count > 0`. When the full suffix exists but cannot be acquired on this tick — for any of the unavailability causes listed in the **viable-but-unavailable rule** — the call returns `appended_resource_count = 0` with `reached_target = False` and the existing path is left intact for a later retry. When no legal suffix exists, it fails with `failure_kind = no_viable_path`.
- In `best_effort` mode, `extend_path(...)` must keep the same `path_id` and append the furthest forward acquirable suffix it can add to the current path. The `resource_sequence` therefore grows in place on the same live path instead of creating a new path. No outcome stores the caller's requested target on the `Path`; the record holds only the geometry actually acquired.
  - When at least one resource is appended, return `appended_resource_count > 0`, with `reached_target` reporting whether `Path.reaches_target(requested_destination_block_id)` is now true.
  - When no resource can be appended but the dispatcher can prove the existing path is still a legal prefix to the requested target, return `success=True` with `appended_resource_count = 0` and `reached_target = False`, leave `resource_sequence` unchanged (the derived `Path.get_authority_end_block_id()` is therefore unchanged too), and let `RouteExecutor` retry later. Why the suffix could not grow does not change this outcome: every unavailability cause in the **viable-but-unavailable rule** lands here. The controller's `received_path_plan` property continues to return the same `path_id`, `resource_sequence`, and `authority_end_block_id` projection on its next read; the requested target this call echoed is recorded route-side on `RouteRun.task_runs[i].resolved_target`, never in that projection.
  - When no legal forward suffix to the requested target exists at all, return `success=False` with `failure_kind = no_viable_path` and leave the existing path unchanged.
- The same three truncation-terminal rules — one terminal preference and two exclusions — that govern `create_path(...)` also govern the appended suffix and Observe authority truncation (see **Authority truncation**, above), and the item-11 canonical rule owns each of them: the holding-point preference (a terminal choice among eligible prefixes), the reversal-trap exclusion, and the junction-fouling exclusion. Where item 11 fails a create because no legal terminal remains, `extend_path(...)` instead appends nothing and returns the `appended_resource_count = 0` / `reached_target = False` success, because the existing live path is still valid and the right caller behavior is to keep it and retry. Growth that would land the new terminal block on an excluded block is not committed; dispatcher truncates to the nearest legal terminal instead, and appends nothing when none is available.
- While the path is still truncated short of the caller's current requested target, the stored `resource_sequence` terminates on the current last acquired block; the derived `Path.get_authority_end_block_id()` reflects that terminal automatically.
- Every successful `extend_path(...)` updates the dispatcher's `Path` record in place. A result with `appended_resource_count > 0` carries the grown `resource_sequence`; a result with `appended_resource_count = 0` carries the unchanged geometry and stores nothing. The controller's `received_path_plan` property reads any growth live on the next access. When the live authority finally reaches the requested target, `Path.reaches_target(requested_destination_block_id)` becomes true and the call reports `reached_target = True`.
- Extend outcomes are branchable without parsing `reason`. Every `success=True` result preserves a valid live path: `reached_target = True` means there is nothing left to extend, and `reached_target = False` means `RouteExecutor` keeps the path and retries later, whether or not the call appended anything. `success=False` with `failure_kind = no_viable_path` means no legal walk from the live authority end reaches the requested target, so waiting cannot clear it, and `RouteExecutor` must latch cancellation before a fresh create attempt.

**Cancellation**

- `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(path_id, error, kind, deviation=False, run_complete=False)` is the single canonical cancellation entry point in v1. `error` is the diagnostic `ErrorRecord` that flows directly into the `cancel_path` event's `error` field for logs/UI, and is `None` only on a `run_complete` release; nothing inside it may be used as a condition by planning or routing logic. Recovery classification uses only the two mutually-exclusive booleans: `deviation` for movement deviation and `run_complete` for normal run authority release. All other recovery branching is driven by controller state, runtime latches, current span coverage, and task-kind rules.
- Release owned blocks through `BlockManager.release_path_block_reservations(...)` instead of direct `block.release()` calls. Cancellation release clears future reservation ownership only; it never clears physical occupancy.
- Path cancellation or revocation effects are owned entirely by `PathDispatcher`, and the cancellation commit happens only in Action. `RouteExecutor` or `TrainController` may request cancellation only by recording controller-owned Action handoff state such as `pending_path_cancel_request`; they must not call `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)`, clear authority, or release resources directly from Plan or the Action command/control code. If Plan route logic decides that the current live path must be revoked, it records or refreshes that cancel request and then stops planning for that train for that tick; later eligible Plan passes follow the same latch-only rule while the incompatible live path still exists. A later eligible Plan may resume ordinary create/extend planning only after three things have happened: the same train's later Action consumes that request, `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` completes, and the ordinary cancellation callback clears route-side live-path correlation. When Action commits the cancellation through `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)`, dispatcher transitions `Path.status` to `CANCELLED`, which by definition makes the controller's `received_path_plan` property return `None` on its next read.
- Power-off uses this same dispatcher cancellation workflow through the inclusive-latch fan-out: see the **Power-off procedure** for the canonical four-step sequence (`98d3` → `278a` → `534f` → `886a`).
- On `ACTIVE -> CANCELLED`, `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` follows the cancellation-specific order in step `09b0`: release future resources with `completed=False`, set status `CANCELLED`, then deliver only the route-side cancellation callback. Cancellation clears future reservation/authority only; physical occupancy and train-owned protection remain until tail-vacate. A same-train new path is allowed once the old path is non-active, subject to ordinary conflicts and controller recovery gates.
- Future switch/flank release for both `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` and `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(...)` goes through `SwitchManager.release_path_locks(path_id)`. The manager scans the stored `Switch.locks` collections and removes every still-future claim whose stored `claim.path_id` matches, including both main and flank claims. It does not recompute flank neighbours from the switch's current persisted fields or infer releases from `Path.resource_sequence`; stored claim identity is authoritative even if topology or flank fields changed after acquisition. The release is idempotent and naturally no-ops for claims already consumed on physical entry. It must not clear `Switch.physical_occupants` or `Switch.train_protection_claims`; those remain physical/train-owned until later controller-reported switch tail-vacate.
- Reservation / physical state ownership in v1 must be read literally:
  - dispatcher-owned future reservation state: `Block.reserved_by_path`, `Block.reserved_for_train`, `Block.reserved_direction`, `Switch.locks`, flank-protection lock ownership for resources the train has not entered yet
  - block physical state owned by `BlockManager` and mutated only through `BlockManager` entry/tail-vacate APIs invoked by `PathDispatcher` on detector-confirmed observations (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection): `Block.occupied_by`, `Block.caution`. Two documented Observe exceptions also clear `Block.occupied_by` without a detector observation — `BlockManager.release_train_occupancy(train_id)` on the ghosted-train teardown and the unidentified-train adoption re-key (see **Power**, Ghosted trains and Unidentified trains) — and the pre-first-tick `RailwayNetwork.place_train(...)` seed sets it (see **Power**, Placement and restore are seeded, not re-detected)
  - dispatcher-mediated switch physical state, written by `PathDispatcher` on controller-reported resource-entry / tail-vacate observations rather than directly by `TrainPhysics`: `Switch.physical_occupants` and `Switch.train_protection_claims` (the `Switch.occupied_by` read is a derived projection of `physical_occupants`, not a separately written store)
  - a block has at most one physical `occupied_by` train at a time. Switch occupancy is different: `Switch.physical_occupants` may contain multiple trains on mutually non-conflicting routes, and conflict is decided by `switch.routes_conflict(...)`, not by the single-value diagnostic `Switch.occupied_by` projection. A single train may hold multiple path records layered over physical ownership; path membership stays on dispatcher `Path` records.
  - cancellation / completion release clears only future block reservations and future switch locks that have not already been consumed by head entry
  - physical entry / tail-vacate observations committed through `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` are the only runtime path that clears or sets `BlockManager`-owned block physical state or dispatcher-mediated switch physical state (block observations are detector-confirmed per **Power**, Block occupancy detection; switch observations are controller-reported traversal), except for the two documented Observe teardown clears through `BlockManager.release_train_occupancy(train_id)` (ghosted-train teardown and adoption re-key) and the pre-first-tick `RailwayNetwork.place_train(...)` seed
  - once a resource is physically occupied, later tail-vacate clears physical occupancy and train-owned protection rather than path-owned residue
- Cancellation commits only on a stopped train (the latch's `is_stopped()` gate), so the controller observes `received_path_plan` turn `None` at rest: the canonical lookahead becomes the no-authority empty payload and ATC holds the train there. When the cancellation was deviation-driven, the stop itself was forced earlier by the zero-limit / EB protocol in step `826a` of the **Controller tick order** (the `"deviation"` reason code while the path was still live). The operator clears EB through `TrainController.eb.release()` once the cancel has committed and authority is cleared; that command clears only `eb.active`, and the ordinary post-command state evaluation then moves the stopped authority-free controller to `READY`. Physics keeps integrating live network state during the EB brake; a pending cancellation releases nothing ahead of the rolling train, and the committed cancellation does not unlock a physically occupied switch.
- After a `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` call commits its lower-layer mutation, dispatcher calls its injected `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(train_id, path_id, error, was_deviation=False, was_run_completion=False)` callback. A `committed = False` idempotent no-op delivers no callback at all. Dispatcher forwards `was_deviation = deviation` and `was_run_completion = run_complete`; validation rejects a call where both are true. Nothing inside `error` drives either branch. For ordinary cancellation/deviation, `RouteExecutor` records the recovery diagnostic and defers target selection until a later eligible Plan. For `was_run_completion == True`, the callback performs no `path_cancelled`, `path_cancel_was_deviation`, or `display_state` write: Plan step `6a0d` owns successful run completion after it observes the stopped no-authority state. The whole `ErrorRecord`, when the cancellation carries one, remains on the mandatory `cancel_path` event and is stored nowhere else.
- **`cancel_path` event.** This is the canonical event surface for cancellation diagnostics. `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` emits one `cancel_path` event through `NotificationCenter` as the last step of the canonical cancellation flow, after the dispatcher mutation has committed and the route-side `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(...)` callback has been invoked. Only a call that returned `committed = True` emits it; an idempotent no-op emits nothing, so a path is never announced as cancelled twice. UI/log consumers use this event as the canonical surface for cancellation diagnostics. The notification carries:
  - `notification_id` — assigned by `NotificationCenter` per the canonical notification rule
  - `event_time` — system-time Unix seconds. Immediately before writing `Path.status = CANCELLED`, `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` samples `time.time()` once and stores that value locally. It uses the same retained value for `Path.last_status_updated_time` and for this event after the route callback returns; it does not resample at emission time.
  - `source` — `"PathDispatcher"`
  - `operation` — `"cancel_path"`
  - `kind` — the level the writer declared on the `pending_path_cancel_request` payload, passed through unchanged. `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` derives nothing: it does not inspect `error`, `deviation`, or `run_complete` to pick a level. Because the whole most-recent same-tick payload wins, all fields describe the request actually committed.
  - `entities` — refs naming the train, the cancelled path, and the train's `RouteRun` when it has one
  - `message` — one line naming the train, the path this call cancelled, and what ended it in plain words: `deviation` when `deviation` is `true`, `run complete` when `run_complete` is `true`, and otherwise the plain-words form of the writer's `error.origin` (emergency brake, operator cancelled, power off, revoked, idle-hold release, contention release). This is where a reader sees "deviation"; `error.origin` stays the machine label `"out_of_sequence"` and no code reads either one
  - `error` — the diagnostic `ErrorRecord` the writer committed, regardless of `kind`. It is `None` only on a `run_complete` release because that release is successful progress with no diagnostic failure.
  - `payload`:
    - `deviation: bool` — `True` only for movement-derived deviation
    - `run_complete: bool` — `True` only for Plan run step `6a0d`; mutually exclusive with `deviation`
    - `latch: str` — the constant `"path_cancel_request"`, naming the latch whose consumption this event is, so a log reader can group it with the latch's other diagnostics
    - `origin: str` — the machine label the writer put on `error.origin` (for example `"out_of_sequence"`, `"operator_cancelled"`, `"power_off"`, `"revoked"`), or the literal `"run_complete"` on a run-completion release where `error` is `None`. This is the machine-readable twin of the plain-words cause in `message`
**Path invariants**

- In v1 the dispatcher path lifecycle is exactly `ACTIVE` / `COMPLETED` / `CANCELLED` (see the **Path status state machine**): acquisition is synchronous inside `create_path()`, so a live path has the single state `ACTIVE`. Whether the train has started moving, entered the terminal resource, or is stopped at the stop point is represented by controller state, `current_resource_index`, and explicit completion predicates, not by separate path lifecycle values.
- `current_resource_index` must track `sequence_index`, not the first occurrence of a raw resource ID.
- A path must not hold the same resource twice at once. Both `create_path()` and `extend_path()` must reject any candidate whose walk would put one block or switch into the path's live holdings a second time. This is the **repeated-resource rule**, and this bullet is its canonical home. For `extend_path(...)`, a candidate whose only walk to the requested target would revisit a resource the path still holds fails with `no_viable_path`, and `RouteExecutor` cancels the path and re-plans; by the next eligible plan the train's tail may have cleared that resource, letting a fresh `create_path(...)` / `extend_path(...)` take it. Dispatcher does not distinguish a revisit whose hold would clear as the train advances from one that never could — there is no own-length feasibility filter that measures the walk against the train's length, so every revisit of a still-held resource is a viability failure, not an availability retry. Because a path may still take authority back into a resource the train has already passed and released, one `resource_id` may appear at more than one `sequence_index`; the **Head-mapping rule** in the **ControllerProgressReport schema** is what resolves the train head to the right occurrence.
- What counts as held is the live claim, not the traversal record. `Path.resource_sequence` keeps every resource the path has ever authorized, including ones the train has already rolled through. Tail vacate never trims this history or renumbers its `sequence_index` values. A block is held while `Block.reserved_by_path` names this path or while this path's train still occupies it; head entry consumes the reservation and tail vacate clears the occupancy (see `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated()`), after which the block is free and any path, this one included, may acquire it again. A switch is held while a live claim on the switch names it: a `Switch.locks` claim whose stored `claim.path_id` is this path, or an entry in `Switch.physical_occupants` / `Switch.train_protection_claims` owned by this path's train. Held is computed from the claims stored on the resource; there is no path-owned hold flag, and a path only ever manages the claims it placed. Head entry consumes this path's main switch lock and converts its flank locks into train-owned protection (see `SwitchManager.on_physical_entry(...)`), and switch tail vacate removes the train's `physical_occupants` entry and clears that train-owned protection (see `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(...)`), after which the switch carries no claim from this path and any path, this one included, may acquire it again.
- Reading the rule against live holdings is what lets a `CIRCULAR` route close its lap. The route walk wraps back to the resources the run started from; by then the train has entered and vacated them, so no live claim from this path remains and taking authority into them again is an ordinary acquisition. A seam that falls on a switch closes the same way, since a vacated switch carries no claim either; where the stored authority may end is set separately by the block-terminated live authority rule under **Resource acquisition**.
- Switch resources contribute `0 cm` to forward-distance accumulation. Any helper that sums per-resource physical length must therefore add `0` for `resource_type == "switch"` and continue the cumulative axis across the surrounding block geometry.
- `FLANK_PROTECTION_DISTANCE_CM` must be a global config, not a per-path setting.
- In v1, switch locks are a multi-owner compatibility set: multiple paths may hold compatible same-state lock claims on the same switch, but conflicting required states are not allowed. Physical occupancy is likewise route-keyed and may be multi-train only for mutually non-conflicting routes.
- `PathDispatcher` does not run a behind-train release sweep; block release is fully owned by `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated()` and is triggered by detector-confirmed Observe progress. Controller/physics traversal remains the vacate source for switches only.

## Route And RouteExecutor

**Route data**

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `route_id` | `str` | Unique route identifier |
| `name` | `str` | Display name |
| `tasks` | `List[RouteTask]` | Ordered route definition — see **RouteTask data** |
| `mode` | `RouteMode` | One of `ONE_OFF`, `CIRCULAR`, `ROUND_TRIP` |
| `assigned_train_ids` | `List[str]` | Stored list of train IDs assigned to the route. Canonical mutators are `Route.assign_train(train_id)` (appends if not already present) and `Route.unassign_train(train_id)` (removes if present); both are idempotent. The field is written from these canonical entry points only — see **Route assignment writers** below. |
| `is_active` | `bool` | Route execution enabled. Defaults to `False` at construction. Written only by `Route.activate()` (`True`) and `route.deactivate()` (`False`) — see **Route activation**. |
| `started_at` | `Optional[float]` | System-time Unix timestamp when activated |
| `created_at` | `float` | System-time Unix timestamp when the Route record was constructed. Sampled by `Route.__post_init__` via `time.time()` at the write site (see **Time sampling** under the **Units contract**). Written exactly once at construction; never mutated by edit, assignment, activation, deactivation, or any other handler. |
| `last_edited_at` | `Optional[float]` | System-time Unix timestamp of the most recent route-definition edit. `None` for a freshly-constructed Route that has never been edited after creation. Written only by the canonical route-definition edit writers — see **Route edit timestamps** below. Not touched by `Route.assign_train` / `Route.unassign_train` (assignment) or `Route.activate` / `Route.deactivate` (lifecycle). |
| `priority` | `int` | Route-executor scheduling priority, `0..9` where `9` is highest and `0` is lowest (default `5`) |
| `acquisition_mode` | `PathDispatcher.AcquisitionMode` | Default route path-acquisition policy (default `AcquisitionMode.best_effort`) |
| `timing_basis` | `"operating" \| "realtime"` | Which clock this route's duration-based dwell and `delay_class` calculations measure against (default `"operating"`). Under `"operating"`, an operator stop does not consume a dwell authored with `task_time` and does not add to a waypoint/stop lateness calculation. Under `"realtime"`, those calculations use wall time. The setting never governs an absolute dwell `target_time`, which remains a wall-clock instant under either basis, and never governs a `run` task's `run_elapsed_seconds`, which always accumulates playback-scaled simulated time (see **Task time semantics**). In v1 it has no request-service edit path — it is set only by full-snapshot load, not by the create/update route services or their handlers — but when it does change it takes effect on the next evaluation with no run teardown, because every `RouteTaskRun` row already stores both stamps. |
| `manual_override` | `bool` | Operator override for `manual` resources (default `False`). Set `True` only on operator-initiated routes (the Quick Route tool exposes the option when the operator explicitly chooses to use manual resources). `RouteExecutor` passes the assigned route's `manual_override` into every `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` / `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` call for that run, which forwards it through the acquisition chain and pathfinder per the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags** canonical home; `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` applies the same flag to its `manual` target filtering and to its `Block.allowed_travel_directions` direction filtering. Edits take effect on the next create/extend attempt with no run teardown. |
| `start_mode` | `RouteStartMode` | Default for which stop a fresh run begins at: `FIRST` (default), `NEAREST`, or `SPECIFIC`. Consulted once when Plan allocates a fresh run; not a live override. See **Run start-mode seeding**. |
| `start_task_index` | `Optional[int]` | Stop index used only when `start_mode == SPECIFIC` (the index into `Route.tasks` of the stop to begin at). `None` otherwise. See **Run start-mode seeding**. |

**Route assignment writers**

`Route.assigned_train_ids` is mutated only through these canonical writers:

- `Route.assign_train(train_id)` and `Route.unassign_train(train_id)` are the two stored-list helpers; both are idempotent. Request services do not call them independently when a live run exists.
- **Assignment request entry.** Every HTTP/UI/admin assignment writer calls `RouteExecutor.request_route_assignment(train_id, requested_route_id: Optional[str], start_override=None)`. `requested_route_id = None` means unassign. If no `RUNNING` run exists, the method clears older pending route/start state, removes the train from any old route, assigns the requested route when non-`None`, and stores the new start override. If a `RUNNING` run exists and the request names that same route, the request is an idempotent no-op; a supplied start override is rejected because the run already consumed its start mode. For a different route or `None`, the method first calls `controller.route_hooks.phase_latches.set_route_abort(...)`, which clears older pending state and writes the inclusive cancel, then stores `{requested_route_id, start_override}` in `RouteExecutor._pending_route_assignments[train_id]`. It does not mutate either route's `assigned_train_ids` yet.
- **Action commits a replacement.** `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)` changes the old run to its historical `DEACTIVATED` state, calls `Route.unassign_train(train_id)` on that run's route, then consumes `_pending_route_assignments[train_id]`. When the stored `requested_route_id` is non-`None`, it calls that route's `assign_train(train_id)` and moves the stored start override to `_pending_start_overrides[train_id]`; when it is `None`, the train remains unassigned. These writes are one Action procedure, so no stored assignment points at the new route while the old run is still live.
- HTTP/UI/admin entry points use that request method (existing v1 routes; their exact paths and payload shapes are unchanged from current code unless this document overrides them):
  - `POST /api/train-routes` requests the route for each train in its `assigned_train_ids` body.
  - `PUT /api/train-routes/<route_id>` diffs the existing list against the requested list and requests assignment/unassignment per change.
  - `PUT /api/trains/<train_id>/assign-route` requests the named route. This is a plain reassignment entry point; `PUT /api/paths/<path_id>/extend` uses the same method as part of operator retargeting.
- Internal teardown writers that call `Route.unassign_train(train_id)`:
  - `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)` (called by Action abort, power-off, and deactivate consumers). These already run only once the abort/power-off/deactivate latch has torn the run down, so the guard above does not apply to them.
  - `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)` (called by Plan terminal-walk completion). This unassigns the same train whose walk it just finished, atomically with the `FINISHED` write, so there is no `RUNNING` run left for the guard above to catch.
- Operator retargeting and route swap call `RouteExecutor.request_route_assignment(...)`; they do not mutate either route list around a live run.

`RouteExecutor.assigned_route_id_for(train_id)` first returns `RouteExecutor.execution_state_for(train_id).route_id` when a live `RUNNING` run exists, then falls back to the route whose stored `assigned_train_ids` contains the train. While a live run tears down, both sources name the old run's route; `_pending_route_assignments` is request state and is not reported as an assignment. `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(...)` changes the historical status, removes the old stored assignment, and commits any replacement in one Action procedure. The live run and stored list must agree whenever both are present; disagreement is an invariant violation rather than a third lookup rule.

- **Single-assignment rule.** A train appears in at most one `Route.assigned_train_ids` at a time. A requested replacement lives only in `_pending_route_assignments` until Action removes the old run and stored assignment.
- **The assign-to-allocation window.** After a route is stored in `assigned_train_ids` and before the next eligible Plan step `9c4f`, the train has that assignment and no `RUNNING` run. That condition is the canonical signal for allocating the fresh run. It occurs immediately for a train without a live run, or after Action commits a held replacement.
- **Start-mode stash timing.** A per-assignment start-mode input stays beside a held replacement in `_pending_route_assignments`. It moves to `RouteExecutor._pending_start_overrides[train_id]` only when the stored route assignment commits, then Plan step `9c4f` consumes it (see **Run start-mode seeding**).

**Route edit timestamps**

`Route.created_at` is sampled exactly once via `time.time()` inside `Route.__post_init__`. No other writer touches it.

`Route.activate()` is the canonical route-activation entry, symmetric with the route-deactivation service. It validates, writes `is_active = True`, and samples `started_at`; it refuses while an assigned train holds `pending_route_deactivate`. The activate/deactivate handlers call their request services and map the result.

`Route.last_edited_at` is sampled via `time.time()` only by request services that mutate the route definition. The set of fields whose mutation bumps it is exactly: `name`, `tasks`, `mode`, `priority`, `acquisition_mode`, and `manual_override`. `Route.start_mode` and `Route.start_task_index` are editable but do not bump it — they are consulted only when a fresh run is allocated (see **Run start-mode seeding**), so an edit there changes nothing already recorded. `Route.timing_basis` has no request-service edit path in v1 (it is set only by full-snapshot load), so it never bumps it either. Lifecycle and assignment fields do not bump it.

The canonical route-definition edit entry points are:

- `POST /api/train-routes` — its service writes `last_edited_at = time.time()` once when at least one edit field is supplied. A bare create leaves it `None`.
- `PUT /api/train-routes/<route_id>` — its service writes `last_edited_at` once only when an edit field actually changed. Assignment-only requests do not bump it.

`Route.priority`, `Route.acquisition_mode`, and `Route.manual_override` edits bump `last_edited_at` even though they do not trigger the structural-edit teardown described in **Route Edit And Reconciliation**: `last_edited_at` records the time of the last definition write, not the time of the last structural change. Of these, `priority` and `acquisition_mode` are the v1 RouteRun override allowlist (`manual_override` is route-level only, not per-run overridable) — see **RouteRun overrides** for the per-field push semantics that distribute later edits to existing runs. UI/log consumers that need to distinguish structural from non-structural edits cannot do so from `last_edited_at` alone in v1; they observe the teardown side effects instead.

**Canonical ownership split**

- `Route` is the shared plan definition only: ordered tasks plus route-level policy such as mode and acquisition mode. It does not own per-train mutable execution cursors.
- A route may be assigned to multiple trains in v1, but each train may run at most one route task at a time. Each assigned train has at most one `RUNNING` `RouteRun` at a time; the live read is `RouteExecutor.execution_state_for(train_id)` (computed by searching the registry for the `RUNNING` `RouteRun`). Historical `RouteRun` rows for the same train (state `FINISHED` or `DEACTIVATED`) are kept indefinitely in `RouteExecutor._historical_runs` as a parallel history; only the active-state predicate is single-instance. The run's `route_id` identifies which shared `Route` definition that train is currently following. That `RouteRun` is the per-train runtime instance of the shared plan, and it owns only per-train mutable execution state: the task cursor, the current traversal direction, per-task timing and resolved-target state (`task_runs`), route-version reconciliation state, and the current route status. Shared route execution state across trains is not allowed.
- `Route` is live shared execution input in v1, not a snapshot source that is copied into each run. Active runs read the current shared `Route` through `RouteRun.route_id`, and later structural route edits immediately latch teardown of every assigned train's currently-`RUNNING` `RouteRun` (each committed in that train's later Action once the train has stopped, per the stopped-train gating in **Action latched-cancel consumption**), followed by fresh `RouteRun` allocation; see **Route Edit And Reconciliation**.
- In helper prose below, when an active-run helper still shows a `route` parameter, read that as the current shared `Route` resolved from `RouteRun.route_id` unless the paragraph explicitly says a new dedicated route assignment is being created.
- Because multi-train assignment is supported, `RouteRun` is the only canonical runtime progress store. `Route` carries no runtime progress fields; consumers read per-train progress from each `RouteRun` (a route-level progress summary is out of scope — see the **Out of Scope** table).
- Per-train route/path errors are emitted as error events with `kind = "warning"` and `ErrorRecord.origin = "planning_failed"` per **Error events**; neither `Route` nor `RouteRun` keeps a stored error summary in v1.
- Departure is not a route-level policy in v1. Plan writes `phase_latches.departure_request` on every eligible Plan pass with live authority for the current target; the ATO-vs-manual behavioral difference is owned inside that call per the **`TrainController.depart()` canonical contract**. The driver in manual mode sees that depart has been accepted (state == `RUNNING_MOVING`) and starts moving the train; there is no separate operator-confirmation button.
- `acquisition_mode` at route level is the policy for how this route wants dispatcher authority to be acquired (`all_or_nothing` or `best_effort`), with default `AcquisitionMode.best_effort` when the route definition omits it. `RouteExecutor` reads `RouteRun.effective_acquisition_mode(route_registry)` (the override-aware read of the shared `Route.acquisition_mode`; see **RouteRun overrides**) for both `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` and later `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` retries on the same planning chain.
- `priority` at route level is the canonical route-executor scheduling priority, with default `5`. Priority values are integers in `0..9`, where `9` is highest and `0` is lowest. `RouteExecutor` sorts runnable route runs by `RouteRun.effective_priority(route_registry)` (the override-aware read; see **RouteRun overrides**); later shared-route edits and per-run overrides may therefore legitimately reshuffle later tick order for active runs. Trains with no current `RouteRun` use effective priority `5` when `SimulationController` merges them into the per-tick runnable-train order.
- `ResolvedRouteTarget` carries exactly `requested_destination_block_id` and `requested_destination_direction`.
  - **Direction is block-relative.** `requested_destination_direction` is always the block-relative direction for `requested_destination_block_id`. `Platform` has no direction field, no platform-frame direction, and no direction-conversion helper in v1.
  - **Platform/station resolution.** `PlatformTarget` and `StationTarget` resolution chooses a concrete platform-end block, then derives the resolved direction from `Block.ordered_tiles`. It validates that direction against `Block.allowed_travel_directions` unless the run's route stores `Route.manual_override = True`, then stores that block-relative result.
  - **No persistent cache.** There is no persistent per-task resolved-target cache outside `task_runs`. Every route-side attempt that arms a new target block resolves a transient candidate live — from the current shared `Route`, current platform availability, train span, and task policy — via `_find_next_task_target(train_id)`. While the same target block stays armed, Plan reuses the stored `resolved_target` pair instead of resolving again, per **Live-path target re-resolution**. The helper is read-only over existing rows and returns one candidate per call; its `after_walk_position` form may append exactly the next directed-walk row when lookahead extends beyond the current `task_runs` tail, but it never changes an existing row's `resolved_target` or `RouteRun.direction`.
  - **Canonical writer.** Plan's authority-acquisition step is the only canonical writer of `RouteRun.task_runs[i].resolved_target`, after a successful `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` / `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` for that candidate.
