  - **Candidate count by target kind.** For a `StationTarget` task, `_find_next_task_target` returns one candidate per call, and Plan retries with successive candidates by re-invoking the helper after a failed `create_path(...)` attempt within the same tick. A failed `extend_path(...)` with `failure_kind == no_viable_path` does not enter this candidate loop; it follows the **Structural failure_kind rule** and stops planning after latching cancellation. A `PlatformTarget` or `BlockTarget` task has only one candidate per tick.
  - **Dispatcher contract vs. route record.** If a path request succeeds, the accepted `(requested_destination_block_id, requested_destination_direction)` pair is returned in the create/extend result and recorded once on `RouteRun.task_runs[i].resolved_target`. The `Path` record stores only `resource_sequence`; the live authority end is read through `Path.get_authority_end_block_id()`. See **Path field schema**.
  - **Operator edits don't rewrite a live segment.** Operator/admin edits to platform/block target-resolution inputs (for example platform block membership/order, `Block.disabled` / `Block.manual` toggles, `Platform.disabled` / `Platform.manual` / `Station.disabled` / `Station.manual` toggles, or `Block.allowed_travel_directions` changes) do not rewrite an already-successful live segment. They take effect the next time Plan commits a new successful create/extend attempt.

**Canonical Next-Target Selection**

- **`ResolvedNextTaskProjection` schema.** The return type of `_find_next_task_target(train_id, exclude=None, after_walk_position=None)` is `Optional[ResolvedNextTaskProjection]`. The optional `exclude` argument is a caller-owned set of already-attempted `ResolvedRouteTarget` values for the current planning problem; the helper itself stores no per-tick state. The optional `after_walk_position` argument returns the first non-finished walk-position strictly after that index on the directed walk. When that position would be exactly one row beyond the current tail, this form calls `RouteRun._append_next_walk_task(from_walk_position=after_walk_position)` once to append exactly that next directed-walk row; it never appends more than one row per call. This is how the **Waypoint lookahead** in step `66aa` reaches past the task the train is physically working on. `None` (the default) returns the next non-finished walk-position and never appends for lookahead. `None` means no next task on the current directed walk (terminal). Otherwise the projection carries:

  | Field | Type | Meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `walk_position` | `int` | Walk-position index in `RouteRun.task_runs` of the next non-finished walk-position on the directed walk. The underlying `RouteTask` is `Route.tasks[task_runs[walk_position].task_index]`. |
  | `task_kind` | `"waypoint" \| "stop" \| "dwell" \| "run"` | The task's kind, copied from the underlying `RouteTask.task_kind` for caller convenience. |
  | `direction` | `"forward" \| "reverse"` | The route walk direction at this task (may have flipped at a `ROUND_TRIP` reflection). |
  | `resolved_target` | `Optional[ResolvedRouteTarget]` | The resolved block + direction for `waypoint`, `stop`, and `run` tasks (for `run`, only the direction seed). `None` for `dwell` tasks and for tasks whose target cannot be resolved in the current attempt. |
  | `failure_kind` | `Optional[TargetResolutionFailureKind]` | Why resolution produced no target; set exactly when the task cannot be served. `missing_target` when the `task_location` ID (block, platform, or station) is not present in the network — a **broken** task; this applies to every `task_kind`, including `dwell` (a dwell names a location too, and a dwell whose location is gone is broken exactly like its paired stop). `target_unavailable` when the target is present but cannot resolve to a usable block this tick (`disabled`, or `manual` under the run's `Route.manual_override = False`, or a `StationTarget`'s platforms are all filtered or held); never set for `dwell` tasks (they carry no dispatcher target to acquire). `None` for a `dwell` task whose `task_location` is present and whenever `resolved_target` is present. Drives the broken-vs-unreachable split in **Unreachable and broken task handling**. |
  | `failure_reason` | `Optional[str]` | Human-readable diagnostic that accompanies `failure_kind` when `resolved_target is None` for a non-dwell task (e.g. `"Block <block_id> is set to manual"`, `"all platforms in station <station_id> are disabled or manual"`, `"every candidate for <station_id> already attempted this tick"`). Plan carries it straight into the `ErrorRecord.text` of the error event it emits (see **Error events**) so the operator sees why the task is stalled instead of an empty diagnostic. `None` for dwell projections, which need no resolver-level error string. It is the prose counterpart to the structured `failure_kind`; consumers branch on `failure_kind`, not on this string. |

  The helper is **read-only over existing rows**: it never writes any existing `task_runs[walk_position].resolved_target`, never changes any other field of an existing `RouteTaskRun`, and never changes `RouteRun.direction`. Its one permitted `RouteRun` side effect is the single-row append described above when the `after_walk_position` branch needs the next directed-walk row beyond the current tail. The canonical writer of an existing `task_runs[walk_position].resolved_target` is Plan's authority-acquisition step, after a successful `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` / `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` for that task. All callers other than the lookahead form consume the helper's return value without changing `RouteRun` storage.

  `TargetResolutionFailureKind` has v1 values `missing_target` (the `task_location` ID — block, platform, or station — is not present in the network; applies to all task kinds, including `dwell`) and `target_unavailable` (the target is present but cannot resolve to a usable block this tick: it is `disabled`, or `manual` under the run's `Route.manual_override = False`, or a `StationTarget`'s platforms are all filtered or held by other trains; never set for `dwell`). It classifies target *resolution* failures only; a target that resolves but whose authority cannot be acquired is classified by `PathAcquisitionFailureKind` instead and is always treated as unreachable, never broken. See **Unreachable and broken task handling**.

- **`CompletionTaskProjection` schema.** `RouteExecutor.find_next_completion_task(train_id) -> Optional[CompletionTaskProjection]` is the public read used only by `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path()`. It returns the lowest non-finished walk-position without appending or resolving a new target. The projection carries `walk_position`, `task_index`, `task_kind = Route.tasks[task_index].task_kind`, and `stored_resolved_target = task_runs[walk_position].resolved_target`. It returns `None` when no `RUNNING` run or no unfinished row exists. `PathDispatcher` never indexes route storage itself.
- **`ArmedTaskProjection` schema.** `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id) -> Optional[ArmedTaskProjection]` is the public derived read for the task whose target the live authority was most recently acquired toward. It requires a `RUNNING` run and active dispatcher path, then selects the greatest non-finished walk-position whose `resolved_target` is non-`None`; append-only walk order and step `66aa` (Authority acquisition)'s single writer make that the most recently acquired row, including a waypoint-lookahead row ahead of the physically served task. It carries `walk_position`, `task_index`, `task_kind`, and `stored_resolved_target`. It never resolves, appends, or writes. It returns `None` when there is no live authority or no acquired row.
- **Separate cursor model.** `RouteExecutor._find_next_task_target()` resolves the next planning candidate, `RouteExecutor.find_next_completion_task()` identifies the next physical task eligible for stop completion, and `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task()` identifies the acquired authority target. `RouteRun.current_waypoint_index` remains only the derived physical-progress cursor. Callers use the named projection matching their question; none derives an armed row through raw index arithmetic.
- `RouteExecutor._find_next_task_target(train_id)` is read-only with respect to existing `RouteRun` rows. It reads the projected row's `walk_direction` — including the `ROUND_TRIP` group reflection — and reports it in the projection, but never writes `RouteRun.direction`; Plan commits that value after successful authority acquisition (see **Route-run state**, the `direction` row). Only `RouteExecutor._find_next_task_target(..., after_walk_position=...)` may grow storage, by appending exactly the next directed-walk row when the requested projection lies one row beyond the current tail.
- For a station task with multiple compatible platform-end candidates on the current tick, `_find_next_task_target(train_id, exclude=...)` picks one candidate per call. The helper itself does not maintain any per-tick state: the caller (Plan's per-tick retry loop) owns the `exclude` set of already-attempted resolved targets for this planning problem and passes it on each call. The helper enumerates the current candidate ordering, skips any candidate present in `exclude`, and returns the next untried one. When every candidate has already been attempted this tick, the helper returns the ordinary `ResolvedNextTaskProjection` for that walk-position with `resolved_target = None` and `failure_kind = target_unavailable` — the same shape and failure kind as any other same-tick resolution failure — never `None`, because a next task still exists on the walk (see the failure-shape rule below). For a `PlatformTarget` or `BlockTarget` task, only one candidate exists per tick. Callers other than Plan's authority-acquisition retry loop — for example the Plan dwell-complete step, steps `c481` (Look up the next non-finished task) / `592a` (Re-resolve the next target), and the Observe head-advance callback — pass `exclude=None` and receive the first candidate under the canonical ordering; that candidate is deterministic for the same shared `Route` + physical-progress + platform-availability inputs.
- **Terminal-walk rule.** When `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` returns no next task on the current directed walk, the current walk is terminal.
  - **Live path still exists.** This is reachable only when every remaining task was broken-skipped, per **Unreachable and broken task handling**. Plan latches the ordinary cancel instead of finishing the run and returns for the tick. A later eligible Plan pass, once that cancel has committed and no live path remains, reaches this same check again.
  - **No live path exists.** Plan calls `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)` directly inside `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)`, which sets `current_route_status = FINISHED` (`RouteExecutor.assigned_route_id_for(train_id)` automatically returns `None`) and, for `RouteMode.ONE_OFF` routes whose unassign left no assigned trains, calls `Route.deactivate()`, which sets `Route.is_active = False` with nothing to latch. The `RouteRun` is preserved as a historical `FINISHED` row in the run history (`RouteExecutor._historical_runs`). Plan then returns for that tick. In the ordinary case the matching live path has already been cleared by stop-completion in the prior Observe batch, so `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(...)` itself needs no new dispatcher cancel.
  - **`CIRCULAR` / `ROUND_TRIP` exemption.** For `RouteMode.CIRCULAR` and `RouteMode.ROUND_TRIP`, `_find_next_task_target` never returns `None` — it wraps or reflects instead — so this terminal-walk branch never fires for those modes.
  - **All-broken cyclic walk.** When every task on a `CIRCULAR` / `ROUND_TRIP` walk is broken, the run does not finish — it holds in the no-reachable-task stall instead (see **Unreachable and broken task handling**), gated the same way on no live path remaining.
- **Failure-shape rule.** If a next task exists but no legal concrete platform/block target can be resolved under the task's targeting policy on this attempt — including the retry loop exhausting every same-tick `exclude` candidate — the helper returns a `ResolvedNextTaskProjection` whose `walk_position`, `task_kind`, and `direction` describe that walk-position and whose `resolved_target` is `None`. The helper returns overall `None` only for the terminal-walk condition (the `RouteMode.ONE_OFF` terminal case defined in the **Terminal-walk rule** above); a next task existing on the walk always produces a projection, never a bare `None`. If no live authority exists and Plan has exhausted all same-tick candidates, Plan stops for that train for that tick. If live authority exists, leave the live path and route status unchanged unless a later `extend_path(...)` result proves structural incompatibility.
- Callers must not rewrite `direction` or `task_runs[i].resolved_target` through raw increment/decrement index arithmetic or by indexing `Route.tasks` outside the helper. Next-task selection comes from `_find_next_task_target(...)`; committed progress advances through the head-advance callback recording `finished_at`, through Plan dwell-complete step recording `finished_at`, and through Plan's covered-task index advance for already-passed `waypoint` tasks and covered stopped-at-destination `stop` tasks.
- `Route.mode` is consumed when the directed walk grows through `RouteRun._append_next_walk_task(from_walk_position)`:
  - `RouteMode.ONE_OFF`: if no next task exists, return `None` (terminal).
  - `RouteMode.CIRCULAR`: wrap from the last task to the first task.
  - `RouteMode.ROUND_TRIP`: reflect task groups at the route ends and flip `walk_direction` when moving to the next group after an end.
- A **task group** is one non-`dwell` task followed by all of its contiguous `dwell` rows. Reflection changes group order, never row order inside a group. For groups `[A, B, C]`, the walk is `A forward → B forward → C forward → B reverse → A reverse → B forward`; the apex group is not repeated. If `B` is `[B(stop), dwell(B)]`, both rows run in that order on both visits.

**RouteTask data**

Retained current-code enums used by route data:

- `RouteMode`: `ONE_OFF`, `CIRCULAR`, `ROUND_TRIP`

`RouteTask` is the unified route-task schema in v1. Every entry in `Route.tasks` is a `RouteTask`.

| Field | Type | Applies | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `task_kind` | `"waypoint" \| "stop" \| "dwell" \| "run"` | all | Required task behavior discriminator. `waypoint` is a pass-through traversal (no stop, no dwell). `stop` is a platform stop that is served by the **Stop-arrival check**. `dwell` is a hold at a location after a stop. `run` is a timed roll: the train departs and keeps rolling while authority permits for `task_time` simulated seconds, then the controller applies the canonical service-stop command and brings it to a smooth stop wherever it is (position-agnostic) — its `task_location` is only a direction seed, never an arrival target. A run whose seed block sits close to the departure point stops there and waits out the remaining timer under the **Authority termination rule**, the same as any other authority-end stop. |
| `task_location` | `BlockTarget \| PlatformTarget \| StationTarget` (tagged union) | all | The concrete target for this task. `BlockTarget(block_id: str)` for direct block targets, `PlatformTarget(platform_id: str)` for fixed concrete platforms, `StationTarget(station_id: str)` for logical stations resolved at runtime. The tagged union enforces that exactly one targeting mode is present. For a `run` task it names the block the train heads toward while rolling; the run ends on its timer, not on reaching it. |
| `task_time` | `Optional[float]` | all | Semantics depend on `task_kind`. For `waypoint`/`stop`: expected travel time in seconds from the previous task's location to this task's location; used to classify arrival as early/on-time/late when the `RouteTaskRun` timing data is available; omit when no timing classification is needed. For `run`: required finite duration greater than `0`, in seconds of **simulated** time, measured by `RouteTaskRun.run_elapsed_seconds` as accumulated per-tick `delta_seconds` while the run is the active task and its direction-seed target resolves to a present usable target on that Plan pass (not wall-clock). For `dwell`: how long in seconds to remain at the location; omit to allow departure immediately. |
| `task_direction` | `Optional["forward" \| "reverse" \| "either"]` | all | Route-level block-relative traversal preference. `RouteExecutor` resolves `"either"` to a concrete direction before any dispatcher call; the dispatcher never receives `"either"`. Defaults to `"either"` when omitted. |
| `target_time` | `Optional[float]` | `waypoint`, `stop`, `dwell` | Optional absolute wall-clock Unix timestamp. For `waypoint` / `stop` it is the expected arrival time, informational (schedule-adherence / ETA classification) and gates nothing. For `dwell` it is the scheduled **departure** time: the dwell holds until it and departs at it, so an early arrival waits for the schedule and a late arrival departs on arrival (see **Task time semantics**). A `dwell` row carrying a `target_time` does not read its own `task_time`. It is read in wall time whatever the route's `timing_basis` is, because an absolute instant does not move when the session is stopped. A `run` task must omit `target_time`; its only clock is its simulated-time accumulator. |

Route-task authoring rules:

- A typical platform stop with a hold is authored as two consecutive tasks: `stop(task_location=PlatformTarget(platform_X), task_time=expected_travel_seconds)` followed by `dwell(task_location=PlatformTarget(platform_X), task_time=hold_seconds)`. The `stop` is served by the **Stop-arrival check**; the `dwell` holds the train in `RUNNING_AT_STATION` until the dwell timer elapses.
- A terminal stop with no hold is authored as a single `stop` task with no following `dwell` task. A missing `dwell` task is the correct encoding.
- A pass-through is a single `waypoint` task. It resolves to a concrete `ResolvedRouteTarget` for authority planning, is completed by head entry into the resolved block, and does not invoke dwell logic or `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()`.
- `task_kind` is required. Missing, null, or unrecognized `task_kind` is a validation error at task creation time; `RouteExecutor` must never infer a default kind.
- A terminal task must not be `waypoint`. If the train must stop and reverse immediately with no dwell, the terminal task is `stop`. A `run` may be a terminal task: it brings the train to rest at its timed smooth stop.
- For target resolution and path acquisition, `waypoint` and `stop` tasks use the same resolution chain and the same dispatcher target contract. Both resolve to a `ResolvedRouteTarget` for authority planning. The behavioral difference: a `stop` arrival is decided by the **Stop-arrival check**, and the route's `RouteTaskRun` records `finished_at` at that arrival; a `waypoint` is completed by head entry with no stop, no dwell, and no `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()`.
- A `dwell` task does not create or require new dispatcher authority. While a `dwell` task is the current active task, Plan does not create or extend authority. The `dwell` task is complete when `RouteTask.should_depart(...)` is satisfied per **Task time semantics**, at which point the Plan dwell-complete step inside `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` sets `finished_at`, writes `station_exit_request`, and returns for that train; the Action station-exit consumer performs `TrainController.finish_dwell()`, and step `c481` resolves the next task on the next eligible Plan.
- **`run` task lifecycle.** A `run` task keeps the train rolling while authority permits for `task_time` simulated seconds and then finishes at a smooth stop.
  - **Timer.** While a `run` is the active task, its direction-seed target resolves to a present usable target on this Plan pass, and `RouteTaskRun.run_elapsed_seconds < task_time`, Plan step `6a0d` adds this tick's `delta_seconds` to that task-run field and acquires or extends authority toward the run's `task_location` exactly as for a `waypoint`; the run never completes on arrival at that block, because it is only a direction seed. A missing or currently unavailable seed pauses accrual for that pass and follows the ordinary broken/unreachable handling. Authority still terminates at the seed block per the **Authority termination rule**, so a run whose seed block sits near the departure point stops there and waits out the remaining timer rather than continuing to roll.
  - **Service stop.** When the timer elapses, step `6a0d` sets the `ops.service_stop_active` latch through `TrainController.begin_service_stop()` — the controller-level operational deceleration command, never an emergency cut, and valid in both ATO and manual control — then writes `pending_path_cancel_request` with `run_complete = True` (with `error = None` and `kind = "info"`, per the `pending_path_cancel_request` payload contract) when live authority exists. The ordinary stopped-train cancel gate releases that authority without setting `RouteRun.path_cancelled` or projecting `display_state == "CANCELLED"`.
  - **Finish.** Only after the train is stopped, the release request has been consumed, and `received_path_plan is None` does step `6a0d` consume the latch through `TrainController.consume_service_stop()` and call `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(...)` to set `finished_at` and advance the walk; it then returns so the next task (typically a `dwell`) starts on a later Plan.

  Where the train comes to rest is not part of the contract; a `run` that must hold after stopping is authored as a `run` followed by a `dwell`.
- Station/platform distinction is explicit:
  - `Station` is a logical grouping of platforms used by route planning and platform selection.
  - `Platform` is the concrete physical stop. When a waypoint's task_location is a `PlatformTarget` or `StationTarget`, dispatcher path requests, block IDs, and directions are always derived from one resolved concrete platform, never from a station group directly.
  - The current attempt may resolve one concrete `platform_id` when resolution goes through a platform. For a `BlockTarget` waypoint, no platform resolution is needed.
- `Platform.ordered_segments(network)` is the derived ordered list of segment IDs in the platform — computed from the platform's stored tiles through the segment reverse index — used to identify the two platform-end segments (and, through the segment -> block reverse index, their owning blocks) and preserve edit stability. `Platform` carries no direction, no platform-local forward/reverse semantics, no per-segment alignment mapping, and no user-facing directional option. A platform is created and edited from tiles: backend platform-creation/edit logic validates that the tiles form one connected switch-free run of matching orientation, growing and shrinking only at the ends, and `ordered_segments(network)` follows from those tiles — so a mid-platform segment split shows up as its child segments with no membership edit. Removing a platform's last tile — its last segment — deletes the platform rather than leaving it empty, per the **Non-empty parent rule** under **Tile**.
- `Platform` carries no direction or platform-side helper. To make a platform serve only one direction, the user must configure the underlying end block's `Block.allowed_travel_directions` so only that traversal is allowed.
- `requested_destination_direction` is the resolved traversal constraint at the requested target.
  - **Route-authored input is block-relative.** Task authors express the route-level preference as `forward`, `reverse`, or `either` on `RouteTask.task_direction`; those values are block-relative preferences, not platform-relative ones. By the time `RouteExecutor` builds `ResolvedRouteTarget`, it must have resolved that preference into one concrete block-relative `"forward"` or `"reverse"` for the chosen `requested_destination_block_id`.
  - **Platform-resolved filtering.** For a task that resolves through a concrete platform, the canonical candidate comparison defined in **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload**, applied by the platform resolution subsection below, evaluates terminal traversals through the platform end block(s):
    - when `task_direction == "forward"` or `"reverse"`, it filters out candidates whose terminal traversal does not match that authored block-relative direction, or is not allowed by `Block.allowed_travel_directions`;
    - when `task_direction == "either"`, it applies no route-authored direction filter, but every candidate must still satisfy `Block.allowed_travel_directions`, and `RouteExecutor` still stores the chosen block-relative concrete direction.
  - **BlockTarget resolution.** When the task_location is a `BlockTarget`, `"forward"` / `"reverse"` are read directly in that block's immutable internal traversal order, and `"either"` means `RouteExecutor` picks whichever block-relative direction is reachable under the same current-span comparison and allowed by `Block.allowed_travel_directions`.
  - **`manual_override` relaxation.** When the run's route stores `Route.manual_override = True`, `RouteExecutor` skips every `Block.allowed_travel_directions` check named above, per the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags** canonical home. The route-authored `task_direction` filter still applies.
  - **Dispatcher never sees `"either"`.** The dispatcher never receives `"either"` in the v1 path contract; route resolution must always eliminate it before calling `create_path(...)` or `extend_path(...)`. `RouteTask.task_direction` (the route-author input, which may be `"either"`) and `ResolvedRouteTarget.requested_destination_direction` (the strict subtype `"forward" | "reverse"` passed to the dispatcher) are deliberately two distinct types. Implementations must reflect this difference in their static types, so that handing an unresolved `RouteTask.task_direction` to `PathDispatcher.create_path()` / `PathDispatcher.extend_path()` is a type error rather than a runtime branch.
- Define the exact dispatcher terminal frame separately. The terminal frame is the explicit directed geometry used for controller braking and diagnostics: `path_tiles`, `entry_edge`, and `exit_edge` for the relevant terminal block. When a live path exists, dispatcher derives that frame from the chosen terminal `resource_sequence` block entry. Boundary/safety-margin projection must never infer that frame from `requested_destination_direction` alone.
- Resolve waypoint targets through one canonical chain: `station -> platform -> block`. If the task_location is a `PlatformTarget`, resolution starts at `platform`. If it is a `BlockTarget`, resolution skips station/platform lookup and targets that block directly.
- When a task_location is a `StationTarget` rather than a `PlatformTarget`, `RouteExecutor` must resolve one concrete platform before path creation. In v1, platform availability is evaluated relative to the train for this route attempt. A platform is unavailable when any linked block is held by another train's physical occupancy or another train/path's live reservation. `CAUTION` by itself does not make a platform unavailable: a caution block may still be reserved/acquired when ordinary reservation rules allow it, and the caution state is consumed by `TrainController` lookahead as a lower ATC speed cap. The current train's own physical occupancy or current live authority must not make that platform unavailable to itself; same-train coverage is handled by Plan's covered-task index advance and same-train path conflicts are handled by the shared pathfinder/acquisition rules. Deterministic tie-breaking is required and follows the canonical candidate-order rule below.
- Platform/station target selection in v1 is:
  - if the task_location is a `PlatformTarget`, resolve exactly that platform for this tick. For a new path, pick its single best compatible platform-end candidate by the canonical graph comparison. If that `create_path(...)` attempt fails, wait until the next eligible tick. Once a live path exists, every retry uses its armed `stored_resolved_target` and calls only `extend_path(...)`; it does not reconsider another platform end.
  - if the task_location is a `StationTarget` and no live path exists, build the complete ordered transient candidate list of all compatible available platform-end candidates across every platform in `Station.platform_ids`, sorted by the cross-query comparison defined in the **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload** home: estimated travel time first when the run's train max speed is supplied, then `tile_count`, then `walk_length_cm`, with ties broken by platform-end identity (deterministic iteration order over `Station.platform_ids`) rather than by `candidate_rank`, since these candidates come from separate per-platform-end queries. In that same Plan pass, `RouteExecutor` may try `create_path(...)` once for each distinct resolved `(requested_destination_block_id, requested_destination_direction)` pair, stopping at the first success. Once one create succeeds, that pair is armed; later ticks call only `extend_path(...)` for the stored pair and never try another station candidate while that path remains live.
  - if the task_location is a `BlockTarget`, resolve exactly that block/direction for this tick. If the create/extend attempt fails without creating or growing authority, wait until the next eligible tick rather than inventing alternatives.
- A waypoint that wants "try any platform in this station" must use a `StationTarget`; a waypoint that uses a `PlatformTarget` targets that one concrete platform.
- Station candidate enumeration preserves the route-specified `requested_direction` literally as a block-relative traversal preference. If the waypoint specified `forward` or `reverse`, candidate platform ends are compatible only when their terminal traversal satisfies that direction under the candidate block's `Block.allowed_travel_directions`. If the waypoint specified `either` (or omitted the field, which is treated as `either`), any `Block.allowed_travel_directions`-compatible terminal traversal may be used. The `Block.allowed_travel_directions` half of that compatibility test is skipped when the run's route stores `Route.manual_override = True`, per the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags** canonical home.
- Later retries re-enumerate platform/station candidates only when no live path exists. A live path freezes the armed pair until completion or cancellation; an unavailable stored target is handled by the live-path target re-resolution cancellation flow, never by silently extending toward another platform. If no concrete platform/block candidate can be resolved for a create retry, target resolution fails for that tick.
- For covered normalization and subsequent task service on the current directed route walk, a `PlatformTarget` or `StationTarget` task with `task_kind == "waypoint"` counts as satisfied when the train covers any compatible concrete platform in that task's allowed platform set; a `PlatformTarget` or `StationTarget` task with `task_kind == "stop"` counts as satisfied when the Observe stop-arrival procedure commits that stop through `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(...)`. A following dwell is an independent task and has no bearing on whether the stop row is finished. When either satisfaction rule applies, `RouteExecutor` uses the actually covered or served compatible block/platform only to decide satisfaction and to report diagnostics; it must not force resolution to some other platform or store a second served-platform choice.
- For each concrete platform being considered, `RouteExecutor` resolves the terminal candidate end blocks and picks among them.
  - **Gathering candidate end blocks.** `RouteExecutor` gathers the terminal candidate block at each end of that platform by calling the same shared network-graph walk query that `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` uses, passing the run's `Route.manual_override` as the query's `manual_override` field. For a multi-segment platform, the candidate end blocks are the blocks owning the first and last segments of `Platform.ordered_segments` (through the segment -> block reverse index); for a platform whose segments all lie in one block, both platform ends collapse to that one block, so only it participates.
  - **Which train ends participate.** If a cab is selected, only the current head-side start locator participates in this stop-planning comparison. If no cab is selected, both physical train ends may participate: a switch-side end is first mapped inward to the occupied block at that end of the current span, and is dropped from the comparison set when no such inward occupied block exists.
  - **Direction filter.** Each candidate graph-query result carries the terminal block-relative direction derived from the canonical block-direction helper through `Block.ordered_tiles`. That direction must pass the task direction filter, and must pass `Block.allowed_travel_directions` unless the run's route stores `Route.manual_override = True`.
  - **Selection.** For a `PlatformTarget` task, pick the best successful candidate using the canonical candidate comparison defined in **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload** (fastest when travel-time estimates are populated, shortest otherwise), applied across the remaining current-span end choices. For a `StationTarget` task, keep the full sorted list of compatible successful platform-end candidates as transient same-Plan retry state, and try each distinct resolved `(requested_destination_block_id, requested_destination_direction)` pair at most once in that pass.
  - **Outcome.** The chosen or currently attempted block becomes `requested_destination_block_id`, and the chosen block-relative direction becomes `requested_destination_direction`. This is how task-authored `"either"` is converted into one concrete `"forward"` or `"reverse"` for `PlatformTarget` and `StationTarget` tasks. When no candidate succeeds, the task attempt fails. The chosen/current candidate block is the dispatcher-facing target block for both `stop` and `waypoint` tasks that resolve through a `PlatformTarget` or `StationTarget` task_location.
- For a task-authored `task_direction == "forward"` or `"reverse"`, the same candidate comparison is used, but pairs whose resulting block-relative direction does not match the authored direction are dropped from the comparison before selection. For `task_direction == "either"`, no route-authored direction filter is applied and the best allowed candidate wins (fastest when travel-time estimates are populated, shortest otherwise).
- After resolution, `RouteExecutor` derives the per-attempt `ResolvedRouteTarget` (`requested_destination_block_id`, block-relative `requested_destination_direction`) for the current task and passes only that transient route-owned request contract into `PathDispatcher`. There is no platform-frame direction to convert. Plan's authority-acquisition step, after a successful `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` / `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` for that task, writes the `(requested_destination_block_id, requested_destination_direction)` pair that call returned into `RouteRun.task_runs[walk_position].resolved_target` — the dispatcher's return names the authority it actually holds, which is what later stop-completion lookup must match against, where `walk_position` is the index returned by the same Plan pass's `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` projection. `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` itself never writes that field. Callback-time code may call the helper to recompute live without disturbing `task_runs[i].resolved_target`; the stored value remains whatever Plan's last successful create/extend wrote and is the authoritative match key for later stop-completion lookup. Later planning retries call `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` again whenever Plan needs a fresh resolve, and Plan's next successful create/extend overwrites the bookkeeping value.
- A task with `task_kind == "stop"` may therefore use a `task_location` that is:
  - a `PlatformTarget`, or
  - a `StationTarget`, in which case `RouteExecutor` resolves a concrete `platform_id` for the current attempt before path creation, or
  - a `BlockTarget`, in which case no platform resolution is required.
- Direction compatibility depends only on block-level `Block.allowed_travel_directions` (relaxed by the run's `Route.manual_override`, per the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags** canonical home) plus current availability — there is no `required_platform_side` or platform-side direction helper.
- Route arrival for tasks with `task_kind == "stop"` uses explicit stop-policy data:
  - the resolved destination block for the task attempt
  - the block-relative traversal direction for that attempt
- Every per-attempt `ResolvedRouteTarget` carries an explicit route-owned traversal-constraint field, `requested_destination_direction`. Before path creation, `RouteExecutor` must resolve the task-authored `task_direction` into one concrete block-relative `"forward"` or `"reverse"` for `requested_destination_block_id` and store that value on `ResolvedRouteTarget`. Dispatcher still derives the exact terminal frame from explicit terminal geometry, but it does so after route resolution has already eliminated `"either"` from the request contract.
- If the task_location is a `StationTarget` or `PlatformTarget`, `requested_destination_block_id` is resolved only after `RouteExecutor` has picked a concrete platform for that train's current attempt and then applied the canonical shorter-path platform-end selection rule above. If the task_location is a `BlockTarget`, that block becomes `requested_destination_block_id` directly, but a disabled block is never a valid direct target, and a manual block is a valid direct target only when the run's route carries `Route.manual_override = True` (the forwarded override lets the dispatcher call accept it; with `manual_override = False` the resolution attempt fails). The same availability rule applies to platform/station resolution: `RouteExecutor` excludes any platform whose own `Platform.disabled` is `True` and every platform belonging to a station whose `Station.disabled` is `True`, and applies the same filter to `Platform.manual` / `Station.manual` unless the run's route carries `Route.manual_override = True`. See the **Platform And Station** availability flags and the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags** canonical home. In all cases, the stored `requested_destination_direction` is the block-relative direction for that resolved block; there is no raw platform-level direction token in the route definition or resolved runtime state.
- Do not define a separate stop-window tolerance or route-authored stop-position field in v1. The controller safety margin is used by controller lookahead and ATO braking to shape the train's stop, but route completion does not manually verify a centimeter tolerance around any route value.
- For tasks with `task_kind == "stop"`, task arrival is not simply "the train is in the task block", but it is also not gated by an exact-stop tolerance check in v1. A stop task enters dwell only after its arrival is committed — either by the **Stop-arrival check** against the live authority, or, for the head-anchored covered-stop case (train stopped, no active path, head in the destination block), Plan's covered-task index advance. The stop's own `finished_at` is recorded at that arrival through `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(...)`; the stop and any following `dwell` are independent rows (see **Task time semantics**), and the route as a whole completes only after that `dwell` task's timer elapses (or at the stop itself when no `dwell` follows). `task_kind == "waypoint"` is reached by train-head entry / physical pass of its resolved block. Controller deviation cases produce a `cancel_path` event with `deviation = true` and one `ErrorRecord` whose `origin` is `"out_of_sequence"` on the event payload.
- **Boundary-projection helper.** One shared helper, such as `RailwayNetwork.project_authority_boundary_delta(ordered_walk, head_locator, authority_end, safety_margin_cm) -> delta_cm`, is the single home for boundary projection.
  - **`ordered_walk`** is the live authority's ordered directed walk, in the same order the controller reads for progress. It is a required input because a directed walk may enter the same resource twice — a run that laps through a block carries that block at two steps — so a locator on its own does not name one place on the walk, and a closed lap would otherwise have two separations to choose between.
  - **`head_locator`** is a `GraphLocator` carrying `tile`, `edge`, and `distance_cm` for the live train head.
  - **`authority_end`** carries `block_id` and `terminal_frame: DirectedBlockFrame` (whose `path_tiles`, `entry_edge`, and `exit_edge` describe the directed terminal frame for the authority-end block).
  - **Return value.** The helper measures along `ordered_walk`, forward from the head's resolved occurrence on that walk, and returns the signed centimeter separation between the live train head and the safety-margin-adjusted authority boundary: positive means the train head is past the safety-margin boundary, negative means it is still short of it, and zero is on-target. The head's occurrence is the one the **Head-mapping rule** resolves for the live path, so this projection and the controller's reported `current_head_sequence_index` always describe the same physical position.
  - **Scope.** In v1 this helper is for braking/diagnostic projection only; it is not the authoritative path-completion gate, and `RouteExecutor` must not compare live train position against it itself.

**Task time semantics**

- Every stored route/task *absolute instant* is a wall-clock Unix second. A duration measures against the clock the route's `timing_basis` names, and an absolute instant is read in wall time under either basis (see **Clocks** under the **Units contract**). A route-run row may additionally carry the runtime-only `_operating` duration anchor beside its wall instant; that anchor is not itself an absolute instant.
- `RouteTask.target_time` is the *expected* time for a task: expected arrival for `waypoint` / `stop`, and the scheduled departure for `dwell`. On `waypoint` / `stop` it is informational only and gates nothing.
- `RouteTask.should_depart(now_wall, now_basis, dwell_started_at_basis)` is evaluated only on a `dwell` row. `dwell_started_at_basis` is the dwell row's `started_at_operating` under the `"operating"` basis and its `started_at` under `"realtime"`:
  - with `target_time` set: depart when `now_wall >= target_time`. An early arrival waits for the scheduled departure; a train arriving after it departs on arrival. `task_time` is not read on such a row, because the schedule already names the moment.
  - with `target_time` absent and `task_time` set: depart when `now_basis - dwell_started_at_basis >= task_time`.
  - with neither set: depart immediately.
- **A late train is not held for being late.** The schedule names when the train leaves. A hold served on top of an already-passed departure only adds the delay it was meant to absorb to every task after it.
- A `dwell` that must always stand for a fixed time regardless of the clock is authored with `task_time` and no `target_time`.
- A `stop` task is independent of its neighbors. It is completed at route-committed stop arrival through `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(...)` (which writes the stop's `finished_at` and advances the derived route-progress cursor). A `stop`'s own `target_time` is its expected arrival time and is informational only — a bare `stop` with no following `dwell` never holds for a time; a time-gated platform hold must be authored as `stop` followed by a `dwell` carrying `task_time` and/or `target_time`. A following `dwell` task (when present) is a separate row with its own `started_at` / `finished_at` lifecycle. `should_depart(...)` is only evaluated against `dwell` rows.
- A `run` task's timer is not evaluated by `RouteTask.should_depart(...)`. Its window is the stored `RouteTaskRun.run_elapsed_seconds`, incremented by Plan step `6a0d` from the playback-scaled `delta_seconds` only on a pass where the run is active and its direction-seed target resolves to a present usable target. When the window elapses, that step sets the `ops.service_stop_active` latch through `TrainController.begin_service_stop()`, waits for the stopped no-authority state, then consumes the latch through `TrainController.consume_service_stop()` and records the run's `finished_at` through `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(...)`; where it comes to rest is not part of the contract.

**Route-definition validation**

- A valid route definition must contain at least one non-`dwell` task (`waypoint`, `stop`, or `run`). A non-`CIRCULAR` route (`ONE_OFF` / `ROUND_TRIP`) must in addition contain at least one task that brings the train to rest — a `stop` or a `run` — and end in one (see the terminal rule below). Single-stop routes are valid for `ONE_OFF` (e.g. one-off reposition or single-destination delivery); the single stop is both the first and final stop. `ROUND_TRIP` routes are subject to the **`ROUND_TRIP` degenerate-route guard** below, which a single-stop route cannot satisfy. A `CIRCULAR` route never terminates, so it needs no stop at all: a waypoint-only `CIRCULAR` route runs the loop continuously.
- Consecutive stop tasks that resolve to the same concrete target are valid. Route validation must not reject or collapse them merely because their resolved `requested_destination_block_id` / `requested_destination_direction` pair is identical. At runtime the second stop is finished by Plan's covered-task index advance — the train is already stopped with its head in that destination block and no active path, so the covered-stop rule applies — and its following `dwell` row (when present) then runs the ordinary dwell-entry/dwell-exit steps.
- Every task must provide `task_kind` explicitly as `"waypoint"`, `"stop"`, `"dwell"`, or `"run"`. Missing `task_kind`, null `task_kind`, or any other value is a validation error at task creation/update time. A `run` additionally requires a finite `task_time > 0` and must omit `target_time`; route creation/update rejects a run that violates either rule.
- A route made only of `waypoint` tasks is invalid for `ONE_OFF` / `ROUND_TRIP` (they need a task that ends the run at rest). A waypoint-only `CIRCULAR` route is valid and runs the loop with no stop.
- A `CIRCULAR` route must contain at least two non-`dwell` tasks whose `task_location` values differ. A circular walk whose moves all name one location has nothing to travel between: when the walk wraps, the only way to serve the repeated task is authority back into the block the train's head already sits in, and `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` rejects a request whose destination is the train's current head block.
- **`ROUND_TRIP` degenerate-route guard.** A `ROUND_TRIP` route must contain at least two non-`dwell` tasks whose `task_location` values differ. A route with only one distinct `task_location` among its non-`dwell` tasks can never give the reflection rule in `RouteRun._append_next_walk_task(...)` (see **Route-run state**) two distinct locations to reflect between, so it has the same unservable-repeated-task problem as the `CIRCULAR` guard above, and the route editor/API rejects it at creation/update time for the same reason.
- `Route.tasks[0]` must not be a `dwell` task. A dwell is a hold after a preceding task at that location; with no predecessor on the initial walk there is nothing to hold after, so the route editor/API rejects a leading dwell at creation/update time.
- Every maximal sequence of `dwell` tasks must directly follow a `stop` or `run` task, and every dwell in that sequence must name the same `task_location` as that preceding stop/run. A `waypoint` never establishes a stopped, authority-free state and therefore may not be followed by dwell. Route creation/update rejects any sequence that violates this rule.
- **Terminal-task requirement.** For a `ONE_OFF` / `ROUND_TRIP` route, the stored `Route.tasks` list must end in a `stop` or a `run` (optionally followed by a `dwell` at that location) before a `RouteRun` may be created. Those modes must have a defined place for the run to come to rest. The route editor/API must validate that terminal requirement before sending the route to route-run activation.
- **`CIRCULAR` is exempt.** A `CIRCULAR` route never terminates, so its authored list may end in any task (including a `waypoint`, or a `run` followed by a `dwell`) and there is nothing to "complete" at a terminal task.
- **Completion for non-circular modes.** For the non-circular modes the terminal task sequence is part of the route: the route is not complete until any terminal `dwell` task's timer has elapsed, or the terminal `stop` / `run` has come to rest when no `dwell` follows it.
- **Canonical terminal shapes.** A terminal `stop` with no following `dwell` is the canonical "stop and end immediately" shape; a terminal `stop` followed by a `dwell` with `task_time > 0` or `target_time` is the canonical "end after holding at the platform" shape. Both are valid.
- A bulb loop or other turnaround that returns to the same stop must be modeled explicitly in the task list (for example `A(stop) -> bulb(waypoint) -> A(stop) -> dwell(A)`). `RouteMode.ROUND_TRIP` does not infer that geometry from one terminal stop.
- Every `task_kind == "stop"` task must identify a valid stop target through `task_location`: a `BlockTarget`, a `PlatformTarget`, or a `StationTarget` that can be resolved to a platform at runtime.
- `Route.priority` must be an integer in `0..9` (`9` highest, `0` lowest); out-of-range values are a route-definition validation error rejected at creation/update and at activation time, per the rule immediately below.
- `Route.activate()` and the route creation/update services must reject any route definition that violates these rules rather than trying to infer missing stop semantics at runtime; `RouteExecutor` never receives an invalid route definition to plan against.

**Unreachable and broken task handling**

This subsection is the canonical home for what Plan does when the current task on the directed walk cannot be served on a tick. Every Plan step that keys on this behavior refers back here by name. The handling depends on *why* the task could not be served, and the two causes have two different owning steps: a **broken** task is skipped by the target-lookup steps `c481` and `592a`, and an **unreachable** task is waited on by the authority-acquisition step `66aa`. `66aa` may also see a broken row directly through its own lookahead resolve (step `592a`'s and `c481`'s lookups are not the only callers of `_find_next_task_target(train_id)`) — when it does, it neither skips it nor waits on it: it leaves the currently armed authority unchanged for that tick and defers the skip to the next eligible `c481` / `592a` lookup, per the **Broken-task skip (lookahead form)** bullet in step `66aa`. It never calls `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` with a missing target. The two causes:

- **Broken task (missing target).** `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` returns a sentinel projection (`resolved_target is None`) with `failure_kind == missing_target`: the task's `task_location` names a `BlockTarget` / `PlatformTarget` / `StationTarget` whose ID is no longer present in the network — for example a `StationTarget` whose station was deleted when its last `Platform` was reassigned to another station (see the **Non-empty parent rule** under **Tile**). Waiting can never resolve a missing target, so a broken task is never waited on.
- **Unreachable task (target present, not usable now).** Either `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` returns a sentinel projection with `failure_kind == target_unavailable` (the target exists but is `disabled` / `manual`, or — for a `StationTarget` — every platform in `Station.platform_ids` is currently filtered or held by another train), or it returns a concrete `resolved_target` but `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` could not acquire any authority for it on this tick (a live `PathAcquisitionFailureKind`, either `blocked_before_target` or `no_viable_path`). In both cases the target still exists, so the condition may clear on a later tick. No `extend_path(...)` outcome is an unreachable-task wait case: while live authority exists the split is not consulted at all (see the bullet below), and an `extend_path(...)` failure on a live path is governed by the latch-cancellation rule in step `66aa`.
- **When each cause is decided.** The broken half is read straight off the projection `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` returns, so `failure_kind == missing_target` is known at lookup time and the step that made the lookup acts on it at once. The unreachable half is decided later: a `target_unavailable` sentinel is carried forward to step `66aa`, and an acquisition failure is known only after the canonical same-tick retry loop (the `_find_next_task_target(train_id, exclude=...)` retry defined in **`create_path()` flow** step 2) has tried every distinct candidate for the current planning problem without creating or growing live authority, and no live authority exists for the task. Neither half is consulted while live authority for the task still exists — including every `extend_path(...)` success that did not reach the target, where the path remains a valid prefix — or while planning has not yet run.
- **Unreachable task → wait.** Step `66aa` leaves the task armed, emits one error event with `kind = "warning"` and `origin = "planning_failed"` naming the train and the walk-position (per **Error events**), writes no `finished_at`, and does not move the route-progress cursor. The next eligible Plan tick reruns `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` against current conditions. This is the only behavior for an unreachable task; v1 has no per-route "skip instead of wait" option, and a `disabled` / `manual` target is held rather than skipped because it can be re-enabled.
- **Broken task → skip toward the next valid task.** Plan does not wait on a broken task. A task is **valid** when its `task_location` ID is present in the network (whether or not that target is currently available); a broken task is the only non-valid kind. The skip applies to every `task_kind` — `waypoint`, `stop`, `dwell`, and `run` alike — and is performed by whichever lookup step saw the sentinel: step `c481` for the task it looks up at the head of the pass, or step `592a` for a task the covered-task advance in step `a5c6` moved progress onto. Each performs the skip inline and then re-runs its own `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` call; neither hands a broken task on to a later step. The skipping step first checks whether the directed walk still contains any valid task: for `RouteMode.ONE_OFF` it scans the remaining tasks from the current `task_index` onward; for `RouteMode.CIRCULAR` / `RouteMode.ROUND_TRIP` it scans all of `Route.tasks`, because the walk cycles through them.
  - **If a valid task exists**, the skipping step skips the broken task: it samples system time and `AppState.operating_time` locally, writes the pair to `task_runs[walk_position].finished_at` / `finished_at_operating`, and calls `RouteRun._append_next_walk_task(from_walk_position=walk_position)` per the canonical append rule. It emits one diagnostic event with `kind = "warning"` and `origin = "task_skipped"` naming the train and the walk-position, with an `ErrorRecord.text` such as `task <walk_position> skipped: target <id> missing` (per **Error events**). Consecutive broken tasks are skipped this way until a valid task is reached, bounded at one full `len(Route.tasks)` scan per Plan pass, a budget steps `c481` and `592a` share. The same pass then carries on from the skipping step with that valid task in hand — a skip at `c481` runs on into steps `6a0d`–`66aa`, a skip at `592a` runs on into `66aa` — so a broken task costs no tick of its own, and the pass plans the valid task (or waits on it if it is unreachable). A skip writes both finishes, so a skipped task is never retried.
  - **If no valid task exists** (every task on the directed walk is broken):
    - For `RouteMode.ONE_OFF`, skipping the remaining tasks leaves the directed walk terminal, so the next eligible Plan sees `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` return `None`. Per the terminal-walk rule in step `592a`, when a live path still exists at that point — reachable when the last-armed task was a `waypoint` that head entry consumed without releasing authority — this pass latches the ordinary cancel instead of finishing the run, and `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)` runs on the later pass that finds no live path; the run ends `FINISHED` having served nothing only once that path is gone. Each broken-task skip already emits its own event, so neither `finish_route_run` nor the interposed cancel needs special-casing for this case.
    - For `RouteMode.CIRCULAR` / `RouteMode.ROUND_TRIP`, the walk never goes terminal, so the skipping step must not keep skipping and appending. When a live path still exists at that point, this pass latches the ordinary cancel the same way the `592a` terminal-walk branch does and returns without setting the flag; the write below happens on the later pass that finds no live path. Once no live path exists, it sets `RouteRun.no_reachable_task = True` (a direct write — not a latch), emits one error event with `kind = "warning"` and `origin = "run_stalled"` naming the train and the run on the `False -> True` transition (per **Error events**), and returns for that tick without arming authority. The train holds with no authority and sits idle, and the derived `display_state` projects `"STALLED"` (see **Route-run state**). The flag is cleared by the next Plan pass whose `c481` or `592a` lookup finds any valid task on the walk — for example after the missing station/platform is recreated — at which point ordinary planning resumes. `no_reachable_task` is never set for `RouteMode.ONE_OFF`.
- **`dwell` walk-positions.** A `dwell` walk-position is broken (and skipped) when its own `task_location` ID is missing from the network — the normal case alongside its paired stop, since the two share the location, so the same skip loop walks past both. The skip can only happen before dwell entry: a broken stop never reaches arrival, so its dwell is evaluated while still pending; once dwell entry has happened, the dwell-timer rules apply and this handling never interrupts an already-entered dwell. The machine-checkable guard both steps `c481` and `592a` test before broken-skipping a `dwell` row is its own stored `started_at`: the skip applies only while that field is unset (dwell entry per step `3a37` has not yet sampled and written it); once `started_at` is set, `c481` and `592a` leave that `dwell` row alone regardless of whether its `task_location` is still present, and it completes only through step `70c3`'s dwell-complete timer check. A dwell whose own location is present is valid and follows the ordinary dwell-entry rules.
- Terminal-walk handling is otherwise unchanged: `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` returning `None` is the only thing that drives `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)`, and for the reasons above that happens only for `RouteMode.ONE_OFF`.

**Route-run state**

This is the canonical field set for `RouteRun` in v1.

- **Storage split by lifecycle state.** Each train's currently-live run is held in `RouteExecutor.execution_states: Dict[str, RouteRun]`, one slot keyed by `train_id`. When a run reaches a terminal state, its `current_route_status` flips to `FINISHED` / `DEACTIVATED`, and the row moves into `RouteExecutor._historical_runs: List[RouteRun]`, which keeps every terminal run indefinitely so the live slot is free for that train's next run. A train may therefore have many historical `RouteRun` rows over time.
- **Live invariant.** At most one `RouteRun` per `train_id` is live (its `current_route_status == RUNNING`) at a time. `RouteExecutor.execution_state_for(train_id)` is a derived read, not a raw slot read: it returns the train's live-slot run only when that run's `current_route_status == RUNNING`, and otherwise `None`.
- **`RouteExecutor.history_for_train(train_id)`.** This parallel history accessor returns every `RouteRun` (any state: `RUNNING`, `FINISHED`, `DEACTIVATED`) for that train across all routes, ordered by `run_number` ascending. Return type: `List[RouteRun]`. The accessor unions `_historical_runs` with the train's live slot, selects only rows where `run.train_id == train_id`, and sorts by `run_number` ascending.
- **`RouteExecutor.history_for_route(route_id)`.** This route-keyed counterpart unions `_historical_runs` with every live slot, selects rows where `run.route_id == route_id`, and returns them ordered by `(started_at, run_number)`.
- **`exec_state` alias.** Throughout the rest of this section, the name `exec_state` is a short alias for the train's currently `RUNNING` `RouteRun` (that is, the result of `RouteExecutor.execution_state_for(train_id)`). When that read returns `None`, no helper that names `exec_state` runs.

`RouteExecutor.route_registry: Dict[str, Route]` is the registry of shared `Route` definitions keyed by `route_id` (not of runs); the run stores above (`execution_states`, `_historical_runs`) are separate instance fields. None of these are persisted across process restart (persistence is Out of Scope for v1 per the Out of Scope table).

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `run_number` | `int` | Globally unique run-instance number assigned by `RouteExecutor` when this `RouteRun` is created. `RouteExecutor._next_run_number` starts at `1`, supplies the current value, and increments after every allocation regardless of route. Numbers are never recycled or recomputed during the process lifetime. `run_number` is an opaque API/history identity and must not be parsed for `route_id`; the immutable `RouteRun.route_id` field carries that relationship directly. |
| `train_id` | `str` | The train this run belongs to. Stored on the run itself; the live run is keyed by `train_id` in `execution_states`, and historical runs carry their `train_id` on the row in `_historical_runs`. |
| `route_id` | `str` | The shared `Route` definition this run is executing. Established at run creation and never mutated, even if the shared route's content later changes. Operator retargeting and route swap do not rewrite `route_id`; they go through "abort current run + create new run" (see **Route Edit And Reconciliation**). |
| `started_at` | `float` | System-time Unix timestamp sampled locally when this run instance is created and never mutated afterward. Used as the synthetic predecessor sentinel for `task_runs[0]` under `timing_basis == "realtime"`. |
| `started_at_operating` | `float` | `AppState.operating_time` read locally by the same allocation operation that samples `started_at`; written once and never mutated. Used as the synthetic predecessor sentinel for `task_runs[0]` under `timing_basis == "operating"`, so no duration mixes clock domains. |
| `current_waypoint_index` | `Optional[int]` (read-only derived) | Physical-progress cursor: the largest walk-position index `i` in `task_runs` where `task_runs[i].finished_at is not None`, or `None` when no task has finished yet. Computed each access from `task_runs`; not a stored field; no writers — progress is recorded by `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(i)` (runtime), which writes both finish-clock fields as one step of advancing the walk position, and the cursor reflects that update on the next read. (At allocation, start-mode seeding may also pre-finish a skipped prefix; see **Run start-mode seeding**. Plan's broken-task skip finishes a broken walk-position by the same direct paired-clock writes; see **Unreachable and broken task handling**.) The walk-position order is the directed walk order. New rows are appended per `Route.mode` after successful completion or broken-task skipping, and waypoint lookahead may append exactly the next row beyond the tail without finishing its predecessor; none of those appends changes this cursor until a row's `finished_at` is actually written (see the `task_runs` row below). A route-committed stop arrival therefore advances this cursor when it calls `RouteRun.advance_walk_position()` for the stop; a following `dwell` row is advanced by its own later call. A run with start mode `FIRST` starts with no `task_runs[*].finished_at` set, so `current_waypoint_index` reads as `None` and the first planning target is `task_runs[0]`. With `NEAREST` / `SPECIFIC`, allocation pre-finishes the skipped prefix `[0, s)`, so `current_waypoint_index` reads `s - 1` and the first planning target is the seeded start position — see **Run start-mode seeding**. **Naming note:** this field indexes all task kinds (`waypoint`, `stop`, `dwell`, `run`), not only `task_kind == "waypoint"` tasks. The name is historical. |
| `direction` | `"forward" \| "reverse"` | Effective direction of the task Plan most recently resolved/armed. Initialized to `"forward"`. Its one writer is Plan, at steps `592a` / `66aa`, which set it from the `direction` field of the `ResolvedNextTaskProjection` they consume. It is not the source for extending the directed walk: `RouteRun._append_next_walk_task(from_walk_position)` reads the predecessor row's `walk_direction` and the validated task-group boundaries to derive `CIRCULAR` wrap or `ROUND_TRIP` reflection, so a delayed Plan direction write cannot corrupt row generation. `RouteExecutor._find_next_task_target(...)` projects the appended row's `walk_direction`, and the first later arm past an end updates this field. No code derives a new appended row from `RouteRun.direction`. |
| `task_runs` | `List[RouteTaskRun]` | Per-run directed-walk table. Each entry represents one walk-position. The list grows over the run's lifetime: at run creation it is initialized with `len(Route.tasks)` entries (one per task in the initial walk; entry at walk-position `i` has `task_index = i` and `walk_direction = "forward"`). Start-mode seeding may pre-finish a prefix of these entries at allocation so the run begins at a later stop (see **Run start-mode seeding**). Each completed walk-position is recorded by `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(i)`, which samples both clocks locally, writes both finish fields, computes `delay_class`, and then calls `RouteRun._append_next_walk_task(from_walk_position=i)`. Two other callers may append: Plan's broken-task skip after writing the skipped row's paired finish fields directly, and `RouteExecutor._find_next_task_target(..., after_walk_position=...)` when waypoint lookahead needs exactly the next directed-walk row beyond the current tail. The lookahead append does not finish or otherwise mutate any existing row. For `RouteMode.CIRCULAR` and `RouteMode.ROUND_TRIP`, successful progress and broken-task skipping replenish the directed walk, while lookahead may temporarily add the one next row needed beyond the tail; for `RouteMode.ONE_OFF` the append helper adds no row, so the unfinished suffix shrinks to zero after the terminal task. Each entry owns its visit direction, paired wall/operating timing, and resolved-target bookkeeping — see **RouteTaskRun schema** below. The synthetic predecessors for `task_runs[0]` are the paired `RouteRun.started_at` fields. |
| `path_cancelled` | `bool` | Latch: set by `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(...)` when the matching live path is cancelled; consumed by Plan route-deviation cleanup when `controller.is_recovery_clean` is true. See the Latch Table in the Core Runtime Loop section for the full lifetime rule. |
| `path_cancel_was_deviation` | `bool` | Diagnostic companion to `path_cancelled`, written together with it by the ordinary branch of `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(...)` from the callback's structured `was_deviation` argument and cleared together with it by Plan route-deviation cleanup. `True` only when the consumed request carried `deviation = True`; `False` for another ordinary authority cancellation that keeps the run alive. A `was_run_completion` callback writes neither field. Not a latch — it carries no gating predicate and no Latch-Table entry. Drives the `display_state == "DEVIATED"` vs `"CANCELLED"` split. Default `False`. |
| `no_reachable_task` | `bool` | Set by Plan step `c481` (or by step `592a` when a mid-pass cursor move lands on a broken task) when every task on the current directed walk is **broken** (each task's `task_location` target ID is missing from the network) for a `RouteMode.CIRCULAR` / `RouteMode.ROUND_TRIP` run and no live path remains, so no authority can be planned and the train holds idle; while a live path still exists at that point the step latches the ordinary cancel instead (`origin = "revoked"`, `kind = "info"`) and leaves the flag unset, setting it only on the later pass that finds no live path (see **Unreachable and broken task handling**). Cleared by the next Plan pass whose step `c481` or step `592a` lookup finds any valid (present-target) task on the walk. Not a latch — it has no gating predicate and no cross-stage handoff, so it carries no Latch-Table entry and no writer helper; Plan maintains it by direct write. Drives the derived `display_state == "STALLED"` projection. Always `False` for `RouteMode.ONE_OFF` runs, which finish instead. Default `False`. See **Unreachable and broken task handling**. |
| `current_route_status` | `RouteRunStatus` (`"RUNNING" \| "FINISHED" \| "DEACTIVATED"`) | Always-present scalar route-owned status. Allocated as `"RUNNING"`. It is read by exactly one consumer for control flow: the `RouteExecutor.execution_state_for(train_id)` active-run derived read keys on `current_route_status == RUNNING` to identify the train's currently-active run. Plan, Observe, Action, and route-callback bodies never read it for control flow — they key on `received_path_plan`, the `path_cancelled` latch (see Latch Table), controller cleanup latches, and current span coverage. See the write-contract table below for writers and triggers. The canonical home for resolved targets is `RouteRun.task_runs[i].resolved_target`; `current_route_status` does not carry a parallel resolved-target collection or wrapper object. |
| `display_state` | `"RUNNING" \| "DEVIATED" \| "CANCELLED" \| "STALLED" \| "FINISHED" \| "DEACTIVATED"` (read-only derived) | Derived UI projection computed each access, in priority order: (1) when `current_route_status` is terminal, return it; (2) when `path_cancelled`, return `"DEVIATED"` if `path_cancel_was_deviation` else `"CANCELLED"`; (3) when `no_reachable_task`, return `"STALLED"`; (4) otherwise return `current_route_status` (`"RUNNING"`). Not stored; runtime branching never keys on it. |
| `overrides` | `Dict[str, Any]` | Sparse per-run overrides of a small allowlisted set of route-level operational fields. Keys are field names from the v1 override allowlist (`"priority"`, `"acquisition_mode"`); a key being absent means "use the shared `Route` value for that field." Default: empty dict. See **RouteRun overrides** below for the override allowlist, the effective-value read pattern, and the force-push / soft-push edit-distribution rules. |
| `overrides_updated_at` | `Optional[float]` | System-time Unix timestamp of the most recent `overrides` write on this run, bumped by `RouteExecutor.set_run_override(...)` and `RouteExecutor.clear_run_override(...)` (sampled via `time.time()` at the write site per **Time sampling**). `None` until the first override write. Diagnostic only; no runtime branching reads it. |
| `start_mode` | `Optional[RouteStartMode]` | The resolved start mode this run was seeded with at allocation (`FIRST` / `NEAREST` / `SPECIFIC`). Written once by the start-mode seed during step `9c4f`; diagnostic only (surfaced read-only in the `GET /api/route-runs/<run_number>` run-record payload, see **Data Flow To UI**). NOT a live override — start mode has no meaning after the run's starting walk-position is seeded. See **Run start-mode seeding**. |
| `start_walk_position` | `int` | The walk-position (list index in `task_runs`) this run was seeded to plan toward first — its first real movement target. `0` for start mode `FIRST`; otherwise the seed position `s` after start-mode seeding pre-finishes the prefix `[0, s)`, so `next_planning_walk_position == s` immediately after seeding. Written once by the start-mode seed during step `9c4f`. Read only by the derived `is_starting`. |
| `next_planning_walk_position` | `Optional[int]` (read-only derived) | The first unfinished walk-position: the lowest `i` in `task_runs` with `task_runs[i].finished_at is None`, or `None` when the unfinished suffix is empty. Computed each access from `task_runs`; not a stored field; no writers. Equals `start_walk_position` immediately after start-mode seeding, and only advances over the run, including across `CIRCULAR` / `ROUND_TRIP` wrap-around, because `task_runs` grows without bound (the unfinished suffix never empties for those modes). A terminal `ONE_OFF` run may briefly return `None` after Observe finishes its last task and before Plan archives the run. Read by the derived `is_starting` and by **Run start-mode seeding**. |
| `next_planning_index` | `int` (read-only derived) | The `task_index` (the index into `Route.tasks`) of that same next unfinished walk-position — the task-index-space companion to `next_planning_walk_position`, which is list-position-space in `task_runs`. `0` for an empty walk and before any task finishes; otherwise the `task_index` of the first `task_runs` entry whose `finished_at is None`; the last entry's `task_index` once every entry is finished (a terminal walk). Computed each access from `task_runs`; not a stored field; no writers. The two companions decouple after `CIRCULAR` / `ROUND_TRIP` wrap-around, when `len(task_runs) > len(Route.tasks)`: a caller indexing `task_runs` directly reads `next_planning_walk_position`, and a caller that needs the position within `Route.tasks` reads this. |
| `is_starting` | `bool` (read-only derived) | `True` while this run is still completing its first real movement target — `next_planning_walk_position is not None` and `next_planning_walk_position <= start_walk_position` — and `False` once the train completes the task at `start_walk_position`, including when `next_planning_walk_position is None`. Monotonic: it flips to `False` exactly once and never back, because `next_planning_walk_position` (see its row above) only advances and can become `None` only after the terminal `ONE_OFF` task finishes. It keys on `next_planning_walk_position` rather than `current_waypoint_index` because `next_planning_walk_position` is defined from run start — it reads `start_walk_position` before any task finishes — while `current_waypoint_index` reads `None` until the first finish. Read by the runnable-train ordering as the primary ordering tier — see the canonical ordering rule in **Per-train tick transaction**. A run re-allocated after a structural edit is seeded afresh, so it reads `is_starting == True` again until it completes its new first target. |
| `idle_hold_ticks` | `int` | Count of consecutive Plan ticks on which this run held a truncated best-effort live authority (the run's armed target block fails `Path.reaches_target(...)`) that neither grew nor saw the head advance. Maintained by the Plan authority-acquisition step (`66aa`) by direct write: incremented on each such no-progress tick, and reset to `0` per the counting rule in step `66aa`'s idle-hold maintenance and release (which also lists the meet-ceiling reset cause; this row does not restate it). Not a latch — it has no gating predicate and no cross-stage handoff, so it carries no Latch-Table entry and no writer helper. Drives the timeout branch of the idle-hold release in step `66aa`; the contention-driven release branch in that same step does not depend on this counter and may fire while `idle_hold_ticks` is still below `IDLE_HOLD_RELEASE_TICKS`. Default `0`. |
| `release_cooldown_ticks` | `int` | Post-release acquisition-skip countdown. Set to `IDLE_HOLD_COOLDOWN_TICKS` by step `66aa` when it latches an idle-hold release; while `> 0`, step `66aa` decrements it by one and skips authority acquisition for this run so the just-released reservations and switch locks stay free for higher-priority runs to claim, then resumes normal planning at `0`. Not a latch; Plan maintains it by direct write. Default `0`. |

- Operator/manual reposition is modeled through the ordinary one-off `Route` + `RouteRun` flow, with no special run-level flag. Such a route is created with `RouteMode.ONE_OFF` and follows the ordinary route-definition validation rules below. A one-off reposition can be authored as a single-task route whose only `task_kind == "stop"` task is the destination; with a single stop, start-mode seeding (see **Run start-mode seeding**) resolves to that task and `current_waypoint_index` initializes to `None`, so `_find_next_task_target` resolves that stop as the first executable movement task. A destination block where the train is already stopped with its head in it (and no active path) is finished by the covered-stop rule in Plan's covered-task index advance (no dispatcher authority is created); any other destination goes through the general Plan / `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` flow.

`ErrorRecord` is defined once in **Design Direction**, **Errors and diagnostic classification**. The run stores none: route and run errors are emitted as events per **Error events**, so the message, its time, its origin, and its level always travel together on one event.

**RouteRun overrides**

This subsection is the canonical home for `RouteRun.overrides`, the per-run effective-value read helpers, and the operator-driven push semantics that distribute later route edits to existing runs.

- **Override allowlist (v1).** Exactly two route-level fields may be overridden per run: `priority` and `acquisition_mode`. Every other route field — `name`, `mode`, `tasks`, `assigned_train_ids`, `is_active`, `created_at`, `last_edited_at`, `started_at`, `route_id`, `start_mode`, `start_task_index`, `manual_override`, `timing_basis` — is shared and not overridable. (`start_mode` / `start_task_index` are not live overrides, but they do accept a one-shot per-assignment input consumed at allocation — see **Run start-mode seeding**.) Any attempt to write a key outside the allowlist is a validation error on the override-edit endpoint; storage rejects the request rather than silently ignoring the unknown key.
- **Storage shape.** `RouteRun.overrides` is a sparse `Dict[str, Any]` keyed by the allowlisted field name. A key being absent means "use the shared `Route` value for that field." A key being present means the value at that key is the effective per-run value, regardless of what the shared `Route` currently holds. The stored types match the route-level types exactly (`priority: int`, `acquisition_mode: AcquisitionMode`); validation runs at write time.
- **Effective-value read helpers.** `RouteRun` exposes one read helper per allowlisted field, each returning the per-run effective value: `RouteRun.effective_priority(route_registry)` and `RouteRun.effective_acquisition_mode(route_registry)`. A `RouteRun` stores no owner back-reference.
