Each helper receives the read-only route registry, resolves `route_id`, returns `self.overrides[<field>]` when that key is present, and otherwise returns the matching field from the shared `Route`. The helpers recompute each access, so later operator edits to either the run-level override or shared route take effect on the next read. Every Plan and ordering consumer supplies `RouteExecutor`'s route registry and uses the corresponding helper rather than reading `Route` or `overrides` directly. `RouteExecutor.order_runnable_trains(...)` reads `RouteRun.effective_priority(route_registry)` per assigned run, and authority acquisition reads `RouteRun.effective_acquisition_mode(route_registry)`.
- **Override write entry point.** Operator/admin writes to `RouteRun.overrides` route through one canonical handler: `RouteExecutor.set_run_override(train_id, field, value)` sets one allowlisted field on the train's currently `RUNNING` `RouteRun`. The handler validates the field name is in the allowlist and the value's type/range matches the shared route's validation rule for that field; on success it writes `overrides[field] = value` and bumps a single same-run audit timestamp `overrides_updated_at` for diagnostics. A symmetric `RouteExecutor.clear_run_override(train_id, field)` removes one key from `overrides`, restoring the shared-route value for that field; clearing a key that is not present is a no-op success. Both helpers are no-op success when the train has no `RUNNING` `RouteRun`. Historical (`FINISHED` / `DEACTIVATED`) runs reject override edits — their `overrides` snapshot is frozen as part of the historical record.
- **Push semantics.** When the operator edits a shared `Route` field (through `PUT /api/train-routes/<route_id>`), the edit may carry a per-field push policy on each changed allowlisted field, encoded as the `push` parameter on the route-edit payload: `push = "force"`, `push = "soft"`, or `push` omitted (default). The route-edit service applies one rule per changed allowlisted field, against every currently `RUNNING` `RouteRun` for that route:
  - **`force`** — overwrite any existing `RouteRun.overrides[field]` with the new shared value. Equivalent to calling `RouteExecutor.clear_run_override(train_id, field)` on every `RUNNING` run for that route after writing the shared field. The shared route now holds the truth and no per-run override remains on this field.
  - **`soft`** — leave any existing `RouteRun.overrides[field]` intact; runs without an override for this field automatically pick up the new shared value through the effective-value helpers. No per-run write happens.
  - **omitted / default** — equivalent to `soft`; the shared edit lands on the route definition and runs without an override start using the new value on the next read, but no override is cleared.
  - Push policies are per-field; one route edit may carry `priority: {value: 7, push: "force"}` and `acquisition_mode: {value: "all_or_nothing", push: "soft"}` in the same request body. Non-allowlisted fields (e.g. `tasks`) ignore the `push` key — they have no per-run override to push to.
  - Push policies apply only to the route's shared field write; if the same request also edits a structural field (`tasks` or `mode`), that field follows the **Route-definition field edit classification** teardown rule unchanged, and any other live non-allowlisted field it edits (`name`, `timing_basis`, `start_mode`, `start_task_index`) takes effect live per that same classification, with no `push` to apply.
- **Historical runs.** Push policies never touch `FINISHED` or `DEACTIVATED` runs. Their `overrides` snapshot is part of the historical row and remains as written when the run was active.
- **API surface.** `PATCH /api/route-runs/<run_number>/overrides` body `{field: value}` (single field) or `{overrides: {field: value, ...}}` (batched) calls `RouteExecutor.set_run_override(train_id, field, value)` per entry. `DELETE /api/route-runs/<run_number>/overrides/<field>` calls `RouteExecutor.clear_run_override(train_id, field)`. Both endpoints reject historical runs with HTTP 409. `PUT /api/train-routes/<route_id>` accepts per-field push policies under the existing edit body; the encoding is `{<field>: {value: ..., push: "force"|"soft"}}` for allowlisted fields and the bare `{<field>: value}` shape continues to work for non-allowlisted fields and for allowlisted fields when no per-field push policy is needed (defaults to `soft`).

`RouteRunStatus` is a scalar enum with exactly `RUNNING`, `FINISHED`, and `DEACTIVATED`; it is not a record with a nested `state` field. `RUNNING` covers ordinary execution, including dwell and unarmed time between legs. `FINISHED` means the directed task walk ended and Plan called `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)`. `DEACTIVATED` means the run ended early through route deactivation, operator abort/retarget/swap, or power-off cleanup; all three teardown consumers call `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)`. Both terminal values move the run into `_historical_runs`; Plan does no further work on that row. The run records no separate teardown-cause field, so UI/log consumers use the canonical `cancel_path` and command-result events when they need that distinction.

`RouteRun.current_route_status` has this v1 write contract. Its three Action teardown consumers below — `pending_route_abort`, `pending_power_off`, `pending_route_deactivate` — each run their own teardown only after any inclusive `pending_path_cancel_request` they wrote (with the `error.origin` named in the row, and written only when a live path existed at write time) has committed earlier in the same Action pass, per the Latch Table; none of the three branches on active-path emptiness — the `pending_path_cancel_request` consumer already owns that. Each row states only its own teardown:

| Writer | Trigger | `current_route_status` after write | Other required writes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Plan (after a successful create/extend) (`66aa`) | a run resolves a fresh next target via `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` and Plan's authority-acquisition step succeeds in `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` / `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` for that target | `RUNNING` | Plan sets `direction` to the resolved direction and writes `task_runs[walk_position].resolved_target` (where `walk_position` is the index the helper returned for the target this tick armed) to the candidate that the successful create/extend used. |
| `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(...)` ordinary branch (`b0fb`) | the matching live path is cancelled or revoked with `was_run_completion == False` AND `RouteExecutor.execution_state_for(train_id) is not None` | unchanged — `display_state` projection follows `path_cancelled` + `path_cancel_was_deviation` | set `RouteRun.path_cancelled = True` (see Latch Table) and `RouteRun.path_cancel_was_deviation = was_deviation` (the callback's classification argument). The callback does not clear `task_runs[i].resolved_target`; whatever Plan's last successful create/extend wrote stays in place. For a non-terminal run the derived `display_state` then reads `"DEVIATED"` when `was_deviation` is true and `"CANCELLED"` otherwise. The `was_run_completion == True` branch writes neither field, cursor, nor task timing and returns after correlation validation. A missing live `RouteRun` is an invariant violation, not a normal callback branch — see the canonical **`RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(...)`** definition. |
| Plan route-deviation-cleanup step (`5fc7`) | `RouteRun.path_cancelled == True` and `controller.is_recovery_clean` is true | unchanged — `display_state` projection follows `path_cancelled` + `path_cancel_was_deviation` | clear `path_cancelled` and `path_cancel_was_deviation` together; the derived `display_state == "DEVIATED"` / `"CANCELLED"` clears with them; the next eligible Plan plans normally |
| Plan terminal-walk detect — direct `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)` (`592a`, terminal-walk branch) | `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` returns `None` on the directed walk in the same Plan pass — whether because a terminal `stop` (and optional `dwell`) or terminal `run` has finished, or because every remaining task on the walk was broken-skipped — AND `PathDispatcher.active_path_id_by_train(train_id) is None`. When the walk goes terminal by the broken-skip cause while a live path still exists (an armed `waypoint` that head entry consumed without releasing authority), this branch instead latches the ordinary cancel per **Unreachable and broken task handling** and returns; this row's write fires on the later pass once that cancel has committed, so the run ends `FINISHED` having served nothing only once no live path remains. | `FINISHED` | clear `path_cancelled` and `path_cancel_was_deviation` if either is still set (the broken-skip case's interposed cancel may not yet have been consumed by step `5fc7`'s `is_recovery_clean` gate on this same pass); call `Route.unassign_train(train_id)`; move the `RouteRun` into `_historical_runs` as the historical `FINISHED` row (the active-state predicate flips and `assigned_route_id_for(train_id)` returns `None`); if this `ONE_OFF` route now has no assigned trains, call `route.deactivate()` (its latch walk is empty); then return. No dispatcher cancel is needed here because either terminal stop completion or terminal run step `6a0d` already cleared the live path, or (in the broken-skip case) the interposed cancel above already did. |
| Action — `pending_route_abort` consumer (`5d2c`) | the `pending_route_abort` latch is consumed (operator/admin route-abort, retarget, or swap) | `DEACTIVATED` | The consumer calls `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)`; the helper writes `DEACTIVATED`, unassigns the train, and (when the controller is `RUNNING_AT_STATION`) writes `station_exit_request` (the Action station-exit consumer performs the transition). Clear `pending_route_abort`. |
| Action — `pending_power_off` consumer (`9a81`) | the `pending_power_off` latch is consumed (set by the Action operator drain or by the Observe ghosted-train rising edge — the consumer does not branch on which) | `DEACTIVATED` | The consumer calls `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)`; the helper writes `DEACTIVATED`, unassigns the train, and (when the controller is `RUNNING_AT_STATION`) writes `station_exit_request` (the Action station-exit consumer performs the transition). `TrainController.complete_power_off()`, per its canonical contract in **TrainController**, follows the helper return. |
| Action — `pending_route_deactivate` consumer (`4f6e`) | the `pending_route_deactivate` latch is consumed (operator/admin or `route.deactivate()` ran while this run had not yet finished) | `DEACTIVATED` | The consumer calls `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)`; the helper writes `DEACTIVATED`, unassigns the train, and (when the controller is `RUNNING_AT_STATION`) writes `station_exit_request` (the Action station-exit consumer performs the transition). When the structural-edit teardown recorded a held re-assignment for this train AND this consumer owned the run teardown (its own `remove_train_route_run(train_id)` cleared a still-`RUNNING` run), the consumer re-applies it (`Route.assign_train(train_id)`) after that clear; if an earlier abort/power-off consumer (or a natural finish) had already ended the run, the consumer instead discards the held re-assignment, per the **Shared-route edit teardown**. Clear `pending_route_deactivate`. |

The teardown cause is not a write. It travels only as the `ErrorRecord.origin` the writer helper put on the inclusive `pending_path_cancel_request` — `"operator_cancelled"` for abort, `"power_off"` for power-off, `"revoked"` for deactivate, per the **Writer-helper rule** — and reaches consumers on the resulting `cancel_path` event. When no live path existed, those helpers write no inclusive cancel, so the teardown carries no cause and the helper's own latch-write event is the only record of it.

`RouteExecutor` owns these direct status writes and the latch/diagnostic writes that feed the derived `display_state` projection. Other entities such as `BlockManager`, `PathDispatcher`, and switch/resource callbacks may trigger the route callback that causes a status change, but they do not write `RouteRun.current_route_status` directly. The `display_state` priority order is defined once in its field row above. Two things matter for control flow: runtime branching never keys on `display_state`, and the active-run predicate is a separate derived read on `current_route_status == RUNNING`, the only runtime control-flow read of that scalar. The `"DEVIATED"` / `"CANCELLED"` and `"STALLED"` projections clear when their backing flags clear. UI/log consumers that need the precise originating kind subscribe to the canonical `cancel_path` event on `NotificationCenter`.

**RouteTaskRun schema**

`RouteTaskRun` is the per-run task-state entry. `RouteRun.task_runs` is a `List[RouteTaskRun]` indexed by walk-position on the run's directed walk. It is allocated with `len(Route.tasks)` entries at run creation (walk-position `i` carrying `task_index = i` and `walk_direction = "forward"`) and grows through `RouteRun._append_next_walk_task(from_walk_position)` as walk-positions finish, broken tasks are skipped, or waypoint lookahead needs the next row beyond the current tail; `task_index` is the back-reference into `Route.tasks` and stops equalling the walk-position after the first `CIRCULAR` wrap or `ROUND_TRIP` reflection, while `walk_direction` records the direction of that particular visit. The unfinished rows are always a contiguous suffix. For cyclic modes that suffix initially has `len(Route.tasks)` rows and shrinks as the original leg finishes; once progress reaches the original tail, every completion/skip append replenishes exactly one unfinished tail row, while waypoint lookahead may temporarily add exactly one extra unfinished row beyond it. For `ONE_OFF`, no replenishment occurs and the suffix may shrink to empty. `RouteTaskRun` is the canonical owner of per-task timing and the resolved dispatcher target. Task-related failures are `NotificationCenter` events whose entity references identify the train, run, and walk-position; no error field is stored on `RouteTaskRun`.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `task_index` | `int` | Back-reference into `Route.tasks` for the underlying `RouteTask` this walk-position represents. With the growing-`task_runs` model, walk-position `i` (the index of this entry in `task_runs`) is no longer guaranteed to equal `task_index` — for `RouteMode.CIRCULAR` and `RouteMode.ROUND_TRIP`, walk-positions and `task_index` decouple after the first wrap/reflection. Readers needing the underlying task definition use `Route.tasks[task_index]`. |
| `walk_direction` | `"forward" \| "reverse"` | Direction of this visit on the directed walk. Initial rows are `"forward"`. `RouteRun._append_next_walk_task(...)` copies it while advancing within a task group and flips it only when a `ROUND_TRIP` walk reflects from one end group toward the next group. `RouteExecutor._find_next_task_target(...)` reports this value in `ResolvedNextTaskProjection.direction`; no caller infers direction from increasing/decreasing raw task indices. |
| `resolved_target` | `Optional[ResolvedRouteTarget]` | Block and direction that Plan's most recent successful `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` / `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` for this walk-position returned. Written exclusively by Plan's authority-acquisition step on success; never written by `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` itself, never written by Observe head-advance callback and Observe stop-arrival step, never cleared by any callback. The "what is the next target?" answer for live decisions is recomputed by `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` and consumed in place. `task_runs[i].resolved_target` is the authoritative target record the **Stop-arrival check** compares the live authority terminal against, so for `task_kind == "stop"` the stored value reflects the platform/block the run is actually serving. `None` until Plan successfully creates/extends authority for this walk-position at least once; `None` for `dwell` walk-positions (which carry no dispatcher target). |
| `started_at` | `Optional[float]` | For a `dwell` row this is a stored system-time Unix timestamp sampled locally by `RouteExecutor` step `3a37`, immediately before that step writes `station_entry_request`, and `None` before that write. That same step also reads `AppState.operating_time` into `started_at_operating`. For every other row this is a read-only derived value with no writers: for walk-position `i == 0` it equals `RouteRun.started_at`, otherwise `task_runs[i - 1].finished_at`, or `None` if that predecessor has not finished yet. Walk-position order is the directed walk order. Consumers use the paired `_operating` derivation when `timing_basis == "operating"`. |
| `finished_at` | `Optional[float]` | System-time Unix seconds when this walk-position ended. `waypoint`: head-entry consumption. `stop`: route-committed stop arrival or the head-anchored covered-stop exception. `dwell`: dwell timer satisfied. `run`: Plan step `6a0d` after its simulated-time window, service stop, and authority release. Successful service writes route through `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(...)`. Two explicit exceptions write directly: allocation-time start-mode seeding sets skipped-prefix timestamps to `RouteRun.started_at` without append, and Plan broken-task skip writes the missing-target row and appends; both leave `delay_class = None`. No other writer exists. |
| `started_at_operating` | `Optional[float]` | Runtime-only operating-clock counterpart to `started_at`. On `dwell`, stored by `RouteExecutor` step `3a37` in the same write that samples the wall value, before that step writes `station_entry_request`. On every other row, derived from `RouteRun.started_at_operating` or the predecessor's `finished_at_operating` exactly as the wall field is derived. `None` whenever the matching wall anchor is unavailable; never persisted. |
| `finished_at_operating` | `Optional[float]` | Runtime-only `AppState.operating_time` reading sampled locally in the same `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(walk_position)` call that writes `finished_at`. Start-mode seeding copies `RouteRun.started_at_operating`; broken-task skipping samples the current operating clock alongside its wall finish. Never persisted. |
| `run_elapsed_seconds` | `float` | Stored simulated-time accumulator used only when the underlying task has `task_kind == "run"`; initialized to `0.0` for every task-run row. Plan run step `6a0d` is its only writer and adds the non-negative playback-scaled `delta_seconds`, capped at the run task's required `task_time`. Head-entry, coverage, dispatcher callbacks, wall-clock reads, and replay never write it. It remains on the historical row after completion for diagnostics. |
| `delay_class` | `Optional["early" \| "on_time" \| "late"]` | Timing classification for `waypoint` and `stop` rows. It is stored run history, not an error classification: the **Errors and diagnostic classification** rules and the `ErrorRecord` shape do not apply to it, and no runtime code branches on it. Its readers are the run panel and the event-log viewer, which display the served walk-position's timing. Computed when `finished_at` is recorded by comparing their expected-travel `Route.tasks[task_index].task_time` with the actual elapsed time since the predecessor walk-position's finish (use `RouteRun.started_at_operating` for walk-position `0` under `"operating"`, `RouteRun.started_at` under `"realtime"`). That elapsed figure is measured against the clock the route's `timing_basis` names — the `finished_at_operating` pair under `"operating"`, the `finished_at` pair under `"realtime"` — so one route classifies its lateness on the same basis its dwells hold on, and the walk-position-`0` predecessor is never a wall instant subtracted from an operating-clock one. The comparison uses `DELAY_CLASS_ON_TIME_TOLERANCE_SECONDS`, adjustable as `delay_class_on_time_tolerance_seconds` in **Runtime settings**: elapsed below `task_time - tol` is `early`, above `task_time + tol` is `late`, otherwise `on_time`. `None` when expected-travel `task_time` is absent or the row has not finished. Never computed for `dwell` or `run`: dwell time is a hold duration, and run time is a simulated-time movement window tracked separately by `run_elapsed_seconds`. A row pre-finished by start-mode seeding or skipped as broken also keeps `delay_class = None`. |

`ResolvedRouteTarget` is the resolved dispatcher request contract for one task attempt: `requested_destination_block_id: str` and `requested_destination_direction: "forward" | "reverse"`.

The armed authority target is the derived `ArmedTaskProjection` returned by `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)`, not `current_waypoint_index` and not the next unfinished projection. There is no stored `_arm_next_target` flag. The projection derives the most recently acquired unfinished row from the append-only run record and exposes its stored target without changing it.

For predecessor timestamp lookup (used by `delay_class` and any other "elapsed since predecessor" computation on a non-`dwell` row): the predecessor is the directly-preceding walk-position. For walk-position `0` on a newly created `RouteRun`, the predecessor is the synthetic route-start sentinel `RouteRun.started_at` under `"realtime"` and `RouteRun.started_at_operating` under `"operating"` — the same clock split every other predecessor lookup observes, so walk-position `0` never subtracts a wall instant from an operating-clock one. The derived `task_runs[i].started_at` returns `RouteRun.started_at` for `i == 0` and `task_runs[i - 1].finished_at` otherwise (and `task_runs[i].started_at_operating` returns `RouteRun.started_at_operating` for `i == 0` and `task_runs[i - 1].finished_at_operating` otherwise), **except on a `dwell` row, where `started_at` / `started_at_operating` are the stored sample `RouteExecutor` step `3a37` wrote before writing `station_entry_request` (per the `RouteTaskRun` schema) and are not derived from the predecessor at all** — the dwell timer therefore reads the dwell row's own stored `started_at`, not its predecessor's `finished_at`. A row appended early for waypoint lookahead may temporarily derive `started_at = None` while its predecessor is unfinished; tasks still finish in walk-position order, so that predecessor timestamp exists by the time the appended row becomes the physical active task.

**`RouteRun.advance_walk_position(walk_position)`** is the canonical helper that advances one successfully served walk-position to completion during runtime. Callers pass no clock value. In one call it samples `now = time.time()` and `now_operating = AppState.operating_time`, then (1) writes the row's `finished_at = now` and `finished_at_operating = now_operating`, (2) computes `delay_class` from the matching clock pair on `waypoint` and `stop` rows only — it leaves `delay_class = None` on `dwell` and `run` rows, per the `RouteTaskRun` schema — and (3) calls `RouteRun._append_next_walk_task(from_walk_position=walk_position)`. Successful progress sites route through this helper: the head-advance callback, Observe stop arrival, Plan dwell completion, Plan run step `6a0d` after stopped authority release, and Plan covered-task advance. Two explicit exceptions write paired finish fields without this helper: allocation-time start-mode seeding copies the run's paired start fields, and Plan broken-task skipping samples both clocks locally; both leave `delay_class = None`, and only the broken-task skip appends. No other writer exists.

**`RouteRun._append_next_walk_task(from_walk_position)`** is the sole internal append step for `task_runs`. Its closed caller list is: `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(...)` after the paired timestamp / `delay_class` writes commit; Plan broken-task skipping after it writes the skipped row's paired finish fields directly; and `_find_next_task_target(..., after_walk_position=...)` when waypoint lookahead asks for the next directed-walk row exactly one position beyond the current tail. Each caller passes the row from which the walk continues. The lookahead caller invokes it at most once per helper call and does not finish or mutate an existing row. No other caller appends `task_runs`. The helper selects the next `task_index` to append per `Route.mode`:

- `RouteMode.ONE_OFF`: do not append. After the terminal task finishes, `task_runs` stops growing.
- `RouteMode.CIRCULAR`: append a new `RouteTaskRun` whose `task_index` is `(task_runs[from_walk_position].task_index + 1) mod len(Route.tasks)`.
- `RouteMode.ROUND_TRIP`: validation has already divided `Route.tasks` into task groups, each consisting of one non-`dwell` row followed by its contiguous dwell rows. Read `task_runs[from_walk_position].walk_direction`. While another row remains in the current group, append that next row with the same direction. At the group boundary, append the first row of the next group in the current direction. Forward from the final group reflects to the first row of the preceding group with `walk_direction = "reverse"`; reverse from the first group reflects to the first row of the second group with `walk_direction = "forward"`. The end group is not repeated, and dwell rows retain their authored order on the reverse visit. Only Plan steps `592a` / `66aa` copy the projected `walk_direction` into `RouteRun.direction`; the append helper never reads or writes `RouteRun.direction`.

The appended `RouteTaskRun` initializes with the selected `task_index` and `walk_direction`, plus `finished_at = None`, `resolved_target = None`, `delay_class = None`, and `run_elapsed_seconds = 0.0`. Its `started_at` reads `task_runs[i - 1].finished_at` on a non-`dwell` row; after a lookahead append that derived value may remain `None` until the predecessor finishes. It stays `None` on a `dwell` row until `RouteExecutor` step `3a37` samples it, immediately before that step writes `station_entry_request`. The helper never re-reads or mutates older walk-positions.

- `RouteRun` is the canonical per-train runtime object for one assigned route. Current-code implementation may still name the class `RouteExecutionState`, but every changed contract in this section refers to that object as the train's `RouteRun`.
- `RouteRun` carries `current_waypoint_index`, `direction`, and `task_runs`.
- `RouteRun.current_route_status` is route-owned temporary per-run status, not a shared route-definition cache. `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(...)` finishes the `walk_position` its caller already resolved through `RouteExecutor.find_next_completion_task(train_id)`; it does not resolve a fresh target. `RouteExecutor.handle_train_advanced(...)` compares the reported block against the next non-finished task via a fresh `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` call, per **Dispatcher progress/completion flow**. Neither callback re-resolves the row it commits: the completion callback commits the row its caller already identified, and the advance callback only reads the live next-task projection to decide whether the reported entry matches it.
- `task_runs[i].resolved_target` is the historical record of Plan's last successful create/extend for task `i`. The only writer is Plan's authority-acquisition step, on a successful `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` / `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` for that task. `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` is read-only over existing rows: even its `after_walk_position` form may only append a newly initialized row and never writes or clears an existing row's `resolved_target`. Head-advance, dwell-complete, and UI consumers consume the helper's return value and do not write `task_runs[i].resolved_target`. No callback ever clears it; it is overwritten only by the next successful create/extend that targets the same task.
- `RouteExecutor` owns a scheduling registry over these `RouteRun` entries. On each Plan tick it orders runnable runs by whether the run is already established, then by descending effective priority (an established run comes before a run still finishing its first task, per `RouteRun.is_starting`), per the canonical ordering rule in **Per-train tick transaction**. Among equal run-state tier and priority, stable existing iteration order is acceptable in v1.
- `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)` is the route-owned removal entry point used by Action abort, power-off, and deactivate consumers (per the **`current_route_status` write contract**). All three Action latch consumers call it with the same single argument; the originating cause is recorded only on the `cancel_path` and command-result events, not on any helper parameter or any field on the `RouteRun`. Natural terminal completion uses Plan's direct `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)` call instead and writes `FINISHED`. When invoked, the method looks up the currently-`RUNNING` `RouteRun`. If none exists, it removes any stored assignment, then consumes `_pending_route_assignments[train_id]` exactly as the assignment-commit contract specifies; this covers a train assigned before its first Plan allocation and an earlier teardown consumer in the same Action pass. If a run exists, it performs the active-run teardown sequence, then commits any held replacement as the last operation:
  - if a live dispatcher path still exists for this train (`active_path_id_by_train(train_id)` is set), the caller must already have cancelled it through `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` before invoking this method (the canonical caller is the same Action cleanup pass that already runs the inclusive-cancel step, so the latch-cancel-then-callback flow handles this naturally),
  - if the controller is currently in `RUNNING_AT_STATION` (the `RouteRun` is dwelling), the method writes `station_exit_request` so the later Action station-exit consumer exits dwell into the **`READY` state**,
  - it calls `TrainController.consume_service_stop()` to clear the `ops.service_stop_active` latch, so an interrupted timed `run` cannot leave service braking armed on the train's next route. The accessor is a no-op when the latch is not set, so this step runs unconditionally,
  - it calls `Route.unassign_train(train_id)` on the run's `route_id` and flips the run's active-state predicate by setting `current_route_status = DEACTIVATED`, so `RouteExecutor.execution_state_for(train_id)` no longer returns it. It then consumes `_pending_route_assignments[train_id]` and applies its requested replacement, if any, per **Route assignment writers**. A structural-edit teardown instead uses its narrower same-route `_pending_reassign` entry, which only the deactivate consumer applies after this method returns (see **Shared-route edit teardown**). Historical rows already in `_historical_runs` are not touched. The torn-down run moves from `execution_states` into `_historical_runs` and remains visible to `RouteExecutor.history_for_train(train_id)`.

  An explicit operator/admin "abort route" request — including operator retargeting and explicit route swap — is delivered through the controller-owned Action latch `pending_route_abort` per the inclusive-latch rule defined in the **Latch Table** preamble. That same Action cleanup calls `remove_train_route_run(train_id)` only when the abort latch is consumed after the dispatcher cancel step (or the dispatcher-cancel-skipped no-active-path branch) has run. Aborting a dwelling train therefore takes that same path: Action cancels any live path (or skips the dispatcher cancel when none exists), then `remove_train_route_run(...)` writes `station_exit_request` (the later Action station-exit consumer exits dwell) and flips the run's active-state predicate.

- Do not add a synchronous `RouteExecutor.continue_route_run_after_eb(...)` hook. EB release is handled through the ordinary conditions and latches: the EB activation has already written `pending_path_cancel_request` with `error.origin = "eb"`, which Action commits and which sets `RouteRun.path_cancelled = True` via the cancellation callback. `TrainController.eb.release()` clears only `eb.active`; the ordinary post-command state evaluation moves a non-dwelling stopped authority-free controller to `READY`. The same train's later Plan route-deviation-cleanup step consumes `path_cancelled` once the controller is `READY` with no live path. The next `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` tick reruns the ordinary planning kernel from the current physical position: covered-task index advance for already-passed `waypoint` tasks, `RouteExecutor._find_next_task_target(train_id)` to resolve the next task, and a brand-new `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)`. This flow does not reuse, complete, or preserve the cancelled pre-EB path chain.
- The derived `current_waypoint_index` reads `None` when no task has finished yet (no `task_runs[i].finished_at` is set). There is no "synthetic current-location start stop" branch: a one-off reposition route is authored as a single-task `stop` route. With start mode `FIRST`, `current_waypoint_index is None` means "no task has been completed yet" and `Route.tasks[0]` is the first planning target; `NEAREST` / `SPECIFIC` seed a later start position instead (see **Run start-mode seeding**).
- `current_waypoint_index` is the route-progress cursor: derived from `task_runs[i].finished_at`, it always marks the last task the train has actually finished. There is no separate stored planning cursor in v1; whenever any stage needs the next-task index, it calls `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` afresh.
- The initial `RouteRun.direction` is `"forward"` through the stored route order. The route plan remains an ordered list in v1. Reversible round-trip behavior comes from the predecessor `RouteTaskRun.walk_direction` and the validated task-group boundaries used by `RouteRun._append_next_walk_task(...)`, never from `RouteRun.direction`, plus the direction `RouteExecutor._find_next_task_target(train_id, ...)` projects and Plan commits to `RouteRun.direction`; there is no second linked or reversed route structure. `RouteRun.direction` only records the most recently armed task's direction — it is not the source the walk reflects from.
- When a new target is resolved, `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` returns the next-task projection and resolved target candidate. Plan sets `direction` to the resolved direction — at step `592a` from the fresh projection, and again at step `66aa` from the accepted projection on a successful create/extend — and after a successful create/extend writes `task_runs[walk_position].resolved_target` (where `walk_position` is the helper's returned index) to the target pair that call returned, per Planning Kernel step `66aa`. Route planning must not look beyond the resolved task in one pathfinder request.
- An `extend_path(...)` call that did not grow authority while a live path still exists, and a `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(...)` for the matching live path, both leave physical progress unchanged. There is no separate planning-cursor rollback; later Plan calls `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` from the current shared route, current physical progress, and the current live authority end or no-authority stopped position as applicable, and that helper resolves the next task fresh. `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` failure follows the same rule: the next Plan simply re-invokes `_find_next_task_target(train_id)`.
- `RouteExecutor` reads the live path id via `PathDispatcher.active_path_id_by_train(train_id)`. A single live path may remain active across multiple task segments. After `waypoint` consumption or `stop` completion — both Observe events — `task_runs[i].finished_at` is recorded for the consumed task (the derived `current_waypoint_index` advances to that index automatically), and only a later progress callback or later Plan may discover the next task on the same `path_id` when authority is still live. `dwell` completion is a Plan event instead: the Plan dwell-complete step writes `station_exit_request` and returns; the next task resolves on the next eligible Plan, after Action performs the dwell exit, per the `dwell` task contract above. A single `RouteExecutor.handle_train_advanced(...)` callback never consumes more than one task.
- UI consumers wanting "why does the train have no live authority?" call `NotificationCenter.latest_error_for("train", train_id)` and show the most recent blocking event whatever its `origin` — `"planning_failed"`, `"task_skipped"`, `"run_stalled"`, `"wedge"`, `"meet_hold"`, or `"dwell_cab_gate"`, per **Error events**, plus the controller's live `lookahead` diagnostics. (Watchdogs and alert notifications are Out of Scope; see the **Out of Scope** section.)
- **No separate cancellation-recovery sub-state.** Do not add a separate controller operational sub-state for cancellation recovery in v1.
- **Deviation braking.** When a deviation invalidates a live path, the cancel latch holds while the zero-limit / EB protocol per step `826a` stops the train (the `"deviation"` reason code applies while the path is still live).
- **Revocation braking.** A revocation under unchanged authority stops the train through ordinary obstruction braking, not the zero-limit protocol. When a revocation invalidates a live path while its `resource_sequence` and the train's mapped head are unchanged — the Observe truncation-failure case under **Authority truncation** — the head stays mappable, so `826a` does not apply. The taken block ahead is now an in-path resource conflict, and ordinary ATC braking under `atc_limit_reason_code = "obstruction"` (see **the canonical `atc_limit_reason_code` enumeration**) stops the train at the ordinary overspeed margin, not the escalation override.
- **Recovery gate.** In either case the cancel then commits at rest and clears controller authority. The deferred recovery gate is the `path_cancelled` latch (see Latch Table). `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(...)` sets it and records diagnostic context immediately in Action, but does not choose a new target or create fresh authority there.
- **Consumption and replan.** Once the train reaches the stopped no-authority state, `TrainController.eb.release()` clears EB and the ordinary post-command state evaluation moves the non-dwelling controller to `READY`. The same train's later Plan route-deviation-cleanup step consumes `path_cancelled`. A later eligible Plan then re-enters ordinary planning: covered-task index advance for already-passed `waypoint` tasks, then `RouteExecutor._find_next_task_target(train_id)` to resolve the next task.
- **Covered-task index advance.** (Canonical home for the **covered-waypoint** and **covered-stop** rules.) At the start of each Plan tick, `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` reads the train's current span via its injected `ControllerRegistry.get_or_create(train_id).get_current_span()` and walks the current directed route from `current_waypoint_index`. For each next non-finished task on the directed walk:
  - **covered-waypoint** (`task_kind == "waypoint"`): the task is covered when its resolved target block (resolved live for this purpose) is anywhere inside the current span, and in addition either the walk-position is on the initial walk (`walk_position < len(Route.tasks)`) or the train's head is not in that block. When it is covered, call `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(i)` (the canonical paired-clock writer) and continue. A waypoint the train physically passed mid-span is covered even after the head has moved beyond it, so span membership is the right test for whether the train has been there. The head condition is what separates "already passed" from "has not left yet" on the walk-positions a `CIRCULAR` or `ROUND_TRIP` walk appends: a target block the train's head still sits in is one the walk must travel back to, so the train reaches it by running the walk rather than by standing in it. On the initial walk that same overlap means the train started there, so coverage finishes it.
  - **covered-stop** (`task_kind == "stop"`): finish it through `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(i)` only when the train is stopped, no active path exists, AND the train's **head** is in the destination block (e.g. a route authored while the train already sits at the destination platform, which has no path for the dispatcher to complete). The covered-stop is head-anchored, not span-anchored: a long train at a dead-end can have its tail spill into the next block — which on a turnaround is the very destination it must reverse back to — while its head is still short of it, and a bare span-membership test would wrongly declare that stop complete and finish the route without the train ever turning around. While the train is rolling or a live path exists, coverage never finishes a stop and it is served only by route-committed stop arrival.
  - `task_kind == "dwell"`: return without advancing — dwell is handled by the Plan dwell-entry step inside `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)`.
  - `task_kind == "run"`: return without advancing — block coverage never finishes a run; Plan run step `6a0d` owns its timer, service stop, authority release, and completion.

  There is no separate `_advance_past_covered_waypoints(...)` helper or `_skip_waypoint(...)` helper in v1; the index advance is just a small loop inside `tick_train_plan`.

**Canonical Route-Progress Events**

- `current_waypoint_index` advances automatically (it is a derived read) when any of these route-owned events writes `task_runs[i].finished_at` in v1:
  - head-based `task_kind == "waypoint"` consumption in `RouteExecutor.handle_train_advanced(...)`, at most one task per head-advance callback
  - `task_kind == "stop"` arrival recorded by Observe step `bc55` of the **Stop-arrival procedure**
  - `task_kind == "dwell"` completion after the dwell timer elapses following a route-committed stop arrival
  - Plan step `6a0d` completing a `task_kind == "run"` after its simulated-time window, service stop, and normal-progress authority release
  - Plan's covered-task index advance for already-covered `waypoint` tasks (including post-cancellation reconciliation) and the covered-stop case for `stop` tasks (see the covered-task index advance canonical home)
  - Plan broken-task handling writing a skipped missing-target task directly (the explicit successful-progress-helper exception)
- Head-based `task_kind == "waypoint"` consumption is a route-owned in-motion progress event, not a dispatcher stop-completion event. The canonical trigger chain is `TrainPhysics.tick(...)` → `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)` → `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` → `RouteExecutor.handle_train_advanced(...)`. The callback contract is fully defined once in the **Dispatcher progress/completion flow** section; consult that section. Summary: each callback consumes at most one task. If the reported block matches the next non-finished task's resolved target, the callback records `task_runs[i].finished_at` (the derived `current_waypoint_index` advances with that write) and returns. Non-matching block reports are no-ops on the route side; intermediate tasks the train physically passed are reconciled by the next Plan's covered-task index advance.
- Already-covered `waypoint` normalization is a Plan step: it calls `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(i)` for any next-on-walk `waypoint` task the covered-waypoint test finds covered (see the covered-task index advance canonical home). `task_kind == "stop"` tasks are not skipped this way: they are served only by route-committed stop arrival (except the head-anchored covered-stop case — see the covered-task index advance canonical home). `task_kind == "run"` is never skipped by coverage and is completed only by step `6a0d`. Plan may run the covered-waypoint advance on multiple consecutive tasks in one pass before requesting authority, up to the one-scan-per-pass bound in that same canonical home; post-cancellation covered-task reconciliation uses that same mechanism. V1 has no route-edit or operator-skip request that declares a present-target task finished. There is no separate `_skip_waypoint(...)` helper.
- There is no stored planning cursor in v1. The "next task to plan against" is always the index returned by the latest `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` call — for *planning*; the physically served row is `find_next_completion_task(...)` and the acquired-authority row is `find_armed_task(...)`, per the **Separate cursor model**. `current_waypoint_index` is the only route-progress cursor, but it too is read-only derived from `task_runs[i].finished_at` rather than stored; it changes only when a task is actually served: waypoint head entry/coverage, stop completion, dwell exit, run completion, or broken-task skip. A successful `create_path(...)` / `extend_path(...)` writes `resolved_target` but does not change it.

**Route-executor state reads**

- `RouteExecutor` must read live operational state from `TrainController`, not from mirrored runtime fields on `Train`.
- Departure, retry, arrival, dwell, and waiting decisions must use controller state as the operational source of truth.
- `Train` may still expose persisted or UI-facing state, but route-control decisions must not depend on it being a live mirror.
- Manual driving is `control_mode == manual`, not a separate operational state. A route-managed manual train still uses ordinary `READY` / `RUNNING_*` states and dispatcher authority; the difference from ATO is how movement begins and is driven, not whether `RouteExecutor` owns the waypoint plan. In particular, manual `READY` must not block route-side path creation. It changes only what `depart()` means after authority exists.

**Contention snapshot**

- `PathDispatcher.get_waiting_conflict(train_id, stored_resolved_target, acquisition_mode, manual_override, acquisition_cap_block_id=None, required_candidate_resource_keys=None) -> Optional[WaitingConflict]` is the canonical forward-resource acquisition read for a blocked waiter. `stored_resolved_target` is the `ResolvedRouteTarget` from `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)`; the remaining arguments are the same effective route policy and tick-start meet constraints Plan would pass to `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)`. `WaitingConflict` carries `waiting_block_id`, `failed_resource_type`, `failed_resource_id`, and `holding_train_ids`. Dispatcher reruns that exact pathfinder/eligibility walk, identifies the first failed resource, and resolves holders from live state: physical occupants first; then a block reservation's path owner or every conflicting switch lock/protection owner; duplicates removed and train IDs sorted by runnable order. A same-train holder is retained. It returns `None` when authority reaches the supplied target, no active path exists, no viable suffix exists, or the failure has no live train owner. `PathDispatcher.get_waiting_for_block_id(train_id, stored_resolved_target, acquisition_mode, manual_override, acquisition_cap_block_id=None, required_candidate_resource_keys=None)` is the read-model projection of `waiting_block_id` from this full result; it forwards the complete request and does not rerun the walk.
- `RouteExecutor` builds one **contention snapshot** per tick after `RouteExecutor.order_runnable_trains(...)` returns and before the first Plan. For each train with an armed task, it obtains `stored_resolved_target` from `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)`, resolves the run's effective acquisition mode and manual override from the route registry, and calls the full `PathDispatcher.get_waiting_conflict(...)` interface above with `acquisition_cap_block_id=None` and `required_candidate_resource_keys=None`. Meet assignment is computed later from this snapshot, so no meet constraint exists yet; the snapshot measures the unconstrained live conflict that meet coordination must resolve. The snapshot has `edges: List[{waiting_block_id, waiting_train_id, holding_train_id, effective_priority}]`, one edge for every holder in each `WaitingConflict`, in runnable-order then holder-order. It also has `highest_waiter_by_block: Dict[block_id, {train_id, effective_priority}]`, derived from those edges with highest priority first and runnable order as the tie-break. The release rule reads the map; wedge and meet detection read the complete edges. A block with no waiter has no map entry.
- The snapshot reads tick-start committed state only through the full injected `PathDispatcher.get_waiting_conflict(...)` projection plus the override-aware route-registry read. It is recomputed every tick, retained across no ticks, and carries no gating predicate, so it is not a latch, has no writer helper, and holds no Latch-Table entry. UI/read-model code calls `PathDispatcher.get_waiting_for_block_id(...)` with the same complete request payload; neither consumer reimplements the walk.
- Two consumers read it in v1. The contention-driven release branch of Planning Kernel step `66aa` (**idle-hold maintenance and release**) reads it to learn whether a strictly-higher-priority run is blocked on a block this run holds as a not-yet-entered future reservation. **Meet coordination** (below) reads the contending pairs it records to seed meet conflict detection.

**Why this shape.** Each train plans alone in its own Plan, so without one shared tick-start view no train can tell that a block it is holding is the block a higher-priority train is stuck behind. The snapshot is the single place that view is assembled. Assembling it once per tick — rather than having every run recompute every other run's `waiting_for_block_id` — keeps each Plan authority step a constant-time read per held block.

**Wedge detection**

- A **wedge** is a set of trains that are each stopped with nowhere to go, where every member is waiting for a resource another member holds. The one-train case counts: a train whose own body holds the resource its authority needs next is a wedge of size one. `RouteExecutor.wedge_report` is the per-tick view of the wedges present, built alongside the contention snapshot, once per tick after `order_runnable_trains(...)` returns the runnable order and before the first train's Plan begins — so it reads tick-start committed state only. Like the contention snapshot it is read-only coordinator state — recomputed every tick, retained across no ticks, carrying no gating predicate — so it is not a latch, has no writer helper, and holds no Latch-Table entry.
- A train takes part only when it is **stopped with nowhere to go**: `TrainController.is_stopped()` is true (the canonical stopped predicate) and it is standing at its live authority boundary with no clearance left to advance, which is the zero-clearance hold `lookahead` reports against that live authority. A train that is still rolling is never a member, because the resource it waits for may clear before it gets there — and when the waited-for resource is held by its own tail, advancing is exactly what clears it.
- Each participating train contributes the matching edges from `RouteExecutor.contention_snapshot.edges`. A cycle in that graph is a wedge, and an edge that points back at the train that drew it is a one-train wedge. Holder identity therefore works for block occupancy/reservation and for switch lock/protection conflicts; wedge detection does not try to infer a switch holder from the waiting block.
- Detection covers trains that hold live authority, which is what the complete `PathDispatcher.get_waiting_conflict(...)` request evaluates before `PathDispatcher.get_waiting_for_block_id(...)` projects its block ID. A train with no live authority is not wedged: it holds nothing it acquired, and why its task could not be served is already recorded by **Unreachable and broken task handling**, which emits its own error event and projects `"STALLED"`.
- `RouteExecutor` emits one event per wedge, with `operation = "build_wedge_report"`, `kind = "warning"`, and `ErrorRecord.origin = "wedge"`, naming the trains in the cycle and the blocks the cycle runs through, on the tick that wedge first appears, and not again until its payload changes, per **Emit on change, not per tick** in **Error events**. It carries the ordinary fields defined in the **Event schema**, and the **Event log** records it like any other event.
- The report changes no runtime state. It gates no planning step, caps no acquisition, and cancels no path. The only release path for a stalled hold remains the idle-hold maintenance and release rule in Planning Kernel step `66aa`.

**Why this shape.** Clearing a wedge takes a train moving, moving takes authority, and the missing authority is what makes it a wedge — so the resolution is physical, and an operator taking manual control is the one actor who can carry it out. What the operator needs from the software is therefore the diagnosis: which trains are involved and which blocks the cycle runs through, said once, rather than several trains that each separately project `"STALLED"` with nothing to show that they are waiting on each other. Cancelling a path returns only reservations a train has not yet entered, so for trains already standing on the contested blocks there is no cancellation the detector could order that would free anything.

**Meet coordination**

- After the contention snapshot (above), `RouteExecutor` computes a per-tick **meet assignment**. Each train's entry carries `meet_ceiling_block_id: Optional[str]` and `candidate_resource_keys`, the selected candidate's ordered list of `(resource_type, resource_id, entry_edge, exit_edge)` values. The ceiling caps how far the train may reserve authority this tick, and the candidate keys make the later dispatcher request use the same route that meet coordination evaluated. Like the contention snapshot, the assignment is read-only tick-start coordinator state — recomputed every tick and retained across no ticks — so it is not a latch, has no writer helper, and holds no Latch-Table entry. v1 stores no persistent cross-train meet plan.
- **Conflict detection.** For each distinct `(waiting_train_id, holding_train_id)` pair in the complete contention edges, `RouteExecutor` resolves both trains' current next targets through `_find_next_task_target(...)`, then calls the same `RailwayPathfinder.query_graph_walks(...)` comparison Plan uses for every eligible current-span end and target candidate. Candidate lists keep canonical order. It examines candidate pairs in lexicographic `(waiting candidate rank, holding candidate rank)` order and selects the first pair whose walks remain individually viable. It then finds each maximal run of resources the two walks traverse with conflicting frames — opposing block traversal direction, or a shared switch whose two routes `routes_conflict`. Those runs are the contested zones. If either target cannot resolve, either candidate list is empty, or no candidate pair has a contested zone, this contention pair produces no meet assignment. Routes that share only non-conflicting frames produce no assignment.
- **Capacity.** A contested zone has sufficient capacity when the contenders can be given non-conflicting routes through it (distinct blocks, every shared switch on routes that do not `routes_conflict`); otherwise capacity is insufficient — a single bidirectional track, or a crossover/throat whose required routes `routes_conflict`.
- **Existing commitment decides before priority.** Before comparing priorities, meet coordination checks the contested zone's live occupancy and reservations. If one contender already occupies or holds authority on any resource in the zone, that contender stays admitted and every opposing contender is held. This commitment ends only when that train has neither occupancy nor reservation anywhere in the zone. A priority edit cannot reverse authority or physical entry that has already committed the meet.
- **Assignment when the zone is uncommitted** is a deterministic function of `RouteRun.effective_priority(route_registry)` (per **RouteRun overrides**) and the stable tie-break order `RouteExecutor.order_runnable_trains(...)` uses:
  - Sufficient capacity: each contender keeps a distinct non-conflicting route, and its `meet_ceiling_block_id` is the far entry of the contested zone on its route, so neither reserves the other's exit track before reaching the zone. Both proceed and pass within the zone; a contender's ceiling lifts on the first tick its route no longer conflicts with the others.
  - Insufficient capacity: the highest-priority contender is admitted with no ceiling — it reserves to its normal route target through the zone — and each lower-priority contender's `meet_ceiling_block_id` is the furthest holding point (`Block.is_holding_point`, per the **Block** field schema) on its route before the contested zone. A lower-priority contender that has no holding point before the zone receives no ceiling and falls back to ordinary best-effort truncation; `RouteExecutor` emits one `kind = "warning"` event with `ErrorRecord.origin = "meet_hold"` recording that the layout offers no holding place to meet at.
- **Plan consumption.** The meet event names `operation = "compute_meet_assignment"`.
  - **Passing the selected candidate and ceiling.** Planning Kernel step `66aa` passes the assignment's `candidate_resource_keys` as `required_candidate_resource_keys` on `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` / `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)`. When the assignment also carries a `meet_ceiling_block_id`, it passes that value as `acquisition_cap_block_id` while keeping `requested_destination_block_id` (and the `task_runs[walk_position].resolved_target` written on success) equal to the route task's real target, per the **Acquisition-cap rule**. Dispatcher may acquire only the matching candidate. If live state has made that candidate unavailable, the call returns the ordinary no-growth/blocked result and the next tick recomputes the assignment; it must not silently choose another candidate that meet coordination did not evaluate.
  - **Effect on authority.** The dispatcher caps the acquired authority at the ceiling, so the derived `Path.get_authority_end_block_id()` lands on the ceiling while the requested target stays the farther route stop. Because `Path.get_authority_end_block_id() != requested_destination_block_id`, the capped authority does not complete and the train holds at the ceiling. The route target is unchanged. On the first tick the train carries no ceiling, step `66aa` passes no cap and requests it. A train aimed at a holding-point ceiling therefore receives clean authority to that holding point and waits there, instead of relying on best-effort truncation to land it there.
  - **Contradictory acquisition mode.** When the assignment writes a ceiling short of the train's requested target while that run's `RouteRun.effective_acquisition_mode(route_registry)` is `AcquisitionMode.all_or_nothing`, the two are contradictory and the train will hold without acquiring anything until the ceiling lifts (per the **Acquisition-cap rule**).
  - **Operator event.** Meet coordination emits one `kind = "warning"` event with `operation = "compute_meet_assignment"` and `ErrorRecord.origin = "meet_hold"` at the moment it writes that ceiling, carrying `train_id`, the assigned `meet_ceiling_block_id`, the run's `requested_destination_block_id`, and the effective acquisition mode, so the operator can see why the train is stopped. It follows **Emit on change, not per tick** in **Error events**, so a ceiling that moves to a different block is a changed payload and a new event: the acquisition calls themselves stay silent and are retried every eligible Plan tick for as long as the meet holds.
- **Stability.** The assignment is recomputed every tick. Effective priority chooses the admitted contender only while no contender has occupancy or authority in the contested zone. Once a contender enters or reserves the zone, that live commitment keeps it admitted until its occupancy and reservations have cleared the zone. Priority edits during that interval do not reverse the current meet; they apply when the zone next becomes uncommitted. If the selected train failed to acquire anything in the zone, there is no commitment, so the next tick may legitimately choose again from current priority and world state.
- **Composition.** The meet assignment constrains candidate selection and may cap acquired authority; it never changes a route target and never reserves a resource. All acquisition still runs through the interlocked `BlockManager` / `SwitchManager` path with flank protection and the item-11 truncation exclusions intact. A stale candidate constraint fails closed for that tick instead of selecting an unevaluated route. Meet coordination reduces how often best-effort truncation, the contention-driven release (step `66aa`), and the reversal-trap exclusion fire, but those stay the safety floor — including for trains the assignment never governs, such as manual or unrouted trains.

**Why this shape.** A meet is a global decision — which train takes the shared track and where the other waits — that no single train's Plan can make from its own view, so it is computed once per tick, before the first train's Plan begins, where the global cross-train view exists. Re-deriving it each tick avoids retained cross-train planning state. Live occupancy and reservations supply the stability after commitment, while effective priority chooses only before commitment. Passing the selected candidate to dispatcher makes Plan act on the same route the global decision checked. Resource locks remain owned by `BlockManager` and `SwitchManager`; a stale assignment can only prevent acquisition for one tick.

**Planning Kernel**

- Plan is a state-machine: each canonical step has explicit preconditions and is a no-op when those preconditions are not met. The kernel never creates fresh authority while the train has not yet reached a stopped recovery point, while any teardown/recovery latch is still dirty, while the controller is `OFF`, or while the `RouteRun` is pending/inside a dwell step.
- Eligibility precondition for the planning kernel's authority-acquisition step (step `66aa`) and the re-resolve step (step `592a` when it would lead to acquisition): `RouteExecutor` may run those steps only when one of the following is true:
  - the train has live authority (`PathDispatcher.active_path_id_by_train(train_id) is not None`) AND `controller.active_conditions ∩ {PATH_CANCEL_PENDING, ROUTE_ABORT_PENDING, ROUTE_DEACTIVATE_PENDING} == ∅`, in which case only step `66aa`'s `extend_path(...)` branch is allowed. The latch exclusion prevents Plan from extending a live path that Action is about to cancel; or
  - `RouteExecutor.is_clean_for_create(train_id)` is true per the **`ControllerCondition` set** canonical home, in which case the create branch is allowed.
- **Steps run in order, gated by their own preconditions.** Steps `5fc7`, `70c3`, `c481`, `a5c6`, and `3a37` (deviation cleanup, dwell-complete, helper lookup, covered-task advance, dwell-entry) are reached on every Plan entry, but a step whose precondition does not hold is a no-op. Step `c481`'s dwell branch routes a valid `dwell` projection to step `3a37`; `a5c6` and `6a0d` have nothing to do for that task kind.
  - **Teardown outranks normal progress.** While any of `pending_path_cancel_request`, `pending_route_abort`, `pending_power_off`, or `pending_route_deactivate` is set, steps `70c3`, `6a0d`, `a5c6`, and `3a37` make no timing, progress, dwell, departure, or authority write. Step `5fc7` may still clear an older cancellation-recovery latch when its own gate holds, and `c481` may read only far enough to determine that no normal work may commit. Action owns teardown; `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(...)` writes `station_exit_request` when the controller is in `RUNNING_AT_STATION`, and the later Action station-exit consumer performs the exit.
- The derived `display_state == "DEVIATED"` / `"CANCELLED"` projection is not itself a gate; it clears automatically when `path_cancelled` (and its `path_cancel_was_deviation` companion) is consumed by the same Plan route-deviation-cleanup step (step `5fc7`).
- If the controller is `OFF`, Plan is skipped. If eligibility preconditions are otherwise unmet (still braking, dirty handoff), Plan returns and waits for a later tick.
- A train with an open **Lighting-voltage calibration** run is skipped for this tick's Plan entirely, the same way an `OFF` train is. A train with an open speed-calibration pass is not skipped: Plan step `c9e1` may create and assign only the pass's current calibration one-off route, after which the ordinary Plan steps allocate and advance it. A request for a non-calibration route abandons the pass and holds that assignment until the calibration route's Action teardown has completed, so Plan never sees both routes assigned.
- For the EB case, the same eligibility rule applies: while `eb.active == True`, `controller.is_recovery_clean` is false per the **`ControllerCondition` set** canonical home and Plan produces no authority. After `TrainController.eb.release()` clears the condition and the ordinary post-command state evaluation reaches `READY`, the next eligible Plan runs the planning kernel normally.
- One Plan pass owns the planning-side `RouteRun` mutation in this canonical order (for the `RouteRun` writes made outside Plan, see the Observe, Plan, and Action Table's Observe and Action rows, the **`current_route_status` write contract**, and **RouteRun overrides**). `RouteExecutor` is the canonical owner of every step; `SimulationController` invokes the kernel through `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(train_id, delta_seconds)`, and `RouteExecutor` resolves the controller through its injected controller registry. Steps:
  0. `c9e1` — **Prepare the active speed-calibration leg.** When the train has an open speed-calibration pass whose current leg is ready, create and assign the pass's calibration one-off `Route` and write `CalibrationRun.active_leg_route_id` (see **Speed calibration**). A train with no open speed-calibration pass does nothing here, and this step never touches a non-calibration route — the ordinary allocation at step `9c4f` picks the assigned route up. Continue to step `9c4f`.
  1. `9c4f` — **RouteRun (re)allocation.** Look up the train's currently-`RUNNING` `RouteRun` (`RouteExecutor.execution_state_for(train_id)`). If one exists, continue to step `5fc7`.
     - Otherwise, scan the route registry for the `Route` with `train_id ∈ Route.assigned_train_ids` and `Route.is_active == True`. At most one exists, per the single-assignment rule in **Route assignment writers** — this is the train's upcoming route. If none is found, Plan returns (no work).
     - If one is found, allocate a new `RouteRun` against that `route_id`:
       - write `route_id`;
       - sample `RouteRun.started_at = time.time()` and read `RouteRun.started_at_operating = AppState.operating_time` in the same allocation operation;
       - set `direction = "forward"`;
       - allocate `task_runs` with `len(Route.tasks)` entries — one per task with `task_index = 0..N-1`, `run_elapsed_seconds = 0.0`, and all Optional fields `None`;
       - set `current_route_status = "RUNNING"`;
       - seed the starting walk-position per **Run start-mode seeding** (for `NEAREST` / `SPECIFIC` this pre-finishes the skipped prefix so the run begins at the chosen stop; `FIRST` leaves the run at `task_runs[0]`).
     - The newly-allocated run is the canonical home of all subsequent Plan mutation for that train this tick. Continue to step `5fc7`.
  2. `5fc7` — **Route-deviation cleanup** (multi-tick latch). When `RouteRun.path_cancelled == True` AND `controller.is_recovery_clean` is true, clear `path_cancelled` and `path_cancel_was_deviation` (the derived `display_state == "DEVIATED"` / `"CANCELLED"` projection clears with them).
  3. `70c3` — **Dwell-complete timer check.** Finish the dwell when all four hold:
     - `TrainController.ops.state == RUNNING_AT_STATION`;
     - `controller.eb.active == False`;
     - `RouteTask.should_depart(...)` is satisfied per **Task time semantics**;
     - no path-cancel, route-abort, power-off, or route-deactivate latch is set.

     Finishing the dwell means: call `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(walk_position)` (which samples and writes both finish clocks and appends the next walk-position, leaving `delay_class = None` on this `dwell` row); then write `station_exit_request` and return for that train. The Action station-exit consumer performs `TrainController.finish_dwell()`; the next task resolves on the next eligible Plan, because the controller stays `RUNNING_AT_STATION` through this pass and cannot depart until Action has performed the exit.
     - Dwell completion is ineligible while `ControllerCondition.EB_LATCHED` is active, under the general rule that EB blocks every Plan branch that would complete dwell, create/extend authority, or depart. Once `TrainController.eb.release()` clears the condition, the next eligible Plan pass may finish the dwell.
  4. `c481` — **Look up the next non-finished task** on the directed walk by calling `_find_next_task_target(train_id)`.
     - If it returns `None`, continue directly to step `592a`, which owns terminal-walk completion.
     - When the projection's `failure_kind == missing_target` — the task's own `task_location` is gone, whatever its `task_kind` — broken-skip it per **Unreachable and broken task handling** and re-run the lookup. Repeat until the lookup returns a valid task, the walk goes terminal, or the pass's `len(Route.tasks)` scan budget is spent; this step and step `592a` share that one budget.
     - When the scan finds no valid task at all on a `RouteMode.CIRCULAR` / `RouteMode.ROUND_TRIP` walk, this step follows the no-valid-task rule in **Unreachable and broken task handling**: when a live path still exists it latches the ordinary cancel (`origin = "revoked"`, `kind = "info"`) and returns without setting the flag — unless `phase_latches.path_cancel_request` is already set, in which case it writes nothing and returns — and it sets `RouteRun.no_reachable_task = True` and returns only once no live path remains. Any lookup that finds a valid task clears the flag.
     - Then branch on the valid projection: `task_kind == "dwell"` goes to step `3a37` (dwell-entry); every other kind continues to step `6a0d`.
     - Step `c481` reads the next task only to run the broken-skip and pick the branch here (terminal walk, no-reachable-task stall, dwell-entry, run timer, or covered-task advance). It does not carry the resolved target past a cursor-moving step, so step `592a` still re-resolves the acquisition target.
  5. `6a0d` — **Run timer, service stop, and normal-progress authority release.** This step applies when the projection from `c481` is a present-target `task_kind == "run"` task and no higher-priority teardown latch is set.
     - **Timer.** Add this tick's non-negative `delta_seconds` to `task_runs[walk_position].run_elapsed_seconds`, capped at the task's required `task_time`. While the stored elapsed value remains below `task_time`, continue to step `a5c6` and ordinary authority acquisition.
     - **Service stop.** Once it reaches `task_time`, set the `ops.service_stop_active` latch through the idempotent `TrainController.begin_service_stop()`. If live authority exists and no run-completion release request is already pending, call `set_path_cancel_request(error=None, kind="info", run_complete=True)`. Then return while any of these holds:
       - the train is moving;
       - that release request remains pending;
       - `received_path_plan is not None`.
     - **Finish.** Once the train is stopped with no live authority and no pending release request, call `TrainController.consume_service_stop()`, then `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(walk_position)`, and return for the tick. The gating predicate above belongs to this step; the accessor itself only clears the latch.
     - This step is the only writer of `run_elapsed_seconds`; head entry, coverage, stop arrival, and the cancellation callback never finish a run. A missing/unavailable run target is handled later by the ordinary broken/unreachable path and does not accrue timer time on that tick.
  6. `a5c6` — **Covered-task index advance.** While the next non-finished task is `task_kind == "waypoint"` and the covered-waypoint test in the covered-task index advance canonical home finds it covered, call `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(i)`. The advance stops when the next task is:
     - `task_kind == "stop"` — except finish it in the covered-stop case, per the covered-task index advance canonical home; while the train is rolling or a live path exists, block coverage never finishes a stop;
     - `task_kind == "dwell"` — continue to step `3a37`;
     - `task_kind == "run"` — run step `6a0d` is its only completion owner;
     - or no further task fits coverage.

     This advance covers at most one full `len(Route.tasks)` scan within a single Plan pass — its own budget, the same size as the one steps `c481` and `592a` share for the broken-task skip in **Unreachable and broken task handling**. `RouteMode.CIRCULAR` and `RouteMode.ROUND_TRIP` keep appending walk-positions as each one finishes, so the scan bound is what ends the pass and hands the tick back.
  7. `3a37` — **Dwell-entry transition.** Write `station_entry_request` (the Action station-entry consumer calls `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()`) when all five hold:
     - the next non-finished task has `task_kind == "dwell"`;
     - the predecessor task's `finished_at` is set;
     - `controller.is_recovery_clean` is true;
     - `controller.cab ∈ {"A", "B"}`;
     - no path-cancel, route-abort, power-off, or route-deactivate latch is set.

     `RouteExecutor` samples the dwell row's `started_at = time.time()` and `started_at_operating = AppState.operating_time` locally and writes them to `RouteRun.task_runs[walk_position]` before writing `station_entry_request`, so the dwell window begins when the train is actually standing at the platform. The Action station-entry consumer calls `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()`, which performs the state transition only; it never reads or writes `RouteRun`. Return for that tick — no path creation while dwell is pending or active. If the controller is already `RUNNING_AT_STATION` at step `3a37`, return before any of that write, since the dwell row's `started_at` / `started_at_operating` were already sampled on the tick dwell entry actually happened. When the first three conditions hold but `controller.cab ∈ {"A", "B"}` does not, the train is held out of dwell with no cab selected; per **Emit on change, not per tick**, this step emits one `kind = "warning"` event carrying an `ErrorRecord` with `origin = "dwell_cab_gate"` and `text` naming the train and stating that dwell entry is waiting on a cab selection, the first tick it observes the block and not again while the same cab-gate condition persists, so `NotificationCenter.latest_error_for(...)` can answer why the run is not progressing.
  8. `592a` — **Re-resolve the next target.** Call `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` afresh. The `c481` lookup picked the Plan branch but predates any progress move made by step `a5c6`, so this resolve is the one that feeds authority acquisition. A completing step `6a0d` returns for the tick, and step `3a37` enters dwell without moving route progress and also returns.
     - If it returns `None`, the directed walk is terminal. When `PathDispatcher.active_path_id_by_train(train_id) is not None` — reachable only when every remaining task was broken-skipped, since a terminal stop or terminal run already clears the live path before its walk goes terminal — this step does not call `finish_route_run(...)` yet: when `phase_latches.path_cancel_request` is not already set, it calls `controller.route_hooks.phase_latches.set_path_cancel_request(error, kind="info", ...)` with `error.origin = "revoked"` per the **Writer-helper rule**; when a request is already pending it writes nothing. Either way it returns for the tick. Otherwise (no live path) it calls `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)` directly and returns for that tick, per the terminal-walk rule in **Canonical Next-Target Selection**. A later eligible Plan pass, run once the Action cancel has committed and no live path remains, reaches this same terminal-walk branch and finishes the run. This fires only for `RouteMode.ONE_OFF`; `RouteMode.CIRCULAR` / `RouteMode.ROUND_TRIP` never resolve to `None`.
     - When the fresh projection's `failure_kind == missing_target`, broken-skip it per **Unreachable and broken task handling** and re-run this resolve, drawing on the same per-pass scan budget as step `c481` and following the same no-valid-task rule on the same condition — latch the ordinary cancel and return, unless already pending, with `no_reachable_task` set only once no live path remains. This branch exists because step `a5c6` can move progress onto a task step `c481` never looked up.
     - Otherwise use the returned projection's `walk_position` and set `direction` from that projection.
     - Read `armed = RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)`. When it is not `None` and the live path already holds `armed.stored_resolved_target`'s block as its armed target, the request contract for this attempt is that stored pair; otherwise this arms a new target block and the freshly resolved projection's `resolved_target` is the candidate, per **Live-path target re-resolution**. Do not write `task_runs[i].resolved_target` yet.
  9. `66aa` — **Authority acquisition.**
     - **Waypoint lookahead.** Before acquiring, decide which target this tick arms. Arm the next unfinished task's target instead of re-arming the currently armed one when both hold:
       - the currently armed task has `task_kind == "waypoint"` and the live authority already reaches it;
       - the count of `block` resources in `resource_sequence` strictly after the train head's `current_resource_index` is below `WAYPOINT_LOOKAHEAD_BLOCKS` (**Runtime settings**).

       This way the extend attempt happens before the train has to brake for the current terminal. Plan reaches that task by calling `RouteExecutor._find_next_task_target(train_id, after_walk_position=<the currently armed waypoint's walk_position, from RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)>)`; when the next position lies beyond the current tail, that helper appends exactly the next directed-walk row through `RouteRun._append_next_walk_task(from_walk_position=<that same armed walk_position>)`. The Plan caller never indexes `task_runs` or `Route.tasks` directly, and the helper never mutates an existing row or `RouteRun.direction`.
     - While a lookahead target is armed, `walk_position` is the returned lookahead index, not the served waypoint's, at the two writes this step performs: the `resolved_target` write below and the accompanying `RouteRun.direction` write. Later `extend_path(...)` retries in **Exact `RouteExecutor` tick calls** and the `Path.reaches_target(...)` idle-hold predicate do not re-derive `walk_position` from a fresh resolve; they read the acquired row directly through `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)`. Arming a lookahead target therefore flips `RouteRun.direction` when that target sits past a `ROUND_TRIP` apex.
     - Arming stays one target at a time: the newly armed target becomes the authority terminal, and the next eligible tick may repeat the step for the target after it.
