The walk-forward stops at the first `stop`, `run`, or `dwell` target. A `stop` or `run` target terminates the authority per the **Authority termination rule**. A `dwell` target arms nothing — it carries no dispatcher target — and this step leaves the current authority unchanged for that tick; dwell entry itself is decided by the dwell-entry step `3a37`, not by this lookahead.
     - A blocked extend is not a failure of this step — the authority simply stays where it is and the train brakes toward it.
     - **Unreachable-task wait.** When the projection carries `resolved_target is None` and `failure_kind == target_unavailable`, per **Unreachable and broken task handling**: make no `PathDispatcher` call, emit one `kind = "warning"` event with `ErrorRecord.origin = "planning_failed"` and `ErrorRecord.text` taken from the projection's `failure_reason`, and return for that tick.
     - **Broken-task skip (lookahead form).** When the projection instead carries `resolved_target is None` and `failure_kind == missing_target`, this step does not wait: it does not arm a lookahead target this tick. It leaves the currently armed task's authority exactly as it stood before this step ran, and returns for the tick without calling `PathDispatcher`. The broken row itself is skipped by the next eligible Plan's `c481` or `592a` lookup, per **Unreachable and broken task handling**; this step never performs the skip itself, because doing so would duplicate that skip's writes for a row `c481`/`592a` has not yet reached.
     - **The create/extend call.** Otherwise call `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` or `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` for that one armed target only, passing `manual_override` from the run's route (`Route.manual_override` resolved through `RouteRun.route_id`).
     - **Meet candidate and ceiling.** When **Meet coordination** has assigned this train an entry for this tick, pass its `candidate_resource_keys` as `required_candidate_resource_keys`. When the entry also carries `meet_ceiling_block_id`, pass it as `acquisition_cap_block_id` and keep `requested_destination_block_id` equal to the route task's real target, per the **Acquisition-cap rule**. A train outside a meet passes neither constraint and requests its route target normally.
     - **On a successful create/extend**, write `RouteRun.task_runs[walk_position].resolved_target` (where `walk_position` is the index the helper returned for the target this tick armed) to the target pair the create/extend call returned — the dispatcher's own report of what it planned toward, never the meet `acquisition_cap_block_id`, and never a fresh re-resolve of the task on this tick. This is the only canonical writer of that field in v1; under the **Waypoint lookahead** it may write a row ahead of the one the train is physically working on.
     - **On a failed `create_path(...)`**, emit one error event with `origin = "planning_failed"` naming the train and the walk-position per **Error events**. A `StationTarget` planning problem may then try its next same-tick resolved target under the candidate-loop rule below; a single-target task stops planning for that train for the tick.
     - **On a failed `extend_path(...)` with `failure_kind == no_viable_path`**, handle it per the **Structural failure_kind rule** below; do not emit the create-failure `origin = "planning_failed"` event or try another same-tick resolved target for this failed extend.
     - **Departure request.** When this Plan pass has live authority for the current target (`TrainController.path_projection.received_path_plan is not None`), write `phase_latches.departure_request` through `set_departure_request()`. This write happens on every eligible Plan pass with live authority for the current target, not only on the pass that first acquired it and not only when this pass's create/extend attempt grew or succeeded — a blocked extend that leaves the same live authority standing still writes it. The Action transition consumer calls `TrainController.depart()`; the request is idempotent per the **Latch Table** and is re-written each eligible pass.
     - **Idle-hold maintenance and release (best-effort hoarding guard).** This step is the canonical home for releasing a stalled best-effort hold; it maintains `RouteRun.idle_hold_ticks` and `RouteRun.release_cooldown_ticks`. An idle hold is a run keeping its reserved blocks and switch locks while making no progress toward its target.
       - **Cooldown window.** While `release_cooldown_ticks > 0`, this step does no acquisition: it decrements `release_cooldown_ticks` by one and returns for that train this tick. The just-released reservations and switch locks stay free for higher-priority runs through the cooldown window.
       - **Counting.** Otherwise, after the create/extend attempt, increment `idle_hold_ticks` by one when all three hold:
         - the live authority is a truncated best-effort prefix — the run's armed target block fails `Path.reaches_target(...)`;
         - the authority did not grow this tick — the create/extend call reported `appended_resource_count == 0`;
         - the head did not advance.

         Reset `idle_hold_ticks` to `0` when any of these holds:
         - the authority grew;
         - the head advanced;
         - the acquisition reached the full target;
         - a meet ceiling capped this tick's acquisition;
         - there is no live path.

         A meet-capped run is deliberately parked at the meet point, not hoarding, so it must not time out and release.
       - **Timed release.** When `idle_hold_ticks` reaches `IDLE_HOLD_RELEASE_TICKS`, release the held truncated authority the system-replan way: call `controller.route_hooks.phase_latches.set_path_cancel_request(...)` with an `ErrorRecord` whose `origin` is `"idle_hold_release"` per the **Writer-helper rule**, stop planning for that train this tick, set `release_cooldown_ticks = IDLE_HOLD_COOLDOWN_TICKS`, and reset `idle_hold_ticks = 0`.
     - **Contention-driven release.** Independently of the no-progress count: when this run holds a truncated best-effort authority, and the tick's contention snapshot (per **Contention snapshot**) records a waiting train whose `RouteRun.effective_priority(route_registry)` is strictly greater than this run's on any block reserved for this run's live path (`Block.reserved_by_path == path_id`) that the train does not yet physically occupy (`Block.occupied_by is None`), then this run gives up the held truncated authority the same system-replan way: call `controller.route_hooks.phase_latches.set_path_cancel_request(...)` with an `ErrorRecord` whose `origin` is `"contention_release"` per the **Writer-helper rule**, stop planning for that train this tick, set `release_cooldown_ticks = IDLE_HOLD_COOLDOWN_TICKS`, and reset `idle_hold_ticks = 0`.
       - This release does not wait for `idle_hold_ticks` to reach `IDLE_HOLD_RELEASE_TICKS`: when the higher-priority run is blocked on one of the held-but-unentered reservations, this run gives them up at once.
       - Equal-priority contention does not trigger it. The strictly-greater test stops two same-priority runs from releasing in turn; the no-progress timeout above stays their backstop.
       - Action then commits that cancel (the train is already stopped under zero ATC clearance), freeing the not-yet-entered reservations and switch locks. The ordinary post-cancel replan reruns from the train's real position on a later eligible Plan tick once the cooldown has elapsed.
     - A full authority — one whose `Path.reaches_target(...)` is true for the armed target — is never truncated, so `idle_hold_ticks` stays `0` and neither release fires for a train that already holds authority to its real target.
     - `IDLE_HOLD_RELEASE_TICKS` (the consecutive-no-progress tick budget) and `IDLE_HOLD_COOLDOWN_TICKS` (the post-release acquisition-skip window) are adjustable fields in **Runtime settings**.
- A single Plan pass may loop locally through these steps.
  - **`StationTarget` same-tick candidate retry.** For one planning problem, Plan may try multiple distinct same-tick resolved targets only when the current task is a `StationTarget` task and the dispatcher attempt is `create_path(...)`. Plan owns a local `tried` set of already-attempted resolved targets for this planning problem, and calls `_find_next_task_target(train_id, exclude=tried)` repeatedly, appending each returned `resolved_target` to `tried` after a failed `create_path(...)` attempt. The helper itself stores no per-tick state; Plan has all the information needed to decide which candidates have been attempted. The helper returns the next compatible candidate each time; when every candidate has already been attempted, it returns the projection with `resolved_target = None` and `failure_kind = target_unavailable` per the **Failure-shape rule** above — never `None`, since the current task is still on the walk.
  - **Single-candidate task kinds.** A `PlatformTarget` task, `BlockTarget` task, or explicit local-reposition task has only one resolved pair for that tick; if its `create_path(...)` attempt fails without creating authority, the run waits until a later eligible tick rather than trying alternatives in the same pass.
  - **Exhausted candidates.** If every same-tick candidate is exhausted without authority creation, `RouteExecutor` stops Plan for that train for that tick.
  - **Partial `extend_path()` success.** If an existing live path remains and `extend_path(...)` returns `success=True` with `reached_target = False`, keep `current_route_status = RUNNING`, preserve that live path unchanged, and retry on later eligible ticks. Step `66aa`'s idle-hold maintenance applies when that retained authority satisfies its separately stated truncated-best-effort predicate.
  - **Structural `extend_path()` failure.** A `success=False` extend failure — `failure_kind == no_viable_path` in v1 — follows the **Structural failure_kind rule**: it latches cancellation and stops planning for the train for the tick before any candidate retry or fresh create attempt.
- `RouteExecutor` never asks dispatcher/pathfinder to solve a whole multi-task route in one search. Longer authorities are formed only by repeated point-to-point segments appended onto the same live path identified by `path_id`.
- In normal route-managed execution, v1 arms exactly one target per Plan pass and never concatenates two targets on the same tick. Across ticks the armed target may run ahead of the train's task progress: the **Waypoint lookahead** arms the next target while the current `waypoint` is still unserved, so more than one unfinished `waypoint` row can carry a `resolved_target` at once. Those are separate cursors and always have been — `Path.current_resource_index` is authority progress and `RouteRun.current_waypoint_index` is physical task progress. A `waypoint` is still consumed only by the head-entry callback chain, whatever the authority terminal is at the time.
- **Authority termination rule.** This is the canonical home. A live authority terminates at the currently armed target block, whatever that task's kind. Dispatcher must not grow it past the resolved target of a `stop` or `run` task before that task is served: authority beyond an unserved `stop` would let the train roll through the place it was sent to stop, and a `run` is finished by its own Plan timer rather than by arrival, so authority past it would run the train on under an already-satisfied plan. A `waypoint` target is an ordinary terminal — the train is meant to pass through it, so Plan's **Waypoint lookahead** arms the next target and grows the authority forward through consecutive waypoints, one armed target at a time. Between arming steps the authority legitimately ends on a waypoint block, and the train brakes toward it if the next arm cannot acquire; that braking is correct, because an authority that cannot grow is exactly as long as the train is allowed to run.
- `task_kind == "stop"` versus `task_kind == "waypoint"` changes only what happens when the resolved target is reached: `stop` enters dwell (or the `dwell` task that follows it) through the **Stop-arrival check** — or, when the route is authored with the train already stopped at the destination, through Plan's head-anchored covered-stop finish — while `waypoint` advances immediately without dwell. It does not change the dispatcher path API shape.

**Run start-mode seeding**

This subsection is the canonical home for which stop a fresh `RouteRun` begins at. It is consulted once, when Plan step `9c4f` allocates a fresh run, and seeds the run's starting walk-position.

- **Start mode.** `RouteStartMode` has three values:
  - `FIRST` (default) — start at `task_runs[0]`. The covered-task index advance then walks past any already-covered `waypoint` tasks exactly as before; stops are never skipped by coverage. This is the v1 behavior when no start mode is set.
  - `NEAREST` — seed the run at the best `task_kind == "stop"` task for the train to begin at. A stop is eligible only when the train has a viable path to its resolved block in the block-relative direction that stop's task requires — the same directed graph-walk the stop-planning rule under **RouteTask data** runs to plan a real move there, which already filters on the task's `task_direction` and on `Block.allowed_travel_directions` (the latter relaxed when the run's route stores `Route.manual_override = True`). So a stop the tracks merely touch, but that can only be reached against its task's direction or against block travel-direction, is not eligible, and the ranking falls through to the next viable stop. Eligibility and track distance both come from that one shared directed graph-walk query (the **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload** comparison, run with the stop's required direction), so this subsection does not restate the metric or the direction filter. Among the eligible stops, rank each by four things in order, each one breaking ties left by the ones before it:
    1. **No reversal first.** Prefer a stop the train can drive straight on from. A stop is a *reverse stop* when, after arriving there, the train's next route move would have to leave it back through the same block the train arrived through — it has to turn around in place. A drive-on stop is preferred even when a reverse stop is a little closer. (The next move is resolved from this candidate stop's walk-position by `RouteExecutor.find_next_move_target_from(walk_position, train_id)`, which shares its forward task-walk kernel — the next non-`dwell` task, wrapping for `RouteMode.CIRCULAR` and reflecting at `RouteMode.ROUND_TRIP` ends — with `RouteExecutor.find_next_move_target(train_id)`, the same next-move rule the **reversal-trap exclusion** under best-effort `create_path()` applies from the occupant's current cursor.)
    2. **Free first.** Prefer a stop no other train has taken. A stop is *taken* when its resolved block is either occupied by another train or is the live next-move target of another train already running this route. Reading other runs' current next move is what spreads a yard-full of trains across distinct stops instead of all of them picking the same nearest one; because it reads each run's *current* move, a train that has already driven past its own seed no longer holds a claim on it.
    3. **Nearest.** Prefer the shorter track-distance walk.
    4. **Lowest task index** breaks any remaining tie.

    If no stop has a viable directed path, fall back to FIRST.
  - `SPECIFIC` — start at the stop named by the effective `start_task_index`. The index must be in range and name a `task_kind == "stop"` task; otherwise fall back to FIRST.
- **Where it is set.** The route-level default is `Route.start_mode` / `Route.start_task_index`. A single assignment may override it through `PUT /api/trains/<id>/assign-route`. `RouteExecutor.request_route_assignment(...)` clears older pending assignment/start state first. When the assignment can commit immediately, it writes the one-shot value to `_pending_start_overrides[train_id]`; when a live run must tear down first, it stores the value beside the requested route in `_pending_route_assignments` and Action moves it to `_pending_start_overrides` only when that route becomes the stored assignment. Plan removes it when the fresh run consumes it. The effective value is the per-assignment input if present, else the route default, else `FIRST`. It is not a live `RouteRun` override: start mode has no meaning after the starting walk-position is seeded.
- **Seeding mechanism.** At allocation (step `9c4f`), after `task_runs` is initialized with `len(Route.tasks)` entries, let `s` be the chosen start task index. For `FIRST` (and any fallback to FIRST), `s = 0` and nothing is seeded. For `s > 0`, the run is allocated with the skipped prefix already finished: for every `i` in `[0, s)`, write `task_runs[i].finished_at = RouteRun.started_at` and `task_runs[i].finished_at_operating = RouteRun.started_at_operating`, leaving `delay_class = None` because those positions were not travelled. `next_planning_walk_position` then lands on `s` and `current_waypoint_index` reads `s - 1`. This prefix-finish is allocation-time initialization, distinct from `RouteRun.advance_walk_position()`, and it appends nothing. Because the initial walk holds only the forward leg (`task_index == walk_position` for `0..N-1`) and `s ≤ len(Route.tasks) - 1`, the apex is never pre-finished and `RouteRun.direction` stays `"forward"`; ROUND_TRIP reflection is handled normally by `RouteRun._append_next_walk_task(from_walk_position)` when the genuine apex later finishes. The resolved mode is recorded on `RouteRun.start_mode` for diagnostics, and the chosen start index `s` on `RouteRun.start_walk_position`.

**Route Edit And Reconciliation**

- **Route-definition field edit classification.** This is the canonical home for whether editing a `Route` definition field latches structural teardown. Every field is exactly one of two kinds:
  - **Structural (latches teardown).** `Route.tasks` (a change to the waypoint set, ordering, or task-kind composition) and `Route.mode` both change the walk structure that `RouteRun._append_next_walk_task(...)` walks live on every append — `mode` selects the `CIRCULAR` wrap / `ROUND_TRIP` reflection / `ONE_OFF` terminal behavior that append reads on each call, so a live `mode` flip could put a running walk into a shape **Route-definition validation** would have rejected outright (for example, a `ONE_OFF` route with no terminal `stop`/`run` task). An edit to either field immediately latches teardown of every assigned train's currently-`RUNNING` `RouteRun` for that `route_id` — the per-train `pending_route_deactivate` latch plus its inclusive cancel, each committed in that train's later Action once the train has stopped (a moving train with still-valid authority first runs out to its `authority_end_block_id`, per the stopped-train gating in **Action latched-cancel consumption**) — followed by fresh `RouteRun` allocation against the edited `Route` on the next eligible Plan. There is no in-place reconciliation in v1 and no version stamp on the run. The fresh run picks its starting walk-position per **Run start-mode seeding**: because the per-assignment start input is one-shot (already consumed by the original allocation), a re-allocation after a structural edit uses the route-level `Route.start_mode` default.
  - **Live (no teardown).** `Route.priority`, `Route.acquisition_mode`, `Route.manual_override`, and `Route.name` take effect live with no teardown because they do not change the walk structure. `Route.start_mode` and `Route.start_task_index` also take effect with no teardown, because **Run start-mode seeding** already consults them only once, at allocation — a live edit changes nothing about any currently-`RUNNING` run and applies only starting with the next fresh allocation. `Route.timing_basis` has no request-service edit path in v1 (it is set only by full-snapshot load), but when it does change it likewise takes effect live with no teardown, per the field's own row in **Route data** above.

  Allowlisted-field edits (`priority`, `acquisition_mode`) may carry per-field `push = "force"` / `push = "soft"` policies that distribute the new value across existing `RouteRun.overrides` per the **RouteRun overrides** subsection. The structural edits (`tasks`, `mode`) and the live edits `name`, `priority`, `acquisition_mode`, and `manual_override` bump `Route.last_edited_at` per the **Route edit timestamps** subsection; `start_mode`, `start_task_index`, and `timing_basis` do not (see that subsection for why).
- A `RouteRun`'s `route_id` is established at run creation and never mutated.
- **Shared-route edit teardown.**
  - **Latching the teardown.** When the shared-route edit service accepts a structural edit, it walks `Route.assigned_train_ids` and writes the per-train deactivate and inclusive cancel latches.
  - **Committing the teardown.** Each train's later eligible Action commits the inclusive cancel and the deactivate teardown through the standard latch consumption flow: the deactivate consumer calls `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)`, which writes `current_route_status = DEACTIVATED` on the old run and (when `state == RUNNING_AT_STATION`) writes `station_exit_request` (the later Action station-exit consumer performs the exit). The historical row stays in `_historical_runs`.
  - **Why re-assignment must be held.** Because teardown unassigns the edited route, its service records `RouteExecutor._pending_reassign[train_id] = route_id` after writing the deactivate latch and does not re-add the stored assignment up front.
  - **Applying the held re-assignment.** The same train's Action `pending_route_deactivate` consumer, after its own `remove_train_route_run(train_id)` has torn the old run down and unassigned the train, applies the held re-assignment by calling `Route.assign_train(train_id)` on the recorded route and clearing the stash — but only when that consumer actually owned the teardown (its `remove_train_route_run(train_id)` cleared a still-`RUNNING` run, i.e. `RouteExecutor.execution_state_for(train_id)` was not `None` when the deactivate step began).
  - **When another teardown wins instead.** The Action consumer order is `pending_route_abort` → `pending_power_off` → `pending_route_deactivate`, so an operator abort or power-off for the same train runs first. When it (or a natural finish) already ended the run, the deactivate consumer finds `execution_state_for(train_id) is None`, discards `_pending_reassign[train_id]` without re-assigning, and the operator/admin teardown wins — a powered-off or aborted train is never silently re-assigned to the edited route.
  - **Next Plan.** The next eligible Plan then sees the train assigned to the edited route with no `RUNNING` `RouteRun` and allocates a fresh `RouteRun` against the edited `Route.tasks` per Plan's RouteRun (re)allocation step.
  - **Retargeting/swap uses the general held-assignment mechanism.** Operator retargeting / route swap stores the different route in `_pending_route_assignments`; it does not use the same-route `_pending_reassign` entry. `_pending_reassign` is consumed only by the `pending_route_deactivate` consumer for structural edits.
- **Route deletion waits for live teardown.** `DELETE /api/train-routes/<route_id>` never removes a route used by a live or pending run inline.
  - The service first rejects new assignment and activation by setting `Route.is_active = False` and recording `route_id` in `RouteExecutor.pending_route_deletions`.
  - For every assigned train it clears any pending same-route re-assignment, calls `controller.route_hooks.phase_latches.set_route_deactivate(...)`, and lets the inclusive cancel plus Action deactivate consumer perform the ordinary authority and run teardown. A route pending deletion is never re-applied by `_pending_reassign`.
  - The active route registry retains the `Route` while any train remains assigned, any `RUNNING` `RouteRun` names it, or any teardown latch for it remains pending. `RouteExecutor.get_route(route_id)` therefore continues to resolve for every live run during Plan and Action.
  - After each Action teardown or natural finish, `RouteExecutor.finalize_pending_route_deletions()` removes a pending route from the active registry only when it has no assignments and no live run. It moves the immutable final definition to `RouteExecutor._historical_routes` before removal, so historical `RouteRun.task_runs[*].task_index` and run-panel serialization can still resolve the task definitions they reference.
  - If the route has no assignment, live run, or pending teardown when DELETE begins, the same finalization runs immediately. Repeating DELETE while teardown is pending or after archival is idempotent.
- The fresh `RouteRun` starts with `direction == "forward"` and `task_runs` initialized from the edited `Route.tasks`, then seeds its starting walk-position per **Run start-mode seeding** (re-allocation after a structural edit uses the route-level `Route.start_mode` default, since the per-assignment input is one-shot). For start mode `FIRST` this leaves `current_waypoint_index == None`; `NEAREST` / `SPECIFIC` pre-finish a skipped prefix. Plan then runs the ordinary planning kernel: the covered-task index advance walks past any `task_kind == "waypoint"` tasks the train already covers, and `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` returns the first non-finished walk-position for the next planning step. Stops are not skipped by coverage, so the fresh run lands on the first non-covered stop or waypoint at or after its seeded start position automatically.
- Operator retargeting and explicit route swap call `RouteExecutor.request_route_assignment(...)` with the new route. For a newly constructed one-off route, the service first activates it through `Route.activate()`. With a live old run, the request method stores the new route in `_pending_route_assignments`, writes the abort and inclusive cancel latches, and leaves both stored route lists unchanged. Action consumes the cancel and abort, archives and unassigns the old run, then commits the held new assignment. The next eligible Plan sees that assignment with no `RUNNING` run and allocates a fresh run. The handler only maps the service's accepted/pending result.

**Exact `RouteExecutor` tick calls**

- `RouteExecutor.update(delta_seconds)` refreshes route-managed scheduling inputs for this tick.
  - **Delta and timestamps.** `delta_seconds` is the per-tick movement-window length (the gap between consecutive ticks at the simulation's current playback rate). It is used by physics integration and by callers that need a per-tick delta, but `RouteExecutor` does NOT maintain a separate `simulation_time` accumulator. All stored route/run absolute instants use system-time Unix seconds (`time.time()`); there is no v1 `RouteExecutor.simulation_time` field. Stored route/run instants such as `Route.started_at`, `RouteRun.task_runs[i].started_at`, `RouteRun.task_runs[i].finished_at`, and `RouteTask.target_time` use system-time Unix seconds; so does the `event_time` on every event (see **Error events**) — except the runtime-only `_operating` anchors (`RouteRun.started_at_operating`, `RouteTaskRun.started_at_operating` / `finished_at_operating`), which are `AppState.operating_time` readings, not wall instants (see **Clocks**).
  - **Runnable-train ordering.** `RouteExecutor` owns the final runnable-train ordering through `RouteExecutor.order_runnable_trains(candidate_train_ids)`. Every candidate train resolves to one run-state tier (established versus still finishing its first task, per `RouteRun.is_starting`; trains without a current `RouteRun` use the established tier) and one effective priority. The merged set is sorted first by run-state tier, then by effective priority descending (`9` highest, `0` lowest), with stable existing iteration order as the only tie-break, per **Per-train tick transaction**. Route-managed and non-route trains at the same tier and priority interleave in stable order. `SimulationController.update(...)` executes the returned IDs and applies no second sort.
  - **What this call does and does not do.** `RouteExecutor.update(delta_seconds)` prepares the route-managed Plan work that `SimulationController` will invoke by train; it must not itself call `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` for every train in a world-wide pass. Trains without a current `RouteRun` still remain in the `SimulationController` loop and simply have no route-managed Plan work for that tick.
- `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(...)` is the canonical public Observe route surface for a served stop: `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(train_id)` calls it once the authority is released, and it owns the step `bc55` commit. It is one of the route-executor entry points outside Plan, alongside the `handle_train_advanced(...)` / `handle_path_cancellation(...)` callbacks.
- `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(train_id, delta_seconds)` is the canonical public Plan surface and is the entire Plan route-executor tick for one train. `SimulationController.update(...)` calls it immediately before that same train's `SimulationController._act_train(train, delta_seconds)` transaction. Dwell handling, covered-task index advance, live target resolution, station candidate iteration, and `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` / `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` attempts all live here. `tick_train_plan` creates or reuses the train's `RouteRun` (current-code class may still be named `RouteExecutionState`). If the controller is `OFF`, Plan route work is skipped and power-on is handled by the Action command slot. If the next non-finished task on the directed walk has `task_kind == "dwell"`, dwell is the active route step: Plan returns for that tick (Plan dwell-entry step inside `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` handles the transition into `RUNNING_AT_STATION`).
- Before any create/extend decision, `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` must call `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` and receive a legal `ResolvedNextTaskProjection` for the current shared route and current physical progress. The returned `resolved_target` is the transient request candidate for this attempt. If the helper cannot currently resolve a legal concrete platform/block target under the task's fixed/flexible platform policy, the retry fails at target resolution and `RouteExecutor` must not call `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` for that tick.
- Before any create/extend decision, the current attempt's resolved target is the route-owned request contract for the `walk_position` returned by `_find_next_task_target(train_id)`: the task target block and the route-owned `requested_destination_direction` constraint. While the live path already holds that target block as its requested target, the contract is the stored pair read through `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)` rather than a fresh resolve, per **Live-path target re-resolution**. It must not resolve or pass any stop-position centimeter field. Dispatcher and controller use the chosen terminal frame plus controller safety margin for braking/boundary projection.
- Route-managed path building is always segment-by-segment along the current directed route walk. On each create/extend attempt, the resolved target represents exactly one resolved task target, never a bundled multi-task search request. After one segment is successfully created or appended, route planning stops for that train on that tick; if the armed target is `task_kind == "waypoint"`, a later tick arms the next task's target per the **Waypoint lookahead** in Planning Kernel step `66aa`, which may arm it before the current waypoint is physically consumed.
- `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` must ensure the train's `TrainController` exists before it reads controller state or calls `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)`. A route-managed train already has a controller by the time authority is assigned in Plan. `SimulationController` owns only the 1:1 binding between `train_id` and `TrainController`; it does not construct or write authority projections.
- Before resolving a new task or retrying the current one, `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` runs the covered-task index advance (a small loop inside the method) so the route does not keep targeting a task the train already physically covers.
- The operational state checks inside `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` must read controller state rather than `train.state`.
- If controller state is `OFF`, `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` is not invoked for normal route planning. A powered-off train must not create, extend, or rely on dispatcher authority, and the system must not auto-power-on it. `TrainController.commands.power_on_cmd()` is accepted only through the Action command slot; route planning resumes on a later tick after the controller is powered and in an eligible state. The canonical power-off release/removal order follows the standard stage workflow per the **Power-off procedure**.
- If the next route task is `task_kind == "dwell"`, `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` must treat dwell as the active route step before any departure/path planning and return for that tick. The Plan dwell-entry step inside `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` transitions the controller to `RUNNING_AT_STATION` automatically when the step-`3a37` preconditions in the **Planning Kernel** hold. Plan must not advance past the dwell task or request authority until the Plan dwell-complete step inside `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` marks the `dwell` task finished.
- If controller state is `READY` and there is no pending/active dwell task, `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` must run its authority-acquisition step (**Planning Kernel** step `66aa`). Path creation/retry is allowed from `READY` regardless of cab selection. The behavioral difference between ATO and manual is only departure execution after authority exists: ATO may auto-select/start, while manual mode leaves actual movement to the driver.
- If controller state is `RUNNING_MOVING`, `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` must not poll for `stop` task arrival; normal stop arrival comes only from the **Stop-arrival check** in Observe. `task_kind == "waypoint"` consumption is also not polled inside `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)`; it is driven by the head-advance callback chain `TrainPhysics.tick(...)` -> `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)` -> `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` -> `RouteExecutor.handle_train_advanced(...)`. Each `RouteExecutor.handle_train_advanced(...)` callback compares one reported block advance with the current route task pointer and may consume at most that one task; it must not arm the next planning target or create/extend authority. `waypoint` consumption is head-based route progress only; the later physical release of earlier path resources still waits for tail-vacate callbacks. Plan still runs step `6a0d` to accrue and complete an active timed `run`, and step `66aa` may retry an eligible `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)`; those steps do not re-implement head-entry or stop-arrival detection.
- If controller state is `RUNNING_AT_STATION`, `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` must run its Plan dwell-complete step (which may call a helper such as `RouteExecutor._check_dwell_complete(train, route, exec_state)`) before any covered-task or planning work; if dwell does not complete on this pass, the run is dwelling/on hold and the rest of Plan proceeds through the Planning Kernel step order without new path or departure planning, per the **Planning Kernel** step chain — step `3a37` returns immediately because the controller is already `RUNNING_AT_STATION`. The dwell-complete helper is owned by Plan only and is never invoked from Observe, Action, or from `RouteExecutor.update(...)`.
- If a live path is short of `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id).stored_resolved_target.requested_destination_block_id`, `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` keeps retrying `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` on that same path using that stored pair. If a fresh resolve for the projection's `walk_position` produces a different target **block**, Plan latches cancel-and-replan per **Live-path target re-resolution**. Arming the next task on a live path is ordinary progress. Each retry preserves the stored pair, and no fresh path is requested while `received_path_plan` remains present.
- More generally, dynamic best-effort extension is allowed in any controller state except `OFF`. The common zero-clearance retry case is when ATC is holding the train at the live-authority boundary, but if a still-live path remains short of its requested target while the train is still moving or otherwise stopped under authority, `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` may proactively retry `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` on later ticks without waiting for a state change, as long as it does not create a second live path.
- `RouteExecutor` does not call any stop-position resolver and does not pass stop centimeters into dispatcher. Route callers pass only the resolved block/direction request contract.
- The authority-acquisition step (**Planning Kernel** step `66aa`) is the route executor's normal "make progress toward the current task" entry point. The same function is used for the initial departure attempt and for retries after `PathDispatcher` has cancelled/revoked the previous path once the train has reached a fresh stopped no-authority state. If the cancellation stop escalated into EB, that retry point occurs only after `TrainController.eb.release()` has cleared the condition and the ordinary post-command state evaluation has reached `READY`; active-path completion still comes back from `PathDispatcher`, not from `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` polling for end-of-path.
- `RouteExecutor` writes `phase_latches.departure_request` whenever live authority exists for the current route target, regardless of `control_mode`; the Action transition consumer calls `TrainController.depart()`. There is no route-level `departure_mode` policy in v1; the ATO-vs-manual behavioral difference is owned inside `TrainController.depart()` itself per the **`TrainController.depart()` canonical contract**.
- After EB release, the EB-interrupted path has already been cancelled by the EB activation flow. `RouteExecutor` must wait for EB release, then make a fresh `create_path(...)` or `extend_path(...)` decision from the current route state; it must not try to reuse that cancelled path. Once fresh authority exists, the next eligible Plan writes `phase_latches.departure_request` per the same rule.

- **Departure-to-waypoint flow**

- The canonical step ordering and gating for one Plan pass live in the **Planning Kernel** subsection (steps `c9e1`–`66aa`). This subsection only states the manual-vs-ATO behaviour at depart-acceptance time and the per-controller-state guards on the authority-acquisition step; it does not redefine the kernel's step order, eligibility precondition, latch checks, or per-step writes. Where this subsection's prose appears to differ from the kernel, the kernel wins.
- `RouteExecutor` owns task targeting; `PathDispatcher` owns authority acquisition and terminal authority geometry; `TrainController` owns stop/braking behavior from that authority geometry using the controller safety margin. The departure flow is: resolve task block/direction, request or extend dispatcher authority as needed, and write `phase_latches.departure_request` once live authority exists.
- The stop, covered-stop, and dwell-entry rules in this subsection apply only to tasks with `task_kind == "stop"`. Tasks with `task_kind == "waypoint"` do not call arrival/dwell helpers; they constrain route geometry only.
- A `task_kind == "waypoint"` task uses the same block/direction resolution rules and the same point-to-point create/extend contract as a `stop` task. The difference is route behavior only: when that task's resolved target is reached, `RouteExecutor` advances immediately without dwell and leaves the next target to the next planning tick.
- A longer multi-task route is implemented as repeated point-to-point segments across later planning ticks. A pathfinder call never receives "go through all remaining tasks"; each `create_path(...)` / `extend_path(...)` request is made from the then-current live authority end to whichever task `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` currently resolves — the just-served task's successor once physical route progress consumes it, or an earlier task's successor already armed under the **Waypoint lookahead**. Physical route progress still waits for `waypoint` head entry or `stop` arrival.
- `RouteExecutor` owns task-chain progression on the route side. `PathDispatcher` grows authority geometry; it does not own task progression. A `waypoint` task is consumed only when the train head first enters that task's resolved block. Live `resource_sequence` coverage may be inspected for diagnostics or extension planning, but coverage alone does not advance `current_waypoint_index` and does not retarget dispatcher authority away from the currently armed task. Tail-based resource release is a separate physical-lifecycle concern owned by tail-vacate observations (detector-confirmed for blocks per **Power**, Block occupancy detection; controller-reported traversal for switches) and dispatcher-mediated resource release.
- For a train departing from rest under route control, `RouteExecutor` does not try to grow authority past the currently armed task inside the same departure call. Departure uses the current live authority only; later ticks may extend or recreate authority after physical route progress advances and the next task becomes the armed target.
- The route-side already-covered handling has two shapes, both in Plan's covered-task index advance. For `task_kind == "waypoint"` targets it is a skip: when the covered-waypoint test in that canonical home finds the current `waypoint` task covered, `RouteExecutor` treats that task as already missed/skipped, does not request a `create_path(...)` for it, and immediately advances route planning toward the next task on the current directed route walk. For `task_kind == "stop"`, coverage finishes the task only in the covered-stop case, per Plan's covered-task index advance (its canonical home); while the train is rolling or a live path exists, a stop is served only by route-committed stop arrival. Operator/manual reposition uses the ordinary one-off route flow as a `stop` task and follows this same rule.
- `RouteExecutor` does not resolve or compare stop-position targets at all. For any `stop` task that still needs authority, it passes only `requested_destination_block_id` and `requested_destination_direction`. Dispatcher stores authority geometry and the controller owns safety-margin braking from that geometry. The route/task resolution step must still provide `requested_destination_direction` as a route-level constraint; dispatcher must not guess it from local geometry, and must not treat it as the exact terminal frame by itself.
- `RouteExecutor` uses `RouteRun.effective_acquisition_mode(route_registry)` for both `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` and any later `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` retries while it is still pursuing that same planning chain. `AcquisitionMode.best_effort` is therefore a route/run policy choice, not a one-off branch invented mid-chain.
- For a `waypoint` task, the create/extend chain is still block-based: the current per-attempt resolved target still carries `requested_destination_block_id` and `requested_destination_direction` just like a `stop` task. The difference is not the path API shape; the difference is that once the train head enters that task's resolved block, `RouteExecutor` consumes the `waypoint` immediately, advances the route cursor, and leaves the next create/extend step to a later planning tick.
- The canonical create-vs-extend decision for `RouteExecutor` is driven by `TrainController.path_projection.received_path_plan` presence, not by any route-side re-evaluation of whether the current waypoint is reachable on an empty map. For the currently armed waypoint:
  - if `controller.path_projection.received_path_plan is None`, the train has no live authority, so `RouteExecutor` must call `PathDispatcher.create_path(train_id=..., ...)`
  - if `controller.path_projection.received_path_plan is not None`, the train is already on a live path, so `RouteExecutor` must call `PathDispatcher.extend_path(path_id=controller.path_projection.received_path_plan.path_id, ...)` on that same `path_id` rather than synthesizing a second path
  Because `controller.path_projection.received_path_plan` is derived from the dispatcher-owned active path, this rule is well-defined in v1: a cancelled/completed path transitions out of `ACTIVE`, so the next controller read returns no live plan and the next planning tick naturally falls into the `create_path(...)` branch. A pass-through waypoint at which the train happens to be stopped with no live plan is therefore a `create_path(...)` case, not an `extend_path(...)` case.
- **Structural failure_kind rule.** When live authority exists for this train (`PathDispatcher.active_path_id_by_train(train_id) is not None`), the authority-acquisition step must treat that live authority as the current route path and must not request a second `create_path(...)`. It calls `extend_path(active_path_id, ...)`. Any `success=True` result leaves the existing path valid, so Plan keeps it, and a result with `reached_target = False` is retried later. When `extend_path(...)` instead returns `success=False` with `failure_kind == no_viable_path`, `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` calls `controller.route_hooks.phase_latches.set_path_cancel_request(...)` with an `ErrorRecord` whose `origin` is `"revoked"` and with `kind = "info"`, stops planning for that train for the tick, and waits for the ordinary Action cancel/callback/recovery flow before any fresh path request.
- If `PathDispatcher.create_path(..., acquisition_mode=best_effort)` returns a live path whose current authorized target is still short of the route's current planning target, that is not a failure. It is a degraded but valid live authority: let the controller treat it as normal movement authority toward the current authorized end, and let `RouteExecutor` keep retrying `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` on the same `path_id` toward that same pending waypoint, passing the stored `resolved_target` request contract unchanged on each retry (per **Live-path target re-resolution**), on later ticks in any controller state except `OFF`. A best-effort create request counts as success whenever it creates one new path record with a non-empty block-terminated live `resource_sequence`; a best-effort extend request counts as success whenever the live path is still a valid authority toward the requested target afterwards — whether it grew, was already at the target, or is temporarily held back by live resource ownership.
- Once such a live path exists, `RouteExecutor` writes `phase_latches.departure_request` when this target is otherwise route-ready. Any immediate zero-clearance hold is controller-owned and comes from lookahead/ATC against that live authority rather than from a special route-side suppression rule.
- On successful path, do not write train-side path cache fields from `RouteExecutor`. `PathDispatcher` owns the authoritative path-progress view; any controller/UI-facing path tiles or path-progress reads must be read as a projection of dispatcher state rather than as a train mirror.
- Do not set destination-block fields directly on `Train` or `TrainController` from `RouteExecutor`; controller authority comes only from the live `controller.path_projection.received_path_plan` projection.
- `PathDispatcher` owns the `Path` record underlying `controller.path_projection.received_path_plan`; `controller.assigned_path_id` must be only a derived read of `controller.path_projection.received_path_plan.path_id`, so `RouteExecutor` does not write that field.
- On any successful `create_path(...)` / `extend_path(...)` call, `RouteExecutor` must update route-owned state for the immediate live task carried by that path: set/keep `current_route_status = RUNNING`, set `direction` from the accepted projection, and write `task_runs[walk_position].resolved_target` (where `walk_position` is the index the helper returned for the target this tick armed) to the target pair that call returned, per the **`current_route_status` write contract**. Later planning retries against the same live path read `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)` and use its `stored_resolved_target`. If a fresh resolve for the armed target's walk-position would change that row's target **block** while authority is live, Plan uses cancel-and-replan rather than rewriting the live target under the existing path; while the same block stays armed, Plan passes the stored pair into the next `extend_path(...)` call and must not resolve the direction again, per **Live-path target re-resolution**. Returned `resource_sequence` geometry alone does not advance `current_waypoint_index`, which remains physical route progress, and v1 does not arm a second waypoint target on the same tick.
- After any successful `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)`, `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)` follows the **`ArmedTaskProjection` schema**: it returns the greatest unfinished walk-position whose `resolved_target` is non-`None`. A `stop` remains armed until it is served. A `waypoint` ceases to be the armed row as soon as waypoint lookahead successfully acquires and stores the successor row's target, even though the waypoint itself remains unfinished until its physical head-entry callback. Later retries always use the newest armed row's `stored_resolved_target`; physical progress remains separate and `current_waypoint_index` advances only when the train actually consumes a task through its canonical completion path.
- `TrainController.depart()` is the controller's departure-acceptance command once a valid path plan exists. `RouteExecutor` writes `phase_latches.departure_request` on every eligible Plan pass with live authority, regardless of `control_mode`, and the Action transition consumer calls `depart()`. ATO vs manual effects on acceptance are owned per the **`TrainController.depart()` canonical contract**.
- When `TrainController.depart()` returns `success == False`, the caller must treat that as a failed departure attempt, not as movement. The controller leaves itself in its current stopped state, records or emits the diagnostic `reason` through `NotificationCenter`, and the next planning tick re-evaluates from current controller state and `controller.path_projection.received_path_plan` presence. If authority was cleared before the call, the normal create-path branch handles recovery on that later tick; if EB or power/state made departure invalid, the existing EB/power/stopped-state rules decide when retry is allowed.

**Exact departure calls**

- Every `RouteExecutor` access to a train's controller goes through its injected `ControllerRegistry.get_or_create(train_id)` dependency. It never calls `SimulationController` or reads a controller dictionary directly.
- If the covered-waypoint test in Plan's covered-task index advance finds a `task_kind == "waypoint"` task covered, the authority-acquisition step must not call `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` for that `waypoint` task. Plan's covered-task index advance has already advanced past it by recording `task_runs[i].finished_at` (which makes the derived `current_waypoint_index` advance) before the depart helper is reached, so the helper continues planning toward the next task on the current directed route walk. If the resolved target block for a `task_kind == "stop"` task is the block the train's head already sits in, Plan's covered-task index advance has already finished it whenever the covered-stop case applied (per the covered-task index advance canonical home); the authority-acquisition step therefore only ever sees such a covered stop while the train is rolling or a live path exists, and in that case it makes no create/extend call for it — the stop is served by the normal **Stop-arrival check** and the release of the live path that follows it.
- For any `stop` task that still needs authority, `RouteExecutor` does not compute or compare a centimeter-level local stopping target. It passes only the task's `requested_destination_block_id` and `requested_destination_direction` into `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)`.
- **Operator repositions are route-backed.** Explicit operator repositions are route-backed in v1 through the ordinary one-off `Route` flow with no special run-level flag.
  - **Construction.** A direct operator/API local-reposition request (the Quick Route tool) constructs a `RouteMode.ONE_OFF` route with a single `task_kind == "stop"` task whose `task_location` is a `BlockTarget`, `PlatformTarget`, or `StationTarget` for the destination, and stores the request's `manual_override` (default `False`) on that route per the **Route data** table. Because a single-task reposition route has only one stop, start-mode seeding (see **Run start-mode seeding**) resolves to that task and `Route.tasks[0]` is the first executable target.
  - **Direction resolution.** The operator/API construction step stores the requested `RouteTask.task_direction` under the ordinary task-authoring contract, including `"either"` or its normal omitted-field default. `RouteExecutor._find_next_task_target(...)` resolves it through the same current-span candidate comparison used by every other `stop` task and produces the concrete `ResolvedRouteTarget.requested_destination_direction` before any dispatcher call. Quick Route has no construction-time direction-resolution or rejection branch.
  - **Execution.** The run is executed through the ordinary Plan / `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` flow. If the destination stop block is already covered when planning runs, the covered-stop rule applies: once the train is stopped with no active path, Plan's covered-task index advance finishes the stop in place and the run completes without creating authority.
  - **No separate position field.** These routes carry no separate target-position field; the controller uses the standard safety-margin stop logic.
- When the current attempt uses `AcquisitionMode.best_effort`, read `armed = RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)`. When `armed` is `None`, no extend retry is due this tick. Otherwise test `Path.reaches_target(armed.stored_resolved_target.requested_destination_block_id)`; if false, keep calling `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` on that same `path_id` using the projection's stored request pair; do not synthesize a new path.
- If the authority-acquisition step sees current live authority already present on the controller (`TrainController.path_projection.received_path_plan is not None`), do not call `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` again. First perform any eligible `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` retry for the currently armed target; after that create/extend decision is complete for this Plan pass, write `phase_latches.departure_request` for that current live authority. ATO vs manual effects are owned per the **`TrainController.depart()` canonical contract**.
- `RouteExecutor` does not write `current_path`, `path_index`, `train.assigned_path_id`, `controller.ato_path_id`, or any destination field. `PathDispatcher` owns path-progress; `controller.assigned_path_id` is derived from the live `received_path_plan` projection.
- Route-driven movement requires a dispatcher path plan and reaches departure acceptance only after `RouteExecutor` writes `phase_latches.departure_request` and the Action transition consumer calls `TrainController.depart()`. The controller infers "no path authority" from an empty `received_path_plan`.
- If initial path creation fails before departure in `all_or_nothing` mode, `RouteExecutor` must emit one error event with `kind = "warning"` and `origin = "planning_failed"` carrying that route/path error per **Error events** and keep the train in `READY`; the train never had authority, so no special controller waiting command is needed.
- In `best_effort` mode, only "no authority at all could be created" is a creation failure. A truncated but live path is not a failure path; the train may run under that current authority and later wait at the current authority boundary while `RouteExecutor` keeps retrying `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` on the same `path_id`.
- On cancel/revoke, the latched cancel commits once the train is stopped: `PathDispatcher` transitions `Path.status` to `CANCELLED` (the controller's `received_path_plan` property then returns `None` on its next read; a still-rolling train is first stopped by the zero-limit / EB protocol in step `826a`), and recovery follows the canonical recovery table. Plan is gated by `controller.is_recovery_clean`; it never reads the cancellation `error`. If the next planning attempt fails, fall through to the ordinary pre-departure route/path error path — no recovery-only state machine.

**Arrival detection**

- The **Stop-arrival check** owns arrival observation for a `stop` task, and `RouteExecutor` owns the commit. There is no separate platform-position arrival gate.
- Step `bc55` records arrival by finishing the matched stop's walk-position through `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(...)`, which samples and writes the row's wall and operating finish fields locally. The derived `current_waypoint_index` then advances to `walk_position`. It does not call `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()`; that transition happens in the next eligible `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` dwell-entry step.
- `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()` is the controller-side dwell-entry transition, called by the Action station-entry consumer of the `station_entry_request` that Plan step `3a37` writes. The controller does not detect dwell entry on its own; it never reads or writes `RouteRun`. The transition is valid only from the **`READY` state**. `RouteExecutor` step `3a37` is the single writer of the dwell row's paired `started_at = time.time()` and `started_at_operating = AppState.operating_time` samples, written before it writes `station_entry_request`.
- On the next eligible tick after `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(...)` records the stop's `finished_at`, `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` performs the dwell-entry step: when `controller.is_recovery_clean` is true, the route's next non-finished task has `task_kind == "dwell"`, the predecessor task's `finished_at` is set, and `controller.cab ∈ {"A", "B"}`, `RouteExecutor` samples the dwell row's `started_at`, per the **RouteTaskRun schema**, writes it to `RouteRun.task_runs[walk_position]`, and writes `station_entry_request` (the Action station-entry consumer performs the transition). Sampling at this step, rather than inside the controller call, means the dwell window measures time standing at the platform rather than time since the predecessor task finished. The train does not plan a new target while dwell is pending or active.
- The dwell-complete check is a Plan step inside `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)`, invoked before covered-task index advance. It runs only while controller state is `RUNNING_AT_STATION`. It calls `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` to live-resolve `walk_position` (the walk-position of the next non-finished task on the directed walk), then calls `RouteTask.should_depart(...)` with the arguments **Task time semantics** defines, sampling each clock it names at the moment of the check.
- Stop arrival sets `finished_at` for that stop directly through `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(...)`, which makes the derived `current_waypoint_index` advance. The stop task is independent of its neighbors: a following `dwell` task (when present) is a separate row with its own `started_at` / `finished_at` lifecycle; a `stop` with no following `dwell` simply has no dwell-entry / dwell-complete steps to run, and the next eligible Plan either plans the next task or calls `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)` for terminal completion.
- A route is complete only after the terminal task sequence (stop + any following dwell) has finished. Route completion handling never fires before the terminal dwell (if any) exits.
- If dwell/timing says depart, the Plan dwell-complete step calls `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(walk_position)`, writes `station_exit_request`, and returns for that train. It does not write `RouteRun.direction`; the Action station-exit consumer performs `TrainController.finish_dwell()`, and on the next eligible Plan target resolution runs and step `592a` commits `RouteRun.direction` from the fresh `ResolvedNextTaskProjection`.
- If no task remains after the completed stop+dwell pair, the dwell-complete step has already returned (having written `station_exit_request`); on the next eligible Plan, step `c481`'s `None` branch reaches step `592a` — the owner of terminal-walk completion — which calls `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)` directly inside `tick_train_plan(...)` and returns for that tick (no live path remains after the completed stop, so the terminal-walk gate is satisfied). `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)` performs the route-completion teardown (set `current_route_status = FINISHED`, possibly trigger `route.deactivate()` for one-off routes with no remaining assigned trains) per the **`current_route_status` write contract**. `RouteExecutor.assigned_route_id_for(train_id)` automatically returns `None`. Dwell exit (`finish_dwell()`) has already run before this call; the `RouteRun` is preserved with `current_route_status = FINISHED` indefinitely as a historical record.
- `route.deactivate()` is the admin-driven entry point for switching off a shared `Route` while one or more assigned `RouteRun`s have not yet finished. It sets `Route.is_active = False` and walks every assigned train, writing `pending_route_deactivate` on each train's controller per the inclusive-latch rule defined in the **Latch Table** preamble. `route.deactivate()` is idempotent; calling it on an already-inactive route with no assigned trains is a no-op. The actual per-train teardown happens in each train's later Action `pending_route_deactivate` consumer, which calls `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)` after the inclusive cancel has committed; the helper writes `current_route_status = DEACTIVATED` and (when applicable) writes `station_exit_request` (the Action station-exit consumer performs the transition). There is no separate `RouteRun.deactivate()` method, and `route.deactivate()` does not delete any `RouteRun` — the runs are kept as historical `DEACTIVATED` records.
- `finish_dwell()` is a **dwell-exit state-transition command only**, named `finish_dwell` rather than `depart_from_station` because it does not start movement. It transitions the controller out of `RUNNING_AT_STATION` to the **`READY` state**. Its single caller is the Action station-exit consumer of `station_exit_request` (written by the Plan dwell-complete step or by a teardown consumer). `RouteExecutor` is still responsible for deciding whether more route work remains, clearing route assignment when complete, and removing the execution-state entry; those are route-level bookkeeping, not controller state.
  `TrainController.finish_dwell()` must not touch `received_path_plan` (the property is derived from the dispatcher-owned active path; authority for the served target already transitioned out of `ACTIVE` in `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(...)` before dwell began), must not call `TrainController.depart()` / `TrainController.ato.go()`, and must not initiate physics movement. The next target's route-side restart happens only on a later tick's Plan pass, through the authority-acquisition step -> `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)`, after which `RouteExecutor` writes `phase_latches.departure_request` once live authority exists. ATO vs manual effects are owned per the **`TrainController.depart()` canonical contract**.

**Dispatcher completion handling**

**route path-event callback schema**

- This is the single canonical callback contract for `PathDispatcher -> RouteExecutor` path-terminal notifications. Dispatcher notifies the route on both terminal transitions: `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(train_id)` calls `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(...)` after release, and `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)` calls the injected `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(...)` callback after a committed cancellation.
- The canonical callback signatures are exactly:
  - `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(train_id, path_id, walk_position)`
  - `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(train_id, path_id, error, was_deviation=False, was_run_completion=False)`
  Parameters are listed positionally above; callers may pass them by name. No other parameter is accepted in v1. Dispatcher derives the two mutually-exclusive booleans from the structured cancel-request fields, never from anything inside `error`. `was_deviation` feeds `RouteRun.path_cancel_was_deviation`; `was_run_completion` suppresses the ordinary `path_cancelled` diagnostic writes because step `6a0d` owns that successful progress event. Neither callback carries a timestamp parameter: every route-side timestamp this chain records is sampled fresh with `time.time()` at the write site per **Time sampling**. `PathDispatcher` independently samples its own status timestamp.
- The callback payloads are exactly:
  - completion context: `train_id`, `path_id`, `walk_position`
  - cancellation context: `train_id`, `path_id`, `error`, `was_deviation`, `was_run_completion`
  This callback is invoked synchronously by `PathDispatcher` immediately after committing the path-status transition, so its `path_id` always identifies the just-terminated path. There is no path-id correlation step.
- In that cancellation context:
  - `error` is diagnostic context only and must not be used for branching. UI/log consumers that need the originating kind subscribe to the `cancel_path` event on `NotificationCenter` (its `error.origin` field carries the writer-supplied label). v1 route-side recovery does not branch on the originating kind. EB recovery timing is gated by controller state: Plan cannot run until `TrainController.eb.release()` has cleared the condition and the ordinary post-command state evaluation has reached `READY`. Power-off teardown is driven by `pending_power_off` and the controller transitioning to `OFF`; every other case shares the same recovery path.
- The single v1 recovery table for cancellation / mismatch cases is:

  | Case | Detection point | Immediate effect | Next eligible Plan |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | any cancellation (movement-derived deviation, or explicit operator cancel / revoke / EB) (`7fa0`) | `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(...)` | preserve only confirmed physical progress, set `RouteRun.path_cancelled = True` and `RouteRun.path_cancel_was_deviation` from the callback's `was_deviation` argument (the derived `display_state` then reads `"DEVIATED"` for a movement deviation and `"CANCELLED"` for operator cancel / revoke / EB) | rerun covered-task index advance plus `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` from current physical position once `controller.is_recovery_clean` is true; the next task's behavior follows normal task-kind rules |
  | live-path target re-resolution invalidates a live path — a fresh resolve for the walk-position the live authority was acquired for would yield a different target **block** than that row records (`162a`); advancing to the next task on the walk is not this case, and neither is a direction-only change for the same block — see the live-path target re-resolution paragraph below for why | Plan latch + Action cancel / replan flow | let the cancel callback set `path_cancelled` per the cancellation row of the **`current_route_status` write contract** | rerun ordinary planning under the same `route_id` (the `RouteRun` is kept, never deactivated); later Plan calls `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` afresh |
  | EB interruption (`eddc`) | EB cancellation plus release flow | latch `pending_path_cancel_request` (`error.origin = "eb"`); the live path stays `ACTIVE` until Action commits the cancel once the train is stopped | after the train stops and the cancellation commits, `TrainController.eb.release()` clears only `eb.active`; the ordinary post-command evaluator reaches `READY`, at which point Plan replans normally |
  | power off (`dc91`) | power-off cleanup flow | latch `pending_power_off` (plus the inclusive `pending_path_cancel_request` when a live path exists); Action commits the cancel once stopped, then removes the `RouteRun` and performs OFF cleanup | the `RouteRun` no longer exists and the controller is `OFF`; Plan has nothing to do |

- `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(train_id)` resolves the served row through `RouteExecutor.find_next_completion_task(train_id)`. It reads `CompletionTaskProjection.task_kind` and `stored_resolved_target` and never indexes `RouteRun.task_runs` or `Route.tasks`. A `None` projection makes the arrival predicate false. On success it follows step `09b0`: release not-yet-entered resources, transition the `Path` to `COMPLETED`, then call `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(...)`, which performs step `bc55` for the projection's `walk_position`.
- Every live authority path has a matching `RouteRun` in v1, including one-off operator routes and speed-calibration leg routes. A dispatcher callback that cannot resolve the matching live run raises an internal invariant violation before mutating route state; it is never treated as a valid special case.
- The callback does not write `Train` fields — authority residue lives on dispatcher records and controller-facing projections.
- `PathDispatcher` clears controller authority by transitioning `Path.status` to `COMPLETED`. The controller's `received_path_plan` property then returns `None` on its next read, and the derived reads `controller.assigned_path_id`, `controller.ato_path_id`, and `controller.ato_destination_block_id` disappear automatically.
- Controller destination-block/path release must remain dispatcher-owned: dispatcher transitions `Path.status` and the controller's `received_path_plan` property automatically reads the new state. The controller reaches the **`READY` state** through its reactive stopped/no-authority rule rather than through a push callback. `RouteExecutor` remains responsible, on the next eligible Plan, for requesting dwell entry — writing `station_entry_request`, which the Action station-entry consumer performs as the `RUNNING_AT_STATION` transition — and for marking the dwell task finished in the Plan dwell-complete step.
- The **Stop-arrival check** identifies the stop being served through `CompletionTaskProjection`; its `stored_resolved_target` remains the authoritative record of which platform/block that stop was targeted at.
- **`RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(train_id, path_id, error, was_deviation=False, was_run_completion=False)`** is the cancellation-side counterpart. The lower-to-upper ordering is canonical: dispatcher finishes its path/resource mutation first, then hands the mutually-exclusive classifications upward. The callback takes exactly one of three branches:
  - **Missing-run handling.** When `RouteExecutor.execution_state_for(train_id) is None`, the callback raises an internal invariant violation before mutating route state. Every live path, including a calibration leg path, must be backed by a `RouteRun`.
  - **Run-completion branch.** For `was_run_completion == True` with a live run, the callback likewise returns after correlation/diagnostic validation and writes no `path_cancelled`, `path_cancel_was_deviation`, progress cursor, or task timing field; successful run progress remains owned by Plan step `6a0d`, which finishes the task only after observing stopped/no-authority state.
  - **Ordinary cancellation branch.** For every other (ordinary, run-backed) cancellation, the callback sets `RouteRun.path_cancelled = True` and `RouteRun.path_cancel_was_deviation = was_deviation`, and never chooses a fresh target or creates authority. The derived display reads `"DEVIATED"` for a movement deviation and `"CANCELLED"` for another ordinary authority cancellation until Plan cleanup consumes the diagnostic latch.

  The callback never advances a task or synthesizes arrival, in any branch.
- Every ordinary cancellation source (movement-derived deviation, operator cancel, revoke, EB, power-off) shares that ordinary `handle_path_cancellation(...)` branch; runtime gates produce their recovery timing differences. Normal run-completion release is the only explicit non-writing branch, selected only by `was_run_completion`, not by anything inside the `ErrorRecord`:
  - the Plan eligibility precondition only allows replanning when the controller is in `READY`, which naturally defers EB recovery until `eb.release()` has run;
  - the power-off Action cleanup separately calls `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(train_id)`, which flips the run to its historical `DEACTIVATED` row so no later Plan has anything to replan; `handle_path_cancellation(...)` still records the same diagnostic state, but the run is unassigned moments later by the same Action cleanup.
  Planning and routing logic rely on these runtime gates (controller state, latches, presence of `RouteRun`, current span coverage, and task-kind rules).
- **Live-path target re-resolution** uses this same temporary-status-clear model only after the current live path has already left `ACTIVE`. The trigger is a resolve that changes under a live path, not ordinary forward movement along the walk.
  - **Trigger.** When a fresh resolve for the walk-position the live authority was acquired for would yield a different target **block** than that row's stored `task_runs[walk_position].resolved_target` records because a non-`Route.tasks` input changed — for example a platform turned `disabled` or `manual`, station membership changed, or platform geometry changed — the live path must be treated as potentially stale, because the system cannot prove the already-acquired authority still serves the task. Changing `RouteTask.task_location` is a structural `Route.tasks` edit and always follows **Shared-route edit teardown** instead.
  - **Not this case.** Advancing along the walk is not this case: finishing a task and arming the next one yields a different `walk_position` and a different target block every time, and the **Waypoint lookahead** arms a target ahead of the train's current task by design. Neither latches a cancel.
  - **Response.** Plan therefore latches `pending_path_cancel_request` with `error.origin = "revoked"` (system/non-operator-driven), stops planning for that train, and waits for the ordinary Action cancel/callback/route-deviation-cleanup flow.
  - **Distinct from a structural edit.** This keeps the same `RouteRun`; it is NOT a structural `Route.tasks` edit, which always tears the run down to `DEACTIVATED` via `set_route_deactivate(...)` per the **Shared-route edit teardown**.
  - **Distinct from operator retargeting.** Operator-driven retargeting and explicit route swap take a different path entirely (abort current run + create new run, see **Route Edit And Reconciliation**); the inclusive cancel for that workflow uses `error.origin = "operator_cancelled"` per the **Latch Table** preamble.
  - Only after the live path is no longer active may `RouteExecutor` clear or rewrite the affected route-owned temporary target state and restart ordinary planning from the train's current position under the reconciled route.
- **Direction is resolved once per armed target block.** Plan resolves `requested_destination_direction` only when it arms a target block the live path does not already hold as its requested target. While the same block stays armed, every `extend_path(...)` retry reads `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)` and passes its `stored_resolved_target` pair unchanged, and Plan must not resolve the direction again for it. The extend-identity rule under **Path extension** and the Plan steps `592a` / `66aa` follow this rule.
- **Why this shape.** A `task_direction == "either"` task resolves its block-relative direction against the train's current span (the `requested_destination_direction` rule under **RouteTask data**), and that span moves every tick, so resolving a live target again lets the direction drift away from the terminal frame the path already acquired. The stored pair is what the **Stop-arrival check** compares the live authority's terminal block against, and it is also what every extend retry passes back in. Resolving once per armed block keeps the run's stored pair and the frame the path acquired the same value for the life of that target.
- A same-block direction change is therefore not something Plan can produce against a live path, and it does not trigger the live-path invalidation above. Arming a **new** target block is a fresh resolve, and it is the only route-side direction resolution that runs while a path is live. When that new block is one the live path already holds, `extend_path(...)` succeeds with `appended_resource_count = 0` / `reached_target = True`; the frame that governs arrival stays the one the path acquired, while the returned pair echoes what Plan passed (per **Path extension**), which is why Plan writes `task_runs[walk_position].resolved_target` from what the call returned, per Planning Kernel step `66aa`. `extend_path(...)` still rejects a direction that would require the train to reverse at the current authority end (`failure_kind = no_viable_path`, per **Path extension**), and that rejection is itself a structural extend failure: `RouteExecutor` latches the same `error.origin = "revoked"` cancel for it (per the **Structural failure_kind rule** under **Exact `RouteExecutor` tick calls**), so a new target whose direction is incompatible with the live authority still ends in cancel-and-replan.
- Completion handling may observe a train still physically occupying the terminal block or switch footprint. That is not a contradiction: `RouteExecutor` records arrival at the **Stop-arrival check**, while physical resource release still waits for the later tail-vacate callbacks.

## Train Entity

**Train ownership**

- **Train persistent fields.** `Train` is the persistent train-data entity. In v1 it keeps these fields:
  - identity
  - consist (including length)
  - `max_speed`
  - `total_distance_cm` and `total_run_time_seconds` — runtime-written persisted counters; rules and single writers in **Maintenance counters**
  - `min_radius_cm` — the train's minimum curve radius in centimetres, read by the pathfinder's curve-radius feasibility filter (see the pathfinding home)
  - `max_slope` — the train's maximum climbable grade as a percent, `0.0` meaning unspecified, read by the pathfinder's slope feasibility filter
  - `consist_length_cm` — the train's physical length in centimetres, used to build its span when it is placed
  - `is_unidentified` — `False` on every train the operator places, `True` only on a runtime-created **unidentified train**
  - `roster_entry_id: Optional[str]` — the `RosterEntry` this train was placed from, written once by `SimulationController.add_train(...)` when placement imports a roster entry, and `None` otherwise. It is the only way a runtime procedure reaches the roster entry behind a placed train (see **Train Roster**).
