Arrival enforcement against the requested target belongs to the **Stop-arrival check**, which reads route-owned state.
- `authority_end_block_id` in `received_path_plan` is always the current authority boundary the controller brakes toward, whether or not that authority has reached the run's armed target. The controller does not know the armed target and does not need to: `Path.reaches_target(block_id)` answers that question for the route side.
- `received_path_plan` does not carry a separate cab or head-side field. Its ordered `resource_sequence` is the retained path-origin-to-authority-end traversal history. Controller geometry reads locate the current physical span within that history and ignore entries wholly behind the current tail; the remaining suffix contains the currently covered span plus forward authority. "Tail" means the physical end of the current span farther from `authority_end_block_id`; "authority side" means the physical end closer to the destination and pointing into the path authority. When `TrainController.depart()` runs in ATO, it derives the cab by comparing `TrainSpan.end_a` and `TrainSpan.end_b` against that live suffix and aligns the selected cab to the authority side — selecting one when none is set, or switching a cab that faces the other way — per the **`TrainController.depart()` canonical contract** (manual depart never auto-aligns — it requires a pre-selected cab and rejects when `cab is None`). `end_a` is not a general preferred end in this model; it is only the final dead-heat tie-break when every authority-side comparison between the two physical ends remains exactly tied.
- Treat `assigned_path_id`, `ato_path_id`, and `ato_destination_block_id` as computed reads derived from `received_path_plan`, not as independently written runtime fields. The alias mapping is explicit in v1:
  - `assigned_path_id := received_path_plan.path_id`
  - `ato_path_id := received_path_plan.path_id`
  - `ato_destination_block_id := received_path_plan.authority_end_block_id`
  When `PathDispatcher` clears authority by transitioning `Path.status` to `COMPLETED`/`CANCELLED`, the controller's `received_path_plan` property returns `None` on its next read and all three disappear automatically.
- `lookahead` is a canonical pure derived value computed live on every read; it is the single canonical series used by ATC, ATO, UI, and monitor consumers.
- Target speed and ATC limit are reads from lookahead at distance 0; the controller does not store standalone `target_speed` or `effective_limit` scalars. The exported v1 payload also carries a top-level `speed_limit_reason` field; its canonical source is the distance-0 lookahead speed-curve metadata, surfaced at top level for UI/monitor reads.

**canonical lookahead payload**

- `TrainController.get_lookahead()` is the single canonical exported lookahead payload for ATC, ATO, UI, and monitor consumers. Every producer/consumer must refer back to this subsection by name instead of restating the field list elsewhere.
- **Why this shape.** Lookahead is the single read surface that fuses authority geometry, network state, signals, and current motion into one ordered forward projection. ATC, ATO, monitor UI, and stop-completion all sample from the same payload, so there is one place to add or change a forward-projected datapoint. Speed-curve metadata (including `atc_limit_reason_code`) lives on the same payload so that "why is the train holding at zero?" is answerable from one read instead of three. The empty/no-cab/no-train form preserves the same shape so consumers do not need to branch on payload variant.
- In v1, `get_lookahead()` carries exactly:
  - top level: `train_id`, `head_tile`, `head_distance_cm`, `travel_direction`, `cab`, `speed_limit_reason`, `lookahead`
  - nested `lookahead`: `blocks`, `signals`, `switches`, `stations`, `clearance_cm`, `safety_margin_cm`, `target_stop_cm`, `authority_boundary_delta_cm`, `speed_curves`
- `head_tile` is the current train head tile coordinate or `None` when unavailable. `head_distance_cm`, `clearance_cm`, `safety_margin_cm`, `target_stop_cm`, and `authority_boundary_delta_cm` are centimeters. `target_stop_cm` is the braking-target distance from the head (`clearance_cm` minus the effective `safety_margin_cm`, floored at 0; equal to `max(0, -authority_boundary_delta_cm)` under the sign convention defined on `authority_boundary_delta_cm` below). `travel_direction` is the train's current forward travel direction in the same frame used by movement/traversal. `cab` is the currently selected cab or `None`.
- `blocks`, `signals`, `switches`, and `stations` are ordered forward projections for UI/debug consumers. They are informational read models only; control decisions come from the same payload's clearance and speed-curve data.
- `lookahead.stations` is the payload name for the ordered forward platform projection: each entry refers to a concrete physical platform ahead on the track, not to a logical multi-platform station group.
- Each `lookahead.blocks` entry carries exactly:
  - `id`
  - `name`
  - `state`
  - `start_cm`
  - `end_cm`
  - `length_cm`
  - `tile_count`
  - `speed_limit_kmh`
- Each `lookahead.signals` entry carries exactly:
  - `id`
  - `name`
  - `state`
  - `distance_cm`
- Each `lookahead.switches` entry carries exactly:
  - `x`
  - `y`
  - `name`
  - `position`
  - `distance_cm`
  - `locked`
  where `position` is `"main"` or `"diverging"` for the live switch alignment at that tile, and `locked` is the exported boolean monitor view of whether that switch currently has any future lock claim or train-owned protection claim that blocks conflicting acquisition.
- Each `lookahead.stations` entry carries exactly:
  - `platform_id`
  - `station_id`
  - `name`
  - `distance_cm`
  - `length_cm`
  - `tile_count`
  - `top_speed_kmh`
- `platform_id` in this compatibility payload is the concrete physical platform identifier on the track.
- `station_id` in this compatibility payload is the logical station-group identifier that owns that platform, or `None` when no station group exists. `station_id` must not be reused as the physical platform identifier anywhere.
- Each `lookahead.speed_curves` entry carries exactly:
  - `distance_cm`
  - `atc_limit`
  - `operational_limit`
  - optional `atc_limit_reason_code`
  - optional `atc_limit_reason_detail`
  The limit fields are in `km/h`.
- The canonical `atc_limit_reason_code` enumeration is defined here once. Every consumer (the **Stop-arrival check**, no-authority braking diagnostic, and monitor/UI display) cross-references this set by name and must not use arbitrary strings or redefine the values elsewhere. `TrainController.is_stopped()` is speed-only and does not consume a reason code.
  - `"authority_stop"` (`f169`) — zero-speed restriction at the safety-margin-adjusted end of live authority, including a head that has rolled past that boundary while still mapping into `resource_sequence`; one of the two conditions that satisfy the **Stop-arrival check**
  - `"caution"` (`39ed`) — approaching or inside a caution zone (block in `CAUTION` state or forward block occupied)
  - `"obstruction"` (`05e9`) — an in-path resource conflict that blocks forward progress below safe clearance distance
  - `"speed_limit"` (`5c1d`) — a posted segment speed limit (`Segment.speed_limit_kmh`) below the train's current maximum: a permitted-speed restriction ahead, distinct from `obstruction` (which is an in-path resource conflict, not a posted limit)
  - `"no_authority"` (`7f1a`) — no live path authority; `atc_limit = 0` at distance 0 regardless of block geometry, so ATC holds a stopped train at rest and escalates a rolling train to EB
  - `"deviation"` (`4e2b`) — live authority exists but the train head cannot be mapped into `received_path_plan.resource_sequence`; `atc_limit = 0` at distance 0 so ATC stops the train (escalating a rolling train to EB per step `826a`) while the latched deviation cancel waits for the stop
  - `"no_cab"` (`2ce5`) — no cab selected; ATC limit is zero regardless of authority
  - `"wrong_direction_cab"` (`a54f`) — selected cab points away from live authority direction; ATC limit is zero
  - `"eb"` (`c3ea`) — emergency brake latched; ATC limit is zero
  - `"no_train"` (`7b09`) — the train or network object is not yet wired, so the empty distance-0 anchor still reports a structured reason code rather than a free-form string
  - **Tie-break.** When more than one category above produces the distance-0 minimum, the reported code is the first match in this order: `no_train`, `no_cab`, `eb`, `no_authority`, `deviation`, `wrong_direction_cab`, `obstruction`, `authority_stop`, `caution`, `speed_limit`. `authority_stop` therefore never masks a zero-limit condition that is not an arrival, keeping the **Stop-arrival check**'s first arrival disjunct exact.
- **A changed reason code is an event.** The reason code answers "why is this train limited right now", so the runtime records when that answer changes.
  - **Comparison and emission.** Tick substep `4d7c` compares this tick's distance-0 `atc_limit_reason_code` against the stored `_last_emitted_atc_reason_code`. When they differ, it emits one event through `controller.notifications` per the **Event schema** — `operation = "tick"`, `entities` naming the train, `message` one line naming the previous and new code, and `payload` carrying the previous code, the new code, the new `atc_limit`, and the `atc_limit_reason_detail` — and then writes the new code to `_last_emitted_atc_reason_code`.
  - **Kind selection.** The substep declares `kind` itself, the same way every other writer does, choosing between **either of these two**:
    - `"info"` for `"deviation"` and `"no_authority"` — because those hold the train at zero and an operator wants them in the stream
    - `"debug"` for every other code — because they are ordinary driving restrictions a developer reads back

    The level is written into the emit call, never computed from the code value at run time.
  - **No `ErrorRecord`.** The event carries no `ErrorRecord`: it reports what the limit is, not that something failed, and the failure that caused the restriction is reported by its own emitting operation. Keeping it below `"warning"` also keeps it out of `NotificationCenter.latest_error_for(...)`, so the no-authority banner still answers with a real failure.
  - **Change basis.** The comparison is against the last emitted code, not the last tick's code, so a code that flickers back and forth emits on each real change and a steady code emits nothing. This is its own change detection, because the event carries no `ErrorRecord` and `NotificationCenter`'s suppression covers only error-carrying events (see **Error events**, Emit on change, not per tick). An error-free per-tick emitter that must not repeat owns its own last-emitted state this way.
  - **Payload completeness.** The payload is the whole record: nothing else stores a reason-code history, and the live value stays the lookahead read it always was.
- `atc_limit_reason_code == "authority_stop"` is the canonical reason code for the zero-speed restriction at the active stop/end-of-authority boundary. The **Stop-arrival check**'s first arrival condition must key on this code, not on arbitrary reason strings; its second arrival condition reads head position and no reason code.
- `authority_boundary_delta_cm` is the live signed separation from the train head to the safety-margin-adjusted authority boundary in the same forward distance axis as the `speed_curves[*].distance_cm` samples and the authority-boundary projection helper. With a live path it is derived from `authority_end_block_id` plus the terminal frame; without a live path it is `0.0` because no authority boundary exists. It is diagnostic/control lookahead data, not a route-authored stop-position field.
- Consumers asking "what is the target speed right now?" sample `lookahead.speed_curves` at distance `0`: `operational_limit` at distance `0` is the controller target speed, and `atc_limit` plus its reason metadata at distance `0` is the controller ATC limit/reason. The exported payload carries the top-level `speed_limit_reason` field — the same distance-0 reason metadata surfaced at top level for monitor/UI reads.
- The empty/no-cab/no-train form must preserve this same top-level and nested key shape, with empty lists and zero distances instead of returning a different payload shape. If a compatibility producer cannot compute one of the nested boundary/safety fields on an empty payload, it must still emit the key with `0.0` rather than omitting it.

**Controller tick order**

1. `01f2` — Drain queued operator commands as the first substep of `TrainController.tick(...)`.
1a. `7b40` — Invoke `after_command_drain` exactly once. The callback binds to the early-Action consumers, in order: first the stopped-gated `pending_path_cancel_request` consumer (when no cancel is pending or the train is rolling, it is a no-op and retains the latch as required), then the `departure_request` consumer calling `TrainController.depart()` and the `station_entry_request` consumer calling `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()`, each recording its result and clearing its own request. This runs even when the controller is still `OFF` after the drain (`power_on_cmd()` was not accepted this drain): the consumers self-gate, so an `OFF` train — being stopped — has its `pending_path_cancel_request` consumed and its two transition requests rejected and cleared, while the teardown latches it retains are consumed by a later powered Action, matching the powered-off-transaction rule in **`SimulationController.update()` calls**. This early-Action consumer order is owned by the **Observe, Plan, and Action Table**.
1b. `71ee` — Call `OperationalStateMachine.evaluate_reactive_conditions()` against the post-command, post-cancel, post-transition controller state. It makes a released EB condition and a just-cleared authority visible to the ordinary transition rules.
1c. Obtain any open calibration's drive value against that state through `SpeedCalibration.get_propulsion_override(train_id)`, which validates the open run and returns `None` when no calibration may drive; neither union variant is applied until the safety steps below permit it. Ending an invalid lighting run is a separate `SimulationController` teardown step (`26f5`), run after this tick's voltage write — see the **Observe, Plan, and Action Table**.
1d. `1b7a` — **Authority-clear ATO stop.** Sample `received_path_plan` after the early dispatcher slot. When it is `None` and `ato.running == True`, call `controller.ato.stop()`.
1e. `4d7c` — **Reason-code change event.** Read the distance-0 `atc_limit_reason_code` from `lookahead` and emit/store it on change per **A changed reason code is an event**. This runs ahead of the later early exits.
2. `3ec8` — If no train, return immediately. The drain has already run, so a command queued against a train that is absent from the network fails its own precondition check rather than sitting in the queue. After that drain, if `state == "OFF"`, keep the controller in `OFF`, reset `_last_emitted_atc_reason_code` to `None` (see its schema row), and return from the controller tick's powered decision work. The tick-opening Observe batch has already sampled and attributed the whole layout. It may have skipped `TrainPhysics.tick(...)` and `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)` for this train, but detector-attributed block entries and vacates were still committed through `TrainController.build_detected_progress_report()`. A train pushed by hand, or an unidentified train (see **Power**, Unidentified trains), therefore remains observable. If `TrainController.commands.power_on_cmd()` succeeded during the drain, the controller is no longer `OFF`, so `TrainController.tick(...)` continues through normal powered Action logic and writes the voltage that the next tick's Observe movement calculation will use. Route Plan stays skipped only for the transaction that began while the train was `OFF`; route planning resumes on the next eligible tick.
3. `d483` — If emergency brake is active:
  - Hold the EB state: re-write handle = `EB` and force the ATC limit at distance 0 to `0`. Then early-exit the tick while EB remains latched. The other **canonical EB activation effects** are not re-applied here, because activation already called `controller.ato.stop()` and cleared the `ops.service_stop_active` latch, no path re-enters authority while EB is latched, and Plan run step `6a0d` does not re-arm the service-stop latch while a higher-priority teardown latch is pending, so there is nothing left to re-apply. `manual.manual_power_percent` is the one manual input this step does not own — the driver may re-command it on any EB tick per the **Power/cab/mode command contracts** — and it needs no per-tick reset here, because the forced zero ATC limit keeps it from producing movement while the latch is set and the **driver-control interlock** on `TrainController.eb.release()` keeps a retained value from surviving into the release.
  - Stay in the early-exit loop until the train has stopped.
  - Require explicit `eb.release()` to clear `eb.active`.
  - While `eb.active == True`, `TrainController.tick()` does not perform post-EB restart logic. `TrainController.eb.release()` clears only the condition; on that command's tick, step `71ee` applies the ordinary state rule and may reach **`READY`**. Neither step clears route-owned recovery state. The earlier EB activation already wrote `pending_path_cancel_request` (`error.origin = "eb"`), which Action cancels and which sets `RouteRun.path_cancelled = True` via the cancellation callback. `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` (Plan) owns the route-deviation cleanup step and observes `path_cancelled` once the controller has reached `READY`.
4. `061a` — If no cab is selected, ATC limit is forced to zero and `lookahead` returns the canonical empty payload on every read.
5. `22a9` — Otherwise `lookahead` returns the canonical payload for the current state on every read:
  - With a received path plan, lookahead extends along the path to the current `authority_end_block_id` boundary adjusted by the controller safety margin.
  - With a received path plan whose head cannot be mapped into `resource_sequence` (a pending deviation), the distance-0 anchor reports `atc_limit = 0` with `atc_limit_reason_code = "deviation"`; the forward projections carry whatever geometry remains mappable.
  - Without a path plan, `lookahead` is the canonical no-authority empty payload (same top-level and nested shape as the no-cab case). `speed_curves` carries a single anchor at `distance_cm = 0.0` with `atc_limit = 0.0`, `operational_limit = 0.0`, and `atc_limit_reason_code = no_authority`. `blocks`, `signals`, `switches`, and `stations` are empty lists. `clearance_cm = 0.0` and `authority_boundary_delta_cm = 0.0`. The controller does not project forward through the train's current occupied block when no live path exists. Movement authority is binary on `received_path_plan`, per the **`received_path_plan` schema** rule that there is no second authority source.
6. `c4c2` — Build ATC state from `lookahead`, including structured reason metadata.
7. `914f` — Apply ATC overspeed logic. Ordinarily, escalate through `TrainController.eb.activate()` when `current_speed_kmh > atc_limit_at_distance_0 + OVERSPEED_EB_THRESHOLD_KMH`. One fail-safe override replaces that margin: when the distance-0 limit is `0` and `atc_limit_reason_code ∈ {"deviation", "no_authority"}`, escalate whenever `not TrainController.is_stopped()`. These are the only zero-limit override reasons; all other reason codes use the ordinary margin. Below the EB margin, when `current_speed_kmh > atc_limit_at_distance_0 + OVERSPEED_WARN_THRESHOLD_KMH`, emit one `kind = "warning"` event (`operation = "tick"`, `entities` naming the train) the first tick the condition holds and not again while it stays true, the same change-detection shape as **A changed reason code is an event**; store the emitted state on `_overspeed_warned: bool` and clear it once the margin is no longer exceeded, so the warning re-emits on the next fresh occurrence. This is the canonical home for both `OVERSPEED_EB_THRESHOLD_KMH` and `OVERSPEED_WARN_THRESHOLD_KMH`.
8. `0a4e` — Calculate ATO info.
9. `8d18` — In ATO mode, if `ato.running`, calculate the handle with `controller.ato.compute_handle(delta_seconds)` and write it to `handle_position`; otherwise call `controller.ato.calculate_braking_notch_for_speed(...)` against the live distance-0 `atc_limit` and write the result to `handle_position` through `OperationalStateMachine`, per Module boundaries rule 5.
10. `924d` — In manual mode, write a controller-owned command and let physics convert it to speed:
  - In `simulation` submode, store the driver's handle notch in `handle_position`. This is the raw driver command; it is not itself clamped. `TrainPhysics` reads the live distance-0 `atc_limit` from controller lookahead when it integrates movement for the tick: the notch may never raise speed above that limit, so a driver notch commanding more than ATC currently allows produces motion capped at the limit without `handle_position` itself being rewritten. When current speed already exceeds the limit — including the forced `0` while `eb.active` — physics decelerates toward the limit at the applicable brake rate (`SpeedProfile.emergency_brake_rate` while EB is latched, per EB workflow row `e67d`) rather than snapping the tick's resulting speed down to it.
  - In `power_percent` submode, store the driver's percentage power in `manual.manual_power_percent` as an integer `0..100`, and let physics map it through `SpeedProfile.power_speed_curve` when no braking override is active. This value is positive only. It represents the absolute applied track/motor voltage and its calibrated immediate running speed, not a signed traction-vs-brake effort. `manual.manual_power_percent` is set-and-forget: once a driver `set_manual_power_percent(...)` command writes it, or a safety workflow resets it to `0` through `manual.reset_power_percent_for_safety()`, it stays at that value across ticks until the driver issues a new command. The controller stores no second driver-command copy and never restores a pre-override value automatically.
  - **Canonical power-percent safety-cap ordering.**
    - **EB branch reachability.** This ordering's EB branch is reachable only on the tick that raises EB from inside step `914f` (the ATC/no-authority escalation path): step `d483` runs before `914f` in tick order and only checks `eb.active` as that step begins, so an EB activated moments later by `914f` does not retroactively trigger `d483`'s early exit on this same tick, and command selection continues into this step with `eb.active` now `True`. The lookahead read this step takes is live (per **Lookahead is a pure derived value**), so it correctly reflects the just-activated EB. Operator-issued EB (`eb.activate()`, drained at tick-entry step `01f2`) never reaches this step on its activation tick: `eb.active` is already `True` by the time step `d483` runs, so `d483` early-exits the tick before command selection is reached, and every later activation tick early-exits at `d483` the same way.
    - **Sampling the commanded operating point.** At the start of command selection, sample `commanded_power = manual.manual_power_percent` and derive `commanded_speed = power_speed_curve(commanded_power)`.
    - **When an override is present.** An override is present when **any of these holds** this tick:
      - `eb.active == True` — EB
      - `ops.service_stop_active == True` — service-stop
      - `commanded_speed > atc_limit_at_distance_0` — ATC: the commanded operating point itself exceeds the live cap; a live ATC limit that the commanded speed already respects is not an override
    - **Effective operating point.** With no braking override, the commanded operating point is the effective speed/power/voltage for the tick. With an override, compute `effective_speed = min(commanded_speed, override_cap)`, where `override_cap` is `atc_limit_at_distance_0` for an ATC override (which already reads `0` for an EB override, via `atc_limit_reason_code = "eb"`) and, read directly from `ops.service_stop_active`, `0.0` for a service-stop override; then derive the tick's `effective_power` from the inverse `power_speed_curve` mapping and `track_voltage` from `voltage_power_curve`.
    - **Retained-field reset.** Under an ATC or service-stop override, and only after capturing that effective operating point, call `manual.reset_power_percent_for_safety()`, so the retained field is `0` for later ticks until the driver re-commands it. An EB override caps the tick to zero but leaves the retained field alone: the driver clears it, and `TrainController.eb.release()` is gated on that clear through its **driver-control interlock**. Thus a positive ATC cap can produce a positive capped voltage for the current tick without contradicting the retained reset, while a zero cap produces zero speed, zero power, and the calibrated 0%-power track voltage (`lighting_voltage`, the stopped-but-lit output — see **SpeedProfile**).
    - There is no handle fallback or negative power-percent command.
10a. `b41e` — **Route-owned service-stop override.** When `ops.service_stop_active == True`, this step runs after ordinary command generation. In ATO and manual `simulation`, it calls `OperationalStateMachine.set_service_brake_to_zero()`; it never calls the neutral-reset helper. In manual `power_percent`, step `924d` has already applied the zero cap and called `ManualDriving.reset_power_percent_for_safety()` for this tick per **Canonical power-percent safety-cap ordering**, so this step has nothing further to apply there. EB and ATC may demand stronger braking. The override persists until `TrainController.consume_service_stop()` clears the latch after stopped no-authority confirmation.
10b. `b7ac` — **Same-tick EB re-assertion.** When `eb.active == True` at this point in the tick — including an activation raised moments earlier by this same tick's step `914f` — re-apply the EB Workflow's own `handle_position = EB` write through the Operational-state sub-module, overriding whatever `8d18`, `924d`, or `b41e` produced this tick. This is the step Module boundaries rule 5 means by "afterward": it makes the tick end with `handle_position = EB`, so the voltage written in this Action pass makes the next tick's Observe movement calculation integrate the emergency-brake rate. `d483`'s early-exit hold re-applies the same write on every later tick while EB remains latched; this step covers only the escalation tick itself, before `d483` has a chance to run.
10c. `c2fe` — **Pending-power-off propulsion hold.** When `phase_latches.power_off == True` AND `eb.active == False` at this point in the tick, replace that tick's command with the neutral notch through `OperationalStateMachine.reset_handle_to_neutral()` and call `ManualDriving.reset_power_percent_for_safety()`, overriding whatever `8d18` or `924d` produced this tick. This step is a no-op while `eb.active == True`, so it never overrides step `b7ac`'s same-tick `handle_position = EB` write: EB outranks the power-off propulsion hold, because a rolling ghost train may reach its own EB escalation on the same tick its power-off latch was written, and that tick must still end with the EB voltage for the next Observe movement calculation. This covers the multi-tick Observe ghost writer, whose latch is not stopped-gated and may stay set across several rolling ticks; the stopped-only operator writer already produces a neutral command from `TrainController._apply_power_off_request(...)`'s one-shot neutralization, so this step is a no-op for it (independent of the EB guard).
11. `44e9` — No standalone `effective_limit` or `target_speed` scalar is computed; consumers read controller lookahead at distance 0.
12. `89ba` — `TrainController.tick(...)` does not latch path completion. It builds the current state-machine outputs by reading `lookahead` (which recomputes live from current span/speed/path), but it must not mutate `Path` records, release resources, clear authority, or call route callbacks itself. Earlier in Observe, when movement calculation ran, `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)` wrote `physics_sync.current_span` / `physics_sync.current_speed_kmh`, called `OperationalStateMachine.evaluate_reactive_conditions()`, built the canonical `ControllerProgressReport`, and appended it to `physics_sync.queued_progress_reports`; it did not mutate dispatcher or route state directly. Action step `71ee` called the same evaluator after the command drain.
13. `32dd` — Waiting decisions read controller lookahead plus `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)`, the route-owned projection of the acquired authority target. Path completion is separate: the earlier Observe **Stop-arrival check** used `RouteExecutor.find_next_completion_task(train_id)` for the next physically served task after local progress and deviation handling. On success, `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(train_id)` released authority and handed the arrival to the route. Explicit teardown latches run only after that normal arrival opportunity; `TrainController.tick(...)` never commits completion.
14. `90d3` — A best-effort truncated path stopping at its current authority boundary is not completion when that boundary is short of the route-owned armed stop target. The controller stays in `RUNNING_MOVING` with `is_stopped() == True` (depart was accepted; ATC is holding the train at zero); the same `received_path_plan.path_id` remains live while `RouteExecutor` keeps retrying `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` on it.
15. `826a` — **Zero-limit authority-loss / deviation protocol.** A rolling train whose authority can no longer be used is stopped through the distance-0 zero limit, never through a service-brake-to-boundary path. **Any of these two cases** triggers it:
  - **Deviation under a still-live path.** The deviation latch is pending while the path stays `ACTIVE`, and the canonical lookahead reads `atc_limit = 0` at distance 0 with `atc_limit_reason_code = "deviation"` (head unmappable, per step `22a9`).
  - **No live path at all** (`received_path_plan is None`). The lookahead is the no-authority empty payload (`atc_limit_reason_code = "no_authority"`). Because every cancellation commits only on a stopped train, this case cannot arise from a cancel under a rolling train; a stopped train whose authority was cancelled simply rests under the no-authority zero limit.

  In either case, step `914f` applies its fail-safe override: `not TrainController.is_stopped()` escalates to EB despite the ordinary overspeed margin. The tie-break codes `no_cab` and `wrong_direction_cab` never mask this override for a moving train: `RUNNING_MOVING` requires a selected cab (the cab guard in the **Controller state machine**), so `no_cab` cannot report while the train moves; `wrong_direction_cab` cannot report on a moving train either, because `set_cab(...)` is accepted only while stopped and a mismatched cab's zero distance-0 limit prevents motion from starting in the first place, so a rolling train's zero-limit reason is always `deviation` or `no_authority`. It calls `TrainController.eb.activate()`, which performs the **canonical EB activation effects**. Once the canonical stopped predicate is true and the cancel latch is consumed, the operator clears EB through `TrainController.eb.release()`. No raw `current_speed_kmh > 0` comparison exists.
**ATC speed limit**

- ATC restriction selection does not read signal state. CAUTION restriction comes from a single controller-owned global cap, `CAUTION_SPEED_LIMIT_KMH`, applied when `TrainController` samples a block whose computed `Block.state` is `CAUTION`; signals are display state derived from blocks, not an ATC input. `CAUTION_SPEED_LIMIT_KMH` is adjustable as `caution_speed_limit_kmh` in **Runtime settings**.
- In manual mode with a received path plan, the controller lookahead builds the authority-boundary stop so the effective ATC limit enforces the current authority end correctly: it brakes to the `authority_end_block_id` boundary in the current live authority frame using the controller safety margin.
- Treat ATC reason reporting as structured metadata on the lookahead/curve payload, not only as a free-form controller string.

**ATO handle calculation**

- `controller.ato.compute_handle(delta_seconds)` is the per-tick ATO handle selection. The controller calls it once per tick while an ATO run is active and writes the result to `handle_position` (per **Module boundaries** rule 5); it gets its tick delta as the `delta_seconds` argument the controller passes (the same tick delta used elsewhere that tick), not from any stored field.
- `compute_handle(...)` reads the canonical controller `lookahead` property (itself a pure derived value computed live); it does not build a lookahead of its own.
- If the sampled operational speed curve at distance `0` is already at or below the stop threshold, it returns a direct braking notch immediately.
- It selects the notch from a two-point sampling of the operational speed curve:
  - the operational speed curve at distance `0`
  - one future point at a delta-scaled horizon (the lookahead distance grows with current motion using `delta_seconds`, e.g. `speed_cm_s * delta_seconds * LOOKAHEAD_TICKS`)
  - combined with the active ATC and block caps to choose power, coast, or brake.

**Speed curves**

- Build a unified restriction set for the full clearance/authority area and take the minimum of all relevant curves and local limits at each sample point.
- Carry source metadata on each `lookahead.speed_curves` datapoint, such as `atc_limit_reason_code` and `atc_limit_reason_detail`.
- Preserve metadata for which restriction category produced the current minimum ATC limit so monitor/debug UI can explain the displayed number.

**Driver/operator inputs**

- `TrainController.commands.set_handle()` is the active manual-driving command for `simulation` submode manual control. The command may be accepted while manual mode is active, `manual_mode_type == simulation`, the train is powered, and a cab is selected; the written `handle_position` is the raw driver command, and `TrainPhysics` never lets it raise the resulting speed above the live distance-0 `atc_limit` when it integrates movement (per tick step `924d` (Manual-mode command write)) — including the limit's forced `0` while `eb.active`, since EB reads `atc_limit_reason_code = "eb"` — decelerating at the applicable brake rate when current speed already exceeds the limit, rather than snapping the tick's resulting speed down to it. The command's physical effect is bounded this way without `handle_position` itself being rewritten, and the command never clears `eb.active`. `set_handle()` is rejected (`success=False`) when `manual_mode_type == power_percent`.
- `TrainController.commands.set_manual_power_percent()` is the active driver input for `power_percent` submode manual control; the matching API endpoint/client method and train/editor UI control deliver operator input through `manual.set_power_percent(...)`. It accepts under the same manual-input conditions as `set_handle()` except `manual.manual_mode_type` must be `power_percent`: manual mode active, train powered, and cab selected. Like handle input, the command may be accepted before depart has been accepted (and while `eb.active`), but ATC and EB remain authoritative and apply the **Canonical power-percent safety-cap ordering**. Setting `0` while `eb.active == True` is how the driver satisfies the **driver-control interlock** on `TrainController.eb.release()`. The command clamps to `0..100` and does not start movement by itself. It is rejected when `manual_mode_type == simulation` or any shared acceptance precondition fails.
- `TrainController.depart()` is called by the Action transition consumer of the `departure_request` latch `RouteExecutor` writes whenever live authority exists for the current target, including one-off operator routes created from direct UI/API movement requests. No other component may call `depart()` directly or synthesize departure acceptance by other means.

**Dispatcher/route-executor inputs**

- There is no `receive_path_plan(path_plan)` setter, cache refresh, or atomic replacement API in v1. `received_path_plan` is a read-only property that resolves the active dispatcher-owned path into the canonical **received_path_plan schema** on each read; updates to the dispatcher's `Path` registry surface automatically without any controller-side write.
- `received_path_plan` must follow the canonical **received_path_plan schema**. Its nested authority geometry must follow the canonical **resource_sequence entry schema** and **path_tile entry schema**; the controller must not be asked to recover terminal-frame direction later from tile coordinates alone.
- In v1, `received_path_plan` carries the authorized corridor and current authority boundary, not the create/extend request's requested target. The live stop the controller must brake to on this tick is derived from `authority_end_block_id`, the terminal frame in `resource_sequence`, and the controller safety margin.
- `received_path_plan` must not carry a second lifecycle status enum. For the controller, movement authority is binary: `received_path_plan is not None` means there is live authority, and `received_path_plan is None` means there is not.
- `on_physics_updated(event_time, span_update)` is called by `TrainPhysics.tick(...)` after it computes the next span/speed and tile delta. `TrainController.on_physics_updated(event_time, span_update)` applies the update to controller-owned `current_span` / `current_speed_kmh`, then calls `OperationalStateMachine.evaluate_reactive_conditions()` synchronously so any movement-caused `READY` ↔ `RUNNING_MOVING` / `ato.running` transition commits here in Observe (see **Reactive condition evaluation**). It then builds the canonical progress report from the tile delta, the live `lookahead` (computed from the just-updated span/speed), and `received_path_plan.resource_sequence` when live authority exists, and appends that report to the controller-owned per-train progress mailbox (`physics_sync.queued_progress_reports`). `TrainPhysics` samples that movement pass's timestamp once via `time.time()` and passes it in as `event_time`, and the controller stores it unchanged on the report's `ControllerProgressReport.event_time`; a single movement pass may make several `on_physics_updated(...)` calls (for example a span split across a tunnel boundary), and they all carry the one timestamp because the controller never resamples. The `ControllerProgressReport` is a within-tick transient, not a stored field, so this sampling sits outside the stored-field **Time sampling** rule under the **Units contract**. `SimulationController` drains and clears that mailbox in Observe by calling `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` in order. This method owns span storage and progress interpretation only. It does not mutate dispatcher path records or route state directly.
- `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()` is the dwell-entry transition performed by the Action station-entry consumer. Plan dwell-entry step `3a37` writes `station_entry_request` when `controller.is_recovery_clean` is true, the route's next non-finished task has `task_kind == "dwell"`, and `controller.cab ∈ {"A", "B"}`, after it has itself sampled and written the dwell row's `started_at` (see step `3a37`); Action then calls `enter_station_dwell()`. The controller call transitions to `RUNNING_AT_STATION` only. The controller does not detect dwell entry on its own and does not read or write `RouteRun`.
- Missing path authority is represented entirely by `received_path_plan is None`. The controller has no `wait_for_path(reason)` command.
- `TrainController.depart()`, `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()`, and `TrainController.finish_dwell()` are controller acceptance/transition commands, each called only by its Action transition-consumer step, which consumes the matching request latch Plan wrote: `departure_request` → `depart()`, `station_entry_request` → `enter_station_dwell()`, `station_exit_request` → `finish_dwell()`. `station_exit_request` is written by (a) the Plan dwell-complete step inside `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)`, or (b) `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(...)` when invoked by any of the Action abort/power-off/deactivate consumers with the controller currently in `RUNNING_AT_STATION`. `TrainController.finish_dwell()` is the end-of-dwell state transition; it lands in the **`READY` state** (per the predicate defined in the Controller state machine subsection), does not clear `received_path_plan`, and does not start movement. Cab selection is preserved across route completion.
- Manual trains use the same Plan dwell-entry step inside `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` as ATO. The difference is departure behavior only: in manual mode `TrainController.depart()` records that the current authority has been accepted and the train is ready to go, but it does not itself start movement or call `TrainController.ato.go()`.
- `TrainController.begin_service_stop()` and `TrainController.consume_service_stop()` are the controller-level accessors for the `ops.service_stop_active` latch; the **Latch Table** defines its writer, consumer, and gating state. `begin_service_stop()` is the latch's canonical writer helper: it is idempotent, valid while powered in either control mode, sets `ops.service_stop_active = True`, and calls `controller.ato.stop()`. It does not cancel authority or write route state, and Controller tick step `b41e` owns the actual per-mode braking override. `consume_service_stop()` clears the latch and changes no other operational state; it is a no-op when the latch is not set, so every caller may call it unconditionally. It emits one `kind = "info"` event through `controller.notifications` only on a call that actually cleared a set latch; a no-op call emits nothing, so the unconditional callers below add no traffic when no service stop was armed. The gating predicate and the full set of run-ending clears are owned by the **Latch Table**, row `ops.service_stop_active`. No other component assigns the field.
- `PathDispatcher` calls its injected `RouteExecutor.handle_path_cancellation(train_id, path_id, error, was_deviation=False, was_run_completion=False)` callback only after the dispatcher cancel mutation has committed. The ordinary branch records diagnostic context and the deviation-vs-cancel display classification from `was_deviation`; the run-completion branch records no cancellation diagnostic state because step `6a0d` owns that normal progress. The `ErrorRecord` remains diagnostic-only event data.
- `RouteExecutor` must not set controller path or destination fields directly; controller authority is read live by the controller through its `received_path_plan` projection over the dispatcher's `Path` registry.
- `TrainController.eb.release()` follows the **EB workflow state machine** rows `ad04` and `29a0`; this list does not restate its preconditions or ordinary post-cancellation recovery.

**`TrainController.depart()` canonical contract**

`TrainController.depart()` is the controller's departure-acceptance command, returning `(success, reason)`. It is called by the Action transition consumer of the `departure_request` that Plan writes on every eligible pass with live authority for the current target, regardless of `control_mode`; there is no route-level departure policy in v1.

- Acceptance preconditions are checked in order; any failure returns `(False, <reason>)` and leaves controller state unchanged, so Plan may retry on a later tick:
  - `received_path_plan is not None` — there must be live authority to depart into.
  - `eb.active == False` — a latched EB blocks departure.
  - `pending_power_off` is not set — a pending shutdown blocks departure.
  - `state ∈ {READY, RUNNING_MOVING}` — the second admits **Reactive condition evaluation** having already advanced state ahead of this call.
  - In `manual` mode only: a cab is selected (`cab ∈ {A, B}`) and a facing direction is resolved.
  - `depart()` itself checks no other `phase_latches` field. `pending_route_abort`, `pending_route_deactivate`, and a pending `pending_path_cancel_request` are caller-side concerns instead, gated where they matter to Plan's own step ordering: the Planning Kernel eligibility precondition already excludes `PATH_CANCEL_PENDING`, `ROUTE_ABORT_PENDING`, and `ROUTE_DEACTIVATE_PENDING` from create/extend acquisition (see the **`ControllerCondition` set** and the **Planning Kernel**), so a pending cancel blocks the extend retry that would normally precede a same-pass `depart()` call for existing live authority.
- On acceptance the ATO-vs-manual difference is owned inside the call:
  - In `ato` mode, `depart()` aligns the cab to the authority itself: it derives the cab facing the authority by comparing `received_path_plan.resource_sequence` with `TrainSpan.end_a` / `end_b` (final tie-break: `end_a`), and when that derived cab differs from the currently selected one — because no cab is selected, or the selected cab faces the other way — it stops the train if it is still moving and selects or switches to the derived cab (a switch of an already-selected cab is the correction case; a fresh selection is the no-cab case). ATO departure never rejects solely for a missing cab when authority exists to derive the direction from; it rejects only when no cab is selected and no authority is available. When aligning moves the head to the other physical end, `depart()` applies the **Reversed-frame re-expression** per the **TrainSpan schema**, the same as any other cab writer. It then delegates to `ato.go()`, the canonical writer of `ato.running`: it sets `ato.running = True` and calls `OperationalStateMachine.enter_running_moving()` to move `state` from `READY` to `RUNNING_MOVING` (idempotent from `RUNNING_MOVING`), the same way ATC escalation raises EB by calling `controller.eb.activate()` rather than assigning `eb.active` directly — `ato.go()` applies the transition through the Operational state machine instead of assigning `state` itself.
  - In `manual` mode, `depart()` calls `OperationalStateMachine.enter_running_moving()` directly — the same transition method, without going through `ato.go()` — moving a `READY` controller to `RUNNING_MOVING`; a `RUNNING_MOVING` controller is an idempotent success that changes no state.
- The single canonical depart-acceptance signal other layers read is `controller.state == RUNNING_MOVING`, set by any canonical transition into that state in the **Controller state machine** table — either a successful `TrainController.depart()` call or **Reactive condition evaluation** observing motion from a cab-selected `READY` controller. The two are equally legitimate; stop-completion eligibility, `ato.running` setting, and route progress all key on `state == RUNNING_MOVING` regardless of which transition fired. Manual driving input may command motion under live authority before Plan's `TrainController.depart()` call lands, and ATC still protects the train (see **Manual mode and movement-authority boundary**).

**route/dispatcher command contracts**

- **Read-only, no setter.** `TrainController.path_projection.received_path_plan` is a read-only property. On each read, it resolves the dispatcher's currently active `Path` for this train into the canonical **received_path_plan schema** (or `None`). There is no setter and no atomic-replacement entry point. `PathDispatcher` updates its own `Path` record in `create_path(...)` / `extend_path(...)`, and the controller observes those updates on its next read.
- **Authority-clear ATO-stop is a level test.** When the property reads `None` while `ato.running == True`, tick substep `1b7a` calls `controller.ato.stop()` (see **Controller tick order**). No previous-path field is stored, so this is a level test on each tick's read rather than an edge the controller remembers, because authority clear is a run-ending event. That bookkeeping does **not** write `state`: it does not "set" the `RUNNING_MOVING → READY` move. `OperationalStateMachine.evaluate_reactive_conditions()` owns that move and runs after every physics update and after every Action command drain. Because every cancellation/completion commits only on a stopped train, the evaluator sees the stopped/no-authority conditions and applies the transition without depending on another movement calculation.
- **Single active path invariant.** v1 holds at most one `ACTIVE` path per train. `create_path(...)` requires `received_path_plan is None`, and `extend_path(...)` keeps the same `path_id`, so a new `path_id` can never appear while a live path is still present: the old path always transitions to `None` first, the reactive evaluation lands the controller in `READY`, and a fresh path is then accepted from `READY` by a new `depart()` call.
- `TrainController.depart()` follows the single **`TrainController.depart()` canonical contract** immediately above. This command-contract list intentionally does not restate its preconditions, cab selection, or ATO/manual effects.
- `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()` is called by the Action station-entry consumer of the `station_entry_request` written by the Plan dwell-entry step inside `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)`. Acceptance requires **all three hold**:
  - `state == READY`
  - `eb.active == False`
  - `cab in {"A", "B"}` — rejected with a diagnostic such as `"cannot enter dwell with no cab selected"` when `cab is None`, enforcing the `RUNNING_AT_STATION` row of **Allowed `(state, cab)` pairs**

  The Plan caller additionally enforces the same cab precondition before calling, plus that `controller.is_recovery_clean` is true, the route's next non-finished walk-position has `task_kind == "dwell"`, and the predecessor walk-position's `finished_at` is set — these are caller-side gates, per step `3a37`. `RouteExecutor` step `3a37`, not this controller call, samples and writes the dwell row's `started_at`; the controller call never reads or writes `RouteRun`. On success, this call transitions the controller to `RUNNING_AT_STATION` and must not create movement or mutate `received_path_plan`. Returns `(success: bool, reason: Optional[str])`; on rejection the call leaves controller state unchanged and emits one `kind = "warning"` event through `controller.notifications`.
- `TrainController.finish_dwell()` is valid only from `RUNNING_AT_STATION`. Acceptance preconditions: `state == RUNNING_AT_STATION`. EB latch state is not a precondition; `finish_dwell()` may run with `eb.active == True` because the Action station-exit consumer may perform it after an abort teardown while EB is still latched. On success, transitions back to the **`READY` state** (per the predicate defined in the Controller state machine subsection), preserves cab selection, does not call `TrainController.depart()`, and does not mutate `received_path_plan`. Returns `(success: bool, reason: Optional[str])`; on rejection the call leaves controller state unchanged and emits one `kind = "warning"` event through `controller.notifications`. Its single caller is the Action station-exit consumer of `station_exit_request`, which the Plan dwell-complete step or a teardown consumer wrote.

**Read accessors**

- `get_lookahead()` is the canonical accessor for UI and debug consumers. Any consumer asking for target speed or speed-limit reason must sample this payload at distance `0`.
- `TrainController.is_stopped_at_authority_end()` is the controller-owned derived read the **Stop-arrival check** (step `8df5`) calls. It returns `True` when **all of these hold**, and `False` otherwise:
  - the train is stopped — `TrainController.is_stopped()` is true;
  - `TrainController.ops.state == RUNNING_MOVING`;
  - `eb.active` is `False`;
  - live authority exists — `received_path_plan is not None`;
  - the lookahead's distance-`0` dominant restriction reason code is `AtcLimitReasonCode.AUTHORITY_STOP`.

  The `AUTHORITY_STOP` reason code is the reachable expression of the authority-end stop, because forward-Euler integration cannot land a step exactly on the boundary, so the literal `atc_limit == 0` never occurs. No head-occupancy test is needed: the dispatcher's `try_complete_active_path(...)` separately verifies the live authority actually reached the requested destination block. Not a stored field; no writers.
- `get_current_span()` is the canonical controller accessor for occupied-span queries. It reads `TrainController.physics_sync.current_span`, the v1 storage home for live physical occupancy and end locators. The payload is general and geometry-first: at minimum it must expose `occupied_blocks` and `occupied_tiles` in physical span order, from one physical end of the train to the other, plus explicit end locators for both physical ends. The ordered occupancy is the block-level ownership view; the end locators are the tile-level precise geometry view. `end_a` and `end_b` are the train's two **physical** ends, and they are cab-independent: they are stable geometric labels for the two ends of the consist and do NOT imply head/tail. The "head" end is whichever physical end matches the currently selected cab in the controller's travel frame. Without a selected cab, `current_span` still carries both physical ends but no head/tail labeling. `RouteExecutor` and `PathDispatcher` consumers that need head-side reasoning derive it from controller cab/travel state plus the span; they must not assume `end_a == head`. `TrainPhysics` is the only normal producer of movement `span_update` values, and `TrainController` is the only normal writer of `TrainController.physics_sync.current_span` (see the carve-outs named under **Train Entity**). `RouteExecutor` / `PathDispatcher` must use `TrainController.get_current_span()` whenever they need the train's current span or physical ends.
- `TrainController.build_detected_progress_report()` produces the detected-progress report for a train whose movement is not calculated this pass — the equivalent of the final `on_physics_updated(...)` progress-report production for a movement-calculated train. It runs on a stopped pass and on a running pass for an `OFF` or ghost-frozen train, per **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs**; the report shape and mailbox contract are defined under **Running and stopped**, the stopped pass.

**TrainSpan schema**

This is the canonical v1 shape of `TrainController.physics_sync.current_span` and the payload returned by `TrainController.get_current_span()`.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `end_a` | `SpanEndLocator` | Stable physical end A of the consist. It is cab-independent and does not imply head/tail. |
| `end_b` | `SpanEndLocator` | Stable physical end B of the consist. It is cab-independent and does not imply head/tail. |
| `occupied_tiles` | `List[Tuple[int, int]]` | Tile-level coverage in physical order from `end_a` to `end_b`. |
| `occupied_blocks` | `List[str]` | Unique block IDs currently covered by the train, in first-seen `end_a` -> `end_b` order. |

`SpanEndLocator` carries exactly:

- `tile` — current tile coordinate for that physical end
- `entry_edge` — `"N"`/`"E"`/`"S"`/`"W"` edge used as the end's current in-tile distance frame
- `distance_cm` — precise in-tile distance from `entry_edge`, in centimeters

Consumers that need the forward/head side derive it from selected cab/travel state plus `end_a` / `end_b`; `TrainSpan` itself never relabels `end_a` or `end_b` as head/tail. The two locators' in-tile frames are always expressed in the current head-forward travel direction: each end's `entry_edge` sits on its rear side for the current head selection, so `distance_cm` grows the way the train travels. The head selection is the cab (`"B"` selects `end_b`; any other selection, `None` included, selects `end_a`). Whenever an accepted cab write moves the head to the other physical end, the cab writer that performed the change re-expresses both locators in the reversed frame — `TrainController.commands.set_cab(...)`, the ATO cab selection inside `TrainController.depart()`, and `TrainController.commands.clear_cab()` alike — `entry_edge` flips to the tile's opposite exit and `distance_cm` becomes `tile_length - distance_cm` — so the ends keep describing the same physical points. A frame left un-flipped would make physics advance the head opposite to the direction the cab commands and draw the head marker pointing into the body.

`PhysicsSpanUpdate` is the canonical payload from `TrainPhysics.tick(...)` into `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)`. It carries exactly:

- `new_span: TrainSpan`
- `current_speed_kmh: float`
- `added_tiles: List[TileTraversal]` in physical traversal order for tiles newly covered by the updated span
- `removed_tiles: List[TileTraversal]` in physical vacate order for tiles no longer covered by the updated span

`TileTraversal` carries exactly:

- `tile_xy` — tile coordinate
- `entry_edge` — `"N"`/`"E"`/`"S"`/`"W"` traversal-frame entry edge
- `exit_edge` — `"N"`/`"E"`/`"S"`/`"W"` traversal-frame exit edge; for tail-vacated block tiles this is the vacated block's forward exit edge for the traversal by which the train left that block, which `TrainController` reads as the block tail-vacate `direction`
- `resource_type` — `"block"` or `"switch"` when the tile belongs to a known resource, otherwise `None`
- `resource_id` — block or switch ID for that resource, otherwise `None`
- `block_id` — owning block ID when applicable, otherwise `None`

`TrainPhysics` computes this delta by comparing the previous controller-owned span it read at the start of the movement step with the newly integrated span. `TrainController` is the only normal writer of the stored `current_span`: it applies `span_update.new_span`, derives resource entry/release observations from `added_tiles` / `removed_tiles`, packages them into one `ControllerProgressReport`, and appends that report to the controller-owned per-train progress mailbox (`physics_sync.queued_progress_reports`) for later delivery to `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` in Observe.

`TrainPhysics.tick(...)` must emit a `PhysicsSpanUpdate` on every running Observe batch in which this train's movement is calculated (per **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs**), even when `added_tiles` and `removed_tiles` are both empty and the integrated `new_span` / `current_speed_kmh` are unchanged. When nothing changed physically, this is an explicit no-change callback. This always-callback rule keeps `TrainController.physics_sync.current_span` / `current_speed_kmh` canonical and gives Observe a deterministic point for local progress consumption and the post-movement stop check. For a train whose movement is not calculated, that deterministic point is `TrainController.build_detected_progress_report()` instead. Action latch consumption remains a later, separate stage.

- One shared neighbor/edge helper, such as `RailwayNetwork.get_connection_edges(tile_a, tile_b) -> Optional[Tuple[str, str]]`, answers two questions at once: are the two tiles track-connected, and if so, which edge on each tile connects to the other. The helper resolves both ordinary grid adjacency (the two tiles share a cardinal edge whose `track_bits` connect) and tunnel adjacency (the two tiles are linked through `RailwayNetwork.tunnels` — see **Tunnels** below). `TrainPhysics` and traversal helpers use this instead of re-deriving neighbor-edge pairs ad hoc. The lower-level neighbor lookup `RailwayNetwork.get_neighbor(x, y, edge) -> Optional[Tile]` follows the same two-step resolution: it returns the grid neighbour first, then falls through to `RailwayNetwork.tunnels.get((x, y, edge))` when the grid cell is empty.

**Tunnels**

- `RailwayNetwork.tunnels: Dict[Tuple[int, int, str], Tuple[int, int, str]]` pairs two dead-end edges so they behave as a single tile-to-tile connection. The map is symmetric: every pair is stored in both directions so lookups are O(1).
- The sole writer is the helper pair `RailwayNetwork.add_tunnel(a, b)` and `RailwayNetwork.remove_tunnel(endpoint)`; no other site assigns to `RailwayNetwork.tunnels` directly. `add_tunnel` enforces the tunnel invariants:
  - Endpoints are distinct.
  - Each endpoint references an existing tile whose `track_bits` include the named edge.
  - Each endpoint is a dead-end at write time — no grid neighbour connects back on the opposite edge. A tunnel fills a dead-end; it does not override real grid geometry.
  - Neither endpoint already participates in another tunnel.
  - The two edges may be any pair, opposite or not (W↔E, N↔S, N↔W, …). A non-opposite pair is needed in layouts such as zig-zag siding loops where, for example, a north-facing dead-end on one side connects to a west-facing dead-end on the other. `Tile._update_dead_ends` uses `RailwayNetwork.get_connection_edges(...)` rather than the cardinal opposite, so the connectivity check follows the actual recorded pair on each tile.
- `RailwayNetwork.propagate_from_tile(...)` runs `_sweep_stale_tunnels()` at the top of every propagation. Any tunnel whose endpoint loses its track, loses the named edge from `track_bits`, or gains a real grid neighbour that connects back, is removed through `RailwayNetwork.remove_tunnel(endpoint)`, so pair symmetry stays owned by the one writer. The propagation that triggered the sweep then sees the cleaned table and recomputes dead-end ports through it. `RailwayNetwork.remove_track(x, y)` calls the sweep explicitly because the removed-tile path does not always touch a grid neighbour propagation.
- `Tile.dead_end_ports` is computed through `RailwayNetwork.get_neighbor(...)`, so a tunneled edge is automatically excluded. Other consumers of dead-end status (the `TRACK_END_SAFETY_MARGIN_CM` trigger, `TrainController.travel_direction` end-of-line fall-through) read through the same `dead_end_ports` field and inherit tunnel awareness without their own table lookups.
- `RailwayNetwork.tunnels` is serialised by `to_dict()` and `to_layout_dict()` as a `tunnels` list of `{"a": {"x", "y", "edge"}, "b": {"x", "y", "edge"}}` records, one per pair, and reloaded by `from_dict()` after all tracks are in place, through `RailwayNetwork.add_tunnel(a, b)` — the same sole writer named above. Its invariant checks are what classify a load-time entry as malformed; malformed entries are logged and skipped without aborting the load.
- Blocks remain grid-contiguous: a tunneled edge is always a block boundary, and `Block.ordered_tiles` does not walk through a tunnel.
- One shared backend network-graph candidate-query / walk-metrics home lives in the common network/pathfinding layer, such as `RailwayPathfinder.query_graph_walks(...) -> List[GraphWalkCandidate]`. Thin adapter methods such as `RailwayPathfinder.find_ordered_walk(...)` or `RailwayPathfinder.measure_along_walk(...)` may still exist, but they must all delegate to this same operational graph home. The candidate query takes tile-precise locators, the caller's `manual_override` flag (default `False`; `True` only when the requesting run's route stores `Route.manual_override = True`), always skips disabled blocks/switches, also skips manual blocks/switches when `manual_override == False` (per the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags** canonical home), and returns zero or more directed walk candidates with whatever ordered tile/block walk payload the caller requested.
- `GraphWalkCandidate` carries exactly this payload. **This subsection is the canonical home for candidate comparison. All other sites cross-reference it rather than restating keys.**

  | Field | Type | Meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `ordered_walk` | `List[GraphWalkStep]` | Canonical directed walk over graph steps in traversal order. Each step contains enough resource/tile/frame data for dispatcher acquisition, route target comparison, and later distance projection. |
  | `ordered_tiles` | `Optional[List[Tuple[int, int]]]` | Ordered tile IDs for callers that requested tile payload. `None` when `return_tiles=False`. |
  | `ordered_blocks` | `Optional[List[str]]` | Ordered block IDs visited by the walk, with consecutive duplicate block steps collapsed only when they represent the same directed block traversal. `None` when `return_blocks=False`. |
  | `start_locator` | `GraphLocator` | The resolved tile-precise start locator used by the graph search, including block/tile membership and optional in-tile position when supplied by the caller. |
  | `terminal_locator` | `GraphLocator` | The resolved tile-precise terminal locator reached by the candidate. |
  | `terminal_block_id` | `str` | Block ID of the terminal block reached by the candidate. |
  | `terminal_block_direction` | `"forward" \| "reverse"` | Terminal block-relative traversal direction derived from the candidate's directed frame against `Block.ordered_tiles`. |
  | `terminal_frame` | `DirectedBlockFrame` | Terminal directed block frame, including path tiles plus `entry_edge` / `exit_edge` metadata needed by dispatcher/controller projection helpers. |
  | `estimated_travel_seconds` | `Optional[float]` | Estimated travel time over the walk, populated exactly when the originating query carries `train_max_speed_kmh`; `None` otherwise. First comparison key when populated. Stored on the candidate so callers comparing results from separate queries retain the same ranking basis. |
  | `tile_count` | `int` | Number of tile steps; first geometry key after travel time. |
  | `walk_length_cm` | `float` | Centimeter walk length; second geometry key. |
  | `candidate_rank` | `int` | Stable deterministic candidate key assigned by the shared graph query, final within that one query's own candidate list. It is not comparable across two separate queries: each query ranks only its own candidates, so a rank value carries no meaning when compared against a candidate a different query returned. When a caller compares best candidates from separate queries, it uses only the first three ordinary keys (`estimated_travel_seconds`, `tile_count`, `walk_length_cm`) and falls straight through to the cross-query tie-break named at that call site on a tie — `candidate_rank` never participates in a cross-query comparison. |

  Candidate comparison within one query's own candidate list is `(estimated_travel_seconds, tile_count, walk_length_cm, candidate_rank)`. Skip the first key when both candidates carry `None`; comparing a populated estimate with an absent one is a caller-contract error because candidates from differently shaped queries must not be mixed. `candidate_rank` derives deterministically from directed-walk identity and is always decisive within one query's own list, so a comparison never reaches it with a tie. No caller substitutes UI order or layer-local heuristics.

  A caller that compares candidates from two separate queries uses only the first three keys (`estimated_travel_seconds`, `tile_count`, `walk_length_cm`), because `candidate_rank` carries no meaning across queries; a caller that mixes it into a cross-query sort is misapplying the comparison. v1 has two cross-query comparison sites: the no-cab `create_path(...)` flow in **Path And PathDispatcher**, which compares the best candidate from two separate per-span-end queries and falls to the `end_a` dead-heat tie-break when the first three keys tie — `end_a` wins by convention — and the `StationTarget` platform-end candidate list in the **Planning Kernel** (step `9c4f`'s target resolution), which merges candidates across every platform's separate per-end query, sorted by the same first three keys, with ties broken by platform-end identity (deterministic iteration order over `Station.platform_ids`) rather than by `candidate_rank` or the `end_a` rule. Both sites are enumerated here; no other caller compares across queries.

  When `GraphWalkQuery.train_max_speed_kmh` is present, the shared query computes `estimated_travel_seconds` from live segment lengths and effective speed limits and stores it on every returned candidate. Geometry-only queries leave it `None`.

- `GraphLocator` carries exactly this payload:

  | Field | Type | Meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `tile` | `Tuple[int, int]` | Tile coordinate anchoring the locator |
  | `resource_type` | `Optional["block" \| "switch"]` | Resource type containing the locator, when known |
  | `resource_id` | `Optional[str]` | Resource ID containing the locator, when known |
  | `block_id` | `Optional[str]` | Convenience block ID when the locator is inside a block; `None` for switch-only locators |
  | `edge` | `Optional["N" \| "E" \| "S" \| "W"]` | Tile edge when the locator is anchored at a graph boundary or caller knows the relevant edge |
  | `distance_cm` | `Optional[float]` | In-tile distance from `edge` along the directed traversal when the caller has a precise position; `None` for tile-only searches |
  | `physical_end` | `Optional["end_a" \| "end_b"]` | Set only for current-train-span start locators so the caller can apply the final `end_a` dead-heat tie-break outside the graph query |

- `DirectedBlockFrame` carries exactly this payload:

  | Field | Type | Meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `block_id` | `str` | Block whose directed traversal is represented |
  | `block_direction` | `"forward" \| "reverse"` | Direction relative to `Block.ordered_tiles` |
  | `path_tiles` | `List[path_tile entry]` | Ordered tile slice through the block using the canonical path-tile entry schema |
  | `entry_edge` | `"N" \| "E" \| "S" \| "W"` | Edge by which the traversal enters the block frame |
  | `exit_edge` | `"N" \| "E" \| "S" \| "W"` | Edge by which the traversal exits the block frame |

- `GraphWalkStep` carries exactly this payload:

  | Field | Type | Meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `step_index` | `int` | Zero-based step index inside `ordered_walk` |
  | `resource_type` | `"block" \| "switch"` | Resource traversed by this step |
  | `resource_id` | `str` | Block or switch ID for the traversed resource |
  | `tile` | `Tuple[int, int]` | Tile coordinate for this graph step |
  | `entry_edge` | `"N" \| "E" \| "S" \| "W"` | Edge used to enter this tile/resource step |
  | `exit_edge` | `"N" \| "E" \| "S" \| "W"` | Edge used to exit this tile/resource step |
  | `block_id` | `Optional[str]` | Block ID when `resource_type == "block"` |
  | `block_direction` | `Optional["forward" \| "reverse"]` | Block-relative traversal direction when the step is inside a block |
  | `switch_required_state` | `Optional[int]` | Required switch state for switch traversal when topology search determines one |
  | `length_cm` | `float` | Physical length contribution of this step |

- **Backend is the sole home for candidate comparison and filtering.** Operational candidate comparison, filtering, and multi-candidate enumeration live only at this backend home. The frontend editor pathfinders in `static/js/pathfinders.js` (`ConstructionPathfinder.findPath(...)` and `ExistingTrackPathfinder.findPathOnExistingTracks(...)`) answer connectivity for the track editor and return a single path. They never apply the canonical **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload** comparison, never apply the disabled-block / disabled-switch / manual-block / manual-switch filters, and never apply `Block.allowed_travel_directions` or `requested_destination_direction`.
- **One comparison implementation site.** The candidate comparison order has exactly one implementation site for the comparison function itself, `RailwayPathfinder.query_graph_walks(...)`; the two enumerated cross-query callers (see the **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload** home) invoke that same function's ordering rather than reimplementing it.
- **Where the availability/direction filters apply.** The availability and direction filters are applied at `query_graph_walks(...)` (planning), at `RouteExecutor` target resolution, and again at `BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)` (acquisition); no frontend pathfinder applies any of them. Callers that need ranked candidates or filter-aware paths — including UI features — route through `RailwayPathfinder.query_graph_walks(...)` rather than re-implementing comparison or filtering on the client.
- **Shared switch-exit primitive.** The frontend and backend must agree on one shared primitive: entering a tile on one segment of a switch limits the valid exits to that segment's paired edge. The frontend encodes this in `ConstructionPathfinder.getExitsForEntry(trackBits, entry)`; the backend encodes it in `Tile.get_exits(entry, use_switch_state=False)`.

**Pathfinding-home migration**

- The current operational backend path search lives in `PathDispatcher.find_paths(start_block_id, end_block_id, train_id=None) -> List[PathSegment]` / `PathDispatcher._bfs_find_paths(...)`. That contract is insufficient for the v1 contracts above because it is block-to-block and distance-sorted only; it does not support **any of these**:
  - direction-aware terminal rejection
  - locator-level (tile-precise) start positions
  - explicit switch-handling mode
  - the canonical **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload** comparison, including estimated-travel-time ranking when a train max speed is supplied
  - measure-along-walk projection

  The refactor must extend or extract that existing backend pathfinding home so it exposes at least:
  - `RailwayPathfinder.query_graph_walks(request: GraphWalkQuery) -> List[GraphWalkCandidate]` — a direction-aware network-graph search that accepts a `GraphWalkQuery` request payload (defined below). It accepts tile-precise start and end locators, not just block IDs.
    - **Availability filter.** It always skips disabled blocks/switches, and also skips manual blocks/switches when `request.manual_override == False` (per the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags** canonical home).
    - **Topology-only search.** The search is topology-only: it plans through switches whatever their current position, because acquisition throws them into the state the walk needs afterwards.
    - **Rejection criteria.** It rejects a candidate when **any of these holds**:
      - its terminal traversal does not satisfy `request.requested_destination_direction`
      - its traversal violates `Block.allowed_travel_directions`, when `request.manual_override == False` (per the same canonical home)
      - it traverses a block or switch leg whose curve radius is tighter than `request.train_min_radius_cm`, when that capability is set — the curve-radius feasibility filter defined below
      - it climbs a block steeper than `request.train_max_slope_percent` in the traversed direction, when that capability is set — the slope feasibility filter defined below
    - **Ranking and output.** It ranks all survivors by the canonical **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload** comparison and returns them with whichever ordered tile/block walk payload the request flags asked for.

  `GraphWalkQuery` carries exactly:

  | Field | Type | Meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `start_locator` | `GraphLocator` | Tile-precise start locator. |
  | `end_locator` | `GraphLocator` | Tile-precise end locator. |
  | `requested_destination_direction` | `Optional["forward" \| "reverse"]` | Optional terminal direction filter; candidates whose terminal traversal does not match are rejected. |
  | `exclude_resources` | `Optional[Set[str]]` | Optional set of resource IDs to exclude from the search (used by retry / extension logic). |
  | `manual_override` | `bool = False` | Operator-override flag per the **`disabled` and `manual` availability flags** canonical home. When `False`, manual blocks/switches are filtered out exactly like disabled ones and `Block.allowed_travel_directions` is enforced. When `True` (forwarded from a run whose route stores `Route.manual_override = True` — operator-initiated routes), manual resources participate normally and `Block.allowed_travel_directions` is not enforced; disabled resources are still filtered. |
  | `train_min_radius_cm` | `Optional[float] = None` | The routed train's minimum curve radius capability in centimetres, or `None` for geometry-only callers with no train context. When set, candidates that traverse a segment (`Segment.min_radius_cm`) or switch leg (`Switch.main_radius_cm` / `Switch.diverge_radius_cm` for the leg the walk uses) whose radius is tighter than this value are rejected by the curve-radius feasibility filter defined below. `manual_override` does not relax this filter. |
  | `train_max_speed_kmh` | `Optional[float] = None` | The routed train's maximum speed in km/h, or `None` for geometry-only callers with no train context. It controls whether `estimated_travel_seconds` is populated; ranking then follows the canonical **`GraphWalkCandidate` payload** comparison without a locally restated tie-break. |
  | `train_max_slope_percent` | `Optional[float] = None` | The routed train's maximum climbable gradient (percent grade), or `None` for geometry-only callers, or `0.0` (the `Train.max_slope` "unspecified" sentinel) for no limit. When set above zero, candidates that climb a segment (`Segment.grade_percent`, sign-flipped for a reverse traversal) steeper than this value are rejected by the slope feasibility filter defined below. `manual_override` does not relax it. |
  | `return_tiles` | `bool = True` | Whether to populate `GraphWalkCandidate.ordered_tiles`. |
  | `return_blocks` | `bool = True` | Whether to populate `GraphWalkCandidate.ordered_blocks`. |

  **Curve-radius feasibility filter.** A train must not be routed through a curve tighter than it can physically take. `query_graph_walks(...)` rejects any candidate that traverses a segment whose `Segment.min_radius_cm` is set and smaller than `request.train_min_radius_cm`, or a switch leg whose active radius (`Switch.main_radius_cm` for the main leg, `Switch.diverge_radius_cm` for the diverge leg) is set and smaller than `request.train_min_radius_cm`. The leg is the one the walk's `GraphWalkStep.switch_required_state` names; when that field is `None` the walk names no leg for that switch, so that step carries no curve limit and never rejects. A `None` block/switch radius carries no curve limit and never rejects; a `None` `request.train_min_radius_cm` (geometry-only callers with no train context) skips the filter entirely. This is a physical capability limit, so `manual_override` does not relax it — unlike the `manual` and `Block.allowed_travel_directions` filters. The capability flows in through the dispatcher: `PathDispatcher` resolves the routed train's `Train.min_radius_cm` and passes it as `request.train_min_radius_cm`; automatic and operator-initiated routes both carry it.

  **Slope feasibility filter.** A train stalls on a climb steeper than it can manage, so it must not be routed up such a grade. `query_graph_walks(...)` rejects any candidate that climbs a segment whose effective uphill gradient exceeds `request.train_max_slope_percent`. `Segment.grade_percent` is signed in that segment's own increasing `ordered_tiles` direction. The effective gradient is therefore `Segment.grade_percent` when the candidate traverses the segment in increasing order and `-Segment.grade_percent` in decreasing order. Because block grouping enforces the stored-orientation invariant above, this is also respectively the block's forward and reverse direction; callers must not maintain a second grade frame. The candidate is rejected when the effective gradient exceeds the train capability.
