Only a climb rejects; a descent never does. `None` grade, `None`/`0.0` train capability, or an unclassified traversal skips the filter. Like the curve-radius filter, `manual_override` does not relax it. `PathDispatcher` resolves `Train.max_slope` and passes it as `request.train_max_slope_percent`.

  - `RailwayPathfinder.find_ordered_walk(...) -> List[GraphWalkCandidate]` — thin adapter over `RailwayPathfinder.query_graph_walks(...)` returning the ranked ordered-walk candidates (best first per the canonical `GraphWalkCandidate` comparison); a caller that needs a single chosen walk takes the first element.
  - `RailwayPathfinder.measure_along_walk(ordered_walk, locator_a, locator_b) -> float` — in-walk centimeter distance projection between two locators on an already-chosen walk, used by lookahead and platform-end pair comparison.
  - `RailwayPathfinder.get_reachable_endpoints(start_block_id, include_stations=True) -> List[str]` — topological reachability enumeration that returns every block (and optionally every station) reachable from `start_block_id`. The walk steps tile-by-tile, so switch tiles do not act as graph barriers. The walk does not consult current switch state, does not apply `Block.allowed_travel_directions`, and knows nothing about any train; callers that need direction filtering use `find_ordered_walk` / `query_graph_walks` instead. Used by the route editor's block-to-block feasibility highlighting, where there is no placed train and any travel direction is allowed.
  - `RailwayPathfinder.get_reachable_endpoints_for_span(head_seeds, occupied_tiles, occupied_blocks, include_stations=True) -> List[str]` — span-aware reachability for one placed train. `head_seeds` is the list of `(tile, outward_edge)` pairs for the train's two physical span ends, where `outward_edge` is the network edge pointing away from the body at that end. The walk starts only from those seeds, in those outward directions. It steps tile-by-tile through switch tiles exactly like `get_reachable_endpoints`, and it never steps onto a tile in `occupied_tiles`; `occupied_blocks` are removed from the result. So it returns exactly the blocks (and stations) the train can reach driving forward out of its head or in reverse out of its tail — never back through its own body, or through a switch its body is sitting on. `PathDispatcher.get_reachable_endpoints_for_train(train_id, include_stations=True)` resolves the train's current span and its two end-outward edges and delegates here; the Quick Route tool's destination highlighting calls it. Each end's outward edge is a purely geometric value — the network edge of that end's tile pointing away from the consist body — computed from the span geometry (`end_a` / `end_b` tile + `entry_edge`) alone, independent of cab selection. It is not derived from `travel_direction` (which is cab-dependent, describes only the cab/head end, and is `None` when no cab is selected). Both span ends always have a well-defined outward edge, so the tool works whether or not a cab is selected.
  - the `GraphWalkCandidate` table above as the only candidate payload contract.
- Every layer that needs pathfinding shares this single home: `RouteExecutor` platform-end selection, `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` start-side and forward candidate selection, `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` suffix selection, and the boundary-projection helpers all route through it.
- The implementation must use the following function table as the canonical operational pathfinding surface. If the shared graph home is implemented as methods on `PathDispatcher` rather than an extracted `RailwayPathfinder` class, keep the inputs/outputs and single-home rule identical.

  | Function | Inputs | Output | Required callers / need | Current nearby implementation |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `RailwayNetwork.get_connection_edges(tile_a, tile_b)` | tile coordinates that are either grid-adjacent or linked through `RailwayNetwork.tunnels` | `Optional[Tuple[str, str]]` edge on `tile_a`, edge on `tile_b` | `TrainPhysics.tick(...)`, graph traversal, directed frame construction | Implemented; consolidates the grid-adjacency check and the tunnel fallback used by `RailwayNetwork.get_neighbor(...)`. See the **Tunnels** canonical home above. |
  | `RailwayPathfinder.query_graph_walks(request)` | `request: GraphWalkQuery` | `List[GraphWalkCandidate]` sorted/comparable by candidate metrics | `RouteExecutor` platform-end selection, `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` start-side selection, `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` candidate selection, `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` suffix selection | Closest backend code is `PathDispatcher.find_paths(...)`, `PathDispatcher._bfs_find_paths(...)`, `PathDispatcher._find_extension_paths(...)`, and `PathDispatcher._bfs_find_extension_paths(...)`; these must be extended/extracted. `static/js/pathfinders.js` has `ConstructionPathfinder.findPath(...)` and `ExistingTrackPathfinder.findPathOnExistingTracks(...)`, but those are editor/construction helpers and are not the runtime operational home. |
  | `RailwayPathfinder.find_ordered_walk(...)` | Same as `RailwayPathfinder.query_graph_walks(...)` | `List[GraphWalkCandidate]`, best first per the canonical comparison; a caller that needs one chosen walk takes the first element | Thin convenience adapter for callers that want the ranked list without naming `query_graph_walks(...)` directly | No exact current equivalent; closest is `PathDispatcher.find_paths(...)` after sorting, but that lacks new frame semantics |
  | `RailwayPathfinder.measure_along_walk(ordered_walk, locator_a, locator_b)` | chosen `ordered_walk` and two `GraphLocator` values on that walk | signed or absolute centimeter distance as specified by caller | lookahead projection, platform-end pair comparison, graph-nearest route reconciliation | Current `PathSegment.distance_cm` is whole-path only and is not sufficient for locator-to-locator projection |
  | `RailwayPathfinder.get_reachable_endpoints(start_block_id, include_stations=True)` | starting block id, station-inclusion flag | `List[str]` of reachable block ids (plus station ids when included) | route-editor block-to-block feasibility highlighting (no placed train, any direction) | Lives at the pathfinder home; `PathDispatcher.get_reachable_endpoints(...)` is a thin wrapper that delegates here so existing callers keep their entry point |
  | `RailwayPathfinder.get_reachable_endpoints_for_span(head_seeds, occupied_tiles, occupied_blocks, include_stations=True)` | the two span ends as `(tile, outward_edge)` seeds, the train's occupied tiles and blocks, station-inclusion flag | `List[str]` of reachable block ids (plus station ids when included), excluding the train's own occupied blocks | Quick Route tool destination highlighting, via `PathDispatcher.get_reachable_endpoints_for_train(train_id, include_stations=True)` | Span-aware companion to `get_reachable_endpoints`: same tile-by-tile switch traversal, but seeded from the train's head/tail outward edges (resolved through its `TrainController`) and forbidden from entering the body's occupied tiles |
  | `RailwayNetwork.project_authority_boundary_delta(ordered_walk, head_locator, authority_end, safety_margin_cm)` | the live authority's ordered directed walk, `head_locator` (a `GraphLocator` carrying `tile`, `edge`, `distance_cm`), plus `authority_end` (carrying `block_id` and `terminal_frame: DirectedBlockFrame`) | signed centimeter delta measured along the walk, forward from the head's resolved occurrence; positive means head is past safety-margin boundary, negative means still short | controller braking diagnostics and stop-boundary projection | No exact current equivalent; the geometry comes from shared graph/geometry helpers and the ordering from the live authority walk, so a lapping route has one answer |

**Manual mode and movement-authority boundary**

- In `simulation` submode, the driver must call `set_handle()`, the controller must store `handle_position`, and `TrainPhysics` must integrate it into speed that never exceeds the live distance-0 `atc_limit`, decelerating toward the limit at the applicable brake rate when current speed already exceeds it rather than snapping down to it, per tick step `924d` (Manual-mode command write).
- In `power_percent` submode, the driver must call `TrainController.commands.set_manual_power_percent()`, the controller must store `manual.manual_power_percent`, and `TrainPhysics` must convert it through `SpeedProfile.power_speed_curve` in the same tick whenever no braking override is active.
- In that same `power_percent` submode, the converted power-percent command is the absolute voltage/speed command and overrides the normal acceleration/deceleration-rate fields while no safety braking override is active. `TrainPhysics.tick(...)` must set the `span_update.current_speed_kmh` for that tick to the calibrated effective speed; the model assumes negligible momentum under direct voltage control, so there is no service-rate ramp between settings. When ATC, service stopping, or EB intervenes, use the **Canonical power-percent safety-cap ordering** in the controller tick: sample the retained driver command and compute the current tick's capped operating point. ATC and service stopping then reset the retained percentage through `manual.reset_power_percent_for_safety()`; EB leaves it retained and blocks `TrainController.eb.release()` until the driver zeroes it. There is no signed negative power-percent command.
- In manual mode with a received path plan, the controller lookahead brakes the train to the current authority end boundary using the controller safety margin — the same authority-boundary stop the lookahead builds in ATO mode.
- Without a received path plan, manual mode receives the same no-authority empty lookahead defined in step `22a9` (`atc_limit = 0` at distance 0, `atc_limit_reason_code = no_authority`). There is no fallback to the current-block boundary; a stopped train with no plan is held at rest, and a deviated rolling train is stopped through the zero-limit / EB protocol in step `826a`.

**Completion ownership and timing**

- `TrainController` is the sole owner of the post-physics stopped/authority-boundary state, `RouteExecutor` the sole owner of the arrival decision, and `PathDispatcher` the sole owner of the release commit. The controller exposes whether the train is now stopped at the usable end of live authority; the route decides whether that stop serves the armed task and records it; dispatcher then mutates path and resource state.
- `TrainController` reaches the **`READY` state** through its reactive stopped/no-authority rule when live authority disappears; it does not decide independently that a path-backed run is complete.
- `PathDispatcher` is the sole owner of the `Path` record underlying `TrainController.path_projection.received_path_plan`; the controller reads that projection and never mutates authority.
- Path completion is emitted only after two things hold: the train has already moved for that tick, and the **Stop-arrival check** says the train is standing at the stop it was sent to. `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(train_id)` releases the authority and then hands the arrival to `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(...)`, so the recorded arrival always follows the release that made it final.
- On that same accepted completion, dispatcher also calls the controller end-of-run hook `TrainController.on_path_complete()` (per step `09b0`). The hook ends the ATO run through `TrainController.ato.stop()` and runs `OperationalStateMachine.evaluate_reactive_conditions()`; it makes no state-transition write of its own, so the reactive stopped/no-authority rule is still what moves the controller to `READY` (or leaves it held under EB). Ending the ATO run here does not decide completion — completion was already decided by the **Stop-arrival check** — it only stops the automatic driver now that the authority it was running on is gone. Cancellation calls no controller hook.

**Controller invariants**

- There is no `self.target_speed` field. Lookahead at distance 0 is the canonical source of target speed.
- Controller-owned live control and physical state must stay cleanly separated from persistent train data.
- Controller ATO destination state comes only from `received_path_plan`. There is no fallback read against `Train`.
- `SimulationController.get_or_create_controller(train_id)` must keep the 1:1 train/controller pairing and must not recreate authority from train-side runtime mirrors. Its only job is to make sure a controller object exists and is registered for this `train_id`. In v1, the controller must exist before any dispatcher path creation or extension: callers must make sure of this before `create_path(...)` or `extend_path(...)`. `SimulationController` must not build or write a path payload itself. There is no late-bind recovery hook such as `PathDispatcher.on_controller_available(train_id)`, because `received_path_plan` is a property that resolves live, so no late controller write is needed.

## TrainPhysics

**Movement-authority input in `TrainPhysics`**

- `TrainPhysics` runs physical integration: the speed update, the span and end-locator update, occupancy tracing, and tail tracing. But the canonical live storage is `TrainController.physics_sync.current_span` and `TrainController.physics_sync.current_speed_kmh`. `TrainPhysics.tick(...)` computes each `span_update` (`new_span`, `current_speed_kmh`, ordered `added_tiles`, ordered `removed_tiles`, and traversal frame metadata) and passes it to `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)`, which performs the controller-owned storage write. `TrainPhysics` must not own path identity, dispatcher authority state, progress interpretation, completion, or a separate canonical position store on `Train`.
- **The two physics halves, and `tick()`.** `TrainPhysics.tick(delta)` pairs `TrainPhysics.integrate_movement(delta)` — the Observe movement calculation that advances the span and passes each `span_update` to `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)` — with `TrainPhysics.apply_track_voltage()` — the Action step that drives the occupied blocks' track voltage for the next tick. The live per-tick loop calls the two halves directly: `integrate_movement(...)` in the Observe batch (`SimulationController._observe_train(...)`) and `apply_track_voltage()` in that train's Action pass (`SimulationController._act_train(...)`). `tick()` runs them back-to-back as one movement-then-voltage step.
- Each tick `TrainPhysics.tick(...)` caps the distance it moves the train so the calculated span stays inside what the block detector confirms (canonical home **Power**, "The calculated span never runs ahead of the detector"). The cap limits distance only. It does not change the speed solution, it never moves the train backwards, and every consumer — the controller's braking and stopping logic, the voltage emission, the progress reports — reads the capped span as that tick's position with no branch for having been capped.
- To choose exits on ambiguous geometry, `TrainPhysics` normally needs a read-only authority-geometry projection from the controller, derived from `TrainController.path_projection.received_path_plan.resource_sequence`. The least it needs is the ordered `resource_sequence` / `path_tiles` geometry from that active plan, plus enough local direction context to pick the correct next edge through the current tile.
- `TrainPhysics` does **not** need dispatcher ownership fields such as `path_id` to step the train, and it does not need requested or authorized centimeter stop targets for physical integration. Centimeter stop-target fields are not part of the v1 path/controller contract. Controller braking logic uses authority-boundary geometry plus the controller safety margin.
- `TrainPhysics` obtains that geometry projection from `TrainController.path_projection.received_path_plan`; it is the only path-geometry movement input.
- `TrainPhysics` must read the current live position through the controller-owned span. It must write movement only by sending `span_update` to `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)`, never through a train-entity position field. Initial placement is set by the API `SimulationController.add_train(...)` flow, which writes `TrainController.physics_sync.current_span` before the first tick. (Persistence and save-data migration are Out of Scope; see the **Out of Scope** section.)
- Exception for cancellation/revocation braking: if the dispatcher-owned path has already left `ACTIVE` while the train is still rolling, `TrainPhysics` must keep moving the train according to its speed and the current live network state. That post-revocation movement relies on the physical `Switch.position` and live track geometry in the network at that moment, not on retained authority locks or a second copy of path ownership kept in the controller.
- Because live switch state is owned by `Switch`, `TrainPhysics._advance_end()` and tail tracing must call the `Tile` traversal helpers using the resolver input defined by the `Tile` helper contract above.

**Block occupancy**

- Route normal tail-vacated transitions through `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)` and `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)`. That chain routes block releases through `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated()`, so `OCCUPIED -> CAUTION -> FREE` stays in one state machine.
- `TrainPhysics` must not write `Block` fields directly, and must not call block-state mutators for normal occupancy, CAUTION, or release. It computes movement `span_update` values, and the controller/dispatcher feedback chain does all block writes through `BlockManager`.
- Block tail-vacate observations come from the Observe detector (debounced no-current; see **Power**, Block occupancy detection), never from tile-level span arithmetic. `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)` includes a block in `tail_vacated_resources` only when the detector slice carries that block, so `PathDispatcher` calls `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated()` only on clears the detector confirmed and the train's calculated tail has earned (see **Power**, A clear read from under the train is a detection fault).
- Normal CAUTION clearing happens inside `on_block_tail_vacated()` via `_reevaluate_caution_blocks()`, plus the **Opposing-traversal caution clear** inside `BlockManager.reserve_blocks_for_path(...)` when a path reserves a caution block for a traversal out of its other end. Both are `BlockManager` writes; there is no separate `clear_block()` / `release_block()` step.

**Tail-vacate flow in `TrainPhysics`**

- `TrainPhysics` does not call `BlockManager` mutators directly; CAUTION transitions go through `on_block_tail_vacated()` via the detector-confirmed tail-vacate path (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection).
- **Tail-vacate reporting.** On tail-vacate, `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)` includes a typed resource-release observation in `tail_vacated_resources`, packages it into the same `ControllerProgressReport`, and appends that report to the controller-owned per-train progress mailbox (`physics_sync.queued_progress_reports`) for the train's Observe consume pass.
- **Vacate authority differs by resource type.**
  - **Block**: the controller reports the vacate only when the Observe detector slice has confirmed the block is clear (debounced no-current per **Power**, Block occupancy detection). The calculated span is not the block-vacate authority. Block IDs arrive directly on the detector slice.
  - **Switch**: a tile-level vacate of the switch resource in the calculated span is enough. Switch IDs come from `Tile.switch_id` on switch tiles, via the same tile-lookup mechanism used for entry detection.
- **Direction field.** The controller report carries the block tail-vacate `direction` as the vacated block's forward `exit_edge` for the traversal by which the train left that block.
- **Observe routing.** During Observe, `PathDispatcher` routes the release through `ResourceCoordinator.release_tail_vacated(resource_type, resource_id, train_id, direction, route)`.
  - Blocks go through `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated(block_id, train_id, direction)`, so `OCCUPIED -> CAUTION -> FREE` stays in one state machine.
  - Switches go through `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(switch_id, train_id, route)`, which removes the matching `Switch.physical_occupants[route]` entry first, and then, only when no entries remain for that train, clears train-owned protection sourced from that vacated switch.
- `TrainPhysics` does not track its own `_caution_blocks`; `BlockManager` owns the full release lifecycle.

**Voltage behavior**

- **Three distinct values.** `track_voltage`, `power_percent`, and `speed_kmh` are three different values.
- **Canonical home for `track_voltage` is `TrainPhysics`.** It is computed each tick from the authoritative source for the active mode.
  - In ATO and manual-simulation mode, that source is the controller/physics speed solution.
  - In manual `power_percent` mode, `manual.manual_power_percent` is mapped to `track_voltage` through the inverse of the train's resolved `voltage_power_curve` (the stage-1 `(track_voltage, power_percent)` curve), while the calibrated `speed_kmh` for that same operating point comes from its resolved `power_speed_curve`. Both curves are read through `SpeedProfileRegistry.resolve(...)`, the one accessor that fills a train's profile from its instance and model records (see **SpeedProfile**, Model profiles and instance profiles).
  - While a **Lighting-voltage calibration** run is open for the train, that run's candidate voltage is the authoritative source instead, in place of whatever the two modes above would otherwise output.

  `track_voltage` is always reached through `voltage_power_curve`, never through `power_speed_curve` (which has no voltage axis).
- **`track_voltage` is a magnitude, not a direction.** It says how hard to drive a block, not which way. Direction is added per block when the value is emitted (see **Power**, A block voltage carries a direction), so every mapping on this page runs from `0` up to the profile's `max_voltage` and no calibration curve carries a sign.
- **`track_voltage` is per-tick derived state.** It is not stored on `TrainController` and not persisted on `Train`. It is owned by `TrainPhysics` and emitted to `BlockPowerController` as that tick's hardware output.
- `TrainPhysics` must pass the current `track_voltage` value to `BlockPowerController` as the software-to-hardware output layer for block voltage emission. This block-voltage application is `TrainPhysics.apply_track_voltage()`, an Action-stage operation: it runs inside the per-train Action pass (`SimulationController._act_train(...)`) after command generation, and is distinct from the Observe movement step `TrainPhysics.integrate_movement(...)` that runs earlier in the tick (see the **Observe, Plan, and Action Table** Action row).
- The active mode decides which value is authoritative (see **Canonical home for `track_voltage` is `TrainPhysics`**, above). In manual `power_percent` mode, the manual power command sets the absolute calibrated voltage/speed point, instead of being integrated through the normal service acceleration/deceleration rates.
- In manual `power_percent` mode, that authority applies only while no controller braking override is active. There is no handle-based speed-up/speed-down integration in this submode. Without an override, `TrainPhysics` uses the calibrated `power_percent -> speed_kmh` result directly for that tick. With ATC/service-stop/EB intervention, it receives the effective speed/power/voltage produced by the controller's **Canonical power-percent safety-cap ordering**; under ATC or service stopping the stored percentage has already been reset for later ticks, while under EB it stays retained until the driver zeroes it, and either way the current tick may still use a positive capped operating point computed from the sampled command. A zero cap produces the calibrated zero-power, zero-speed outcome.
- In `power_percent` manual mode, `TrainPhysics` must use the profile's voltage/power/speed calibration directly. It must not use scalar target-speed fields, and must not apply the service acceleration/deceleration rates to the manual-power command. The calibration must work in both directions, so physics can convert between the authoritative value for the active mode and the derived outputs it needs to maintain. `SpeedProfile` owns these mappings, and they must be documented exactly this way:
  - `track_voltage <-> power_percent`
  - `power_percent <-> speed_kmh`
- When `TrainPhysics` needs `track_voltage`, it derives it from the current authoritative mode input. In ATO and manual `simulation` mode, that is `speed_kmh -> power_percent -> track_voltage`. In manual `power_percent` mode, it is `manual_power_percent -> track_voltage`, plus the calibrated absolute `speed_kmh` command. In manual `power_percent` mode without a braking override, that calibrated `speed_kmh` is written into the same `PhysicsSpanUpdate.current_speed_kmh` that carries the movement result.
- Do not add extra names for these concepts. The doc speaks in voltage, power percent, and speed, and the three mappings stay distinct.

**Physics invariants**

- `TrainPhysics` must not own manual-mode policy; it must execute controller commands and maintain physical state only.
- Future authority is held by `Block.reserved_by_path` / `Block.reserved_for_train` on the block side and `Switch.locks` on the switch side. `TrainPhysics` holds no path-lock state of its own. Movement is geometry-driven. Once the train enters a resource, switch integrity during traversal is enforced by `Switch.occupied_by` plus any `Switch.train_protection_claims`.

## SpeedProfile

`SpeedProfile` carries motion-rate data plus calibration measured from a locomotive, in the vocabulary the rest of the system must use directly: voltage, power percent, and speed. The calibration defines two-way mappings: between `track_voltage` and `power_percent`, and between `power_percent` and calibrated `speed_kmh`. A record is one of two kinds — a model profile describing a locomotive model, or an instance profile describing one physical locomotive — and **Model profiles and instance profiles** below is the canonical home for that split.
- `SpeedProfile` fields:
  - `profile_id`: unique profile identifier.
  - `name`: display name for UI/debug/profile selection.
  - `derived_from`: the model profile this record overlays, unset on a model profile and set on an instance profile. It is the field that says which of the two kinds a record is (see **Model profiles and instance profiles**).
  - `model`: the locomotive model this profile describes, written the same way `RosterEntry.model` writes it. It is what makes a measured curve worth keeping: a second locomotive of that model starts from the curve the first one produced instead of from the seeded linear default. **Train Roster**, Profiles are matched by model, is where a roster entry uses it. It is carried by model profiles only; an instance profile leaves it unset and resolves it from the model profile it derives from. It is blank on a model profile seeded at train creation, because nothing has yet said which model that train is.
  - `calibrated_at`: the wall-clock date and time **Speed calibration** last wrote this profile's `power_speed_curve`, unset while that curve is still the seeded linear default. It is the one field that says whether a profile is measured or a placeholder, and it is how a roster entry chooses between two model profiles naming one model (see **Train Roster**, Profiles are matched by model). It is one of the three fields an instance profile may carry (see **Model profiles and instance profiles**).
  - `max_voltage`: top of the usable `track_voltage` range for the first mapping stage. A model profile seeded at train creation (see `power_speed_curve` below) defaults to `DEFAULT_SEEDED_MAX_VOLTAGE_V`, a `constants.py` value. It is carried by model profiles only.
  - `voltage_power_curve`: stored calibration mapping `(track_voltage, power_percent)` for the first stage. Its v1 default is linear across the usable range, from `lighting_voltage` (0%) to `max_voltage` (100%). It is carried by model profiles only: an instance profile stores no curve of its own, and its resolved curve is the model profile's curve re-anchored at the instance's resolved `lighting_voltage` (see **Model profiles and instance profiles**). **Speed calibration** does not write it; **Lighting-voltage calibration** is what moves its bottom anchor, by committing a new `lighting_voltage`.
  - `power_speed_curve`: stored calibration mapping `(power_percent, speed_kmh)` for the second stage. Its v1 default is linear from `0%` -> `0 km/h` to `100%` -> the owning train's configured `max_speed`. This default is seeded on the model profile `SimulationController.add_train(...)` creates at train creation when placement imports no profile, anchoring the `100%` point to that train's own `max_speed` so the curve matches the train whose creation seeded it. It is one of the three fields an instance profile may carry, and **Speed calibration** is what writes a measured one.
  - `lighting_voltage`: the single voltage at which the train is lit but not yet moving. The stopped-but-lit states output it, and it is also the 0%-power point (bottom) of `voltage_power_curve`: at exactly this voltage power is 0 and the train holds, and just above it the train begins to move. It is therefore the highest `track_voltage` at which the train is lit and still holds. It is one of the three fields an instance profile may carry, and it is the one every locomotive is expected to carry its own value of, because a lamp, a motor and a gearbox differ between two items of one model. Its value is set, in the ordinary case, by **Lighting-voltage calibration**; a seeded default or an imported roster entry can also carry one. A model profile seeded at train creation defaults to `DEFAULT_SEEDED_LIGHTING_VOLTAGE_V`, a `constants.py` value chosen below the Hardware Setup default `current_sense_min_drive_v` so a freshly placed train satisfies **Occupancy source follows drive state**'s bound without immediate recalibration (see **Lighting-voltage calibration**, What a candidate may be).
  - `acceleration_rate`: service acceleration rate in `km/h/s`.
  - `deceleration_rate`: service braking rate in `km/h/s`.
  - `emergency_brake_rate`: emergency-brake deceleration rate in `km/h/s`.
  - `friction_rate`: passive/coasting deceleration rate in `km/h/s`.
  - `operational_decel_ratio`: comfort-braking fraction used when ATO builds operational braking curves.
  - `air_resistance_enabled`: whether the drag model is active.
  - `drag_coefficient`: drag strength used by the drag model.
  - `reference_speed_kmh`: reference speed used to scale the drag model.
  - `power_multipliers`: per-notch table mapping each power handle position to the fraction of `acceleration_rate` that notch applies, so different train models can have different power-notch response. Stored on the profile and read directly by the physics integration and ATO (not from any module-level default); the v1 construction default is the standard notch table.
  - `brake_multipliers`: per-notch table mapping each brake handle position to the fraction of the operational brake rate (`deceleration_rate × operational_decel_ratio`) that notch applies. Stored on the profile and read directly by the physics integration and ATO; the v1 construction default is the standard notch table.

**Model profiles and instance profiles**

- **A record is a model profile or an instance profile, and `derived_from` is what says which.** A model profile leaves `derived_from` unset and describes a locomotive model. An instance profile names a model profile in `derived_from` and describes one physical locomotive.
- **A model profile carries the shape.** It stores base values for every field in the list above, including `lighting_voltage`, `power_speed_curve`, and `calibrated_at`, both mapping curves, `max_voltage`, the motion rates, the drag fields, and the two notch tables. The three fields in the next bullet may also be present on an instance profile as per-locomotive overrides; they are not absent from the model profile.
- **An instance profile carries only what was measured on that one locomotive.** It may carry three fields and no others:
  - `lighting_voltage`
  - `power_speed_curve`
  - `calibrated_at`
- **A field an instance leaves unset is read from its model profile.** That is what lets a correction to a model profile reach every locomotive of that model that has not measured the field for itself.
- **An instance profile stores no `voltage_power_curve`.** Its resolved curve is the model profile's curve with its bottom anchor moved to the instance's resolved `lighting_voltage`, because that anchor is the 0%-power point by definition (see the `lighting_voltage` field above). Building it drops every model-profile point below the new anchor — each one names a voltage that does not move this locomotive — and resolves the `0%` anchor point itself to the instance's `lighting_voltage`.
- **`SpeedProfileRegistry.resolve(profile_id)` is the one accessor that applies the overlay.** It returns a complete profile with every field filled: from the instance where the instance carries the field, and from the model profile everywhere else. `TrainPhysics`, the ATO computer, the hardware readiness evaluator, and the UI all read a train's calibration through it, and no other site merges the two records.
- **A train and a roster entry both name an instance profile.** `Train.speed_profile_id` and `RosterEntry.speed_profile_id` name the instance and never the model profile, so a measured locomotive keeps its own numbers across placements (see **Train Roster**).
- Why this shape: the two things a calibration pass measures sit at different levels. A power/speed sweep mostly describes a model, and a lighting voltage describes one item's lamp, motor, and gearbox. A record at each level lets each pass write the level it measured, so the operator is never asked at commit time which level a number belongs to, and moving a measurement from one item up to its model stays a deliberate act (see **Speed calibration**, What commit writes).

**SpeedProfile constraint**

- `SpeedProfile` is not a speed-limit object. It holds motion-rate data and calibration (`lighting_voltage`, `max_voltage`, `voltage_power_curve`, `power_speed_curve`), not any kind of speed ceiling. Train maximum speed and block maximum speed are separate constraints, each enforced on its own.

**Speed-profile addition**

- Calibration wording uses three explicit values: `track_voltage`, `power_percent`, and `speed_kmh`.
- The calibration has two bidirectional mappings and both must be stated directly in the doc:
  1. `track_voltage <-> power_percent`
  2. `power_percent <-> speed_kmh`
- `voltage_power_curve` is the stored `(track_voltage, power_percent)` mapping used by the first step. `lighting_voltage` is the highest `track_voltage` at which the train is lit and still holds; just above it the train begins to move (and it is the voltage the stopped-but-lit states output). `max_voltage` is the top of the usable range. In v1 the default `voltage_power_curve` is linear across that usable range, from `lighting_voltage` (0%) to `max_voltage` (100%). So reversing from `power_percent` back to `track_voltage` uses the inverse interpolation of this same stored curve.
- `power_speed_curve` is the stored `(power_percent, speed_kmh)` mapping used by the second step. `power_percent` is the normalized control value between voltage and speed; it is not a second name for either of them. Its v1 default is linear from `0%` -> `0 km/h` to `100%` -> the owning train's configured `max_speed` (seeded at default-profile creation; later per-train tuning replaces the curve (see **Speed calibration**), and the stored curve — not `max_speed` — stays the calibration authority). It is always stored explicitly as profile calibration data, never inferred ad hoc elsewhere. Reverse lookup from `speed_kmh` to `power_percent` uses the inverse interpolation of this same stored curve.
- The motion-rate fields (`acceleration_rate`, `deceleration_rate`) govern ATO, manual `simulation` handle integration, service/emergency braking, and coasting. They do not shape manual `power_percent` response (that submode applies the calibrated speed immediately, see TrainPhysics).
- A model profile is a shared record and an instance profile is not. Several instance profiles may derive from one model profile, and that is what makes measuring a locomotive worth the pass: the operator calibrates one item of a model and promotes the result, and every locomotive of that model runs on the measured curve. `model` is the field that says which model a model profile describes, and **Speed calibration**, **What commit writes**, is where an operator decides whether a measurement stays on the one item or becomes the model's.
- Every train must name an instance profile, so `power_percent` manual mode always has a defined voltage/power/speed mapping, even before per-locomotive tuning. `SimulationController.add_train(...)` guarantees one at creation time: when placement imports a **Train Roster** entry that names an instance profile, the train uses that instance; otherwise `add_train(...)` creates a model profile whose `power_speed_curve` `100%` point is anchored to the train's configured `max_speed`, plus an empty instance profile deriving from it, and the train names the instance. An unidentified train, which Observe's layout-wide detector snapshot creates instead (see **Power**, Unidentified trains), gets that same pair and never uses it.

## Speed calibration

Speed calibration measures one locomotive's real power/speed response and writes it into that locomotive's instance profile as measured points, in place of the seeded linear `power_speed_curve`. `SpeedCalibration` is the class that owns and runs this procedure, keyed per train; it holds that train's `CalibrationRun`, the transient working record of the pass in progress. The **SpeedProfile** section is the canonical home for the two stored curves (`voltage_power_curve`, `power_speed_curve`) and for the model-profile / instance-profile split; this section is the canonical home for the procedure that fills the second one, and for **What commit writes**, which record receives the result. Calibration is the per-locomotive tuning the **SpeedProfile** section names: it is the one way a profile's `power_speed_curve` moves off its seeded linear default.

- **A pass commands a power percent and measures the speed that comes back.** It must work this way round: `power_speed_curve` is the curve that turns a wanted speed into a control value, and it is the very thing the pass is building, so the pass must not ask for a target speed while building it. Each step commands one `power_percent`, `TrainPhysics` drives the rails at the `track_voltage` that percent maps to through `voltage_power_curve`, and the pass reads the resulting `speed_kmh` back from measured motion.
- **The sweep runs in `CALIBRATION_POWER_STEP_PERCENT` increments up to `100%`.** At the v1 increment of `10` that is ten measured steps, `10%` through `100%`. The `0%` point needs no measurement: `0%` power is `lighting_voltage`, the voltage at which the train is lit and holds, so `(0%, 0 km/h)` is the curve's origin by definition and the pass writes it as such. That makes **Lighting-voltage calibration** the pass to run first: every step of this sweep is a percentage of a range whose bottom that one sets.
- **A pass measures the second stage only.** Each step yields one `(power_percent, speed_kmh)` point, and the finished set of points is the new `power_speed_curve`. `voltage_power_curve` is not measured and a pass must not write it. There is nothing about it a timed run can see: `power_percent` is the app's own normalized control value rather than a physical quantity, so a step can only command the voltage that curve already assigns to its percent, and reading that voltage back would restate the curve instead of testing it. The first stage stays the mapping the profile states between `lighting_voltage` and `max_voltage`, and **Lighting-voltage calibration** is the pass that moves its bottom anchor.
- **`CalibrationRun` is the transient working record of one pass**: the ordered power steps, the samples gathered so far, the train under calibration, and `active_leg_route_id: Optional[str]`, which names the calibration-created one-off route for the current leg or is `None` between legs. Like all runtime movement state it is in-memory only (per **Out of Scope**); only its committed result persists, through ordinary `SpeedProfile` persistence. Measuring every step does not commit the run: it holds its finished sample set until the operator picks a commit target, and **What commit writes** is what happens then.

**Auto profiling**

Auto profiling is the automatic measurement mode. It times the locomotive across one block of known length using the block detectors the layout already has, runs it back and forth across that block, and repeats that over the power sweep. It is the canonical home of the timed run; **Manual marking** below is the fallback for a layout the detectors cannot time.

- **The operator names the measured block.** A pass is set up by naming one block — the measured block, B — and `B.length_cm` must be greater than zero, because that one length is the whole of what the measurement rests on. The pass finds B's two neighbours itself, by walking the track out of each end of B through the points as they are actually aligned, the same forward tile walk `TrainPhysics` uses to resolve a train's next reserved block (see **Power**, Only the next reserved block is pre-energized). Those two neighbours are A and C. The operator names one block rather than three because the other two are not a choice: they are whatever the points are set to, and naming a stretch the points do not lead to would name a run the train cannot make.
- **The clock is two confirmed entries.** The train starts standing in A. The clock starts the moment B is confirmed occupied and stops the moment C is confirmed occupied, so what it times is the head crossing B end to end. `B.length_cm` over that elapsed time, converted through the same model-scale helper physics integrates distance with (see **Units contract**), is that crossing's measured `speed_kmh`. The pass watches only the confirmed entries attribution has credited to the calibration train (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection), so another train moving elsewhere on the layout cannot start or stop its clock. `SpeedCalibration` reads the same detector slice every other consumer reads: it checks the calibration train's `physics_sync.pending_detected_entered_blocks` inside Observe, immediately after that tick's attribution has written it and before the per-train loop begins, so it sees a confirmation the same tick Observe credits it and before the train's own final Observe callback folds and clears the slice. It writes nothing into the slice; it only reads it.
- **Why the middle block and not the first.** Timing from the moment power was applied to the moment B confirms would measure an unknown distance: the model never knows where inside a block a train sits (see **Power**, The calculated span never runs ahead of the detector), so how far the locomotive stood from A's far seam is not a number the pass has. Timing between two entry confirmations measures exactly one block, whatever the start position was. The two stamps are also the same kind of event — a confirmed OCCUPIED transition — so the detector's fixed lag, the one-tick read lag plus the `OCCUPANCY_ON_THRESHOLD` debounce reads, lands on both of them and cancels in the difference (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection). A one-sided interval would carry that lag as a bias in every sample.
- **The pass turns the train around at each end.** When the far outer block confirms occupied, the pass commands `power_percent = 0`, waits for the train to satisfy the canonical stopped predicate (see **Units**, `TrainController.is_stopped()`), issues `TrainController.commands.set_cab(...)` for the train's other end, and commands the same power step again. The reversal is that ordinary stopped-only cab command and nothing else (see **TrainController**, Power/cab/mode command contracts); calibration adds no reversal mechanism of its own. Driving the stretch back and forth is what lets a plain length of track measure a locomotive: a run that only ever went one way would need a loop the train can take, and a layout without one could not be calibrated at all.
- **Both directions are measured, and a step's sample is their mean.** A step runs `CALIBRATION_ROUND_TRIPS` round trips, so it collects twice that many crossings of B, half in each direction, and their mean is the step's sample. Two things make the mean the right number rather than one crossing's. A stretch is rarely dead level, and a grade makes the uphill direction measure slow by very nearly the amount it makes the downhill direction measure fast, so equal counts each way cancel it. And `power_speed_curve` carries no sign — `track_voltage` is a magnitude and neither stored curve is per-direction (see **TrainPhysics**) — so the single number the curve stores has to describe the locomotive driven either way.
- **The outer blocks are the run-up and the stopping room.** Each leg starts from a stand in an outer block, so that block is all the room the locomotive has to reach the speed the step commands, and the block at the far end is all the room it has to stop in. When the outer blocks are too short for the locomotive to finish accelerating in, the pass times a still-accelerating train across B and the curve reads low at its top steps. That is a property of the stretch the operator picked rather than of the locomotive, so the panel names both outer blocks it resolved before the pass starts (see **The panel**).
- **A leg that overruns the stretch fails the pass.** When a block past the far outer block confirms occupied and attribution credits it to the calibration train, the locomotive needed more stopping room than the stretch has. `SpeedCalibration` abandons the pass, commands `power_percent = 0`, and reports the reason on the command-result stream. The far outer block is the leg's authority end, so the rail past it is dead and the overrun is bounded to the one block a locomotive can coast into — but coasting into it at all means the measurement was made on a stretch too short for this locomotive, so the pass reports it rather than measuring on.
- **A step that does not move the train records `0 km/h`.** The low steps may not overcome the locomotive's stiction at all. A step whose B confirmation does not arrive within `CALIBRATION_STEP_TIMEOUT_S` records `0 km/h` and the pass moves to the next step. The train never left the outer block it stood in, so the pass does not turn it around: the next step commands from where it stands, facing the way it already faces. The flat bottom this leaves on the curve is that locomotive's real stall band, and physics reading `0 km/h` back for those commands is reading what the locomotive actually does.
- **A leg that starts crossing and never arrives fails the pass.** When B has confirmed but the far outer block has not within `CALIBRATION_STEP_TIMEOUT_S`, the locomotive stopped somewhere inside the stretch. That is a different fault from the stall band above, and it is not recorded as a slow step: a part-crossing is no measurement at all, and timing one would put a speed on the curve the locomotive never held.
- **A sweep in which no step moved the train fails the pass.** When every step measured `0 km/h`, `SpeedCalibration` reports the stretch rather than offering the result to commit. An all-zero curve is not the curve of a locomotive that cannot move — a locomotive that cannot move at `100%` is not one the layout was driving — it is a stretch the pass could not measure on, most often one too short for the consist to clear the measured block between crossings. Storing it would say the locomotive stands still at full power, and every speed the app later asked of it would map back to that.
- **The train must be standing in one of the two outer blocks.** That is where a leg starts from, so it is checked when the pass opens, and it is also what says which way the opening leg runs: toward the outer block the head is not in. Every later leg re-reads the head's block the same way when it arms, so a leg never asks for authority to the block the locomotive is already standing in.
- **Each leg runs as its own one-off route.** A leg arms only when `CalibrationRun.active_leg_route_id is None`, `PathDispatcher.active_path_id_by_train(train_id) is None`, and no `RUNNING` calibration `RouteRun` remains. At Plan step `c9e1`, `SpeedCalibration` prepares a `RouteMode.ONE_OFF` route with one `stop` task at the far outer block, `acquisition_mode = all_or_nothing`, `manual_override = False`; `RouteExecutor` creates, activates, and assigns it and stores its id in `CalibrationRun.active_leg_route_id`. `SpeedCalibration` does not call `PathDispatcher` or mutate route registries itself.
- **Plan acquires leg authority all-or-nothing.** In that same Plan pass, the ordinary steps allocate the matching `RouteRun` and perform the ordinary `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` call. Until `controller.received_path_plan` is present, `TrainController.tick(...)` selects zero calibration power and the step timeout does not run. If acquisition is blocked, Plan retries normally. This makes a busy stretch delay the pass instead of failing the step. All-or-nothing prevents a partial authority from stopping the locomotive inside the measured stretch.
- **A leg finishes through ordinary stop completion.** When the far outer block is confirmed and the train stops at the terminal, Observe step `9d8b` completes the path and its callback finishes the one-stop `RouteRun`. Plan then performs the ordinary one-off terminal teardown and unassigns that route. On the next Plan step `c9e1`, the absence of an assigned active route or live run clears `CalibrationRun.active_leg_route_id` and prepares the next leg. The requested cab reversal is part of the calibration state that `TrainController.tick(...)` validates and applies through the ordinary stopped-only cab rule before selecting propulsion. A stalled step is different: its leg route never reached the far outer block, so the pass tears that route down and re-arms a fresh leg from where the train stands, facing the way it already faces (see the stall bullet above), rather than holding a spent authority.
- **Pass-abandonment cases command a stop and deactivate the leg route.** When any of these holds, the pass commands `power_percent = 0` and calls `set_route_deactivate(reason, has_active_path=...)` for the active calibration route in the same step:
  - an overrun
  - a never-arrives leg
  - a braking override
  - a generation change
  - operator Stop
  - a request to assign a non-calibration route
  - a mid-run panel close
- **An existing teardown is not duplicated.** If `pending_route_deactivate` is already set, the pass writes no second deactivation. If another writer already set `pending_path_cancel_request`, `set_route_deactivate(...)` follows the ordinary most-recent-payload rule while adding the route teardown request. The pass abandons its samples either way.
- **External assignment waits for calibration teardown.** A writer that requests a non-calibration route while a speed pass is open first tells `SpeedCalibration` to abandon the pass, then uses the ordinary held same-train reassignment flow: it records the requested route, calls `set_route_deactivate(...)` for the active calibration route, and does not assign the requested route yet. The Action deactivation consumer tears down and unassigns the calibration route, then applies the held assignment. Because Plan has already run for that train in this tick, the requested route cannot allocate or move until the next Plan pass.
- **The stretch is energized by the ordinary power rules.** Auto profiling adds no power rule and takes no exception from one. The leg's path reserves the stretch ahead of the train, so the block the train stands on carries `track voltage` under its span and the next reserved block carries it as the one block pre-energized ahead (see **Power**, Block power-controller role, and **Only the next reserved block is pre-energized**). A, B and C go live in turn under the rule every train already runs under, in whichever order the leg's direction takes them. That rule is also exactly the protection this pass needs: the whole reason for the run is that the profile does not yet describe this locomotive, so nothing further ahead than the block it is entering may be live, and the rail past the far outer block — the leg's authority end — is dead.
- **A braking override voids the pass.** ATC, service stopping, and EB outrank calibration output. `TrainController.tick(...)` checks those safety conditions before accepting the active calibration's requested `power_percent`; when any applies during a measured crossing, it selects the safety output, abandons the pass before voltage application, reports the reason on the command-result stream, and leaves the profile's previous curve in place. A step's ordinary deceleration after the far outer block confirms is not an invalidating override, because the measurement ended on that confirmation before the stop command applied.
- **A step that measures slower than a lower-power step is measured once more.** `power_speed_curve` must stay invertible, so the samples have to rise with power (see **What commit writes**, The measured curve must stay invertible). One re-measure is what tells a noisy crossing apart from a locomotive that really does run slower at more power; a second slow reading is the second answer, and the pass fails and reports it rather than carrying a sample the commit will refuse.

**Manual marking**

- **Manual marking times the locomotive between two operator marks.** The operator sets two marks a known distance apart — that distance is the marker spacing — runs the train at the step's commanded `power_percent`, and issues a calibration `record` command as the head passes each one. The marker spacing over the time between two consecutive `record` commands is that crossing's measured `speed_kmh`. As in **Auto profiling** the crossings are averaged, `CALIBRATION_ROUND_TRIPS` round trips of them, so one noisy crossing does not set a point.
- **The operator drives the shuttle in this mode.** Nothing confirms a block entry for the pass to turn the train around on, so each end's reversal is the operator's, made with the same stopped-only cab command the pass issues for itself in **Auto profiling**. `SpeedCalibration` commands each step's power and counts marks; where the train is belongs to the operator.
- **Manual marking is the path when block detection cannot time the run** — when no block the pass can walk two neighbours out of exists, or when the measured block's `length_cm` was never recorded.
- Both modes produce the same `(power_percent, speed_kmh)` samples, hold them in the same `CalibrationRun`, and feed the same commit, including its non-decreasing and all-or-nothing rules (see **What commit writes**). `CALIBRATION_POWER_STEP_PERCENT`, `CALIBRATION_ROUND_TRIPS`, and `CALIBRATION_STEP_TIMEOUT_S` are constants in `constants.py`.
- Every calibration interval is measured against `AppState.operating_time` (see **Units**, Clocks). Wall time would count an operator's stop as distance covered: the session stops, the locomotive stops, and the interval goes on growing. `operating_time` advances only while the session runs, so a pass paused mid-crossing resumes on the same measurement. It also carries the playback multiplier, so a Simulation pass at four times playback measures the model's own km/h rather than four times it, and in Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware, where `simulation_speed` is `1.0`, it advances at wall rate and the pass is a real-world measurement.

**The panel**

- **The calibration group names the locomotive before either pass opens.** The Speed Profile panel's calibration group carries a locomotive row, and both this pass and **Lighting-voltage calibration** drive the train it names; neither pass picks a train for itself. The row holds three things:
  - a train picker listing every placed train whose resolved profile is the profile on screen — every train naming an instance profile that derives from it, and every train naming it directly — showing each train's car number and state
  - Take control, which puts the named train into the state both passes require
  - a readiness line naming every opening condition the named train does not yet meet, so the operator reads them together rather than one at a time
- **Take control sets `manual` control mode and selects a cab.** It issues the ordinary Action manual commands and takes no exception from their contracts (see **TrainController**, Power/cab/mode command contracts): `set_mode(...)` for `manual`, then `TrainController.commands.set_cab(...)` for the cab the train already has, or `A` when it has none, which also powers a powered-off train up as its documented side effect.
- **Take control clears no other opening condition.** An assigned route and an open pass of the other kind are reported on the readiness line for the operator to resolve. Those two conditions say another procedure owns the train, and taking it away from that procedure is a decision the operator makes rather than a side effect of pressing a button in this panel.
- **The operator does not choose the cab.** A locomotive's power/speed response is the same driven either way, so which end drives is not a measurement the operator makes. Both passes need a cab because a block's `track voltage` is signed by the cab that picked it (see **Power**, A block voltage carries a direction), and Take control is what provides one.
- **The Calibrate speed control opens this pass.** It sits in the same calibration group, beside the lighting-voltage row that **Lighting-voltage calibration**, The panel, is the canonical home for.
- **Before the pass starts the panel holds three things**: the measured block, which the operator names; the two outer blocks the pass resolved out of that block's ends, shown so the operator sees which stretch the train will run before it runs it; and Start.
- **While the pass runs the panel holds three things**: which step is being measured and how many of its crossings are done, the points measured so far drawn against the profile's stored curve, and Stop. Stop is a pass-abandonment case: it ends the pass the way a braking override does — it commands `power_percent = 0`, deactivates the active calibration one-off route per **Each leg runs as its own one-off route**, and writes nothing to either profile record.
- **When every step is measured the panel holds the result and the two commit controls**: the measured curve drawn against the stored one, **Save to this locomotive**, and **Promote to model**. **What commit writes** states what each control does.
- **Nothing is written until the operator picks one of the two.** Closing the panel without picking discards the pass; a mid-run panel close is also a pass-abandonment case, ending the pass exactly like Stop — it commands `power_percent = 0` and deactivates the active calibration one-off route. A measured curve says what one locomotive did on one stretch, and whether that is the model's curve or only this item's is a judgement about a physical locomotive that the operator is the one able to make.

**What commit writes**

- **Commit writes two fields and no others**: `power_speed_curve` from the pass's samples, and `calibrated_at` from the wall clock. It must not write `voltage_power_curve` — **Lighting-voltage calibration** is the one procedure that moves that curve's anchor — and it must not write a motion rate or a notch table, which describe how the model behaves rather than how fast the measured locomotive ran. `model` is edited on the model profile in the panel like any other model-profile field, so a commit never writes it.
- **Save to this locomotive** writes those two fields onto the instance profile the calibrated train names. That train runs on the measured curve from that moment and no other locomotive changes. It is the control for a locomotive that does not run like the rest of its model, and for keeping a working model curve while measuring one item beside it.
- **Promote to model** writes those two fields onto the model profile the calibrated train's instance derives from, and clears both fields from that instance in the same commit. Every locomotive whose instance leaves them unset runs on the new curve from that moment, the calibrated one included, because clearing them is what puts it back to following its model. That is what a model profile is for: one item is measured, and every locomotive of that model gets the measurement.
- **Commit is all or nothing.** A pass that has not measured every step writes nothing, whichever target the operator picks. A partly replaced curve would be part measured and part seeded with nothing on the profile to say which part is which, and no later reading of it could tell.
- **The measured curve must stay invertible.** Physics reads `power_speed_curve` in both directions, and the reverse lookup from `speed_kmh` to `power_percent` is an inverse interpolation that needs speed to rise with power (see **SpeedProfile**). On commit the assembled samples must be non-decreasing in `speed_kmh`, and a commit that finds them otherwise fails and reports it rather than storing a curve half the system cannot read backwards.

**Where it runs**

- **Opening a pass requires all of these**, and every one of them is a condition the commands the pass issues already carry:
  - the train is placed, and it stands in one of the measured block's two outer blocks — a leg starts from a stand in an outer block, so anywhere else is not a place a step can start
  - `control_mode` is `manual` and the manual submode is `power_percent` — both `set_manual_power_percent(...)` and `set_cab(...)` are manual-only commands
  - the train is `READY` and stopped
  - a cab is selected — the pass reverses by writing the other end, so there must be an end it is writing away from
  - the train has no assigned route — `RouteExecutor.assigned_route_id_for(train_id) is None` — and has no **Lighting-voltage calibration** run open (that pass states the same exclusion from its side). After opening, only the route named by `CalibrationRun.active_leg_route_id` may be assigned while the pass remains valid
- **Where it runs.** Plan step `c9e1` advances the speed-calibration sequence, evaluates step progress against `CALIBRATION_STEP_TIMEOUT_S`, and prepares the next leg route or requested reversal. `RouteExecutor` performs route creation/assignment and all path acquisition during Plan. During Action, `TrainController.tick(...)` calls `SpeedCalibration.get_propulsion_override(train_id)` after its ordinary command drain and before propulsion selection. The return type is `Optional[CalibrationPropulsionOverride]`, where the closed union is `{kind: "power_percent", value: float}` for speed calibration or `{kind: "track_voltage", value: float}` for lighting calibration. The helper validates the open run and returns `None` when no calibration may drive. A requested reversal uses the same stopped-only cab validation as the ordinary cab command. Calibration never enters `SimulationController._act_train(...)` as a special pre-controller call and never queues pretend operator commands.
- **The pass drives the train through ordinary surfaces, not new ones.** It is a dedicated controlled pass, but it drives the train the way an operator in manual mode drives one, through surfaces that already exist.
  - **Leg authority uses the ordinary route path.** Step `c9e1` supplies the leg definition; `RouteExecutor` creates and assigns the one-off route, allocates its `RouteRun`, and calls `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` in Plan. `SpeedCalibration` never creates, extends, completes, or cancels a path directly.
  - **Controller owns calibration output.** Speed and lighting calibration share the `CalibrationPropulsionOverride` mechanism above; there is no speed-only control bypass. `TrainController.tick(...)` selects the returned value during its ordinary Action decision and does not copy it into `manual.manual_power_percent`, `handle_position`, or the operator-command inbox. The override replaces the ordinary traction source. The speed pass's `power_percent` variant feeds the speed solution, so it stays below EB, ATC, service stopping, pending power-off, and output safe state like any traction request. The lighting pass's `track_voltage` variant is a magnitude-only sub-drive holding voltage (handle `N`, no motion) that feeds no speed and moves the train not at all by itself, so it is gated only by EB, pending power-off, and output safe state — which propulsion selects before it — and the ATC and service-stop caps, which meter the speed solution, do not apply to it.
- **Every calibration path has a matching `RouteRun`.** Calibration has no exception to the route-backed-authority rule or to dispatcher completion handling.
- **Leg completion and abandonment use ordinary route flows.** A successful leg uses terminal stop completion. Abandonment calls `set_route_deactivate(...)`; the Action consumer cancels any live path and removes the `RouteRun` through the standard teardown order.
- **Braking overrides retain the same authority over the pass as over any manual command.** ATC, service-stop, and EB retain the same authority over the pass that they hold over any manual command (see **A braking override voids the pass** above and the **Canonical power-percent safety-cap ordering**).
- `CalibrationRun` captures `SimulationController.safe_state_generation` when it opens, and `SpeedCalibration` compares the live generation before issuing each command and before accepting each detector or marker sample. A changed generation means a session stop or another safe-state request occurred, so the pass abandons its samples, commands `power_percent = 0`, and reports the reason on the command-result stream. A pass that has measured every step is past that check: it issues no further command and accepts no further sample, so its result is a finished set of numbers a later session stop cannot corrupt, and the operator may still commit it. This generation comparison is the complete handoff; `OutputSafety` never calls into calibration.
- Calibration adds no persisted state of its own. What it writes is the two `SpeedProfile` fields **What commit writes** names, on the one record the operator's commit target names. It must not open a new event sink; progress and the final result are reported as ordinary command-result events on the one stream owned by `NotificationCenter` (see **Core Runtime Loop**, Runtime notifications).
- In Simulation the measured speed comes from the happy-path train model, so a calibration pass reproduces the model's own curve. In Virtual Hardware it comes from the controllable fake device, which lets the procedure and its fault handling be exercised against a complete Hardware Setup. In Real Hardware it comes from the physical locomotive's true response. The procedure is identical in all three environments; only the source of the measured response differs.

## Lighting-voltage calibration

Lighting-voltage calibration finds the one voltage at which a locomotive is lit and still holds, and writes it to `lighting_voltage` on that locomotive's instance profile (**SpeedProfile** is the canonical home for what that field is, which record carries it, and what else reads it). It is the first calibration a newly added locomotive gets: `SimulationController.add_train(...)` seeds a placeholder value, and every other calibrated number sits on top of it, because a **Speed calibration** sweep takes its bottom step from `lighting_voltage`. `SpeedCalibration` owns this pass as it owns the speed pass, keyed per train.

**The operator's eye is the measurement**

- This pass commands a voltage and asks the operator whether the locomotive moved. Nothing on the rig can answer that question at this level. A current channel reads whether a locomotive is drawing on the block, not whether it moved, and first movement is a creep of a few millimetres, far below what timing a head across two block seams can resolve. A person watching the locomotive is the one instrument that reads it, so the operator's judgement is the sample this pass collects, and there is no measured value to write down.

**The panel**

- **The pass drives the locomotive the calibration group names.** The train comes from the locomotive row both calibrations share, and Take control is what puts it into the state this pass requires (**Speed calibration**, The panel, is that row's canonical home).
- **The lighting-voltage row is the panel.** The profile's lighting-voltage field sits in the same calibration group, and the Calibrate control beside it opens the run in place on that row: the row then holds the candidate voltage as it stands, a step-up control, a step-down control, Save, and Revert. The voltage/power curve stays on screen with its bottom anchor following the candidate, so the operator sees what Save will write before writing it.
- **The lighting-voltage field is read-only.** **Lighting-voltage calibration** is the one procedure that moves a profile's stored `lighting_voltage` in the ordinary case (see **Power**, Occupancy source follows drive state); seeded and imported values arrive with the profile itself. So the field displays the resolved value, and the step controls are the one way to move it.
- A step changes the candidate by `LIGHTING_VOLTAGE_STEP_V` and puts the new value on the rails at once, so every press is answered by the locomotive in front of the operator. `LIGHTING_VOLTAGE_STEP_V` lives in `constants.py`.
- The value to save is the highest step at which the locomotive still held still, because `lighting_voltage` is the lit-but-not-moving voltage: the operator steps up until it creeps, steps back down one, and saves.
- The step-up control stops at the ceiling in **What a candidate may be**, so the panel cannot show a value Save would refuse; the step-down control stops at `0`.
- **Save and discard are the two operator-driven endings.** Save commits the candidate and ends the run. Discarding it ends the run just as completely, and it happens on any of these:
  - Revert
  - leaving the profile or closing the panel
  - naming a different train in the locomotive row

  Either way the run ends and that train's `track_voltage` returns to what its state ordinarily outputs. See **What the run drives** for the conditions that end a run without operator action.

**What the run drives**

- Opening a run requires the train to be placed, in `manual` control mode, `READY` and stopped, with a cab selected, with no assigned route (`RouteExecutor.assigned_route_id_for(train_id) is None`), and with no **Speed calibration** pass open for it. A cab must be selected because ordinary per-block emission needs `TrainController.travel_direction` to sign the candidate magnitude separately for each block (see **Power**, A block voltage carries a direction); the calibration group's Take control is what provides one (see **Speed calibration**, The panel). `stopped` and the no-concurrent-**Speed-calibration** rule are opening preconditions only: neither is re-checked while a run is open, so a run survives the train creeping under the candidate voltage.
- A run ends the moment any of these conditions holds, not only on Save or panel-close: the train leaves `READY`, leaves `manual` control mode, loses its cab, is powered off, has EB activated, or is assigned a route. Step `26f5` re-evaluates those conditions in `SimulationController._reevaluate_lighting_run(train)` during the Action teardown (`_commit_train_act`), after `TrainController.tick(...)` has selected propulsion and `TrainPhysics.apply_track_voltage()` has written this tick's voltage, and calls `SpeedCalibration.cancel_lighting(train_id)` when any condition fails. It is a `SimulationController`-level step because the route-assignment condition reads `RouteExecutor.assigned_route_id_for(train_id)` and the remaining conditions read `SpeedCalibration.lighting_run_still_valid(...)`. The run therefore ends on the same tick its condition is met; the candidate is dropped and the train's `track_voltage` returns to what its ordinary state outputs on the following tick. The one voltage already written on the ending tick moves nothing, because `SpeedCalibration.get_propulsion_override(...)` withholds the candidate under EB, pending power-off, and the other safety caps while propulsion is selected, and a still-valid candidate is a sub-drive-threshold holding voltage. A session stop or safe-state generation change does not end a run: unlike **Speed calibration**, a lighting run accumulates no timed sample for a stop to corrupt, so the candidate is left in place and reaches the rail again through the ordinary energized-set emission of the next `start`, the same general de-energize/resume mechanism every other train's `track_voltage` goes through. A fatal-halt clear does end a run: `SimulationController.clear_failed_runtime()`'s step-`7c41` fan-out calls `SpeedCalibration.cancel_lighting(train_id)` for every train with an open run, alongside its `TrainController.complete_power_off()` call on each controller, because that fan-out is not an Action pass.
- While a run remains valid, `TrainController.tick(...)` selects the run's exact candidate voltage magnitude instead of the ordinary manual-notch, manual-power, or ATO traction request. It does not copy the candidate into an operator-command field. `TrainPhysics` treats the override's `track_voltage` value as the authoritative magnitude for that tick, and ordinary per-block emission applies the canonical block-relative sign separately to every block. Output safe state, pending power-off, EB, ATC intervention, and service stopping outrank the candidate during propulsion selection, so a candidate the run must not drive is withheld before voltage application; the run itself is cancelled a step later, in the Action teardown after the voltage write (step `26f5`). The candidate does not feed the speed solution, so it never moves the modelled train by itself. It reaches that train's ordinary energized set, and each block follows the ordinary direction rule (see **Power**, Block power-controller role and A block voltage carries a direction). A train that may open a run is stopped with nothing reserved ahead of it, so that set is the rail under the locomotive.

**What a candidate may be**

- A candidate is at least `0`, and it stays below both the profile's `max_voltage` and, in Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware, the Hardware Setup's `current_sense_min_drive_v`. In Simulation the `current_sense_min_drive_v` bound is not evaluated, because Simulation never reads Hardware Setup (see **Simulation is independent of Hardware Setup**); a candidate saved there is bounded only by `max_voltage`. The readiness evaluator under **Occupancy source follows drive state** re-checks the stored value against `current_sense_min_drive_v` at hardware activation, so a candidate saved in Simulation that would fail the hardware bound is caught then rather than at save time.
- The second bound is `current_sense_min_drive_v` (see **Hardware setup**, Occupancy source follows drive state). This pass is the one thing that moves `lighting_voltage`, so it is where that bound is kept.

**What Save writes**

- Committing always writes the candidate to `lighting_voltage` on the instance profile the train names — there is no promote-to-model choice here, unlike **Speed calibration**'s two commit controls. A lamp, a motor, and a gearbox differ between two items of one model, so this value describes the locomotive in front of the operator rather than the model it belongs to. No other train changes, and the model profile is untouched.
- `lighting_voltage` is also the 0%-power point of `voltage_power_curve` (see **SpeedProfile**), so committing moves the bottom anchor of the curve this train resolves. Because an instance profile stores no `voltage_power_curve` of its own, the move is in the resolved curve alone and the model profile's stored curve is unchanged; **SpeedProfile**, Model profiles and instance profiles, is the canonical home for how that resolved curve is built.

**Where it lives**

- `LightingCalibrationRun` is the transient working record of one run: the train, the instance profile the candidate will be written to, and the candidate voltage. Like `CalibrationRun` it is in-memory only; only the committed profile value persists. `SpeedCalibration` exposes the lighting start/step/commit/cancel methods and the shared read-only `get_propulsion_override(train_id)` accessor. `TrainController.tick(...)` reads that accessor after validation; neither it nor `TrainPhysics` reaches into the run registry.
- The run adds no persisted state beyond that one profile field and opens no new event sink. It reports as ordinary command-result events on the one stream owned by `NotificationCenter` (see **Core Runtime Loop**, Runtime notifications), the same way **Speed calibration** reports.
- The value describes a physical motor, so Real Hardware is where a run tells the operator something new: the candidate is a raw voltage substitution on the real rail, and the operator watches the real locomotive to see whether it creeps. The candidate never feeds `TrainPhysics`'s speed solution, so the modelled train's own crawl point stays fixed at the profile's stored anchor regardless of the candidate; in Simulation and Virtual Hardware, where the model is the only thing to watch, a run is therefore a readback of the value already stored rather than a live experiment. The procedure — opening, stepping, Save — is identical in all three environments; only whether the answer is new differs.

## Train Roster

The `TrainRoster` is the catalog of locomotives the operator owns. It is persisted layout data, not runtime state: it is edited with the layout and saved and restored in the layout snapshot (runtime state stays in-memory only per **Out of Scope**; persisted layout data survives, the same split the **Maintenance counters** section draws). Each `RosterEntry` records one owned locomotive and the defaults used to put it on the track.

- `RosterEntry` fields:
  - `entry_id`: unique identifier for the roster record.
  - `name`: display name for the locomotive.
  - `model`: free-text description of the physical item — its manufacturer, product, and box, as written on the packaging. It is also what a measured profile is found by, against `SpeedProfile.model` (see **Profiles are matched by model** below).
  - `purchase_date`: the date the locomotive was acquired.
  - `purchase_price`: the acquisition cost.
  - `consist_length_cm`: the physical length used to build the train's span when this entry is placed (see **Train Entity**).
  - `max_speed`: the locomotive's top speed.
