  - `min_radius_cm`: the locomotive's minimum curve radius — the train-side value the pathfinder's curve filter reads (see **Train Entity**).
  - `max_slope`: the locomotive's maximum climbable grade as a percent, `0.0` meaning unspecified (see **Train Entity**).
  - `speed_profile_id`: the instance profile this locomotive runs on (see **SpeedProfile**, Model profiles and instance profiles). **Speed calibration** and **Lighting-voltage calibration** both write that instance, so a measured curve and a measured lighting voltage stay with the locomotive across placements. Several entries naming one model each carry their own instance and derive them from one model profile (see **Profiles are matched by model** below).
- **Profiles are matched by model.** When a `RosterEntry` is created, or its `model` is edited, and it names no `speed_profile_id`, the roster finds the model profile whose `model` equals the entry's, comparing the two strings exactly, and creates an empty instance profile deriving from it for the entry to name. When more than one model profile carries that model, the instance derives from the one with the most recent `calibrated_at`, and a model profile with none set loses to any model profile that has one. When no model profile carries that model, the entry keeps no profile link, and placement seeds the model profile and the instance under it that **SpeedProfile** describes. The match is made once, at the moment the entry's model is written, and the stored `speed_profile_id` is the link every later read follows: a placement resolves a profile by id, never by string, so renaming a model afterwards moves nothing that is already linked.
- Placing a train may import a `RosterEntry`. When the placement input names one, `SimulationController.add_train(...)` (the placement home in **Train Entity**) seeds the new `Train`'s persistent fields and its instance-profile link from that entry instead of from blank defaults. A roster entry is a template for placement: the placed `Train` is a separate runtime instance, and editing one after placement does not change the other. The instance profile is the one record they share on purpose: it is that locomotive's own calibration, and both the entry and the placed train name it.
- The roster carries the locomotive's identity, purchase record, placement defaults, and profile link only. Cumulative usage stays on the live `Train` and its block and switch counters per the **Maintenance counters** home; the roster stores no second usage total.

## Power

**Hardware interface boundary**

- The runtime drives and reads the physical-world boundary only through abstract interfaces addressed by logical id (`block_id`, `switch_id`), never by pin or wire. There are three: `TrackOutput` for block track voltage, `SwitchOutput` for switch throw, and `OccupancyInput` for detector reads. Simulation constructs its three happy-path model implementations directly and does not read Hardware Setup. Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware construct the same setup-aware HAL implementations as one complete set; their only device difference is in-memory versus physical. A missing role or interface fails the Virtual/Real build — `None` never asks the runtime to install a simulated fallback. `BlockPowerController` holds `TrackOutput` and `SwitchPowerController` holds `SwitchOutput` (both defined below). They are the only callers of the two output interfaces during operation — including the per-channel zero and de-energize writes that `OutputSafety.enter_safe_state()` drives, which it issues through each controller's non-recording device write (`BlockPowerController.zero_device_outputs()` and `SwitchPowerController.de_energize_device_outputs()`; see **Safe state / fail-safe**) rather than the ordinary model-recording write — and they hold no wiring knowledge themselves. A commissioning session is the one other caller, and only while it holds the outputs (see **Commissioning owns the writes; the detectors stay shared**).
- **No wiring knowledge above the interface.** No runtime, control, route, physics, or manager code names a GPIO pin, expander chip, shift-register bit, or bus type. A concrete implementation owns the map from logical id to physical channel and is the only place that knows the wiring. Direct GPIO, a 74HC595 / 74HC165 shift-register chain, and an I²C expander such as MCP23017 are interchangeable implementations of the same interfaces. Choosing one changes which implementation is constructed and nothing else. The map itself is data — the binding table in **Hardware setup** below — that the concrete implementation loads and is the only reader of.
- **Fault injection belongs to Virtual Hardware.** Simulation's default interfaces model happy hardware: every write succeeds and every read agrees with the model. Tests may inject a stub directly into the interface seam, but operator-facing hardware faults are modeled by Virtual Hardware's in-memory device, below the real chip and HAL implementations. The canonical injectable fault kinds are exactly `transaction_refusal`, `timeout`, `device_disconnect`, `invalid_reading` (`OccupancyInput` and the block-voltage readback), `input_hold_or_flicker` (`OccupancyInput`), and `output_disagrees_with_command` (`TrackOutput` readback). Every other site names this set rather than restating it, and `PUT /api/virtual-hardware/fault` takes one of these values. That keeps Simulation focused on algorithms while proving the same hardware-failure path Real Hardware uses.
- **Input / sensing boundary.** `OccupancyInput` is the read side for sensors that no software output drives. v1 reads one thing through it: block current detection, via `read_block_currents()`. (The block track-voltage readback is the output interface reading back its own output, `TrackOutput.get_actual_voltage`, not an `OccupancyInput` read; its one v1 consumer is the diagnostic block-voltage read `BlockPowerController.get_block_voltage(block_id)` — see **Block power-controller role**.) Block current detection is the block-occupancy authority. Its read, debounce, attribution, and position reconciliation are defined in **Block occupancy detection** below. `OccupancyInput` also names the blocks it can answer for, through `detected_block_ids()`. In Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware, activation requires both occupancy bindings for every layout block, so this set is the complete layout block set. For `SimulatedOccupancyDriver` it is empty, because Simulation senses nothing physical and derives occupancy from the model. **Block occupancy detection** reads the set to decide whether detector-gated movement applies. Switch alignment has no sensor read in v1: authority is the commanded `Switch.position`. Treating any sensor as a fault-detection, verification, or recovery source is **Out of Scope** for v1.
- **Safe state / fail-safe.** Each output interface defines a safe state, but the sequence is owned by one session-level entity so track and point outputs cannot disagree about whether the rig is driving. That entity is `OutputSafety`, and it exposes one method: `enter_safe_state()`. It performs the whole sequence itself, in order:
  1. de-energize every point motor through `SwitchPowerController.de_energize_device_outputs()`
  2. command every block voltage to `0` through `BlockPowerController.zero_device_outputs()`

  Both are each controller's non-recording device write: they command the device transport directly and do not touch `Block.track_voltage`, `Switch.position`, or any other recorded model field, so `enter_safe_state()` is safe to call from any thread, including the Real Hardware `OutputWatchdog` daemon thread (see **Loss-of-control watchdog**). Both non-recording writes still pass through the driver, so the per-channel last-commanded voltage that **Occupancy source follows drive state** reads is updated to `0` by the safe state itself; only the recorded model fields (`Block.track_voltage`) wait for the reconciliation described below. Point motors go first because a solenoid is the output that destroys itself if left energized; track voltage only keeps a train moving.
- **Every chip is attempted even when one fails.** A single dead chip cannot leave the rest energized, and the failures are reported together.
- **Reconciling the recorded model fields is a separate, later step.** Reconciling `Block.track_voltage` and the other recorded model fields to match is always owned by the runtime thread, never `enter_safe_state()` itself. `SimulationController.enter_output_safe_state()` performs that reconciliation synchronously, immediately after `enter_safe_state()` returns, for every runtime-thread caller; the watchdog path reconciles instead at trip-record consumption, on the runtime thread's next tick (see **Loss-of-control watchdog**).
- **Runtime-thread callers reach the sequence through `SimulationController.enter_output_safe_state()`.** That wrapper first advances `safe_state_generation`; the Real Hardware `OutputWatchdog` is the sole direct caller of `enter_safe_state()`, and the runtime advances that generation when it later consumes the watchdog trip. Operation stop, commissioning entry, restart/shutdown, and fatal runtime/hardware entry all use the runtime wrapper.
- **Environment behavior for safe state.** Virtual Hardware performs the same sequence against the fake device; Simulation only zeroes its stored values.
- **Safe state is a de-energize, not a lock.** Nothing is withheld from the outputs afterwards: the next `start` drives the layout again with no reactivation, because stopping took away the voltage and nothing else. This is the whole of v1's physical safety mechanism, and its limit is written into what it is — reaching the safe state is a write, so it needs a live process and a working transport. A process or host that dies leaves each board holding its last commanded value, which `activation_report` reports as a Real Hardware readiness warning so activating is an informed act.
- **Loss-of-control watchdog.** Real Hardware only: activation starts one safety-only daemon, `OutputWatchdog`, that reaches the safe state when the runtime thread stops refreshing the outputs. Simulation and Virtual Hardware drive no physical motor, so neither starts it. A landed ordinary output transaction refreshes the deadline; expiry runs only `OutputSafety.enter_safe_state()` under the same transport lock used by ordinary device transactions.
- **The daemon writes only below the model.** The daemon calls `enter_safe_state()` directly, which — per **Safe state / fail-safe** — performs its whole sequence through each controller's non-recording device write (`SwitchPowerController.de_energize_device_outputs()`, then `BlockPowerController.zero_device_outputs()`); those writes go straight to the device transport, below the model, and the daemon records their transport results in its own thread-safe trip record. It may not read or mutate `SimulationController`, trains, routes, notifications, or any other runtime model state, which is exactly what calling only the non-recording write, and never the ordinary model-recording write, guarantees.
- **Trip-record consumption escalates a failed drop to hardware failure.** Consuming the trip record is the one step `SimulationController.update(...)` performs even behind a fatal gate, because a failed safe-state attempt must still escalate to `hardware_failure`. On the next runtime-thread tick, the controller consumes that trip record, reconciles every block's recorded `track_voltage` to `0` (so the model never keeps reporting a block energized past a watchdog-driven drop it did not yet know about — see **A refused write is fatal to a hardware-backed session, and never recorded as voltage**), enters hardware failure if the safe-state attempt failed, and otherwise emits one `kind = "warning"` event through `NotificationCenter`. This trip-record reconciliation is the watchdog path's counterpart to the synchronous reconciliation `SimulationController.enter_output_safe_state()` performs for every other, runtime-thread caller of `enter_safe_state()` (see **Safe state / fail-safe**); the watchdog path is deferred by exactly one tick because the daemon thread cannot perform it itself.
- **A successful drop does not end the session.** A successful safe-state drop protects the layout but does not itself end the session; a recovered loop may drive again on its next write.
- **Arming and disarming the watchdog.** `SimulationController.enter_output_safe_state()` disarms the watchdog before delegating to `OutputSafety.enter_safe_state()`; the watchdog's own expiry call disarms it too. In both cases the next landed ordinary output write re-arms it.
- **Hardware I/O failure is fatal to the physical session.** When any of these occurs, it reports the failure to `SimulationController.enter_hardware_failure(...)`:
  - a failed output write
  - a failed detector transaction
  - a lost controller
  - an inability to complete safe state
- **`SimulationController.enter_hardware_failure(...)` is the sole true writer.** That method, not the reporting entity, is the only writer of `hardware_failure = True`, mirroring `SimulationController.enter_failed_runtime(...)` in the **Fatal physical-entry conflict procedure**. It stops the session (`simulation_running = False`), calls `SimulationController.enter_output_safe_state()` — which advances the generation and delegates to the sequence that attempts every de-energize and zero action even when one of them fails — records every failure in the emitted event payload, stores only the current `environment_activation_generation` as `hardware_failure_activation_generation`, latches the flag, and emits one `kind = "error"` event with `operation = "enter_hardware_failure"`. It retains no `ErrorRecord` or second diagnostic payload across ticks.
- **The affected hardware-backed operation loop stops.** `SimulationController.update(...)` refuses advancement while `hardware_failure` is set only when `active_environment` is `virtual_hardware` or `real_hardware`, including the watchdog trip-record exception in step `ee19` above. An active `simulation` environment continues its full software-defined Observe → Plan → Action loop while the latch remains visible; this is full Simulation operation, not a fallback substituted inside a failed hardware-backed session. The failed Virtual/Real session does not log-and-retry its tick and never replaces its interface with a simulated one. Clearing the latch leaves the session stopped; only a later explicit start resumes ticks.
- **Recovery is reactivation followed by an explicit clear.** Every successful `POST /api/operation/activate` increments `environment_activation_generation` and marks the requested environment active, but deliberately leaves `hardware_failure` unchanged. A latched `hardware_failure` does not block activating or running Simulation: `POST /api/simulation/control` refuses on it only while the active environment is Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware (see the endpoint row under **Hardware setup**, REST surface), so an operator whose Hardware Setup is broken or incomplete can still activate and run Simulation while repairing the hardware, per **Simulation is independent of Hardware Setup**. `POST /api/runtime/clear-hardware-failure` is the sole caller of `SimulationController.clear_hardware_failure()` and that method is the only writer of `hardware_failure = False`. It refuses unless the active environment is Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware and `environment_activation_generation > hardware_failure_activation_generation`, proving that a successful activation occurred after the failure. On success it clears the flag and emits one informational event, mirroring `clear_failed_runtime()`. `SimulationController.clear_failed_runtime()` does not clear the hardware latch. Repair or replace the device, reactivate it, then clear the latch; neither activation nor clearing silently starts operation.
- Virtual Hardware follows the same latch and recovery flow so it can be tested without the rig.

**Hardware setup**

- Hardware Setup is the physical description shared by Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware: a `controller` (the transport bridge), a `chips` list, the binding maps that wire logical ids to chip ports, and detector calibration. It contains no `enabled`, `develop`, or selected-environment flag. Simulation never reads it. The setup is persisted to an app-managed file and inside its layout save file (see **Saved with the layout**); the selected operating environment is stored separately and loading a layout never activates hardware.
- **Completeness is activation policy, not edit policy.** An incomplete setup may be saved and exercised through bounded commissioning while a rig is being built, but it cannot activate Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware operation. Until the setup is complete, the only operating environment that may run the railway is Simulation. Completeness is checked against the loaded layout: every block has one `block_track` binding plus both required occupancy bindings (`block_occupancy` and `block_occupancy_current`); every switch has one `switch_output` binding and one `switch_track_source` binding; every binding names a present compatible chip and unique in-range port; no binding names a deleted entity; every required device is reachable; and every `SpeedProfile` assigned to a placed train has `lighting_voltage` strictly below the setup's `current_sense_min_drive_v` (see **Occupancy source follows drive state**). Absence of a required item is always a readiness blocker. A missing binding, chip, device, or detector source is never interpreted as a clear input, an unpowered/undetected exception, or a request for a simulated fallback.
- **Controller.** The transport a real session drives through. v1 has one, `ch347` — a USB-HID bridge that carries an I²C bus, an SPI bus, and GPIO. It may carry a `device_port`, but `ch347` opens by USB VID/PID, so the port is optional. The controller list stays open, so another bridge is one added entry.
- **Chips.** Each chip has a `chip_id`, a `kind`, a `bus`, and the parameters that kind needs. v1 has five kinds: `pca9685` (PWM) drives track power, `hc595` (shift-out) drives switch throws, and block occupancy has two sources — `hc165` (shift-in), the digital detector, and a current monitor, which reads block supply current directly. A current monitor is either an `ina3221` (3 channels) or an `ina219` (1 channel); the two differ only in how many blocks one chip covers.
- **A chip's interface `role` is derived from its `kind`, never stored.** The occupancy kinds share the `occupancy_input` role and differ by port kind.
- **A chip's `bus` is user-set, not derived.** It is stored, not derived, from the buses its kind allows: `pca9685`, `ina3221`, and `ina219` are I²C only, while a shift register (`hc595` / `hc165`) is `spi` or `gpio`. A shift register clocks its data over the SPI peripheral on either bus; its `bus` names where its **latch line** sits — one of the two hardware chip-select pads (`spi`), or a general-purpose pin (`gpio`). The `gpio` bus exists because the bridge carries only two chip-select pads, so a third shift register must latch somewhere else.
- **The rest of a chip's parameters are user-set as well.** An `i2c_address` for an I²C chip; a latch line (`spi_select`) plus a cascade count (`chain_length`) for a shift register on either the SPI or GPIO bus.
- **Each chip kind contributes a fixed number of channels or bits.** A `pca9685` contributes 16 PWM channels, of which a block's track takes two; a shift register contributes `8 × chain_length` bits; an `ina3221` contributes 3 current-sense channels and an `ina219` 1.
- **A block's track is two PWM channels.** A commanded block voltage is signed — the sign is the block-relative direction the train runs through that block (see **Block power-controller role**, A block voltage carries a direction) — so a block's track is an H-bridge whose two inputs are driven by two `pca9685` channels. The binding names the two `forward` and `reverse`; those are its two slots, and which slot a positive voltage drives is what the binding's `reversed` flag states (see **The rail binding bonds tile order to rail polarity** below). The driver maps voltage magnitude to duty cycle and voltage sign to which of the two channels drives, holding the other at zero, so the two inputs are never driven together. The two are chosen independently, not as a fixed adjacent pair, because a bench build may wire a block's rails to any two channels on the chip.
- **A block at `0` has nothing applied to it.** Zero is a commanded voltage like any other, and the same rule covers it: the channel matching the sign carries the magnitude, and the other rests at zero, so at zero neither channel drives and the H-bridge is given no input at all. That is what an un-energized block is — one the app applies no voltage to. It is not a claim about what a meter reads on those rails. A locomotive's wheelbase bridges an insulated joint as it crosses one, and while it does, the block it is leaving feeds the block it is entering through the locomotive itself; that is a property of the track, not of any voltage the app commanded. Energizing one block ahead is what bounds which block can be fed that way (see **Block power-controller role**, Only the next reserved block is pre-energized).
- **The rail binding bonds tile order to rail polarity.** A block's tile order and its rail polarity are independent facts: the order comes from how the layout was drawn, and which rail a channel drives comes from how the rig was wired. Nothing makes the two agree on their own, and a block driven by the wrong one runs its trains backwards.
- **The `reversed` flag is the bond.** It states which of the two bound channels drives the block in its `forward` direction, so a positive `track voltage` drives the binding's `forward` channel when the flag is clear and its `reverse` channel when the flag is set. Neither value is a fault — they are the two ways a block can be wired — and the **track direction sweep** under **Self-test** is the measurement that establishes which one this block is.
- **The bond is wiring, not layout.** It lives with the Hardware Setup like every other binding and persists independently of the layout, so an operator never needs a layout save for the bond to survive a restart.
- **The bond stays below the hardware interface.** The commanded voltage keeps its block-relative sign everywhere above, so **Occupancy source follows drive state** reads that same value and no layer above the driver carries a wiring branch. **Detector polarity is resolved in the hardware layer** states the same rule for the digital detector.
- **The `forward` and `reverse` channels themselves must not change.** They name two physical rails, and one of those rails may carry the block's idle detection feed; rebinding to flip a block would move that feed. A channel edit that does not name the flag keeps its stored value, so re-picking the rails never silently resets a bonded block.
- **The flag resolves per write.** It is one of the values a driver resolves per write, so correcting it reaches the next track write without rebuilding the session (see **A binding is read per write** below).
- **The flag covers the whole block.** A block is fed as one: the binding feeds every member segment, and a segment carries no polarity of its own. A block with no rail binding has no rails to bond.
- **The sweep resolves the flag the same way the driver does.** It drives the channel a positive `track voltage` would drive on that block first, which is the channel that must move a locomotive toward that block's higher tile indices. A block whose flag does not match its wiring runs the locomotive the wrong way on that first leg and names itself; the same block with the flag corrected runs it the right way, which is the operator's check that the bond is right.
- **A switch throw is a pulse on one of two coils.** A solenoid point motor has one coil per side, so a `switch_output` entry names two `hc595` output bits: `port_main` throws toward MAIN and `port_diverge` throws toward DIVERGE. A throw energizes one coil, waits the fixed throw pulse width, and de-energizes it, so both coils rest low between throws and the alignment is held by the points themselves rather than by a driven output. The pulse is short — a coil left energized burns out — and its width is one value in the driver, used unchanged by an operating session and by the commissioning throw test, so a bench test proves the same drive the runtime issues. `port_standby` is the optional bit wired to a motor driver's standby/enable pin, for drivers that ignore their inputs until it is high. A build whose driver needs no such pin leaves `port_standby` unset. Every shift-out bit the commissioning surface drives is driven this same way, because any bit may be wired to a coil.
- **The order of a throw's writes is part of the contract.** The two coil bits are the motor driver's two inputs, so a throw must write them in this order:
  1. raise `port_standby`
  2. drive the target coil high
  3. drive the *other* coil low
  4. wait the pulse width
  5. drop `port_standby`
  6. drop the target coil

  Two rules in that sequence keep the motor alive, and neither is optional.
  - **The other coil is always driven low, never assumed low.** This makes a throw correct from any prior bit pattern — including the one a shift-register chain powers up in — and it never drives both inputs at once.
  - **`port_standby` drops before the coil.** That write puts the driver's outputs into high impedance. When the coil input drops first, the driver stays enabled with both inputs low, which is its brake mode and shorts the coil. The final coil write then only settles the resting pattern, except on a driver with no standby bit, where it is the de-energize — which is why it is unconditional.

  The de-energizing writes must happen even when the throw fails part-way, so a failed throw leaves no coil driven.
- **Latch lines are named by pad.** A shift register latches on a line named by the CH347 board pad, and the line set depends on its bus: the SPI bus offers `cs0` and `cs1`; the GPIO bus offers `gpio0`–`gpio7`. The `ch347api` library names the SPI lines off by one — its `set_CS1` drives pad `cs0`, its `set_CS2` drives pad `cs1` — so the driver holds the pad-to-library map and the correct active polarity per chip kind. No layer above the driver names a pad or a library call.
- **A GPIO-latched chip borrows a chip-select pad.** The bridge clocks SPI data only while a chip-select is asserted, and it releases that select when the transfer ends. A shift register latched on a GPIO pin must therefore borrow one of the two pads for the length of its transfer. The driver borrows a pad that no `hc595` latches on, because releasing a `hc595`'s latch pad would clock stray bits into that chip and may throw a switch; an `hc165`'s load pad is safe to borrow, since a transfer only freezes and reloads its parallel inputs. A build in which every chip-select pad latches an `hc595` must not also carry a GPIO-latched chip.
- **Bindings.** The binding maps carry the logical-id-to-chip-port wiring, each keyed by logical id:
  - `block_track` (`block_id` to the two PWM channels driving its rails, `forward` and `reverse`, plus the `reversed` flag bonding those channels to the block's tile order — see **A block's track is two PWM channels** and **The rail binding bonds tile order to rail polarity** above)
  - `switch_output` (`switch_id` to its two coil ports plus an optional standby port, see **A switch throw is a pulse on one of two coils** below)
  - `block_occupancy` (`block_id` to a digital-detector port on an `hc165`, see **Detector polarity is resolved in the hardware layer** below)
  - `block_occupancy_current` (`block_id` to a current-sense channel on an `ina3221` or an `ina219`, plus `calibration_id`; `OccupancyInput` resolves `baseline_ma` and `threshold_ma` from `detector_calibration[calibration_id]`)
- **Every layout block must be bound in `block_track` and both occupancy maps.** Every layout block must appear exactly once in `block_track` and in both occupancy maps before Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware may activate.
- **`switch_track_source` wires a switch to its feed block.** One further required map, `switch_track_source`, wires every `switch_id` to the `block_id` whose feed powers that switch's rails; it is the one binding whose value is another logical id rather than a chip port, because a switch's rails have no channel of their own (see **Switch power-controller role** below). It must name the block at the switch's main entrance. `SwitchPowerController` is its only reader.
- **The rest of this binding table is read by the concrete driver alone, with one exception.** The rest of this binding table is the physical-channel map named under **Hardware interface boundary**, and the concrete driver is its only reader, except for `block_occupancy_current`, which Real Hardware's block-voltage readback (`TrackOutput.get_actual_voltage`, see **A refused write is fatal to a hardware-backed session, and never recorded as voltage**) also reads where that chip provides a bus-voltage measurement.
- **A binding must name a valid, uniquely-used chip port.** A binding must name a configured chip whose role matches the map — and, for the two occupancy maps, whose port kind matches (a digital detector bit for `block_occupancy`, a current-sense channel for `block_occupancy_current`) — at a port within that chip's range. A port must not be bound more than once, the two channels of one `block_track` entry must differ, and the two coil ports and the standby port of one `switch_output` entry must all differ.
- **An incomplete setup may be saved and commissioned, but not activated.** The editor may temporarily save any of these maps incomplete, and commissioning may exercise the entries that exist, but the readiness report keeps hardware-backed operation blocked until the complete cardinality and validity rules pass.
- **A binding is read per write.** A binding names a port; a session is built from chips. Those are different lifetimes, and v1 gives each its own: the chips, their transport, and the maps the chips are constructed and range-checked against are captured when Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware is activated, while the values below are looked up on every write, from the setup as it stands at that moment.
  - a switch's `port_main`, `port_diverge`, and `port_standby` (`switch_output`)
  - a block's `reversed` rail-polarity flag on its `block_track` binding
  - a switch's `switch_track_source` rail feed

  These three are the values a rig being wired gets wrong and corrects, and not one of them changes which chips a session builds — each only re-aims an existing chip, or names a block. An operator who re-picks a coil port must see the next throw land on the new bit: a correction that takes effect only after the environment is activated again reads as a control that does nothing, and the operator changes the wiring instead of the setting. Every other part of the setup — the controller, the chip list, a `block_track` binding's two channels, both occupancy maps and their calibration, and the shared drive-zone levels — is captured at activation, because changing it means building different chips. `GET /api/operation/environment` reports whether the saved setup holds captured changes the running session was not built with; the per-write values never raise that flag, because they are already in use.

- **Occupancy source follows drive state.** A block bound in both occupancy maps is read from whichever source is trustworthy this tick. The magnitude of the driver's last-commanded voltage for that block's track channel decides which one, because how hard software is driving the rails is what makes a detector believable; the sign is direction and has no bearing on it.
- **The last-commanded voltage is tracked below the hardware interface.** That last-commanded voltage is held one place below the hardware interface, written by whichever owner currently drives the channel — `BlockPowerController` during operation, a commissioning session while it holds the outputs (see **Commissioning owns the writes; the detectors stay shared**), or the safe-state zero (see **Power**, Safe state / fail-safe, which updates this same store) — so the zone rule always reads the value the rail actually carries regardless of which owner put it there.
- **Two configured levels split that range into three zones.** Both are one value for the whole Hardware Setup, so a rig sets them once: `idle_deadband_v`, at or below which nothing is driving the rails, and `current_sense_min_drive_v`, at or above which the drive is strong enough to put a readable load on a current channel.
  - **Idle** (at or below `idle_deadband_v`): no drive, so there is no current to sense and the block's `hc165` digital detector decides.
  - **Driven** (at or above `current_sense_min_drive_v`): the rail drive swamps the digital detector, but a motor under real drive draws a current the sense channel reads cleanly, so the current channel decides — current is present when `abs(current - baseline_ma)` reaches the channel's `threshold_ma`.
  - **Lighting** (between the two): a stopped-but-lit locomotive. The required current channel decides, the same as in the driven zone, and the digital detector is not read at all. A missing or unavailable current binding is an activation blocker or hardware I/O failure, never a digital fallback. Current present is returned as raw `true` to `BlockOccupancyDetector`, which still applies `OCCUPANCY_ON_THRESHOLD`; it does not confirm occupancy on one interface read. A raw clear must first be earned inside the hardware-backed `OccupancyInput`: that source must read clear on every one of `LIGHTING_CLEAR_HOLD_READS` consecutive reads while the interface continues to return its last reported value. Only after the hold releases does it return raw `false`, at which point `BlockOccupancyDetector` begins its separate `OCCUPANCY_OFF_THRESHOLD` debounce. `LIGHTING_CLEAR_HOLD_READS` lives in `constants.py` and is `30` in v1. Any current-present read resets the lighting hold, and so does leaving the zone.

  The digital detector is silent in this zone because it reads the drive rather than the train. Lighting voltage reaches the rails as a fraction of the full supply switched on and off — a duty cycle — so the detector's comparator sees the full supply for that fraction of every cycle, and asserts on roughly that fraction of reads whether or not a locomotive is there. The current channel tells the two cases apart across the same band by close to a factor of ten, so it is the one source with something to say.

  The clear window exists because a locomotive can still go quiet on the current channel: one drawing less than its channel's `threshold_ma` at standby reads the same as an empty block. Occupancy and drive are a loop — a block that reads clear is released, releasing it cuts its voltage, and cutting its voltage changes which zone it is in and therefore which detector answers. Holding the last reported value until the deciding source has read clear for a whole window keeps a release slow enough that a marginal locomotive cannot ride that loop around, and still gives the hold an exit.
- **`current_sense_min_drive_v` must sit above `lighting_voltage`.** `current_sense_min_drive_v` must sit above the profile's `lighting_voltage` (**SpeedProfile**), so a lit but motionless train lands in the middle zone rather than reading as driven. **Lighting-voltage calibration** is where that bound is kept for the one procedure that moves `lighting_voltage` in the ordinary case, because in Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware the calibration pass caps its accepted candidate at that ceiling (in Simulation the bound is not evaluated, per **What a candidate may be**); it does not by itself guard every other way a profile's `lighting_voltage` or the setup's `current_sense_min_drive_v` can change.
- **This constraint is enforced by the shared readiness evaluator.** This constraint is part of the layout-aware readiness report that `GET /api/operation/environment`, `GET /api/operation/readiness`, and `PUT /api/operation/environment` all return (see **Hardware setup**, the REST surface, and **Completeness is activation policy, not edit policy**): the shared readiness evaluator checks every placed train's resolved `lighting_voltage` against the setup's current `current_sense_min_drive_v`, the same way it checks a missing occupancy binding, when that value does not sit below it — whether that value came from calibration, an imported roster entry, an adoption-seeded default, or a placeholder profile from `add_train`. `POST /api/operation/activate` re-runs the same evaluator and refuses activation on the same blocker. The check is evaluated live at each of those calls; a `PUT /api/hardware/config` or profile edit made while already active takes effect on the next such check, not retroactively against the running session.
- **Both occupancy sources are mandatory.** Both sources are mandatory for every block in Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware. A missing binding blocks activation; a source that becomes unavailable after activation is a hardware I/O failure and enters the fail-closed hardware-failure lifecycle. Missing never counts as clear. This selection lives inside the hardware-backed `OccupancyInput`; the per-block `current present` boolean it returns is the same shape whichever zone answered, so **Block occupancy detection** consumes it without knowing the source.
- **Detector polarity is resolved in the hardware layer.** A shift-in chip carries an `active_low` flag describing how its detector drives the line: a comparator with no inverter stage pulls its output low when a train draws current, so that chain's raw bit reads 0 occupied and 1 clear, while a detector with an inverter reads the other way. Polarity is stated once per chip, because a detector chain is wired one way throughout: every block bound to that chip reads the same way, and a binding carries no polarity of its own. The real `OccupancyInput` applies the chip's polarity as it reads each bit. The boolean it returns must always mean `current present`, whichever way the detector is wired, so polarity is invisible above the interface — no code above it, and no other physical source, carries a polarity branch. Polarity applies to the digital detector only: a current-sense channel is judged on the magnitude `abs(current - baseline_ma)`, which has no polarity to resolve.
- **Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware share one setup.** Both environments build every required chip, binding, interface, occupancy rule, and safety-supervisor contract from the same Hardware Setup. Virtual Hardware supplies an in-memory transport and emulates whatever safety gate the setup maps; Real Hardware supplies the physical transport and external gate. The build is atomic and all-or-nothing. Missing roles, bindings, chips, or required safety facilities are activation blockers, never requests for simulated fallbacks.
- **Simulation is independent of Hardware Setup.** Simulation constructs its model interfaces without opening, validating, pruning, or changing Hardware Setup. A broken or incomplete setup therefore cannot prevent Simulation from running, and running Simulation cannot be mistaken for successfully activating a requested Real Hardware environment.
- **Self-test.** Self-test opens the selected device and probes each chip — an I²C chip must ACK, and a shift register's transaction must complete. The ports of every reachable chip form the pool the binding maps draw from.
- **Commissioning.** Commissioning is an explicit setup session, not an operating environment, and never a tool that borrows outputs from live operation. It may inspect an incomplete setup so the operator can build and bind the rig, but it cannot run trains or grant ordinary operation ownership. Entering it safely stops operation, drives the outputs to their safe state, and gives one bounded commissioning owner the outputs. It takes the outputs and not the device, so the detectors go on being read the whole time it is open (see **Commissioning owns the writes; the detectors stay shared** below).
- **Port-test.** A port-test drives one output port or reads one input port so a single wire can be confirmed before binding.
- **Track direction sweep.** It drives the block's two bound channels one way, off, then the other way, with a hard duration bound and safe-state cleanup. It resolves the block's `reversed` flag as the driver does (see **The rail binding bonds tile order to rail polarity** under **Power**).
- **Switch throw test.** It pulses one coil of a bound switch through the same write order and pulse width an operating throw uses, then records that alignment on the switch through `SwitchManager.record_bench_alignment(switch_id, position)`. That entry is the model-write-without-coil-drive path: it applies the `Switch.position` and runs the `BlockManager` block-reachability notify (`on_switch_position_changed`) but drives no coil, because the bench already pulsed it. It writes model state, and only that: it drives no train and grants no operation ownership. It exists because the operating throw `SwitchManager.request_position_change(...)` refuses while no operating environment is active (the operating-throw gate under **Canonical `Switch.position` mutation workflow**), and no environment is active during commissioning — the state every bench throw runs in — so recording the already-driven alignment cannot go through that entry, and would double-drive a coil the commissioning session has taken if it did. A bench throw is an operator alignment, so `record_bench_alignment` carries the same `manual` override an operator's own throw does.

  The app must record the new alignment because the points have moved, and the app must not go on describing the layout the way it was before the operator watched them move.
- **Block occupancy test.** It drives nothing. When both required bindings exist, it reports both sources, the drive zone, and the resulting verdict. Otherwise it reports the missing source as a readiness blocker rather than synthesizing a result.
- **Exit conditions.** Leaving, timing out, disconnecting, or failing commissioning completes the safe-state sequence before ordinary operation may reactivate.
- **Virtual Hardware** exercises the identical workflow against its fake device.
- **Commissioning owns the writes; the detectors stay shared.** A session opens one device handle and every owner reaches the rig through it. What a commissioning session takes is the exclusive right to **write**: while it holds the outputs it is the only ordinary writer of a track channel or a coil, and no other ordinary owner may drive one. It does not take the reads.
- **The detector pipeline keeps running throughout a commissioning session.** `OccupancyInput.read_block_currents()` is served for the whole commissioning session, so the global read, the debounce, the attribution, and the Observe commit keep running and `Block.occupied_by` stays live (see **Block occupancy detection**, The read does not stop for a commissioning session). This is what a bench is for: an operator opens one to find out why a block reads wrong, and the layout beside it must go on saying what the app currently believes, because that comparison is the diagnosis.
- **The operational loop moves no train during commissioning.** Entering commissioning stops operation, so the route/controller loop performs no movement calculation or propulsion output. A bounded commissioning output test may physically move a locomotive — the track-direction sweep does so deliberately — but that movement is not an operational train command or an extra physics pass. Detector observation and model occupancy commits continue throughout.
- **Ordinary reads and writes run on the runtime thread, with one exception.** The Real Hardware watchdog's safety-only de-energize/zero sequence is the sole thread exception, and it shares the same transport lock, so device transactions never collide.
- **A commissioning owner's writes select the same occupancy zone as operation.** The zone a block is read in follows the voltage commanded onto that block, whichever owner commanded it (see **Occupancy source follows drive state**): a commissioning owner writes the same last-commanded-voltage value that rule reads, so a rail a bench is driving is read in the `driven` zone and its current channel decides, exactly as it would under operation. Detector processing and model commits continue, but the stopped-pass de-energize drain issues no device write while commissioning owns outputs. It clears any queued block IDs as logically handled, because commissioning's mandatory exit safe-state sequence zeros every output before ownership can return; the de-energize stores remain same-tick queues and never become retained latches.
- **Exiting commissioning restores the safe state and returns the writes.** Leaving, timing out, disconnecting, or failing commissioning completes the safe-state sequence, which zeros all outputs before returning output ownership. The reads never stopped, so occupancy needs nothing reactivated to be visible again.
- **Persisted setup; separate selected environment.** A setup `PUT` writes the whole Hardware Setup to an app-managed JSON file. It may be incomplete while edited, but activation performs full layout-aware validation. Setup changes never rewire a running session in place. The selected environment is stored independently; requesting Simulation remains possible with a malformed setup, while requesting Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware yields a structured blocked state rather than falling back. Activation owns safe stop, rebuild, reconnect, and verification; the operator-facing workflow never requires a raw "restart server" step.
- **Saved with the layout.** Saving a layout writes its Hardware Setup into the layout file because bindings are keyed by that layout's `block_id` and `switch_id`. Loading the layout may adopt that setup after validation, but does not import or change the selected operating environment and never activates physical output. A loaded setup replaces the previous setup as a whole; absent sections become empty/default edit-state values and therefore remain explicit readiness blockers wherever required, dangling bindings are reported, and invalid setup is reported without preventing the geometry from loading.

**Hardware REST payload schemas**

- Unknown fields and unknown discriminator values are rejected. Every referenced layout entity and `chip_id` must exist, ports must be integers inside the selected chip's advertised range, numeric values must be finite, and one physical port may appear in only one binding of the same output/input role.
- `HardwareSetupRequest` carries exactly `controller`, `chips`, `detector_calibration`, `block_track`, `block_occupancy`, `block_occupancy_current`, `switch_output`, and `switch_track_source`:
  - `controller` is `{ "kind": "ch347", "device_port": Optional[str] }`.
  - each I²C chip is `{ "chip_id": str, "kind": "pca9685" | "ina3221" | "ina219", "bus": "i2c", "i2c_address": int }`;
  - each shift-output chip is `{ "chip_id": str, "kind": "hc595", "bus": "spi" | "gpio", "spi_select": int, "chain_length": int }`, with `chain_length >= 1`;
  - each shift-input chip is `{ "chip_id": str, "kind": "hc165", "bus": "spi" | "gpio", "spi_select": int, "chain_length": int, "active_low": bool }`, with `chain_length >= 1`; `active_low` is stored only on this chip variant and applies to every digital detector bit in its chain;
  - `detector_calibration` maps detector calibration id to `{ "baseline_ma": float, "threshold_ma": float }`, with both values nonnegative and `threshold_ma > baseline_ma`;
  - `block_track` maps `block_id` to `{ "chip_id": str, "forward_port": int, "reverse_port": int, "reversed": bool }`; both ports address PWM channels on that chip, both are in range, and they must differ;
  - `block_occupancy` maps `block_id` to `{ "chip_id": str, "port": int }`; the referenced `hc165` chip supplies polarity;
  - `block_occupancy_current` maps `block_id` to `{ "chip_id": str, "port": int, "calibration_id": str }`;
  - `switch_output` maps `switch_id` to `{ "chip_id": str, "port_main": int, "port_diverge": int, "port_standby": Optional[int] }`; `port_main` and `port_diverge` must differ, and a populated `port_standby` must differ from both. The operating throw and commissioning throw both use the driver-wide fixed pulse width defined by the switch-output driver; no binding carries a second pulse duration;
  - `switch_track_source` maps `switch_id` to a `block_id` string. Unlike the other binding maps its value is a logical id, not a chip port, so it carries no `reversed`: a switch has no rails of its own, and its rail polarity is whatever the feed block's own `block_track` binding already sets.
- Commissioning bodies all carry `session_id: str` after enter. `enter` carries `{ "timeout_seconds": float }` with `0 < timeout_seconds <= COMMISSION_MAX_SESSION_SECONDS`. `output` is either `{ "session_id": str, "kind": "block_track", "block_id": str, "voltage_v": float }` or `{ "session_id": str, "kind": "switch_output", "switch_id": str, "position": SwitchPosition }`. `pulse` carries `{ "session_id": str, "switch_id": str, "position": SwitchPosition }` and uses the same driver-wide fixed pulse width as an operating throw, which must be no greater than `COMMISSION_MAX_PULSE_MS`. `inputs`, `currents`, and `exit` each carry only `{ "session_id": str }`. Every commissioning response has `{ "success": bool, "session_id": Optional[str], "reason": Optional[str], "data": object }`; `data` is empty except that `inputs` returns `{ "digital": {binding_id: bool} }` and `currents` returns `{ "milliamps": {binding_id: float} }`.
- The raw virtual-hardware input bodies address a block, not a chip port. `PUT /api/virtual-hardware/input/occupancy` takes `{ "block_id": str, "occupied": bool }` — the endpoint resolves the block's `block_occupancy` binding to the chip and latch line. `PUT /api/virtual-hardware/input/current` takes `{ "block_id": str, "current_ma": float }` (nonnegative), resolved through the block's `block_occupancy_current` binding.
- `VirtualHardwareFaultRequest` is `{ "action": "inject" | "clear", "target_kind": "controller" | "chip" | "port" | "transaction" | "readback", "target_id": str, "operation": Optional[str], "fault": Optional[VirtualHardwareFaultKind] }`, where `VirtualHardwareFaultKind` is exactly the canonical set under **Fault injection belongs to Virtual Hardware**: `transaction_refusal`, `timeout`, `device_disconnect`, `invalid_reading`, `input_hold_or_flicker`, or `output_disagrees_with_command`. `fault` is required for `inject` and must be `None` for `clear`; an incompatible target/fault pair is rejected rather than translated to another name.
- `VirtualHardwareScenarioRequest` is one of `{ "action": "place", "train_id": str, "block_id": str, "direction": "forward" | "reverse" }`, `{ "action": "move", "train_id": str, "to_block_id": str }`, `{ "action": "stop", "train_id": str }`, or `{ "action": "remove", "train_id": str }`. These actions change fake detector/current inputs only; they do not mutate operational train/controller state.

- **REST surface.**

| Endpoint | Body | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/hardware/config` | — | Returns the saved Hardware Setup: `controller`, `chips` (including stored bus plus derived role/direction/port metadata), detector calibration, and binding maps, plus a session summary saying which environment is running, whether it is active, and whether the saved setup holds changes the running session was not built with. The layout-aware readiness report itself is served by `GET /api/operation/environment` and `GET /api/operation/readiness`, not here. It contains no selected-environment flag beyond that session summary. |
| `PUT /api/hardware/config` | `HardwareSetupRequest` | Validates the fields and bindings that exist and writes the whole setup, returning the stored config. Incompleteness is allowed while editing or commissioning — it is surfaced by the readiness report (`GET /api/operation/environment` / `GET /api/operation/readiness`) — but it blocks Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware activation; only Simulation may operate until every required binding and device passes readiness. Malformed fields, incompatible chips, out-of-range or duplicate ports, and dangling references are rejected. The running session keeps the chips and maps it was built with until explicit activation; the values named in **A binding is read per write** reach the rig on the next write. |
| `GET /api/operation/environment` | — | Returns `requested_environment` and `active_environment`, each one of `"simulation" \| "virtual_hardware" \| "real_hardware"` (the same union `PUT /api/operation/environment`'s body carries), lifecycle state (`inactive`, `activating`, `active`, `blocked`, `hardware_failure`, or `commissioning`, where `commissioning` means a commissioning session holds the outputs while the detectors are still read — see **Commissioning owns the writes; the detectors stay shared**), readiness blockers, device health, and whether the saved setup holds changes the running session was not built with (the captured parts only — see **A binding is read per write**). This is the single session truth the header and diagnostics read. |
| `PUT /api/operation/environment` | `{ "environment": "simulation" \| "virtual_hardware" \| "real_hardware" }` | Selects the requested environment but does not silently rewire a running session. Simulation needs no setup. Virtual/Real selection returns the readiness blockers that would prevent activation. |
| `POST /api/operation/activate` | — | Safely stops the current session, validates the requested environment, builds all interfaces atomically, reconnects, and verifies the active environment. On success it increments `environment_activation_generation`; it deliberately does not clear a pre-existing `hardware_failure`. A Virtual/Real failure returns the structured blocked state and never activates Simulation as a fallback. |
| `POST /api/runtime/clear-hardware-failure` | — | Calls `SimulationController.clear_hardware_failure()`. It succeeds only for an active Virtual/Real environment whose successful activation generation is newer than the generation captured when the latch was set. It clears only `hardware_failure` and leaves the session stopped. |
| `POST /api/runtime/clear-fatal` | — | Calls `SimulationController.clear_failed_runtime()`. Refused when the runtime is not halted (`failed_runtime` unset). On success it runs the step-`7c41` (Clearing the halt) cleanup and leaves the session stopped; it does not clear `hardware_failure`. |
| `POST /api/simulation/control` | `{ "action": "start" \| "stop" }` | Writes `AppState.simulation_running` for ordinary start/stop, the sole ordinary writer per **Running and stopped**. Refused while `failed_runtime` is set, in every environment. Refused while `hardware_failure` is set only when the active environment is Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware; a latched `hardware_failure` does not block starting an active Simulation environment, per **Simulation is independent of Hardware Setup**. Clearing the applicable halt through its own endpoint is required first wherever the refusal applies. |
| `GET /api/hardware/catalog` | — | Returns the selectable controllers and chip kinds — the buses each kind allows, role, direction, port count, and required parameters — that the setup UI reads. |
| `POST /api/hardware/scan` | `{ "config": {…} }` | Opens the controller and reports which I²C addresses answer right now — per-chip reachability for the I²C chips (the Hardware Setup Detect / Rescan button). It does not probe shift-register (`hc595` / `hc165`) transactions; those chips and individual output ports are exercised interactively through the port-test, track-test, switch-test, and occupancy-test endpoints and commissioning. It runs only while operation does not own physical outputs. |
| `POST /api/hardware/commission/{enter,output,pulse,inputs,currents,exit}` | The closed commissioning body for that action under **Hardware REST payload schemas** | `enter` safely stops operation and transfers exclusive **output** ownership to a bounded commissioning session; the occupancy read is shared and keeps running throughout (see **Commissioning owns the writes; the detectors stay shared**). The actions exercise ports through the same output interfaces and drivers, with the same duration limits, as operation. `exit`, timeout, disconnect, or failure completes the safe state before releasing ownership. These endpoints change no setup. |
| `GET /api/virtual-hardware` | — | Virtual Hardware only. Returns fake-device connection state, raw inputs, measured/current values, output commands/readback, injected faults, and active high-level scenario. Each block reports which outputs and detectors it is bound to, the raw detector bit alongside that bit resolved through the chain's polarity, and the commanded duty on both of its rails alongside the signed voltage those duties mean once the binding's `reversed` flag is applied. |
| `PUT /api/virtual-hardware/input/occupancy` (`{ "block_id": …, "occupied": bool }`) and `PUT /api/virtual-hardware/input/current` (`{ "block_id": …, "current_ma": float }`) | see left | Change fake device input state only, one raw source at a time; the ordinary occupancy pipeline observes it on its next read. `/input/occupancy` sets the block's digital detector bit at the raw level — a digital write sets the register bit itself, so on an `active_low` chain the bit that means `current present` is 0 (see **Detector polarity is resolved in the hardware layer** above). `/input/current` sets the block's fake current-sense reading in mA. Writing one source leaves the block's other source saying whatever it said before, which is how a deliberate disagreement between the two is set up. |
| `PUT /api/virtual-hardware/input/presence` | `{ "block_id": …, "present": true \| false }` | Puts a virtual object on one block's detectors, or lifts it off. It writes every occupancy source the block is bound to in one call — the digital bit resolved through the chain's polarity, and a current clear of that channel's `threshold_ma` above its `baseline_ma` — so the block reads the same way whichever source **Occupancy source follows drive state** selects. A block bound to no occupancy source is rejected. |
| `PUT /api/virtual-hardware/fault` | `VirtualHardwareFaultRequest` | Injects or clears a fake controller, chip, port, response, or readback failure below the real HAL implementation. |
| `POST /api/virtual-hardware/scenario` | `VirtualHardwareScenarioRequest` | Converts a topology-aware virtual train action into raw fake detector/current transitions, one block at a time through the same write `PUT /api/virtual-hardware/input/presence` performs. A step across a block boundary confirms the entered block's detectors and clears the left block's in the same call. It never writes `Block.occupied_by`, controller span, or another operational state directly. |

**Block occupancy detection**

- Each block has its own current detector and is its own occupancy section; its member segments are geometry only and are not independently detected (see **Block**, Detection isolation is separate from geometry). Current present on a block means a train is standing on it; no current means no train is. This detection is the authority for `Block.occupied_by`: it replaces any guess from the calculated train position. Switch occupancy is not detected this way. Switch-alignment authority stays the commanded `Switch.position` (see **Out of Scope**), and a switch's physical entry and exit still come from the train's calculated traversal.
- **One global read per tick.** At the top of each tick the runtime reads every block's detector at once through `OccupancyInput.read_block_currents()`, which returns a plain `block_id -> current present` map with no train identity. In Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware, which physical source produces that boolean — an `hc165` digital detector or a current-sense channel selected by drive state — is defined in **Hardware setup**. In Simulation, `SimulatedOccupancyDriver` derives the same-shaped map from live train spans. The read reflects where trains were at the end of the previous tick, so a block the locomotive just entered is confirmed no earlier than the next tick, and in practice after the `OCCUPANCY_ON_THRESHOLD` debounce reads on top of that (see **Debounce with on/off thresholds**); that lag is the honest sensor latency.
- **The read does not stop for a commissioning session.** A commissioning owner takes the outputs, not the detectors, so this whole pipeline — the global read, the debounce, the attribution, and the Observe commit — keeps running while one is open (see **Hardware setup**, Commissioning owns the writes; the detectors stay shared). What stops is train motion, because entering commissioning stops operation first. A block a locomotive stands on therefore reads OCCUPIED throughout, and the only thing that changed is who may drive the rails.
- **Debounce with on/off thresholds.** Real contacts flicker: a block a train is standing on can briefly read open. `BlockOccupancyDetector` keeps a per-block counter and confirms a block OCCUPIED only after `OCCUPANCY_ON_THRESHOLD` consecutive current reads, and CLEAR only after `OCCUPANCY_OFF_THRESHOLD` consecutive no-current reads. The bias is fail-safe: occupy quickly, clear slowly, so a momentary open circuit inside the train's span does not drop the block. Both thresholds live in `constants.py`. Debounce is the first half of that bias and rides out a dropout shorter than the off-window; the gate on committing a clear is the second half and covers a dropout that outlasts it (see **A clear read from under the train is a detection fault**). Each tick the detector compares the whole confirmed-occupied set against the previous one, so a fast train that enters or clears several blocks in one tick is reported in one pass.
- **Placement is seeded, not re-detected.** `RailwayNetwork.place_train(...)` sets `Block.occupied_by` directly when a train is initially put on the track. This initial placement is the one sanctioned exception to the "runtime entry writes `occupied_by` only through `BlockManager.occupy_blocks(...)`" rule, because it runs before the first tick (the same way `SimulationController.add_train(...)` seeds `current_span` before the first tick). At the top of each tick the detector seeds every already-occupied block as already confirmed, so a block a train was placed on is not reported as a fresh entry. Such a block still clears normally once its current drops for the off-window. Runtime-state save/load is out of scope.
- **Placement seeds switch occupancy too.** A placed span may cover a switch tile (see **SwitchManager**, The body must not reach a block reading no current — a switch tile has no detector to read clear, and a body may cover it). For every switch tile the seeded span covers, `RailwayNetwork.place_train(...)` also seeds a `Switch.physical_occupants[route] = train_id` entry, deriving `route` from the span's own traversal through that tile (the same `frozenset({entry_edge, exit_edge})` shape `SwitchManager.on_physical_entry(...)` records — see **Switch entity**, Occupancy). This is the switch-side counterpart of the `Block.occupied_by` seed on the same line, and it runs before the first tick the same way. It is the only sanctioned exception to "`Switch.physical_occupants` is written only through `SwitchManager.on_physical_entry(...)`". A switch seeded this way carries no `Switch.locks` entry, because seeded already-covered switches are never newly locked (see **SwitchManager**, Intrusion check); the switch-integrity guarantee for a seeded train rests on the seeded `physical_occupants` entry alone, the same as for a train that entered the switch normally and consumed its main lock. Such a switch clears the ordinary way: `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(...)` removes the entry once the train's tail vacates the tile.
- **Attribution.** The raw read carries no train identity, so each confirmed change is matched to a train from the live authority model.
  - **Match order for a newly OCCUPIED block.** Try in order:
    1. the train the block is reserved for (`Block.reserved_for_train`, the reserved-ahead corridor) — and only when that train is standing next to the block;
    2. the train whose live span currently covers it;
    3. an ordinary train holding a block reachable from it through undetected track.

    Standing next to means the same reachability walk in all three steps, so a train never gains a block with another block between it and everything it holds.
  - **A train is not entering a block it is being driven away from.** Standing next to a block says the two are near each other and nothing about which way either is going, so every one of those matches also asks whether the train could be entering that block at all. `TrainPhysics.could_be_entering(block_id)` is the canonical home of this test.
    - A moving train could only have entered a block in front of it, so current appearing on the side it is driving away from is not that train arriving but something else on the track behind it. In front means the same forward walk the span correction uses, which follows the points as aligned and stops at the first `detected block` the detector has not confirmed (see **Physical detection outranks the calculated position**).
    - The test reads only which way the train is being driven, never how far it got: a `SpeedProfile` describes the locomotive it was calibrated for, and a train reaching a block early is the case this exists for, so a distance would be the one number it could not trust.
    - A train that is not moving is not being driven away from anything, and every block next to it stays plausible: the model never knows where inside a block a train sits, so a stationary locomotive may be bridging an insulated joint the model shows it well clear of, drawing current on the block either side of it.
  - **A reservation on its own is not evidence of where a locomotive is.** A train reserves the corridor in front of it before it gets there, so current on a reserved block with a clear `detected block` still between it and the train must not be read as that train: matching it would mean the train skipped the block in between, which is track no detector confirmed. Such current is a different object, and the block the train can no longer reach is taken out of its authority (see **Path And PathDispatcher**, Authority truncation).
  - **Matching runs until it stops resolving blocks**, rather than in one pass: a train fast enough to cross several blocks between two reads has them all confirmed in the same comparison, and each block a train gains in this pass is evidence for the next one, so the second block across is matched to the train that just gained the first.
  - **The third step keeps one locomotive one record.** A locomotive standing across a block boundary draws current on both blocks, and the far one matches no reservation and no span — but it is this train spanning two blocks, not a second object. Reachability is the same connectivity walk unidentified-train identity uses, so only the first block across undetected track counts: current with a block between it and every train is a different object.
  - **A newly CLEAR block** is matched to its current holder (`Block.occupied_by`). The clear is vacated for that train only when the holder's calculated tail has reached the block's exit seam; otherwise the block is held (see **A clear read from under the train is a detection fault**).
  - **A confirmed entry that none of those three steps matches** is attributed to an **unidentified train**: a `Train` Observe's layout-wide detector snapshot creates for it, with its own `train_id` and its own `TrainController` (see **Unidentified trains**). From that point it is an ordinary train to every other rule in this document.
    - Observe writes its `physics_sync.pending_detected_entered_blocks` / `pending_detected_vacated_blocks` exactly as it does for any other train, its final Observe callback folds them into a progress report, and Observe commits its entries and vacates through the same coordinator/manager path — so no occupant needs a side channel into `Block.occupied_by`.
    - A different train that physically enters a block an unidentified train holds is the ordinary `occupied_by_other_train` fatal conflict; claiming what it is standing on is adoption's job, not a second train's (see **Unidentified trains**, Adoption).
    - Under Simulation no unidentified train ever appears: its current map is built from live train spans, so every confirmed-occupied block already matches a train the app controls. An unidentified train may appear in Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware when the hardware-backed input reports current on a block no controllable train covers.
- **The confirmed change flows through the normal Observe path.** Observe writes the affected train's `physics_sync.pending_detected_entered_blocks` / `pending_detected_vacated_blocks` and never writes `Block.occupied_by` itself, for every train without exception. The train's final Observe callback folds those sets into its progress report and clears them; Observe commits block entry/vacate through the ordinary coordinator/manager path. Unidentified trains take this same path, which is why a detected occupant the app does not control is modelled as a train rather than as a second kind of occupant. `physics_sync.pending_block_exit_edges` remains the separate direction buffer, holding an entry across ticks when detector clear lags calculated tail exit and holding one within a single tick for an unidentified train.
- **Physical detection outranks the calculated position.** When confirmed occupancy leads the calculated span, Observe calls `TrainPhysics.reconcile_to_detected_occupancy(train, controller)` directly for that train; the method itself computes a forward-only corrected span and writes it onto `physics_sync.current_span`, before route ordering/Plan. The correction reads that train's confirmed-entered blocks alone.
- **Correction and integration compose sequentially.** The next tick's top-of-Observe integration runs from that corrected span and its `span_update.new_span` replaces it with the ordinary movement result, so correction and integration compose sequentially rather than competing at one apply site.
- **The correction stops at the first unconfirmed `detected block`.** The correction chases only the confirmed blocks the head can reach by moving forward, and it stops at the first `detected block` the detector has not confirmed occupied — the same line the cap holds the head at (see **The calculated span never runs ahead of the detector**). A block on the far side of one is not somewhere this train can be, because reaching it means having crossed track whose detector says it is clear, so the correction never carries a span over a boundary the cap would not let the train cross under power.
- **A confirmed block behind the span is held, not reconciled.** A confirmed block behind the span — the locomotive is further back than the calculated position put it, and attribution has just given that block to this train — cannot be reconciled by a forward-only walk, so the span does not move for it and the block is simply held.
- **A confirmed clear never moves the span.** When the detector confirms a block clear for a train, then `TrainPhysics.reconcile_to_detected_occupancy(...)` leaves that train's span where it is. A span is rigid, so moving its tail forward means driving its head forward, and a block reading clear reports only where a train is not — it carries no statement about where the head is, and a span moved by one would claim head positions no detector reported. What the clear does instead is release the tail cap on that block, so the next tick's top-of-Observe integration carries the tail past the seam (the clear is confirmed during this tick's attribution, after this tick's integration has already run, so the tail advances on the following pass) (see **The calculated span never runs ahead of the detector**).
- **A clear read from under the train is a detection fault.** When the detector confirms a `detected block` clear while the holding train's calculated tail has not yet reached that block's exit seam, then the block is not vacated: `Block.occupied_by` stays with that train, the block keeps its `track voltage`, and the span does not move. This covers every block the train still stands on, whether the tail is short of the seam of the rearmost block it holds or the block sits under the head or the middle of the span. A train standing on a block is the one thing that block's detector cannot see past, so a clear read from under it is the detector losing the train rather than the train leaving.
- **The fault is reported once per block.** `SimulationController` emits one event on the read where a block first reads clear under its holding train, with `kind = "warning"`, an `ErrorRecord` naming the lost detection, and the block and train ids on the payload. It emits nothing further for that block while the fault holds, and reports it again only after the block has read current again in between. A fault that re-emitted every read would bury the stream for as long as one detector stayed quiet.
- **A held clear is re-offered until the tail reaches the seam.** Release follows the confirmed-clear state, not the single read on which the block first went clear. On every later read, a `detected block` the detector still confirms clear, that a train still holds through `Block.occupied_by`, and whose exit seam that train's calculated tail has now reached, is vacated for that train. A clear the tail had not yet earned is therefore never lost: it commits on the first read after the tail arrives.
- **The two sources settle the disagreement themselves.** When a clear is held, then one of exactly two things ends it: the block reads current again, or the train's own integration carries its tail to the seam. Neither outcome needs an operator, because the same read that raised the fault also released the tail cap on that block, so a moving train closes the gap under its own power. A train that is standing still holds the block for as long as it stands there, which is the true answer for a stopped locomotive. When no block in a train's evidence set reads confirmed occupied, that train is ghosted instead (see **Ghosted trains**).
- **An unidentified train's clears commit at once.** Weighing a clear against a second source needs integrated motion, and an unidentified train integrates none, so it has no second source. Its span is exactly the blocks it holds (see **Unidentified trains**, Span), so a clear leaves its span and its `Block.occupied_by` on the same read.
- **Span-writer roles.** `TrainPhysics.reconcile_to_detected_occupancy(...)` is the Observe correction span writer; `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)` is the ordinary top-of-tick Observe span writer for continuing integration (both run in the Observe batch, the correction after the integration).
- **Forward-only protects integrated motion from being snapped backwards.** A train that integrates no motion of its own has none to protect, so for an unidentified train the corrected span is simply its confirmed-occupied blocks (see **Unidentified trains**).
- **The calculated span never runs ahead of the detector.** The rule above pulls a span forward to where the detector says the train already is. This one is its mirror: it holds a span back from where the detector has not yet said the train is. A train's calculated span must not claim a `detected block` the detector has not confirmed occupied, and must not release a `detected block` the detector still confirms. `TrainPhysics.tick(...)` enforces both by capping the distance it moves the train that tick: the head stops at the entry seam of the next `detected block` and waits there until that block confirms occupied; the tail stops at the exit seam of the rearmost `detected block` the span holds and waits there until that block confirms clear.
- **A held head always ends up inside a block.** Switch tiles belong to no block and carry no detection, so a run of them between two blocks is track nothing can vouch for. When the next `detected block` lies beyond such a run, the head is held at the exit seam of the block it is in rather than at that block's edge. A head that is already outside every block is left free to run to the next block boundary, where the hold applies again, rather than pinned where nothing can release it.

  Holding the head on undetected track would claim a position no detector supports, and a head in no block has no current block to resolve, so `PathDispatcher.create_path` could no longer plan for the train.
- **The tighter cap wins.** A span is rigid, so the tighter of the two caps decides the whole tick, and a cap never moves a span backwards — it only shortens the step, down to standing still.
- **A confirmed entry is an exact position fix.** A confirmed entry puts the head on that block's entry seam. It is the only detector reading that moves a span; a confirmed clear moves nothing (see **A confirmed clear never moves the span**). Between two entries, the position inside the block is integrated from the speed solution and is an estimate, because the speed solution describes the locomotive the profile was calibrated for rather than the one on the track.

  The cap is what bounds that estimate: the model may be wrong about where a train sits inside a block, and never about which blocks it is on.
- **Environment differences.** In Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware, every layout block is in `detected_block_ids()`; losing a detector after activation is fatal rather than a reason to bypass its cap. Under Simulation the set is empty, so no train is detector-capped and this rule is inert. An unidentified train integrates no motion of its own, so it has nothing to cap (see **Unidentified trains**).
- **The pending-entry block stays live.** The block a capped head is waiting on is that train's `pending-entry block`, and it carries `track voltage` for as long as the cap holds, because the train has to be driven onto the very block whose detector releases the cap (see **Block power-controller role**). Only the detector releases a cap.
- **A large correction is reported.** A correction is the app agreeing the train is further along than it thought, and at one block it is routine and silent: the cap parks the head on the entry seam of the block it is entering, so every ordinary block entry gains exactly that one block once its detector confirms it. That is sensor latency, and reporting it would bury the stream. A correction that gains `OVERRUN_REPORT_MIN_BLOCKS` or more blocks is different.
