The detector found the train a whole block past where the model had it, which latency does not explain: the locomotive is running faster than its `SpeedProfile` says, so every estimate built on that profile — arrival time, braking distance, where the train sits inside its current block — is wrong in the same direction, and it will be wrong again on the next block. `TrainPhysics` emits one event for such a correction, with `kind = "warning"`, an `ErrorRecord` naming the overrun, and the blocks gained and the distance made up on the payload. The correction itself is unchanged; what this adds is that the app stops making the same correction silently forever. `OVERRUN_REPORT_MIN_BLOCKS` lives in `constants.py`.
- **A held confirmed block behind the span pins the train.** A train can hold a confirmed block its span does not cover and its head cannot reach by going forward: the locomotive is standing behind the calculated position. A moving train is never handed one, because a block behind it is a block it is being driven away from (see **Attribution**). One arrives the other ways a train comes to hold a block — initial placement, adoption, or a block credited to it while it stood still, which its own cab change then puts behind it by reversing which way forward runs. The forward-only correction rule does not move the span for such a block, but the tail rule still applies to it: the span must not run away from a block whose detector says this train is standing there. While the train holds such a block, `TrainPhysics.tick(...)` caps the step to zero, so the whole span stands still with its tail against the detected locomotive. The pin releases through the ordinary vacate path — the locomotive leaves, the block's current stops, the confirmed clear releases `Block.occupied_by` — and the cap lifts on the next tick. The tail is already past the exit seam of a block behind the span, so such a clear is never held.
- **Not a latch.** Debounce is a filter; the detector slice is a named within-tick handoff with a final-callback clear point; the span correction is immediate; the distance cap is recomputed from the confirmed set every tick and retains nothing. A held clear retains nothing either: the set of blocks reading clear under their holding train is recomputed from the confirmed set and the live spans on every read, and the once-per-block report is the difference between that set and the previous read's, the same shape as the confirmed-set comparison itself. None waits across ticks on a gating predicate, so none belongs in the Latch Table.
- **Two views of occupancy.** The calculated span's `occupied_blocks` is where the model puts the train. `Block.occupied_by` is what the detector confirms, held until the tail has earned the seam. Over `detected block`s the two agree at the end of every tick, because the rules above make it so: the span adds only a block the detector has confirmed and refuses to add or drop a block it has not, and `Block.occupied_by` refuses to drop a block the train's tail has not yet cleared. The one thing `Block.occupied_by` may hold that the span does not is a confirmed block behind the span (see **A held confirmed block behind the span pins the train**), and the pin keeps the span parked against it until it clears. What the span carries on top of that set is where inside those blocks the train sits, which is an estimate between confirmed changes. Every layout block is detected in Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware; in Simulation the detector set is empty and the model span is the sole occupancy source. Block track voltage tracks the calculated span in addition to the confirmed set, so the rail under the train is never dead while a block is still clearing (see **Block power-controller role**).
- **Ghosted trains.** A train's evidence set is its span's `occupied_blocks` plus the blocks it holds through `Block.occupied_by`, intersected with `detected_block_ids()`. When that set is non-empty and none of it is confirmed occupied, no physical reading backs the calculated position — for example, the locomotive may have been lifted off the rails — so the span represents nothing detected. Such a train is **ghosted**: an identity the app still holds with no current behind it, the mirror image of an **unidentified train** (see **Unidentified trains**).
- **`presence_unknown` is recomputed each Observe pass, not latched.** Observe computes this pass's verdict, overwrites the stored `presence_unknown`, and publishes it on the controller payload; because Observe overwrites it every pass it is never latched, so detection returning anywhere in the evidence set clears it on the next pass. Observe detects the rising edge by comparing the fresh verdict with the stored value before overwriting — the stored `presence_unknown` is its own edge memory, and there is no separate previous-value field.
- **The rising edge triggers the ordinary power-off teardown.** On the rising edge Observe calls `controller.route_hooks.phase_latches.set_power_off(reason, has_active_path=...)` through `TrainController._apply_power_off_request(...)` — the same general teardown an operator-issued power-off uses (see the **Power-off procedure**) — so the inclusive `pending_path_cancel_request` and `pending_power_off` latches drive the same teardown every other power-off does: future block reservations and switch locks release, the `RouteRun` is removed, and `TrainController.complete_power_off()` performs only its canonical general OFF cleanup. The ghost-only work stays outside that general helper.
- **The rising edge also releases the train's block occupancy.** On the same rising edge Observe calls `BlockManager.release_train_occupancy(train_id)`, clearing every block the train holds through `Block.occupied_by` and synchronously reevaluating caution because no detector observation will ever arrive to vacate those holdings; that occupancy release exercises `BlockManager`'s own occupancy-release writer into its `_blocks_pending_deenergize` store (see **Power**, De-energize against the same source) for the just-cleared holdings.
- **The rising edge excludes the train from the energized set.** Observe also excludes the train from the energized set, so this train's emission set reads empty for the rest of the tick; the ordinary per-tick `TrainPhysics` emission-set difference then queues the rest of the train's prior emission set — including its retained span — into the same de-energize drain, with no separate Observe write.
- **An operator-issued power-off does not perform these ghost-specific steps.** An operator-issued power-off performs none of these ghost-specific steps and leaves `occupied_by` untouched.
- **The rising edge retains switch-side protection.** This rising edge does not release any `Switch.physical_occupants` entry or `train_protection_claims` the train holds: the locomotive may still be bodily on the points even though its evidence set reads unconfirmed, so those switch-side records are deliberately retained rather than cleared alongside the block occupancy above. They clear through the ordinary tail-vacate release (`SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(...)`, see **SwitchManager**) once detection returns and the train moves off the switch under ordinary operation; a ghost frozen mid-switch keeps its physical protection until then.
- **Teardown commits under the ordinary rolling-train gate.** While teardown is in flight, the per-train loop runs the ghosted train's ordinary transaction, exactly as for any other train with a pending cancel, so the latch commits under the same `is_stopped()` gating every cancellation uses.
- **The ghost-only freeze runs once the controller reads `OFF`.** Once that teardown has committed and the controller reads `OFF`, `SimulationController._freeze_lost_train_controller(train_id)` performs the ghost-only freeze: it clears queued operator commands and movement-derived controller progress reports, forces the retained speed to `0`, and suppresses Plan, command drain, control, and movement calculation while `presence_unknown` remains true. It does not suppress the layout-wide detector snapshot, attribution, occupancy reconciliation, or detector-derived progress delivery: those Observe steps run for every train regardless of controller state, and they are what notice detection returning. It does not clear route/resource state or call `TrainController.complete_power_off()` again. The last span stays as the retained position used for attribution and the question-mark display, never as a prediction the app advances.
- **Detection returning admits the train back to ordinary operation.** Detection returning clears the flag on the next Observe read; once the controller is `OFF`, that admits `power_on_cmd()` through the ordinary Action drain for an `OFF` train (per **Per-train tick transaction**) and ordinary operation resumes from the retained position.
- **UI marker.** The UI marks a ghosted train with a question mark for as long as `presence_unknown` reads true.
- **Nothing removes a ghosted train.** The absence of current does not prove the locomotive was physically removed, and train removal is out of scope for v1 (see **Out of Scope**).
- **Environment differences.** In Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware the evidence set covers every block in the span; in Simulation it is empty because `detected_block_ids()` is empty, so the flag stays off.
- **An unidentified train is never ghosted.** It has no identity to outlive its occupancy, so one that loses its blocks is retired instead (see **Unidentified trains**, The gap).

**Unidentified trains**

- An **unidentified train** is a `Train` the runtime creates for current it detects on track that no train the app controls is standing on — a locomotive placed on the rails by hand, a car left behind, a train from before the app started. The app cannot drive it as it stands: driving a train needs a cab, a speed profile, and a route, and this one was never set up with any of them. So the app keeps track of it, which is what keeps every other train clear of it, and it offers the operator the one thing that fixes the situation — saying what the detector found, which turns it into an ordinary train (**Adoption**). It is the mirror image of a **ghosted** train: current on the rails with no identity behind it, rather than an identity with no current behind it (see **Ghosted trains**).
- **Creation and identity.** Observe creates one when it confirms a block OCCUPIED that attribution matches to no existing train — either because it is not reachable from any train's blocks through undetected track, or because the one train it is next to is being driven away from it (see **Block occupancy detection**, Attribution). Adjacency is decided first because an unidentified train is never energized: handing a train's own block to one would drive that block to `0` under the locomotive the app is driving. It gets a fresh `train_id` from the runtime, its own `TrainController`, `is_unidentified = True`, and blank persistent train data with the default `SpeedProfile` described in **SpeedProfile**. Identity follows connectivity: one unidentified train per connected group of blocks held by unidentified trains. When two such groups grow together they are one train, and it keeps the older `train_id`; when one group splits in two, the older `train_id` stays with the part holding the block it held longest and the other part becomes a new unidentified train. `SimulationController` keeps a runtime-only **retired-id set**, which is the canonical home of the never-reuse rule: every `train_id` an unidentified train is retired with (**The gap**) or adopted away from (**Adoption**) goes into it, and no later unidentified train is given one. The set is not saved, so a restart starts it empty (**Runtime only**).
- **Span.** Its span is exactly the blocks it holds. Its length, and where inside those blocks it actually sits, are unknown, so its `current_span` end locators sit at the outer boundaries of its end blocks and `occupied_tiles` lists every tile of every block it holds. This claims the most track the detector allows, which is the safe reading for a train nobody is driving.
- **Movement.** `TrainPhysics.tick(...)` integrates nothing for it: it is never powered, so its speed is `0` and it produces no movement of its own. Detection is its only span source, and it arrives through the ordinary Observe call to `TrainPhysics.reconcile_to_detected_occupancy(...)`. Everything downstream is the normal per-train chain — Observe `TrainController.on_physics_updated(...)`, `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)`, `ResourceCoordinator`, and the two managers.
- **Direction.** It has no cab and no travel direction when it first appears. Once it moves, its direction is the block it moved into: when it vacates a block while still holding a neighbour, the `direction` passed to `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated(...)` is the vacated block's `exit_edge` toward that neighbour, and the block it left behind takes normal `CAUTION`. Observe writes that edge into `physics_sync.pending_block_exit_edges`, the one carrier for a per-block tail-vacate direction, and the final Observe callback consumes it on the same tick — for an unidentified train that entry never waits across ticks, because the edge comes from the detected blocks rather than from a calculated tail exit it does not have.
- **The gap.** Switch tiles carry no detection, so an unidentified train rolling through a switch can hold no blocks at all for a moment. When its last block clears, that block's tail-vacate passes `direction = None` and the block goes straight to `FREE` (see **BlockManager**), but the train itself is held, with an empty span, for `UNIDENTIFIED_GAP_HOLD_S`. `UNIDENTIFIED_GAP_HOLD_S` lives in `constants.py`.
- **A held train reclaims a reachable confirmed entry within the gap window.** Within that window, a confirmed entry no existing train accounts for, on a block reachable from its last held block through undetected track, is that same train continuing its run: it keeps its `train_id`. If more than one held train could account for the entry, the one whose hold began most recently takes it.
- **A train retires when the gap window ends with no blocks held.** One that still holds no blocks when the window ends is retired.
- **Retirement teardown.** Retirement is a runtime-owned teardown in this order:
  1. clear the train's `physics_sync.pending_detected_entered_blocks`, `pending_detected_vacated_blocks`, and `pending_block_exit_edges`
  2. drop its `TrainController` from the controller registry and its physics instance from the physics registry
  3. drop the `Train` from the train registry
  4. add the `train_id` to the retired-id set so it is never reused (**Creation and identity**)

  The train holds no blocks, no reservations, no locks, and no `RouteRun` at this point, so nothing else is released, and nothing about it was ever written to saved state (**Runtime only**).
- **Retirement is the one teardown the runtime performs on a train by itself.** Removing a train the operator placed is a different thing and is out of scope for v1 (see **Out of Scope**).
- **Never driven while it is unidentified.** For as long as `is_unidentified` is `True` the train is never assigned a route, never given a `RouteRun`, never given a `Path`, never given a cab, and never accepts an operator command; the API rejects every such request for its `train_id`, and `PathDispatcher` never creates a path for it. The one command its `train_id` does accept is adoption, which is not a driving command — it is the operator describing what is on the track. Because it has no `RouteRun` it takes its place in the runnable order like any train without one, per the canonical ordering rule in **Per-train tick transaction**, and its Plan is a no-op. Its controller stays `OFF`, so its Action command drain always finds an empty queue, and the Observe occupancy commit runs for it on the ticks Observe attributed a block change to it, which is how its entries and vacates commit (see **Per-train tick transaction**).
- **Adoption.** An unidentified train is a report, not a dead end: the operator has looked at the layout and can say which locomotive it is, how long it is, and which way it is pointing, and that is exactly what it is missing. `SimulationController.adopt_unidentified_train(...)` takes those, plus the `train_id` the train keeps from then on, and turns it into an ordinary train.
- **Adoption is refused when any of these holds:**
  - the train is not unidentified
  - the `train_id` is already held by another train
  - the head tile named is not one the train is standing on
  - the train is holding nothing because it is in the gap
  - the declared consist would reach into a block reading no current

  Under Simulation, the first refusal above already rejects every adoption attempt before reaching any other condition: no unidentified train ever exists there to adopt (see **Ghosted trains** and **Unidentified trains** above, Under Simulation no unidentified train ever appears).
- **What adoption does, once it is not refused:**
  - **The same `Train` record survives, re-keyed.** Adoption does not delete the unidentified train and add a train in its place. `Block.occupied_by` follows the detector, and the detector reports changes rather than levels (**Block occupancy detection**), so releasing a block that is still drawing current would leave it `FREE` under a locomotive standing on it with no future entry to correct it. Instead the `train_id` moves to its new value across every registry that keys on it — the train registry, the controller and physics instances, and the blocks the train holds, whose ownership moves through the ordinary `BlockManager` release-then-occupy writers — `BlockManager.release_train_occupancy(old_train_id)` first, then the adopting train's occupancy write — so no block is ever owned by two ids. `is_unidentified` becomes `False`, and the `train_id` it was adopted away from goes into the retired-id set, so no later unidentified train is handed it (**Creation and identity**).
  - **Placement is the operator's declaration.** An unidentified train claims whole blocks because nobody knows where inside them it sits; the adopted train's span is rebuilt by `RailwayNetwork.place_train(...)` from the declared consist length and facing. With no head tile given, the consist must be centered in the track the detector confirmed: as much unaccounted-for track in front of the train as behind it. That is the whole of what the detector reports — the train is somewhere in these blocks — and standing the train at the first tile of the first block instead would state a position the detector gives no reason to believe. An operator who can see where the train actually stands may give a head tile, which must be one the train claims, and the front then sits at that tile's exit edge in the declared facing. Placement runs before the re-key, so a consist that does not fit the track behind the head leaves nothing half-adopted — the train is still the unidentified train it was. As with any other `RailwayNetwork.place_train(...)` call, this also seeds `Switch.physical_occupants` for every switch tile the rebuilt span covers, per **Placement seeds switch occupancy too** under **Power**.
  - **The body must not reach a block reading no current.** A block the detector reports clear has nothing standing on it, so no adopted train's body can extend into one. A declared consist that would is refused, and the train is left exactly as it was; the operator gives a shorter length, a different facing, a different head tile, or waits until every block the train stands on reads current. Track that carries no detection at all is not such a block: a switch tile has no detector to read clear, and a body may cover it.
  - **What the consist does not reach goes back to being unidentified.** Blocks the rebuilt span does not cover but the train still held are not this train: they are current on track no train the app controls stands on, which is the definition of an unidentified train, so `SimulationController.adopt_unidentified_train(...)` hands them to one through the ordinary Observe attribution and reports which blocks it gave back. They must not stay on the adopted train. A block with `occupied_by` set is not an eligible reservation candidate for anyone, its own holder included (see **BlockManager**), and the dispatcher excludes only the train's span blocks from the candidate set — so a train holding track it does not stand on walls itself off from its own route and never acquires a path. They must not simply be released either: they are drawing current, and the detector reports changes rather than levels, so nothing would re-occupy them and another train could be routed straight in. An operator who meant those blocks to be part of the train adopts it again with the full consist length.
  - **It is a real train from that moment.** It takes an instance profile — the one the operator named, or a fresh model profile and instance anchored to the declared `max_speed`, replacing the blank pair it carried — accepts every operator command, is energized like any other train, and is written to saved state. Nothing downstream has a branch for an adopted train; `is_unidentified` is `False`, which is the whole of what the other rules test.
- **Never energized.** An unidentified train commands no `track_voltage`, and its span is excluded from the energized set and from the de-energize test (see **Block power-controller role**). A block held only by an unidentified train is driven to `0`. Putting voltage on the rail under a train the app cannot steer or stop is the hazard this rule exists to contain.
- **Runtime only.** Unidentified trains are not written to saved state and not restored. A restart re-detects whatever is still drawing current and creates fresh ones for it, from an empty retired-id set. An adopted train is an ordinary train and is saved like one, so adoption is also how an operator makes a hand-placed locomotive survive a restart.
- **Shown as itself.** An unidentified train appears in the train list and on the layout as one, marked apart from the trains the operator controls and offering none of their controls, so the operator can see there is something on the track. What it does offer is the way out: its detail panel reports which blocks it was detected on and carries the form that adopts it.

**Block power-controller role**

- `BlockPowerController` is focused on the software-to-hardware boundary only: it accepts a voltage number and applies it to block outputs.
- `TrainPhysics` computes `track_voltage` from the current authoritative mode input (see **TrainPhysics**, Voltage behavior). `BlockPowerController` applies that already-computed voltage to the hardware-facing block outputs.
- **A block voltage carries a direction.** `track_voltage` is a magnitude and says nothing about which way a locomotive runs; a DC locomotive's direction is the polarity on its rails. So the value `BlockPowerController` commands on a block is that magnitude given a sign: positive when the train runs the block in its `forward` direction, negative when it runs it in `reverse`, where forward and reverse are the block-relative directions over `Block.ordered_tiles` (see **Block**). The sign is per block, not per train. Each block's tile order is drawn on its own, so two blocks a train holds at the same moment may run opposite ways against the train's line of travel; one sign for the whole train would drive the locomotive backwards on every block whose order was drawn against it.
- **A held block's direction comes from the canonical block-direction helper.** The direction for a held block is the block-relative direction of the train's line of travel through that block, computed by the **canonical block-direction helper** (see **Segment**) — the same value `ReservedBlockTraversal.block_direction` carries for a reserved block (see **BlockManager**).
- **The line of travel** is the ordered walk from the train's tail end through its cab end and onward through its pending-entry block and reserved corridor, oriented by `TrainController.travel_direction` (see **TrainController**). A block held through confirmed occupancy that the calculated span does not cover sits at one end of that walk, and extending the walk through it by the connectivity that attributed it gives that block its direction.
- **A train with no cab selected holds every block positive.** It has no `travel_direction`, so every block it holds is driven positive.
- **A cab change re-signs every held block.** A cab change recomputes `travel_direction`, so the next emission re-signs every block that train holds — this is how a train reverses.
- **The signed value is recorded on the block.** `BlockPowerController.set_block_voltage(...)` records the signed value on the block, so the layout reports which way each block is being driven as well as how hard.
- **Which physical channel a sign reaches is wiring.** It is resolved below the hardware interface (see **Hardware setup**, The rail binding bonds tile order to rail polarity); no layer above the driver names a channel.
- **Energized set: where the train stands, plus one block ahead.** For every train `T` the app controls — that is, every train that is neither unidentified (see **Unidentified trains**) nor ghosted (`presence_unknown`, see **Ghosted trains**) — the exact emission set is `T.controller.physics_sync.current_span.occupied_blocks ∪ {block_id | Block.occupied_by == T.train_id} ∪ {T's `pending-entry block`} ∪ {T's `next reserved block`}`. Each tick `TrainPhysics` drives that train's one computed `track_voltage` onto every block in this set, signed per block by the direction the train runs through that block (see **A block voltage carries a direction**). Each term is in the set for its own reason:
  - **The calculated-span term**, not debounced `Block.occupied_by`, keeps a newly entered unreserved/deviated block powered immediately.
  - **The confirmed-occupancy term** is there because the two views of occupancy can disagree about where a train is, and the rail must not go dead under a locomotive on either reading. A block attribution gave this train because it neighbours the span (see **Block occupancy detection**, Attribution) is in neither the span nor the reservations, and a forward-only correction cannot bring a span back onto it, so this is the only term that powers it — and it is the term the locomotive standing there needs in order to move at all.
  - **The pending-entry term** covers the train the detector cap is holding at a block seam: its calculated span stops short of the block it is entering, so without this term the rail the locomotive has to roll onto to release its own cap would be dead.
- **A block's feed is never asked for two voltages.** Because a block shares one feed across its segments and block exclusion prevents another modeled train from owning the same calculated block, a feed is never asked for two voltages.
- **A ghosted or unidentified train's emission set is empty for that tick.** It controls no `track_voltage`, so `TrainPhysics`'s difference against `TrainPhysics.previous_tick_emission_set_by_train_id` (see **De-energize against the same source**) queues every block of its last non-empty set, its retained span, with no additional writer.
- **Only the next reserved block is pre-energized.** A train's **next reserved block** is the first block of its reserved-ahead corridor (`Block.reserved_for_train`) that its head reaches by travelling forward, passing over the blocks it is already standing on. `TrainPhysics` resolves it each tick with the same forward tile walk the seam cap uses, so it follows the points as they are actually aligned rather than as a plan describes them, and it is `None` for a train with nothing reserved ahead of it. The rest of the corridor carries no voltage. One block ahead is the whole of what pre-energizing is for — a locomotive must not cross an insulated boundary into dead rail — and it is also the most that may be live at once. **Rail energized further ahead than the locomotive is authorized to be this instant is rail a train running fast keeps accelerating over.** A speed profile describes the locomotive it was calibrated for, so a real train reaches a seam before the model says it has; with the whole corridor live it runs on through every block of it while the app still believes it is a block back, and the detector confirmations arrive as a correction after the fact. Energizing the next reserved block bounds a reserved-corridor overrun to one block and puts dead rail immediately past the authority end, so the layout itself enforces the limit the app is computing.
- **A train with no reservations is unaffected by the pre-energizing rule.** It holds the rail under it through the span and confirmed-occupancy parts, and the block it is entering through the pending-entry part.
- **De-energize against the same source.** A block leaves the energized set two ways, and each source holds its dropped blocks in its own owner's store — `BlockManager._blocks_pending_deenergize` and each `TrainPhysics` instance's `_blocks_dropped_from_energized` — which `SimulationController` drains together once per tick. This subsection is that mechanism's canonical home. The two stores are world-level collections, not latches: they hold no **Latch Table** row and are not governed by the latch Writer-helper rule. No single `SimulationController` field holds a combined queue; `SimulationController` reads the two stores through their take-methods and never keeps a merged copy.
- **The stores drain once per tick.** `SimulationController` takes both stores — `BlockManager.take_blocks_to_deenergize()` and every `TrainPhysics.take_blocks_dropped_from_energized()` — once per tick, after every train has emitted and before the signal refresh, unions their contents, and clears both, so nothing survives to the next tick.
- **`BlockManager` queues a block when any of these holds**: a calculated span drops the block, a reservation on it clears, or a confirmed-occupancy holding on it is released through `BlockManager.release_train_occupancy(...)` (the ghost-rising-edge case). `BlockManager` adds it to `_blocks_pending_deenergize` through its writer `BlockManager._mark_for_deenergize(block_id)`, and `BlockManager.take_blocks_to_deenergize()` returns only the blocks still unheld at drain time — a block vacated and re-held within the same tick is not returned.
- **`TrainPhysics` queues a block that silently drops out of the next-reserved-block term.** When a block stays reserved but stops being its train's `next reserved block` — the train reversed on its corridor, or a replan reordered it — nothing about the block changed, so `BlockManager` cannot see it. `TrainPhysics` adds it instead to `_blocks_dropped_from_energized`, from the difference between this tick's emission set and the emission set it stored per train from the previous tick (`TrainPhysics.previous_tick_emission_set_by_train_id`).
- **A block is driven to `0` only when it fails all four emission-set terms.** `SimulationController` drives a block from either store to `0` only when all four of these hold:
  - it is absent from every controller's current `current_span.occupied_blocks`
  - it has no `Block.occupied_by` naming that controller's train
  - it is no controller's `pending-entry block`
  - it is no controller's `next reserved block`
- **The drain tests both views of occupancy, never one alone.** The drain tests the calculated span **in addition to** debounced `Block.occupied_by`, never instead of it, so neither view of occupancy alone can zero a rail and a same-tick re-entry prevents zeroing.
- **A reservation the train has not reached is not part of the test.** It is deliberately not part of the test, because it is not part of the emission set either: holding it would leave a block driven and zeroed on the same tick.
- **Ghosted and unidentified trains are excluded from all four tests.** Unidentified-train controllers and `presence_unknown` controllers are excluded from all four tests, so a block held only by an unidentified train, or only by a train no detector can find, is driven to `0` (see **Unidentified trains** and **Ghosted trains**).
- **This makes the routine energized set the global union of steerable trains' four terms.** It is exactly the global union, over the trains the app can steer, of their calculated occupied blocks, confirmed occupancy, pending-entry blocks, and next reserved blocks — the same four terms the emission set carries.
- **A whole-layout sweep is the no-`BlockManager` fallback and the admin/test primitive.** `BlockPowerController.deenergize_unheld_blocks(skip=None)` drops every block no train physically holds (`Block.occupied_by`) to `0` in one pass over all blocks, with `skip` naming the calculated-span, pending-entry, and next-reserved blocks the runtime keeps energized. It is the fallback for a runtime with no `BlockManager` wired, plus an admin/test reconciliation primitive; a normally-wired runtime drives the two event-driven stores above and never reaches it.
- **This differs from the loss-of-control safe state, which zeroes every output at once.**
- `BlockPowerController` owns only voltage emission/readback; controller and physics layers supply all manual-mode decisions and the already-computed voltage.
- **A refused write is fatal to a hardware-backed session, and never recorded as voltage.** Simulation's `TrackOutput.set_voltage(...)` is the happy-path model and accepts a valid block command. Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware cannot activate with a missing binding or chip, so a refusal or exception after activation means the device contract has failed at runtime. `BlockPowerController.set_block_voltage(...)`, the ordinary model-recording write, records the commanded voltage only when the write landed; otherwise it reports the failure to `SimulationController.enter_hardware_failure(...)`, which drives the safe state itself (see **Hardware I/O failure**) and latches the halt, and emits one event with `kind = "error"` and an `ErrorRecord` naming the failed device.
- **A write that fails inside `OutputSafety.enter_safe_state()`'s own sequence does not re-enter it.** `enter_safe_state()`'s sequence calls the non-recording device writes (`SwitchPowerController.de_energize_device_outputs()`, `BlockPowerController.zero_device_outputs()`; see **Safe state / fail-safe**), not the ordinary model-recording writes, but the two report failures into the same per-channel failure-tracking shape: when the caller is that sequence itself, a failed per-channel write is recorded in that run's failure set and the sequence continues to the next channel; the aggregate result is reported once, through the "inability to complete safe state" entry of **Hardware I/O failure** below, never by a second call into `enter_hardware_failure(...)` or a second `enter_safe_state()` from inside the first.
- **Further operating commands are refused until the latch is explicitly cleared.** Further operating commands are refused until the operator successfully reactivates a validated hardware-backed environment and explicitly clears the latch through `POST /api/runtime/clear-hardware-failure`; the clear leaves the session stopped.
- **The model never reports a block energized while the rail is dead.** The model never reports a block energized while the rail is dead, and the runtime never continues operating around missing hardware.
- **A watchdog-driven safe-state drop is reconciled on the next runtime-thread tick.** A watchdog-driven safe-state drop is the one path that writes the physical rail to `0` before any model write records it; the runtime-thread tick that consumes the trip record reconciles the recorded voltages to match (see **Loss-of-control watchdog**), so the invariant holds again from that tick onward.
- The block-voltage read surface (`BlockPowerController.get_block_voltage(block_id)` over `TrackOutput.get_actual_voltage(block_id)`) reports the voltage on a block. Simulation returns the last value accepted by the happy-path model. Virtual Hardware returns the controllable fake device's readback, and Real Hardware reads the block's bound `block_occupancy_current` channel bus voltage where that chip provides one; neither hardware-backed environment silently substitutes the commanded value for a failed read. It returns `None` where the rig has no measurement facility, and `None` plus one `kind = "warning"` event on a failed readback transaction. This is a diagnostic read: it never enters the hardware-failure lifecycle, which is why the fatal "failed detector transaction" of **Hardware I/O failure** does not cover it.

**Switch power-controller role**

- `SwitchPowerController` is the switch-side counterpart of `BlockPowerController`, and it covers a switch's two separate electricals: the `throw voltage` it drives onto the point motor, and the block feed its rails run on. It holds `SwitchOutput` and is the only caller of it during operation — including the safe-state call — so `SwitchManager` requests a throw through the controller and never touches the interface itself. A commissioning session is the one other caller, and only while it holds the outputs, through the same output interfaces and drivers (see **Hardware interface boundary** and **Commissioning owns the writes; the detectors stay shared**).
- **The two electricals are different wires.** `SwitchOutput` is the software-to-hardware boundary for switch *throw* output. It accepts a target alignment (`0 = MAIN`, `1 = DIVERGE`, matching `Switch.position`) and drives the point motor. It holds no wiring knowledge — how a target alignment reaches the motor is the driver's business, defined under **Hardware setup** (see **A switch throw is a pulse on one of two coils**) — and it owns no routing, lock, or availability policy. The rails are the other wire: they carry the `track voltage` of the switch's feed block, which `BlockPowerController` emits. The two are never compared. Simulation supplies `SimulatedSwitchDriver`; Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware supply the setup-aware driver against their respective device.
- **A switch's rails are fed from one nearby block.** A switch has no track feed of its own. Its rails are wired to one nearby block and carry that block's `track voltage`, so the emission `BlockPowerController` already makes for that block is what drives a train across the switch. The wiring is the `switch_track_source` binding in **Hardware setup** (`switch_id` to `block_id`), and `SwitchPowerController` is that map's only reader. The bound block must be the one at the switch's **main entrance**. A train crossing the switch from its main-side entrance is standing on the feeding block itself; a train crossing from the diverge side is entering the switch out of its pending-entry / next-reserved block, which the one-block-ahead rule (see **Only the next reserved block is pre-energized**) already pre-energizes as the feeding block before the train reaches the switch. Either way the feeding block is always a block the ordinary energized set already carries — the block the train stands on, or the block it is about to enter — so a switch is live under a train without any emission, reservation, or channel of its own. This is why the energized set stays exactly the block set defined under **Block power-controller role** — switches add nothing to it.
- **Rail voltage is read, never written.** `SwitchPowerController.get_switch_voltage(switch_id)` reports the voltage on a switch's rails by reading its feed block through `BlockPowerController.get_block_voltage(source_block_id)`. While an incomplete setup is being edited or commissioned it returns `None` when that switch has no `switch_track_source` entry; that state is an activation blocker and cannot occur during Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware operation. It is a UI/diagnostic read — the per-switch hardware view shows which block feeds the switch and whether those rails are live — and no control, routing, or physics decision reads it. `SwitchPowerController` drives nothing onto the rails: the bond is physical, so there is no output to write.
- **Why the switch has its own controller.** `BlockPowerController` takes a voltage number and applies it; a switch is the other shape. Its one output is an alignment, not a voltage, and its one voltage is sourced from a block rather than commanded. Holding both facts in `SwitchPowerController` gives every switch-side electrical question a single answer site, and leaves `BlockPowerController` owning exactly one thing: the voltage on a block.
- **Acquisition always throws.** Lock acquisition drives the coil for every switch it acquires, whether or not `Switch.position` needed changing and whether or not that alignment was the last one commanded. A throw is blind, so having driven a coil once is no evidence the points seated: a solenoid can stall, bounce back, or be moved by hand afterwards, and nothing reports it. Points left on the wrong side carry the train's `track voltage` down the other branch, which both denies the train the rail it is about to run on and lights the current detector on a block the train is nowhere near — read as occupancy on track nothing is standing on. One extra pulse removes that whole class of failure, so acquisition re-throws rather than reasoning about whether it needs to. Outside acquisition the throw is emitted whenever the canonical `Switch.position` mutation workflow (see the **Switch entity** section) issues an alignment the output has not last driven.
- **A throw is blind.** A point motor reports no position back — it has no contact, encoder, or sensed alignment — so `Switch.position` is the commanded alignment and nothing confirms the points seated. `SwitchManager` must not infer a physical alignment from any other reading, and must not treat a successful throw as evidence the switch moved. The rail-voltage read is no exception: it reports the feed block's voltage and says nothing about where the points are.
- **An unissued throw is fatal to a hardware-backed session.** `SwitchPowerController.set_throw(switch_id, target_state)` returns `True` when the command reached the device and `False` when it did not. A missing port binding or chip is rejected before Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware activation; a refusal or exception after activation therefore means the device contract has failed at runtime. The controller reports the failure to `SimulationController.enter_hardware_failure(...)`, which drives the safe state itself, and reports the failed command through `NotificationCenter`. As with a refused voltage write, a throw that fails while it is itself part of `OutputSafety.enter_safe_state()`'s own sequence does not re-enter that sequence (see **A write that fails inside `OutputSafety.enter_safe_state()`'s own sequence does not re-enter it**, above). Any partial lock acquisition rolls back its software locks, but operation does not continue and the throw is never auto-retried. `Switch.position` remains the commanded alignment rather than being rewritten as an inferred physical position.
- **Environment behavior.** Simulation accepts every valid throw and records it. Virtual Hardware can inject any of the canonical fault kinds listed in **Hardware interface boundary** to prove the same observable hardware-failure lifecycle without physical equipment. It does not pretend to observe an uninstrumented point motor mechanically sticking after a successful pulse. Real Hardware enters the hardware-failure lifecycle when the physical device refuses or fails. Missing setup is never a runtime throw outcome in either hardware-backed environment because it blocks activation.

## Data Flow To UI

**API payload ownership**

- Each runtime/entity owner must expose its own API payload through its own `to_dict()` (or equivalent read-model method), rather than merging changed live fields back into another entity's payload. `Train.to_dict()` owns persistent train data. `TrainController.to_dict()` owns live onboard, control, and physical diagnostics, including the stored `presence_unknown`. Dispatcher-owned path progress is exposed through `PathDispatcher.get_active_path_progress(train_id)` plus the route-supplied call to `PathDispatcher.get_waiting_for_block_id(...)` described below.
- **A composite runtime snapshot exposes five sibling payload groups.** In v1, any composite runtime snapshot that returns the network/train view must expose them with this exact ownership split:
  - **`trains`**: the list of `Train.to_dict()` payloads.
  - **`controllers_by_train_id`**: a map `train_id -> TrainController.to_dict()`.
  - **`dispatcher_progress_by_train_id`**: a map `train_id -> {path_id, status, current_resource_index, authority_end_block_id, waiting_for_block_id, resource_sequence}`. The dispatcher-owned path fields come from `PathDispatcher.get_active_path_progress(train_id)`; `waiting_for_block_id` comes from the complete `PathDispatcher.get_waiting_for_block_id(...)` request assembled by `RouteExecutor` below. Each `resource_sequence` entry in this progress projection is a lightweight subset — `sequence_index`, `resource_type`, `resource_id`, `entry_edge`, `exit_edge` — and carries no nested `path_tiles`. A consumer that needs the per-step tile geometry reads the controller payload's `received_path_plan.resource_sequence` (the full canonical **resource_sequence entry schema**, with its nested `path_tiles`) instead of this projection.
  - **`assigned_routes_by_train_id`**: a map `train_id -> route_id` (or `None`), resolved from `RouteExecutor.assigned_route_id_for(train_id)`.
  - **`route_runs_by_train_id`**: a map `train_id -> {route_id, run_number, state, display_state, last_error}` — a lightweight live-run summary. `state` is the run's `current_route_status` value; `display_state` is the derived UI projection; `last_error` is the derived `NotificationCenter.latest_error_for(...)` read for the run, never a stored field. The full run record — the armed requested-target pair (from `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id).stored_resolved_target`), `start_mode`, and the per-walk-position `task_runs` timing projection — is served on demand by the `GET /api/route-runs/<run_number>` detail endpoint (under its `tasks` key), not inlined here, so the per-tick composite snapshot stays small. That `tasks` projection carries, for each walk-position, `{task_index, task_kind, walk_direction, started_at, finished_at, delay_class, elapsed_basis_seconds, elapsed_wall_seconds, resolved_target}`: `task_kind` derived from `Route.tasks[task_index].task_kind`, `walk_direction` stored on `RouteTaskRun`, `elapsed_wall_seconds = finished_at - started_at` for a finished row, and under `timing_basis == "operating"` `elapsed_basis_seconds = finished_at_operating - started_at_operating` (equal to the wall result under `"realtime"`); both elapsed fields are `None` until the row finishes, including an active dwell, and are serialization-only. `RouteRun` owns both the summary and the detail; `TrainController.to_dict()` never merges route-owned fields into its payload.
- **The two route-side maps answer different questions, and both are carried.** `assigned_routes_by_train_id` is the lightweight "which route is this train on?" map the frontend reads to tell assigned trains from unassigned ones; it is non-`None` even between runs, before Plan has allocated a `RouteRun`. `route_runs_by_train_id` is the live run summary (`None` whenever there is no `RUNNING` run). When a run is live, the `route_id` in both agrees.
- **`waiting_for_block_id` is recomputed, not retained.** During composite read-model assembly, `RouteExecutor` resolves `RouteExecutor.find_armed_task(train_id)` and the run's effective acquisition mode and manual override, then passes that request to the canonical `PathDispatcher.get_waiting_for_block_id(...)` projection with `acquisition_cap_block_id=None` and `required_candidate_resource_keys=None`, matching the tick-start contention view. The read model does not reimplement the walk or ask the dispatcher to discover route-owned target state. Best-effort retries may change the result tick to tick, which is why it is recomputed rather than retained; it feeds the "show stuck" overlay.
- **Other endpoints must preserve the ownership split.** Other detail endpoints may present the same owned data in a different wrapper, but they must preserve this ownership split and must not merge controller-owned, dispatcher-owned, or route-owned live fields back into `Train.to_dict()`.

**Elapsed values are server-owned**

- A payload that carries a duration carries it as a number the runtime computed. A client renders it and never derives one from its own clock: a browser clock cannot see a stop, a playback multiplier, or the server's own time, so any elapsed figure it derived would be wrong in all three ways (see **Clocks** under the **Units contract**).
- A client may still format a wall instant the payload carries — `started_at`, `finished_at`, `target_time` — as a local clock time, because those are absolute and need no elapsed arithmetic.
- The run panel reads its per-walk-position elapsed figures from the `tasks` projection of the `GET /api/route-runs/<run_number>` detail endpoint (see **Data Flow To UI**), which carries both the `timing_basis` elapsed figure and the elapsed wall time for each served walk-position, because a run that was stopped for ten minutes is honestly described only by both numbers.

**`Train.to_dict()` payload**

- `to_dict()` must expose all canonical fields owned by the `Train` entity for convenience.
- `Train.to_dict()` exports only the persistent train fields owned by `Train`. Live physical/control diagnostics (position, span, speed, state, target speed, ATO info, lookahead, path/destination IDs, reserved blocks) are not in this payload — they live on the controller payload.
- Read live operational diagnostics from `TrainController.to_dict()` instead.

**`TrainController.to_dict()` payload**

- `to_dict()` must expose all canonical fields owned by the `TrainController` entity for convenience.
- Export all live operational state, including `handle_position`, `manual.manual_mode_type`, and `manual.manual_power_percent`.
- Export live physical state from the controller-owned storage, including `current_span` and `current_speed_kmh`, for UI/debug consumers that previously read position or occupied tiles from `Train.to_dict()`.
- Export ATO state using `ato_destination_block_id` derived from `received_path_plan.authority_end_block_id`.
- Export `received_path_plan` when present using the canonical **received_path_plan schema**. This is the controller/UI projection of active dispatcher authority, and its nested authority geometry must continue to follow the canonical **resource_sequence entry schema** and **path_tile entry schema**.
- Do not make `TrainController.to_dict()` the owner of live path-progress state in v1. `PathDispatcher` stays the only owner of `current_resource_index`. If the UI needs that progress projection, expose it through a dispatcher-owned read model such as `PathDispatcher.get_active_path_progress(train_id)` (the full projection is listed above in this section), resolved from the dispatcher's own active-path registry for that `train_id`. Do not copy ownership into `TrainController`, and do not write per-tick sequence-index updates into the controller.
- UI/debug consumers that need active authority geometry must read `received_path_plan.resource_sequence`; consumers that need current physical occupancy must read `TrainController.get_current_span()`.
- Expose the full canonical lookahead payload as the single source of truth for current target speed, ATC limit, speed-limit reason, and forward curve rendering.

**UI data-flow anchor**

- Treat the controller payload as the source of truth for live operational, manual, and physical state. Treat the train payload as the source for persistent train data.
- A UI asking "what is the train's target speed right now?" must call `controller.get_lookahead()` and sample at distance `0`.

**Signals (display-only)**

- Signals are display-only UI state. `SignalRegistry` stores them and owns their lookup surface (`add_signal`, `get_signal`, `get_signal_at`, `get_signal_at_direction`, `remove_signal`, `update_signal`); `RailwayNetwork` reaches signals only through it. `RailwayNetwork.update_signals_from_blocks()` produces aspect values for the UI once per tick, at the tick tail after every train's Action and the de-energize drain (see the **Per-train tick transaction**). No controller or physics layer uses them as a speed restriction. The CAUTION speed restriction is owned by `CAUTION_SPEED_LIMIT_KMH` through the lookahead / ATC path (see **TrainController**, ATC speed limit).

## Event log

The event log is the operator-facing record of what happened during a run. It is the structured stream `NotificationCenter` already owns (see **Core Runtime Loop**, **Runtime notifications**), kept on disk and presented for review, so an operator can scroll back through a run instead of catching events only as they pass. It is not a second sink: every event still flows through `NotificationCenter`, which assigns the order and the schema, and the event log is that one stream persisted and surfaced.

**What it records**

- **What it records.** The log carries every event `NotificationCenter` emits, at every level:
  - command results
  - the error events defined in **Error events**
  - the latch writes and consumptions defined by the **Writer-helper rule**
  - the operational events that mark what each train did — train placed, departed, arrived, entered or finished station dwell, entered a block, vacated a block, threw a switch, path created / completed / cancelled, and EB activated / released

  Each one is a single event with the fields defined by the **Event schema**, and each names the function that produced it in `operation` (`"add_train"`, `"depart"`, `"occupy_blocks"`, `"on_block_tail_vacated"`, `"request_position_change"`, `"apply_position_change"`, `"create_path"`, `"try_complete_active_path"`, `"cancel_path"`, `"handle_path_completion"`, `"enter_station_dwell"`, `"finish_dwell"`, `"activate"`, `"release"`).
- **`apply_position_change` is distinct from the operator/API `request_position_change` throw.** `"apply_position_change"` is the Plan dispatcher acquisition-time throw (`SwitchManager.acquire_locks_for_segment(...)`, see **Switch entity**), distinct from the operator/API `"request_position_change"` throw.
- **Emitter attribution for the named operations.** `"handle_path_completion"`, `"enter_station_dwell"`, and `"finish_dwell"` are emitted by `RouteExecutor.handle_path_completion(...)`, `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()`, and `TrainController.finish_dwell()` respectively; `"activate"` and `"release"` are emitted by `TrainController.eb.activate()` and `TrainController.eb.release()`.
- **The stored `operation` is the unqualified function name.** The stored `operation` remains the unqualified function name per the **Event schema**.
- **Operational events carry `kind = "info"` and no `ErrorRecord`.**
- **`notification_id` is the log's read-back order.** The increasing `notification_id` is the order the log reads back in.
- Components must not write the log directly. They emit each event through `NotificationCenter` at the points they already report from, the same way as any other notification, so the "no separate sink" rule in **Runtime notifications** still holds. The event log is the persisted projection of that one stream.

**Persistence**

- The event log persists to disk, so a run's record outlives the session and an operator can review an earlier run's incidents later. It holds the same `NOTIFICATION_RETENTION_ROWS` window the in-memory stream holds (see **Runtime notifications**, Retention): one cap governs the whole stream, so a row an operator can no longer see in the viewer is a row no query can reach. This is a deliberate persisted record, separate from live runtime state — occupancy, locks, the train span — which stays in memory per **Out of Scope**. It is runtime-written data that is saved rather than rebuilt each session, alongside the maintenance counters (see **Maintenance counters**).

**Viewer**

- The event-log viewer is a read-only panel in the operator UI. It reads the persisted stream and lets the operator filter it — by entity, by `kind`, by `source`, by `operation`, by `ErrorRecord.origin`, by time — and selecting an entry highlights the entities it names on the canvas. It presents the record only; it never mutates runtime state.

**Replay**

- Replay is an event-timeline visualization, not state reconstruction. It steps or scrubs through retained events, shows the selected event's message and payload, and highlights the entities named by that event on the matching saved layout. When an operation's closed payload contains explicit geometry or before/after values, the viewer may draw those recorded values; it never infers missing train positions, block occupancy, or switch alignment and never interpolates motion between events. Because retention may remove the beginning of a run and v1 stores no replay checkpoint, the viewer makes no promise to reconstruct world state at an arbitrary time. Re-running the simulation engine forward or backward remains **Out of Scope**.

## End-To-End ATO Path Run

**End-to-end path-authority projection**

- `PathDispatcher` stores the active dispatcher-owned `Path`. `TrainController.path_projection.received_path_plan` reads the canonical **received_path_plan schema** projection from that active record. `controller.assigned_path_id` is a derived read of that projection's `path_id`.
- `RouteExecutor` must ensure the train's `TrainController` exists before path authority is created or extended in Plan.
- `RouteExecutor` must not write `assigned_path_id` or `ato_destination_block_id` directly.

**End-to-end ATO run**

This is a high-level walk-through. The canonical contracts live in the relevant sections (see **Stop-arrival procedure**, **Planning Kernel**, **Route-run state**, **Observe, Plan, and Action Table**).

1. Observe runs once before runnable-train ordering: sample every layout detector into one retained snapshot, calculate movement for each train whose movement is calculated this pass (per **Movement feedback runs only when movement is calculated; detection feedback always runs**), then debounce and attribute the retained snapshot across the whole layout for every train regardless of controller state. It then creates/extends/holds/retires unidentified trains, truncates conflicting authority, reconciles affected train spans, drains each train's progress mailbox to commit block entry and tail-vacate and run the route head-advance callbacks, latches any movement-derived deviation (`origin = "out_of_sequence"`, committed later in Action once the train is stopped), evaluates stop arrival (step `9d8b`, skipped when a cancel is pending), and performs ghost rising-edge occupancy/power cleanup and latch writes per the **Observe, Plan, and Action Table**. Its detector-derived handoff and committed positions are ready before any train's Plan begins.
2. Plan: run the covered-task index advance. Resolve the next task via `RouteExecutor._find_next_task_target(train_id)` to get one concrete `(requested_destination_block_id, requested_destination_direction)`. Then call `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` (or `PathDispatcher.extend_path(...)` if a live path exists), using `acquisition_mode = run.effective_acquisition_mode(route_registry)`. If a resolved pass-through (`waypoint`) target block is already covered, the index advance skips it. A resolved stop target block is finished by the same index advance once the train is stopped with its head in that block and has no active path (the covered-stop rule).
3. Action (for each train, after Plan): drain commands, consume `pending_path_cancel_request` through the stopped-gated early-Action dispatcher callback, consume `departure_request` (calling `TrainController.depart()`) and `station_entry_request` (calling `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()`), run reactive-condition evaluation (step `71ee`), evaluate control and set the block track voltage, then consume `pending_route_abort`, `pending_power_off`, and `pending_route_deactivate`, and finally consume `station_exit_request` last (calling `TrainController.finish_dwell()` when dwelling, or its no-op clear). The voltage drives movement calculated in the next tick's Observe. Dwell-complete timing, route-deviation cleanup, and terminal route completion remain Plan procedures.
4. Extension retries use the same `path_id` until authority reaches the requested target. Every `success=True` extend keeps the existing live path, and `reached_target = False` means retry later; a `no_viable_path` failure latches cancel-and-replan.
5. Stop arrival advances the stop task via `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(...)`, which writes its `finished_at`. On the next tick, when the route's next task is `dwell`, the Plan dwell-entry step inside `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` writes `station_entry_request`; the Action station-entry consumer calls `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()`, moving the controller to `RUNNING_AT_STATION`. The Plan dwell-complete step checks `RouteTask.should_depart(...)`, then calls `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(...)` for the dwell row (writing its `finished_at` and advancing the derived `current_waypoint_index`), writes `station_exit_request`, and returns; the Action station-exit consumer performs `TrainController.finish_dwell()`. On the next eligible Plan, if `_find_next_task_target(train_id)` returns `None`, Plan calls `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)` per the terminal route completion contract (state `FINISHED`, the run kept as a historical row) — no live path remains at this point, since the stop's arrival already cleared it. Otherwise it leaves the next target to that later Plan.

**End-to-end manual-arrival note**

- Manual trains use the same route-committed arrival and the same Plan dwell-entry step inside `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` as ATO trains. The only difference is departure. In manual mode, `TrainController.depart()` marks the current authority ready to go by calling `OperationalStateMachine.enter_running_moving()` directly, not through `TrainController.ato.go()`; it does not start movement by itself.

**End-to-end post-EB restart note**

- EB recovery follows the canonical **EB workflow state machine** defined in the **TrainController** section. The pre-EB path is never reused. After EB release, the next eligible Plan creates fresh authority and writes `phase_latches.departure_request`, per the canonical depart contract.

## Glossary

This section defines words that get overloaded across the document. Some mean similar but different things in different layers. Others show up in prose with no stored field behind them. Defining each word once here lets every other site point to it by name instead of restating it.

Three rules govern this glossary:

1. **If a word appears in prose but in no schema, it goes in the glossary, or it does not appear in prose at all.** No informal nouns.
2. **If two words mean the same thing across layers, pick one as the main word and mark the other as a synonym.** Do not let the two drift apart over time.
3. **If a word means different things in different contexts, qualify it every time it appears.** Never write a bare `forward`. Always write "block-relative forward" or "train-relative forward."

**Group A — Action verbs.** Each row names the entity acted on, who initiates the action, and the resulting state.

| Verb | Entity / initiator / resulting state |
| --- | --- |
| `cancel` | `Path` (`status: ACTIVE -> CANCELLED`); initiated by `PathDispatcher.cancel_path(...)`. Writers and gating per the **Latch Table** (`c832`) and the **Physical progress / deviation procedure**. |
| `complete` | `Path` (`status: ACTIVE -> COMPLETED`); initiated by `PathDispatcher.try_complete_active_path(...)` per the **Stop-arrival procedure** |
| `finish` | `RouteRun` (`current_route_status -> FINISHED`); initiated by `RouteExecutor.finish_route_run(train_id)` per the terminal route completion procedure (`879a`) |
| `deactivate` | `RouteRun` (`current_route_status -> DEACTIVATED`); initiated by `RouteExecutor.remove_train_route_run(...)` from the Action abort/power-off/deactivate consumers |
| `abort` | `RouteRun`; operator-driven teardown via the `pending_route_abort` latch per the **Latch Table** (`bc5d`) |
| `revoke` | `Path`; system-driven cancel via `pending_path_cancel_request(revoked)` from route reconciliation, admin route deactivation, structural extend failure, a path left with no valid authority after another train takes a block it reserved (see **Path And PathDispatcher**, Authority truncation), or the broken-skip terminal-walk cancel (steps `c481` / `592a`, latched while a live path still exists on an all-broken or terminal walk — see **Unreachable and broken task handling**) |
| `deviate` | `RouteRun.path_cancelled = True` with `path_cancel_was_deviation = True` (derived `display_state == "DEVIATED"`); writer and consumer per the **Latch Table** (`75cb`). A non-deviation authority cancellation also sets `path_cancelled` but leaves `path_cancel_was_deviation = False`, so it projects `display_state == "CANCELLED"` instead (see **Route-run state**). |
| `depart` | `TrainController.ops.state -> RUNNING_MOVING`; initiated by `TrainController.depart()`, the Action consumer of `departure_request` (written by `RouteExecutor.tick_train_plan(...)` when live authority exists) |
| `dwell` | `TrainController.ops.state -> RUNNING_AT_STATION`; initiated by `TrainController.enter_station_dwell()`, the Action consumer of `station_entry_request` (written by the `RouteExecutor` Plan dwell-entry step) |
| `throw` | `Switch` (moves the point motor to a new alignment and writes the commanded `Switch.position`); owned by `SwitchManager` per the **Switch entity** mutation workflow and **Power**, Switch power-controller role |
| `skip` | `RouteRun` (`task_runs[walk_position].finished_at` set, the route-progress cursor advances past a broken task); initiated by Plan step `c481`, or step `592a` for a task a mid-pass cursor move landed on. Canonical home **Unreachable and broken task handling**. |
| `stall` | `RouteRun` (`no_reachable_task = True`, derived `display_state == "STALLED"`, the train holds idle); initiated by Plan step `c481` (or step `592a`) when every task on a `CIRCULAR` / `ROUND_TRIP` walk is broken and no live path remains — while a live path still exists the step latches the ordinary cancel instead and sets the flag on a later pass. Canonical home **Unreachable and broken task handling**. |

**Group B — Geometry terms.** Each row names the frame of reference. Always qualify the term in prose.

| Term | Frame of reference |
| --- | --- |
| `forward` | Block-relative (matches `Block.allowed_travel_directions`; the tile order is the concatenation of the block's constituent `Segment.ordered_tiles`) OR train-relative (the cab end the train is heading toward). Always qualify which. |
| `reverse` | Block-relative or train-relative. Always qualify which. |
| `head` | Train-relative; the physical end of the current span on the authority side, i.e. closer to `authority_end_block_id`. |
| `tail` | Train-relative; the physical end of the current span farther from `authority_end_block_id`. |
| `cab` | Operator-selected control end of the train; `A` or `B` or `None`. The cab is on the head side when the train is moving forward in the authority frame. |
| `frame` | Generic term for a directed coordinate context; always qualify with one of: block-relative, traversal, terminal, or travel. |
| `traversal direction` | Block-relative; `"forward"` or `"reverse"` for one block as walked by a path. |
| `travel direction` | Network-relative; the train's current motion direction in the network frame, derived from cab and span. |
| `terminal frame` | The directed `path_tiles` / `entry_edge` / `exit_edge` of the terminal block in a `Path.resource_sequence`; used for braking and for completion direction match. |

**Group C — Aggregate nouns.** Each row gives the type, or marks the word as informal prose only and points to the real concrete artifact behind it.

| Noun | Type / canonical schema |
| --- | --- |
| `path` | Stored entity (`Path` record); canonical schema in **Path field schema**. |
| `authority` | Informal prose for "the cleared corridor ahead of the train"; not a stored field. Use `Path` or `received_path_plan` when the concrete artifact is needed. |
| `plan` | Informal prose synonym for `received_path_plan`; canonical schema in **received_path_plan schema**. |
| `run` | `RouteRun` runtime instance; canonical schema in the RouteRun section. |
| `walk` | The directed sequence of walk-positions (`task_runs` entries) of a `RouteRun`, each carrying a `task_index` back-reference; not a stored field. |
| `task` | `RouteTask` authored entry (with `task_kind`); runtime instance is `RouteTaskRun`. |
| `start mode` | Which stop a fresh `RouteRun` begins at (`FIRST` / `NEAREST` / `SPECIFIC`). It comes from the route-level default `Route.start_mode` plus a per-assignment one-shot input. Canonical home **Run start-mode seeding**. |
| `broken task` | Informal prose for a `RouteTask` whose `task_location` ID is not in the network (it resolves with `failure_kind == missing_target`). It is skipped, never waited on. Canonical home **Unreachable and broken task handling**. |
| `unreachable task` | Informal prose for a `RouteTask` whose target exists but cannot be served this tick (`failure_kind == target_unavailable`, or a live `PathAcquisitionFailureKind`). It is waited on, not skipped. Canonical home **Unreachable and broken task handling**. |
| `valid task` | Informal prose for a `RouteTask` whose `task_location` ID is in the network, whether or not it can be served right now. It is the opposite of a broken task. Canonical home **Unreachable and broken task handling**. |
| `holding point` | A block a user marks with `Block.is_holding_point = True` as a safe place to wait. The canonical field lives in the **Block** field schema. It has two consumers: the best-effort truncation holding-point preference (item 11 under **Path And PathDispatcher**) and **Meet coordination**'s `meet_ceiling_block_id` selection. |
| `adoption` | The operator turning an **unidentified train** into an ordinary, driveable train by supplying the identity, consist and facing the detector cannot know. Canonical home **Power**, Unidentified trains. |
| `unidentified train` | A `Train` the runtime creates by itself for a detected block with no app-controlled train accounting for it. It is never driven while it stays unidentified. Canonical home **Power**, Unidentified trains. |
| `ghosted` | Said of a train the operator placed whose detected blocks all read clear. Canonical home **Power**, Ghosted trains. |
| `configuration` | A category word, not one schema, file, mode, or API surface. Do not use it bare. Name the actual owner: **persistent train data**, **layout geometry**, **Hardware Setup**, or **runtime settings**. These have different lifetimes and activation rules. |

**Group D — Electrical / switch-hardware terms.** These separate the two voltages and the two meanings of switch alignment.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `track voltage` | The DC voltage put on a block to drive the train. Each train uses one magnitude, applied to the blocks it stands on plus the block it is entering and the next block reserved ahead of it (see **Power**, Energized set), and every one of those blocks is given its own sign — which way the train runs through that block (see **Power**, A block voltage carries a direction). Because a block shares one feed across its segments, that whole block is powered (see **Block**, one-train-per-Block power domain). This way, when the train crosses a boundary, the next block is already powered instead of dead (see **Power**, Block power-controller role). Canonical home `TrainPhysics` (see **TrainPhysics**). `BlockPowerController` emits it to the block outputs (see **Power**). A switch has no feed of its own; its rails carry the voltage of its `switch feed block`. |
| `throw voltage` | The DC drive put on a switch point motor to move it. Which coil it is put on picks which alignment to move to (see **Power**, Hardware setup). Emitted by `SwitchPowerController` (see **Power**, Switch power-controller role). This is a separate output from `track voltage`: the two are different wires and are never compared. |
| `switch feed block` | The block whose feed also powers a switch's rails. A switch carries no `track voltage` of its own: its rails are wired to the block at its main entrance, so a train standing on the switch is driven by that block's voltage. The wiring is the `switch_track_source` binding in **Hardware setup**, and `SwitchPowerController` owns the relation (see **Power**, Switch power-controller role). |
| `physical channel` | One addressable line on a chip — a PWM channel, a shift-register output bit, a shift-register input bit, or a current-sense channel — that a logical `block_id` or `switch_id` maps to on a given hardware build. A logical entity may take more than one: a block's track takes two PWM channels, a switch takes two coil bits. The physical-channel maps in the binding table in **Hardware setup** (see **Power**) carry it; only the concrete `TrackOutput` / `SwitchOutput` / `OccupancyInput` driver reads them, and no other layer names a channel. |
| `safe state` | Every switch point motor is powered off and every block's `track voltage` is `0`. Canonical home **Power**, Safe state / fail-safe. |
| `detected block` | In Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware, every layout block is a detected block. Canonical home **Power**, Hardware interface boundary. |
| `pending-entry block` | The detected block a train's head is being held out of while it waits for that block to confirm occupied. A train has at most one, and only while the cap holds. Canonical home **Power**, Block occupancy detection. |

**Group E — Session-mode and operating-environment terms.** These name two different layers: the Editor/Operation session-mode split, and the three environments in which Operation may run. Canonical home is **Session mode and operating environment** under **Core Runtime Loop**.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `editor mode` / `operation mode` | The two session modes; a session is in exactly one (binary per session). Editor mode places and wires geometry; operation mode runs the railway — it brings up the runtime (`SimulationController` and its per-tick loop) and drives the trains. |
| `Simulation` | The algorithm-focused operating environment. It needs no Hardware Setup, derives occupancy and train motion from the model, and uses happy-path simulated interfaces whose writes succeed. It does not emulate chips, ports, buses, or wiring. |
| `Virtual Hardware` | The hardware-integration operating environment. It requires the same complete Hardware Setup as Real Hardware and runs the real chip drivers, bindings, HAL, and occupancy pipeline against an in-memory device. Its inputs, responses, disconnects, and failures are controllable. It never opens or energizes the physical controller. |
| `Real Hardware` | The physical-layout operating environment. It requires a complete, validated Hardware Setup. Every required interface is physical; a missing binding, chip, or device blocks activation or faults the session. It never substitutes a simulated interface. |
| `SimulationController` | The runtime engine shared by operation in all three environments. The `Simulation` in its name is historical; it is not a Simulation-environment-only object, and it is not itself a mode. |
| `running` / `stopped` | The two states of an operation session, held in `AppState.simulation_running`. Running advances the whole tick. Stopped runs only the observing steps; stopping drives the outputs to their `safe state`, and starting permits output again. A stopped session is not a frozen railway: in the two hardware environments the layout goes on carrying whatever is on it, and the detectors go on reporting it. Canonical home **Running and stopped** under **Core Runtime Loop**. |
| `authoring step` / `observing step` | The two halves every step of the tick falls into. An authoring step decides what happens next and drives the layout to make it happen; it runs only while the session is running. An observing step reads the detectors and makes the model agree with them; it cannot invent motion, so it runs running or stopped. Canonical home **Running and stopped** under **Core Runtime Loop**. |
| `stopped pass` | One turn of the runtime loop in a stopped Virtual Hardware or Real Hardware session: the observing steps and nothing else. A stopped Simulation session runs no such pass. Canonical home **Running and stopped** under **Core Runtime Loop**. |

## Canonical Entity Index

**Safety functions index**
