Audit them together when reviewing safety behavior: ATC limits and EB (**TrainController**: **ATC speed limit**, **EB workflow state machine**), flank protection (**Flank Protection Computation** plus the **Switch Entity** storage contract), the fatal physical-entry freeze (**Fatal physical-entry conflict procedure** in **Core Runtime Loop**), and the hardware safe state (**Power**, **Hardware interface boundary**).

## Units

**Units contract**

- All deceleration math is expressed in a single unit system. `SpeedProfile.deceleration_rate`, `emergency_brake_rate`, `friction_rate`, and `acceleration_rate` are all in `km/h/s`, and `TrainPhysics` and the controller braking-distance helpers consume them directly in those units (converting to `cm/s` / `cm/s^2` only through the model-scale helpers when integrating distance). There is no second deceleration rate in other units to reconcile: braking is driven entirely by the `SpeedProfile` rates, so no per-layer unit reinterpretation occurs.
- **Canonical stopped predicate.** One stopped predicate is used everywhere: `TrainController.is_stopped()`, comparing controller-owned `current_speed_kmh` against `STOPPED_SPEED_THRESHOLD_KMH = 0.1`. `STOPPED_SPEED_THRESHOLD_KMH` is the global "considered stopped" speed threshold, adjustable as `stopped_speed_threshold_kmh` in **Runtime settings**.
  - It is distinct from any ATC zero-speed limit. The "ATC limit" mentioned elsewhere in this document means the ATC-derived speed cap at distance 0 in the canonical lookahead — when that cap is `0` the ATC is granting no clearance distance.
  - Every consumer of a stop condition uses this same helper instead of introducing a layer-specific stop threshold: controller-reported stop completion, `TrainController.commands.power_off_cmd()`, `TrainController.commands.set_cab()`, `TrainController.commands.set_mode()`, and `TrainController.eb.release()`.

**Time sampling**

- v1 clock samples for a stored field are taken at the write site, never threaded as method or callback parameters. Whenever this document says `current_time` for a wall timestamp, it means `time.time()` sampled when the writer commits the write. Every writer of `last_status_updated_time`, a wall `started_at` / `finished_at`, or event `event_time` samples locally. A writer of a paired route-run timing transition also reads `AppState.operating_time` locally for the matching `_operating` field. Callers pass neither clock value into a write. When one writer records an event time and a related status timestamp in the same step, it samples `time.time()` once locally for both wall fields. This rule governs values written to a stored field; a pure predicate may take clock readings as parameters. `RouteTask.should_depart(now_wall, now_basis, …)` is the one such reader — Plan step `70c3` samples `time.time()` and `AppState.operating_time` locally before the call.
- Every absolute or persisted timestamp is a wall-clock instant. The runtime-only `started_at_operating` / `finished_at_operating` fields are monotonic duration anchors, not absolute timestamps; they are never persisted beyond the process, though they may be held in memory and serialized into UI-facing derived figures (see **Clocks**). Which pair a duration uses is decided by **Clocks** below.

**Clocks**

v1 keeps three clocks. Every duration in this document measures against exactly one of them. Absolute and persisted instants use wall time; runtime route timing may additionally store an operating-clock anchor beside its wall instant.

| Clock | Advances | Playback multiplier | Reset |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| wall | always | not applied | never; it is system time |
| `AppState.operating_time` | only while the session is running | applied | process start |
| `SimulationController.simulation_time` | only while the session is running | applied | process start, and whenever a session builds a new `SimulationController` |

- **Wall** is `time.time()`, system-time Unix seconds. It measures what the world does whether or not the app is running it, and it is the only clock an absolute instant may be written in. Wall fields such as `started_at`, `finished_at`, `created_at`, `last_edited_at`, `target_time`, and event `event_time` are sampled at their writer per **Time sampling** above; `_operating` fields are the explicitly named runtime-only exception because they are duration anchors rather than absolute instants.
- **`operating_time`** is monotonic seconds of operation since process start. Each running pass of the runtime loop adds that pass's wall delta multiplied by `simulation_speed`; a stopped pass adds nothing. It measures how long the app has been conducting, which is what a schedule holds against: a dwell serves its whole hold however long the operator was away, and serves it four times as fast at four times playback. It lives on `AppState` beside `simulation_running` and `simulation_speed`, so loading a layout does not reset it and only a process restart does.
- **`simulation_time`** is the variable physics integrates against. It adds the same wall delta multiplied by `simulation_speed`, capped per pass at `MAX_SIM_DELTA_SECONDS` (lives in `constants.py`) so one stalled pass cannot integrate a single large jump and drive a train past its speed limit. That cap makes it a safe integrator rather than a faithful clock — it discards real time under load, and discards more of it at higher multipliers — so no schedule measures against it. Its consumers are physics integration, the `run` task's window (`RouteTaskRun.run_elapsed_seconds`), and `Train.total_run_time_seconds` (see **Maintenance counters**), so "run 20 s" means 20 s of simulation.
- **An `operating_time` value never leaves the session.** It may be stored on an in-memory `RouteRun` / `RouteTaskRun` for duration arithmetic and for computing the server-owned elapsed figures a UI payload carries, but it is never written to a layout save, an **Event log** row, or another record that outlives the process. The raw anchors themselves are not serialized: the `tasks` projection served by the `GET /api/route-runs/<run_number>` detail endpoint (see **Data Flow To UI**) is the closed field list, and it carries only the derived `elapsed_basis_seconds`, never a raw `_operating` field. Everything persisted is written in wall time.
- **A client derives no durations.** A frontend renders the instants and the elapsed values a payload carries, and never computes an elapsed figure from its own clock (see **Data Flow To UI**, Elapsed values are server-owned).

**Safety margin globals**

**Why this shape.** Two values, not one, because the right standoff distance from a track-end (where overrun has no platform interaction) is different from the right standoff distance at a platform stop (where overrun affects passenger boarding). One global per terminus type captures the operational distinction without forcing each route or block to author its own value. Putting both values inside `TrainController` lookahead computation gives one canonical projection that ATC, ATO, and stop-completion all read. Other layers consume the projected boundary rather than the raw margin number.

- The controller safety margin is two distinct global values, not a single tunable. Both are owned by `TrainController` lookahead computation and are not authored on routes, paths, or per-block fields. Both are adjustable fields in **Runtime settings**.
  - `TRACK_END_SAFETY_MARGIN_CM`: applied when the authority-end block is bounded by a track-end / dead-end / non-station authority terminus.
  - `PLATFORM_SAFETY_MARGIN_CM`: applied when the authority-end block is the resolved terminal block of a platform stop.
- `TrainController` lookahead is the single computation site for these margins. When building the authority-boundary projection in `get_lookahead()`, the controller finds the terminal block entry for `authority_end_block_id`, projects the authority-end block's forward boundary in that directed terminal frame, and counts back from that edge by the selected safety margin to build the ATC/ATO speed curve. ATC is intentionally not trying to drive the train all the way to the physical edge of the cleared/authorized block. This projection is a braking and diagnostics calculation only. It is not route-authored stop-position data and is not a route completion tolerance. Other layers (dispatcher, route, physics, signals) must not re-derive or duplicate this margin; they consume the lookahead-projected boundary instead.

## Runtime settings

v1 exposes a fixed set of ATC, ATO, and route-timing calibration values as settings an operator can change from a live session, with no restart and no code change. `RuntimeConfig` (`runtime_config.py`) is the single authoritative store of the current value of every tunable field; `GET` / `PUT /api/settings` (`routes/settings.py`) is the only entry point that reads or writes it. A `PUT` also mirrors the accepted value onto every module attribute the consuming code reads it from (see below), so a live module attribute is a mirror of `RuntimeConfig`, never a second source of truth.

Each field seeds at process start from a fixed code default — for example, `caution_speed_limit_kmh` seeds from `constants.CAUTION_SPEED_LIMIT_KMH`. A `PUT` writes the accepted value onto the `RuntimeConfig` field and onto every module attribute the consuming code reads that value from, so code that reads the value as a live module attribute observes the change on its next read. The store is in-memory only, per **Out of Scope** (Persistence / save-load of runtime state): a process restart reseeds every field from its code default. Like every admin/API request, a `PUT` is applied between ticks on the runtime's single thread (**Out of Scope**, Multi-threaded runtime), so it never races the per-tick stage loop.

**Settings REST API**

| Endpoint | Body / parameters | Behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/settings` | none | Returns `{"settings": {...}}` with every field's current value. |
| `PUT /api/settings` | `{"settings": {field: value, ...}}`, or a flat `{field: value, ...}` body (a `"settings"` key, if present, is used as the update dict; otherwise the whole body is) | Applies the accepted subset of the request per **Validation** below, then returns `{"status": "success", "settings": {...}}` with every field's current value — the same shape as `GET`, not only the fields the request changed. |

**Validation**

- An unknown field name is ignored: it does not fail the request and is not reported as an error.
- A `null` value for a known field is ignored, leaving that field unchanged.
- An accepted field's incoming value is coerced to that field's own type. A value that cannot be coerced is ignored, leaving that field unchanged; every other field in the same request is still applied. Every v1 tunable is `int` or `float` (see **Tunable fields** below).
- After coercion, every numeric value must be finite and satisfy these field rules; a value that fails is ignored exactly like a coercion failure, while unrelated valid fields in the same request still apply:
  - `overspeed_warn_threshold_kmh >= 0` and `overspeed_eb_threshold_kmh > overspeed_warn_threshold_kmh`, evaluated against the merged post-request pair. If a request would violate the relation, ignore both threshold writes from that request.
  - `atc_signal_lookahead_blocks >= 1`, `lookahead_sample_count >= 1`, `idle_hold_release_ticks >= 1`, `idle_hold_cooldown_ticks >= 0`, `waypoint_lookahead_blocks >= 0`, and `notification_retention_rows >= 1`.
  - `ato_speed_tolerance_min_kmh > 0`, `ato_speed_tolerance_max_kmh >= ato_speed_tolerance_min_kmh`, and `ato_speed_tolerance_ratio > 0`, with the min/max relation evaluated against the merged post-request pair. If a request would reverse the pair, ignore both tolerance-bound writes from that request.
  - `stopped_speed_threshold_kmh > 0`, `min_lookahead_cm > 0`, and `caution_speed_limit_kmh > 0`.
  - `ato_speed_margin_kmh`, `lookahead_headroom`, `brake_deadband_kmh`, `track_end_safety_margin_cm`, `platform_safety_margin_cm`, and `delay_class_on_time_tolerance_seconds` must each be `>= 0`.

**Tunable fields**

Every field below is a top-level key in the `GET` / `PUT /api/settings` payload, named exactly as its `RuntimeConfig` field (snake_case). Where a field backs a value this document already names elsewhere, the module-global name and its canonical home are given and the operational meaning of that value stays defined there, not restated here. Where no such home exists elsewhere in this document, the row's own description is the field's complete definition.

*ATC Computer (`train_controller/atc.py`, `train_controller/__init__.py`):*

| Field | Type | Default | Controls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `overspeed_eb_threshold_kmh` | `float` | `10.0` | Margin, in km/h, above the ATC speed limit at which ATC escalates to EB (`OVERSPEED_EB_THRESHOLD_KMH`; see **Controller tick order**, step `914f`). |
| `overspeed_warn_threshold_kmh` | `float` | `5.0` | Margin, in km/h, above the ATC speed limit at which ATC emits a diagnostic overspeed warning (`OVERSPEED_WARN_THRESHOLD_KMH`; see **Controller tick order**, step `914f`). |
| `atc_signal_lookahead_blocks` | `int` | `3` | Scan depth, in blocks, for `controller.atc.signal_lookahead_blocks` (`ATC_SIGNAL_LOOKAHEAD_BLOCKS`). |

*ATO Computer (`train_controller/ato.py`, `train_controller/speed_curves.py`):*

| Field | Type | Default | Controls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ato_speed_margin_kmh` | `float` | `3.0` | Margin, in km/h, the ATO operational speed limit stays below the ATC speed limit (`ATO_SPEED_MARGIN_KMH`). |
| `ato_speed_tolerance_max_kmh` | `float` | `2.0` | Upper bound of the speed-tracking tolerance band ATO holds around its target speed (`ATO_SPEED_TOLERANCE_MAX`). |
| `ato_speed_tolerance_min_kmh` | `float` | `0.05` | Lower bound of that tolerance band (`ATO_SPEED_TOLERANCE_MIN`). |
| `ato_speed_tolerance_ratio` | `float` | `0.1` | Tolerance band width as a ratio of the reference speed, clamped to the min/max above (`ATO_SPEED_TOLERANCE_RATIO`). |
| `lookahead_headroom` | `float` | `0.5` | Headroom factor in the braking-lookahead distance ATO samples ahead (`LOOKAHEAD_HEADROOM`): `max(min_lookahead_cm, travel_this_tick * (1 + lookahead_headroom))`. |
| `min_lookahead_cm` | `float` | `5.0` | Minimum braking-lookahead distance ATO samples ahead (`MIN_LOOKAHEAD_CM`). |
| `lookahead_sample_count` | `int` | `4` | Number of points ATO samples along the braking-lookahead curve (`LOOKAHEAD_SAMPLE_COUNT`). |
| `brake_deadband_kmh` | `float` | `0.3` | Speed-over-target band inside which ATO holds the current brake notch rather than tightening it (`BRAKE_DEADBAND_KMH`). |

*Stop and safety-margin thresholds:*

| Field | Type | Default | Controls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `stopped_speed_threshold_kmh` | `float` | `0.1` | `STOPPED_SPEED_THRESHOLD_KMH`, the canonical stopped predicate — see **Units**, Units contract. |
| `track_end_safety_margin_cm` | `float` | `25.0` | `TRACK_END_SAFETY_MARGIN_CM` — see **Units**, Safety margin globals. |
| `platform_safety_margin_cm` | `float` | `5.0` | `PLATFORM_SAFETY_MARGIN_CM` — see **Units**, Safety margin globals. |
| `caution_speed_limit_kmh` | `float` | `40.0` | `CAUTION_SPEED_LIMIT_KMH` — see **TrainController**, ATC speed limit. |

*Route timing (`route_executor.py`):*

| Field | Type | Default | Controls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `idle_hold_release_ticks` | `int` | `30` | `IDLE_HOLD_RELEASE_TICKS`, the idle-hold no-progress tick budget — see **Route And RouteExecutor**, Planning Kernel step `66aa`. |
| `idle_hold_cooldown_ticks` | `int` | `20` | `IDLE_HOLD_COOLDOWN_TICKS`, the post-release acquisition-skip window — same home. |
| `waypoint_lookahead_blocks` | `int` | `3` | `WAYPOINT_LOOKAHEAD_BLOCKS`, how few block resources may remain ahead of the train head before Plan arms the next target while the current `waypoint` is still unserved — see **Route And RouteExecutor**, Planning Kernel step `66aa`, **Waypoint lookahead**. Raising it makes trains hold more track ahead of themselves and brake less at waypoints; lowering it frees track for other runs sooner. Tune it together with `idle_hold_release_ticks`, which claws back exactly the kind of unentered hold this setting creates. |
| `delay_class_on_time_tolerance_seconds` | `float` | `30.0` | `DELAY_CLASS_ON_TIME_TOLERANCE_SECONDS`, the tolerance band around a task's expected-travel `task_time` inside which a served walk-position grades `on_time` — see **Route And RouteExecutor**, `RouteTaskRun` schema, the `delay_class` row. |

*Event stream (`notification_center.py`):*

| Field | Type | Default | Controls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `notification_retention_rows` | `int` | `10000` | `NOTIFICATION_RETENTION_ROWS`, how many of the most recent events `NotificationCenter` keeps before dropping the oldest — see **Core Runtime Loop**, **Runtime notifications**, Retention. Raising it lets an operator scroll further back through a long session at the cost of memory and event-log file size; lowering it trims both. |

**Why this shape**

- One store and one endpoint pair give v1 a single place to read or change every calibration value, without a separate admin surface per consumer.
- Coercing to the field's existing type, rather than validating against a declared schema, keeps a field's type anchored to the value already seeded from code, so a field can never end up holding a type its consuming code does not expect.
- **Runtime settings**, **Hardware Setup**, and the **selected operating environment** are distinct surfaces changed only through the application's API (the general rule in **Out of Scope**, Hand-authored config files or env vars for settings). Runtime settings reach the running session on the consumer's next read and reseed from code defaults after restart. Hardware Setup is the persisted controller/chip/wiring description stored with its layout; Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware build a session's chips from it at activation, and resolve the per-write values named in **Hardware setup**, **A binding is read per write** on every write. The selected environment is stored separately, per **Session mode and operating environment**. Changing the environment, or the captured part of the setup, never rewires a running session in place; activation performs the safe stop and session rebuild.

## Scope

Primary files reviewed:

- `simulation.py`
- `train.py`
- `train_controller/` (package: `__init__.py` façade plus `atc.py`, `ato.py`, `commands.py`, `eb.py`, `manual.py`, `notifications.py`, `ops.py`, `path_projection.py`, `physics_sync.py`, `route_hooks.py`)
- `train_physics.py`
- `railway_platform.py`
- `station.py`
- `block.py`
- `block_manager.py`
- `block_grouping_manager.py`
- `segment.py`
- `segment_geometry_manager.py`
- `path.py`
- `path_dispatcher.py`
- `route_executor.py`
- `train_route.py`
- `track.py`
- `switch.py`
- `network.py`
- `speed_profile.py`
- `block_power.py`

Terminology:

- `path`: a movement authority that the dispatcher reserves between blocks.
- `route`: a higher-level travel plan. It is a list of `stop`, `waypoint`, `dwell`, and `run` tasks that each resolve to a concrete block target or, for `run`, a direction-seed target.
- `route run`: the running, per-train copy of an assigned route. It points to one shared `Route` definition but holds that train's own changing state: waypoint cursors, the current resolved target status, dwell timing, and which active path it is tied to. The current code may still name the class `RouteExecutionState`, but the canonical concept is `RouteRun`.
- `block`: the power + occupancy + reservation unit. A switch-free connected run of one or more `segment`s that share one power feed (one `track voltage`) and admit one train at a time. It is the unit the dispatcher reserves and the train occupies. The current code carries this concept across two classes: `PowerDistrict` (which groups blocks onto one power feed) plus the occupancy and reservation half of `Block`. The canonical `Block` unifies them — it is that power grouping, now grouping `segment`s through `segment_ids`, and it owns the occupancy and reservation state lifted up out of what the current code calls `Block`.
- `segment`: a group of tiles with one unified geometry — it owns `ordered_tiles`, `length_cm`, `speed_limit_kmh`, `min_radius_cm`, and `grade_percent`. A segment stores no occupancy, reservation, availability, or power state; those live on its owning `Block`. One `segment` maps to many real-world rail pieces that share its geometry.
- `tile`: one physical rail tile on the grid, identified by its `(x, y)` coordinate and its local 6-bit geometry. A tile is not a group of tiles and is not a block; a `Segment` owns an ordered list of tile entries.
- `platform`: the real, physical place on the track where a train stops. Dispatcher targets are always written against a concrete block traversal frame, never against a logical station group. When a waypoint resolves through station or platform data, the platform supplies the linked blocks and the traversal context used to work out that block target.
- `station`: a logical group of one or more platforms, used only to pick a stop at the route level. When a route targets a station-level stop, `RouteExecutor` must first pick one concrete platform for that attempt, then build the dispatcher request from that platform.

## Out of Scope

This section lists features and concerns that v1 leaves out on purpose. It makes those gaps explicit, so a reader (AI agent or human) can tell that a missing thing is a decision, not an oversight.

An Out of Scope entry is not a wishlist and not a promise to build the thing later. It records that someone asked the question and the answer for v1 was "no." Three rules govern what goes here:

1. **Out of Scope is a clear "no," not a brainstorm.** An entry goes here only when a designer has actively decided to leave a concern out of v1. If no one has raised the question, do not guess.
2. **Out of Scope is not a graveyard.** A concern that was once in scope and then removed does not belong here. It goes nowhere, by the "removed is removed" rule in the Authoring Rules. Only concerns that were never in scope belong here.
3. **Out of Scope does not promise v2.** Listing something here is not a roadmap. v2 will have its own scope discussion.

| Concern | v1 stance | Why Out of Scope for v1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Multi-threaded runtime | No general multi-threaded runtime; all API/UI/admin requests and ordinary hardware transactions run between ticks on the runtime thread. The one exception is the Real Hardware safety-only `OutputWatchdog` daemon described under **Power**. | The "always recompute live" projections (`lookahead`, `received_path_plan`, derived properties) work only because model changes happen between ticks. The watchdog performs only the documented safe-state hardware writes and never reads or writes runtime model state (see **Power**, Loss-of-control watchdog). |
| Persistent / cross-tick lookahead or projection caching | Recompute live on every read across ticks | Performance is fine for v1 train counts. Cross-tick caching adds a place that can go stale, and v1 does not need it. A within-tick memo is allowed as an implementation detail: it is thrown away before the next tick and shadow-checked to match a live recompute (see **Lookahead is a pure derived value**). That memo is not the cross-tick caching this row rules out. |
| Persistence / save-load of runtime state | In-memory only | No use case in v1. |
| Schema migration, backward-compat shims, dual-write transitional fields | None | v1 is the first design; "v1 means v1." |
| Unobservable mechanical outcomes after successful I/O — a signal lamp fails, EB hardware fails to engage, or a point motor accepts a pulse but mechanically sticks | Not inferred, verified, or recovered in v1; the documented commanded state remains the software authority | A point motor reports no position, so software cannot know that the points stuck and must not invent auto-retry, recovery, or a rollback of `Switch.position`. This does not exclude hardware-interface faults: transaction refusal, disconnect, invalid detector/readback data, and failure to reach safe state are in scope. Virtual Hardware injects those observable device/interface failures, and Virtual Hardware and Real Hardware both enter the fail-closed hardware-failure lifecycle defined under **Power**, Hardware interface boundary. |
| Hardware sensors as a fault-detection, verification, or recovery source | Block current detection sets block occupancy (in scope). Using any sensor to detect a mechanical fault, verify a commanded action, or trigger mechanical recovery is out | The block current detector is the authority for block occupancy (see **Power**, Block occupancy detection). The commanded `Switch.position` is the authority for switch alignment, and v1 reads no switch-position sensor. The observable interface failures named in the row above are still fatal; what v1 does not do is infer an unobservable mechanical outcome from some unrelated sensor. |
| Collision modeling | Two trains in one block is a fatal runtime failure via `SimulationController.enter_failed_runtime(...)`, not a physics interaction | Physics does not model contact. |
| Reverse motion under cab | Forbidden; wrong-direction cab forces the distance-0 ATC limit to `0` | Physics never produces backward motion. |
| Authorization / RBAC / multi-user model | All API requests trusted | No user accounts in v1. |
| Logging beyond `NotificationCenter` | `NotificationCenter` is the only runtime sink | Component-local logging is forbidden by design. A component may write one last-resort line to the standard library logger when `NotificationCenter.emit(...)` itself raises, because a failed emit must not be silent. That fallback carries no routine trace: it fires only on the emit failure it reports. |
| Idempotency keys, retry/dedup wrappers on API commands | None | Single-threaded between-tick drain makes them unnecessary. |
| Health checks, metrics export, distributed tracing | None | Operators read `NotificationCenter` and live projections. |
| `Path` / `RouteRun` retention caps | Unbounded for v1 | Retention policy will be added when leak becomes measurable. The runtime event stream is capped separately; see **Runtime notifications**, Retention. |
| Per-train safety margin tuning | Two global settings (`TRACK_END_SAFETY_MARGIN_CM`, `PLATFORM_SAFETY_MARGIN_CM`; see **Runtime settings**) | Per-train tuning is a future calibration concern. |
| Per-tile speed limits beyond `Segment.speed_limit_kmh` | Segment-scoped only | Sub-segment speed restrictions are not modeled. |
| Live editor mutation during operation | Forbidden; Editor and Operation are binary session modes (the split and Operation's three operating environments are defined in **Session mode and operating environment**) | Geometry stability is required by every "always recompute live" rule. |
| Multi-network in one process | One network per `SimulationController` instance | Cross-network interaction has no use case in v1. |
| Re-running the simulation engine (true time-travel of the live model) | None | Visual replay over the recorded **Event log** is in scope (see **Event log**); re-simulating the model forward or backward is not. |
| Schedule adherence / ETA / SLA tracking | None | Only the reporting layer built on top of the stored timing fields is out of scope: ETA projection, SLA dashboards, and lateness alerts. The timestamps under it are not just informational. `RouteTaskRun.started_at` / `finished_at` are inputs to the route-progress cursor, written and read per the **RouteTaskRun schema** and **Route-run state** contracts. The per-walk-position `delay_class` value computed by `RouteRun.advance_walk_position(...)` is also in scope. |
| Pluggable physics or speed-profile backends | None | `SpeedProfile` is the single calibration model. |
| Route-level runtime progress summary | None; `RouteRun` is the only runtime progress store | No route-level summary shape has a v1 consumer; UI and API read per-train `RouteRun` progress. |
| Hand-authored config files or env vars for settings | None | Every v1 setting is changed only through the application's own API, never by hand-editing a file or setting an environment variable. **Runtime settings** hold entirely in memory (reseeded from code defaults on restart). **Hardware setup** (**Power**) is written by its own API to an app-managed JSON file so the wiring survives the session rebuild that applies it — persistence the app owns and writes only through the API, the same way it owns the layout save files, which carry a copy of that setup (see **Power**, Saved with the layout). The selected operating environment is stored separately from layout wiring (see **Session mode and operating environment**). |
| Async/streaming notification protocols (websocket, SSE, push) | None | Frontend reads `NotificationCenter` via polling/projection. |
| Cross-tick latch durability across process restart | None | Process state is volatile. |
| Watchdogs / alert notifications for stuck trains, no-progress | None | Operators read live diagnostics from `lookahead.speed_curves[0].atc_limit_reason_code` and the latest error event for that train (see **Error events**). (The hardware fail-safe watchdog that cuts power to the track and point motors on loss of control is a different mechanism, specified in **Power**, Hardware interface boundary.) |
| Operator removal of an app-controlled train | Not specified in v1; do not implement it | Surface, teardown order, and pending-latch handling are not specified for v1. Retiring an unidentified train is a different thing and is in scope: the runtime built that train for itself, and **Power**, Unidentified trains owns its teardown order. |
| Bulk operations (multi-train commands, batch route assignment) | None | Operators issue per-train commands one at a time. |

## Authoring Rules

These rules apply to every edit of this document. Reviewers must reject any patch that breaks them.

1. **This document is v1. It contains no "removed in v1," "legacy," "deprecated," or "no longer used" text anywhere.** If a field, method, state, or flag is not part of v1, it must not appear here at all. If a row is missing from a schema table, that absence is the statement that the thing does not exist. Any patch that adds tombstone language ("removed in v1," "no longer used," "kept for compatibility," "deprecated," and the like) is incomplete and must be rejected.

2. **No cross-reference drift.** When any rule changes (ownership, a payload field, a state transition, a callback signature, a latch consumer, a recovery gate), every place in the document that refers to the old rule must be found and updated in the same edit. A patch that updates only one section is incomplete. Reviewers must reject any patch that leaves two sites describing the same rule in different ways.

3. **One canonical home per concept.** Each shared schema, latch, predicate, and helper has exactly one canonical home: the single place where it is defined. Every other site refers to it by name. If two sites describe the same concept in different ways, the patch is incomplete.

4. **Latches are described in the canonical Latch Table.** Every latch in the document must appear in the Latch Table (in the Core Runtime Loop section). Each entry lists the writer stage and entity, the consumer stage and entity, and any conditions that let it survive across ticks. Other sections may summarize why a workflow writes or consumes the latch, but must name the Latch Table as the authority and must not introduce a different writer, consumer, gate, or lifetime.

5. **Stage boundaries are described in the canonical Observe, Plan, and Action Table.** The Observe, Plan, and Action Table (in the Core Runtime Loop section) is the authority for which entity acts in which stage. Overview and procedure sections may summarize the ordered work so the document remains readable, but must point to the Observe, Plan, and Action Table and must not define a different owner or stage.

6. **No single-use-case branches in shared contracts.** If a workflow step is written as a branch for one specific case, it must either be rewritten as a general mechanism, or be clearly marked as the one case that the general mechanism cannot cover.

7. **Diagnostic-only distinctions belong on events, not enums.** A distinction that no code acts on must be carried in the `NotificationCenter` event payload, not added as a new enum value on a control-flow type. An enum value written by a genuinely different code path (and that could become functional) may stay. An enum value that exists only so the UI can show a different label must move to the event payload.

8. **Requirement keywords are binding.** `must` and `must not` state required contract behavior. `may` states allowed behavior. `should` is not used in a contract statement: a sentence that states a contract uses `must`, and one that grants permission uses `may`. Readers, including code-generation agents, treat these keywords literally.

## Logic Review Checklist

**Review checklist**

- Is the controller reading the canonical **received_path_plan schema** projection when path-end stopping matters?
- Does each `resource_sequence` entry carry the ordered `path_tiles` slice using the canonical **path_tile entry schema**, with explicit `entry_edge` / `exit_edge` on both the resource entry and each nested tile entry? Controller lookahead and UI geometry need those edges.
- Is controller lookahead the only source of target speed and speed-limit reason?
- Does an **Auto profiling** step time the head between two confirmed block entries — into the measured block and into the one after it — rather than from the moment power was applied? A one-sided interval measures an unknown start position inside the first block and carries the detector's confirmation lag as a bias.
- Does an **Auto profiling** step collect equal numbers of crossings in each direction, turning the train around itself with `TrainController.commands.set_cab(...)` once it is stopped, and average them into one sample? Crossings weighted toward one direction carry the stretch's grade into the curve.
- Does a **Speed calibration** pass hold its measured samples until the operator picks **Save to this locomotive** or **Promote to model**, and does Promote clear `power_speed_curve` and `calibrated_at` from the calibrated train's instance profile in the same commit that writes them to the model profile (see **What commit writes**)?
- In manual mode, does ATC enforce the end of the assigned path as a hard stop through the controller lookahead authority-boundary stop?
- Can any path-complete event still fire while the train is braking or creeping toward the terminal authority end? It must not: release waits for the **Stop-arrival check**, which requires `TrainController.is_stopped_at_authority_end()` (its full condition — stopped, `RUNNING_MOVING`, no EB, live authority, and an `AUTHORITY_STOP` reason code at distance `0` — is defined under **TrainController**, Read accessors).
- Does `controller.ato.compute_handle(delta_seconds)` read only the current tick's canonical lookahead payload, not stale scalar fields?
- Does `RouteExecutor` read controller state rather than mirrored runtime state on `Train`?
- Does `RouteExecutor` resolve waypoint-authored block-relative direction preferences into one concrete `requested_destination_direction` before calling `PathDispatcher.create_path()` or `PathDispatcher.extend_path()`? It must do this without relying on platform-level direction fields.
- Do `RouteExecutor` and `PathDispatcher` use the same shared pathfinder/current-span workflow, including the same deterministic tie-break, for start-side and platform-end selection?
- Do `RouteExecutor` and `PathDispatcher` get head/tail/current-span data only through `TrainController.get_current_span()`? `TrainPhysics` must stay the movement-update producer, and `TrainController` must stay the writer for controller-owned span state.
- For a pass-through waypoint whose resolved target block is already physically covered, does Plan's covered-task index advance skip it? And does it finish a covered stop once the train is stopped, has no active path, and has its head in the destination block (the head-anchored covered-stop rule), with dwell entry and exit then running normally?
- Does `PathDispatcher.create_path(...)` report the head-covered-destination violation (`invalid_request`) only when the requested destination already contains the train head? A block covered by the tail alone remains the explicit turnaround-target carve-out; head-covered stops are left to Plan's covered-task index advance.
- Is a resource the path already holds rejected during both `create_path()` and `extend_path()`, while a block the train has passed and released stays available to acquire again?
- In `best_effort` mode, does the system keep one live `path_id`, extend `resource_sequence` in place, and avoid treating a truncated-but-live authority as a creation failure?
- Does `best_effort` creation fail instead of storing a live authority when the head is on a switch and no forward block can be acquired?
- Does `best_effort` truncation hold the live authority one block back, instead of stopping it on a two-way block entered straight off a switch (the junction-fouling exclusion)? One-way blocks, and two-way blocks in `CAUTION`, stay exempt, so trains may pack tight up to them.
- When a best-effort authority must truncate short of its target, does it prefer a holding-point block (`Block.is_holding_point`) as the scale-back target over the switch-based junction-fouling back-off? It falls back to the switch rule only when the acquirable prefix has no holding point, and it must still honor the reversal-trap exclusion as an absolute floor.
- Does a stalled, truncated best-effort hold release in both cases: after the `IDLE_HOLD_RELEASE_TICKS` no-progress timeout (`error.origin = "idle_hold_release"`), and as soon as the tick's **Contention snapshot** shows a strictly-higher-priority run blocked on a block this hold owns but has not entered (`error.origin = "contention_release"`)? Both use the same system-replan mechanics while retaining distinct diagnostics.
- Does **Meet coordination** compute a per-tick advisory meet ceiling (never a reservation)? It caps a contender's **acquired authority** (via `acquisition_cap_block_id`, leaving `requested_destination_block_id` and `resolved_target` at the route target) at a holding point before a contested zone, or at the zone's far entry when capacity allows, so the held train stops at the ceiling without completing its path. All acquisition still runs through the interlocked manager path, and the assignment is re-derived each tick rather than stored.
- Does `PathDispatcher` resolve controller progress reports against active authority by `train_id`, from its own database rather than from physics or train mirrors? `cancel_path(path_id, ...)` is path-keyed instead, because the caller passes the id it just read from `active_path_id_by_train(train_id)`; `try_complete_active_path(train_id)`, the other terminal call, stays train-keyed. Delayed release of a still-occupied block or switch resolves from the resource itself after authority release.
- Are multi-train routes using per-train `RouteRun` objects as the only canonical progress store, with no route-level runtime progress summary fields?
- Does Plan's covered-task index advance loop resolve `PlatformTarget` and `StationTarget` task targets as needed, advance past already-covered `task_kind == "waypoint"` tasks, and avoid advancing past `task_kind == "stop"` tasks just because the target block is covered?
- On active-run plan replacement (operator retargeting and route swap use abort + new assignment, never a `route_id` rewrite) and on live-path target re-resolution: does `RouteExecutor` clear the affected `path_cancelled` handoff state through the canonical write contract, and replan from the train's current physical position with no synthetic progress jumps? It must keep target identity in `task_runs[i].resolved_target` rather than in `current_route_status`, and must keep no stored planning cursor outside `_find_next_task_target(train_id)`.
- Does a live authority ever extend past an unserved `stop` or `run` target? It must not, per the **Authority termination rule**. The currently armed target is always the authority terminal; unlike a `waypoint`, an unserved `stop` or `run` may not be superseded by arming a later target.
- Does Plan arm the next target while the current `waypoint` is still unserved once fewer than `WAYPOINT_LOOKAHEAD_BLOCKS` blocks remain ahead of the head, and does it arm one target at a time so each acquisition is direction-filtered on its own terminal?
- Is "has this authority reached that target?" always asked through `Path.reaches_target(block_id)` rather than by comparing the block against `authority_end_block_id`, outside the **Stop-arrival check**'s terminal-block equality test (which the **Authority termination rule** makes exact for an unserved `stop`)? An authority that runs past a target has reached it.
- Is the requested target absent from the stored `Path` record — an argument in, an echo in the result, and stored once route-side in `RouteRun.task_runs[i].resolved_target`?
- Does the route decide task completion and the dispatcher only release? No dispatcher-side acceptance test may gate a task being finished.
- Does stop arrival require the **Stop-arrival check**? And do controller deviation cases produce a `cancel_path` event with `deviation = true`, carrying one `ErrorRecord` (`origin = "out_of_sequence"`) on the event payload?
- Does the normal `CAUTION -> FREE` reevaluation require the forward neighbour (reached by the connectivity walk from `block.caution.exit_edge`) to be non-`OCCUPIED`, fire from exactly the three closed triggers (`on_block_tail_vacated()`, `on_switch_position_changed(...)`, and `release_train_occupancy(train_id)`), and read no controller or `travel_direction` state, while still allowing the explicit completion-time `force` exception in `release_path_block_reservations(..., completed=True)` and the **Opposing-traversal caution clear** in `reserve_blocks_for_path(...)` (same end keeps the caution, other end clears it)? (`occupied_by` is always `None` in `CAUTION` — guaranteed by `on_block_tail_vacated()` clearing it — so a separate non-occupied check on the CAUTION block itself is vacuous. `reserved_by_path` is explicitly not a gating condition; if `block.caution` has cleared but `reserved_by_path` remains set, the computed block state is `RESERVED`, not `FREE`.)
- Can any completion or cancellation path still unlock a block or switch that the train physically occupies at full stop?
- Does `TrainController.eb.release()` clear only the EB condition, leaving the ordinary state owner to preserve `RUNNING_AT_STATION` or move a powered stopped authority-free controller to `READY`, and does any cancelled run restart only through ordinary recovery, fresh path creation, and `TrainController.depart()`?
- Does `TrainController.eb.release()` reject a manual `power_percent` driver whose `manual.manual_power_percent` is still non-zero, so no train departs on a percentage retained from before the EB stop? And does `TrainController.commands.set_mode(...)` clear that same retained percentage, so it cannot survive a mode change either?
- Do train-owned flank-protection claims record `source_switch_id` so tail-vacate can release only the protection created from the vacated main switch?
- Is a block's commanded voltage signed per block by the traversal direction the train runs through it, with rail polarity resolved only below the hardware interface through the `block_track` binding's `reversed` flag (see **A block voltage carries a direction**)?
- Is a queued block driven to `0` only when it fails all four emission-set terms — absent from `current_span.occupied_blocks`, no `Block.occupied_by` naming that controller's train, not the `pending-entry block`, not the `next reserved block` — with a still-reserved block that is not the train's `next reserved block` allowed to drop (see **Power**, De-energize against the same source)?
- Are coil ports, rail polarity (`reversed`), and rail-feed (`switch_track_source`) resolved fresh on every write, while the chips, transport, and range-checking maps stay fixed at Virtual Hardware / Real Hardware activation (see **A binding is read per write**)?
- Does block-occupancy attribution refuse to credit a moving train with a block behind it — matching a newly OCCUPIED block only to a train it is physically approaching — while a stopped train's attribution stays permissive (see **Power**, Attribution)?
- Does `SimulationController.enter_hardware_failure(...)` remain the single writer of `hardware_failure = True` and `clear_hardware_failure()` the single clearer, mirroring `enter_failed_runtime(...)` / `clear_failed_runtime()` (see **Hardware I/O failure**)?
- Does an unidentified train's `train_id` retire into the never-reuse set on the gap-hold teardown, and does adoption re-key an existing unidentified train in place rather than deleting and recreating it (see **Unidentified trains**, The gap and Adoption)?
- Does `SpeedCalibration` reject opening a **Lighting-voltage calibration** run unless the train is placed and stopped, `READY`, in `manual` mode with a cab selected, has no assigned route, and has no other calibration run already open? Does it reject continuing an open run — discarding the candidate through `cancel_lighting(train_id)` — the moment the train leaves `READY`, leaves `manual` control mode, loses its cab, is powered off, has EB activated, or is assigned a route (note that a stopped train continuing to stand still does not itself end a run), and does a `clear_failed_runtime()` fatal-halt clear also end it?
- Does a `task_kind == "run"` task finish only through Plan step `6a0d` — timer from playback-scaled `delta_seconds`, `begin_service_stop()`, a `run_complete = True` release with `error = None`, then `consume_service_stop()` and `advance_walk_position(...)` once stopped with no authority — and never through head entry, coverage, arrival, or the cancellation callback?
- Is a `missing_target` task skipped inline by whichever of steps `c481` / `592a` saw it (writing `finished_at`, `origin = "task_skipped"`), while a `target_unavailable` task is waited on at step `66aa` (`origin = "planning_failed"`, nothing written), and does an all-broken `CIRCULAR` / `ROUND_TRIP` walk set `no_reachable_task` rather than skipping forever?
- Does a fresh `RouteRun` seed its starting walk-position per `RouteStartMode` (`FIRST` / `NEAREST` / `SPECIFIC`), pre-finishing the skipped prefix to `RouteRun.started_at` with `delay_class = None` and no appends, with the per-assignment start-mode input consumed one-shot?
- Is `OutputSafety.enter_safe_state()` the one entry point for the safe-state sequence, do all runtime-thread callers reach it through `SimulationController.enter_output_safe_state()` (which advances `safe_state_generation` exactly once, with the Real Hardware `OutputWatchdog` as the sole direct-call exception), does it de-energize every point motor through `SwitchPowerController.de_energize_device_outputs()` before zeroing every block voltage through `BlockPowerController.zero_device_outputs()` — both non-recording device writes that touch no recorded model field — and does it attempt every chip even after one fails rather than stopping at the first failure (see **Power**, Safe state / fail-safe)? Does `SimulationController.enter_output_safe_state()` then synchronously reconcile the recorded model fields to match for every runtime-thread caller, and does the watchdog path instead reconcile them at trip-record consumption on the runtime thread's next tick?
- Is a block bound in both occupancy maps read from whichever source the commanded-voltage drive zone selects, and does the lighting zone report clear only after `LIGHTING_CLEAR_HOLD_READS` consecutive reads on which that zone's deciding source reads clear (see **Power**, Occupancy source follows drive state)?
- Is digital-detector polarity resolved entirely inside `OccupancyInput`, so the boolean it returns always means `current present` regardless of chip wiring, with no polarity branch anywhere above the interface (see **Power**, Detector polarity is resolved in the hardware layer)?
- Is a ghosted train's `presence_unknown` recomputed and overwritten on every Observe pass rather than latched, is the train excluded from the energized set and all four de-energize-drain terms on the same rising edge, does that same edge's `BlockManager.release_train_occupancy(...)` call queue the just-cleared holdings through `BlockManager`'s own writer, and does the ordinary per-tick `TrainPhysics` emission-set difference — not an Observe write — queue the rest of its prior emission set, including its retained span, into `TrainPhysics`'s `_blocks_dropped_from_energized` store (see **Power**, Ghosted trains, De-energize against the same source, and Block power-controller role)?

**Notes**

- Ordinary switch release happens when the train tail vacates the switch tile, not on full path completion. `TrainController.on_physics_updated(span_update)` reports the vacated resource in `tail_vacated_resources`, and `PathDispatcher.on_controller_progress(report)` releases it through `ResourceCoordinator.release_tail_vacated(..., route)`: blocks go through `BlockManager.on_block_tail_vacated(...)`, while switches go through `SwitchManager.on_switch_tail_vacated(switch_id, train_id, route)`, which removes the matching `Switch.physical_occupants[route]` entry first and then, only when no entries remain for that train, releases train-owned protection sourced from that vacated switch through `Switch.release_train_protection_from(...)`. The neighbour-side `source_switch_id` filter protects claims created by other occupied main switches. Both completion and cancellation must respect physical occupancy: if a switch is still physically occupied, its train-owned protection stays in place until the later tail-vacate event.
- `assigned_path_id` is a read-only derived property of `received_path_plan.path_id` on `TrainController`. The underlying `received_path_plan` is itself a read-only value returned by the controller's injected active-path projection reader over `PathDispatcher.get_active_path(train_id)` (which derives over `Path.status == ACTIVE`), so updates and releases surface automatically without any controller-side write step.
